strawson.line: Argues against treating narrativity as the norm, and for "episodic" ways of being a self.

trivers.line: Developed theories of reciprocal altruism and parental investment, and of self-deception as a tool for deceiving others.

vaillant.line: Directed the Harvard Grant Study for decades and traced how defenses mature.

chalmers.line: Gave the hard problem of consciousness its name.

barrett.vs: Basic emotion theorists such as Ekman and Panksepp disagree.

libet.line: Timed the readiness potential against people's reported decisions.
libet.vs: Schurger's noise model challenged how it was interpreted.

cacioppo.line: Founded the scientific study of loneliness, treating it as a biological signal.

marx.line: The early Marx, before the economics, wrote about alienation. Work under capitalism estranges people from what they make, from themselves and from each other.

carstensen.line: Her socioemotional selectivity theory says perceived time shapes motivation.

gilovich.line: Studied regret, counterfactual thinking and the spotlight effect.

adler.line: Broke with Freud. People are driven less by sex than by striving to overcome felt inferiority, and by a need to belong.
adler.vs: Freud saw the past as the cause. Adler saw goals as the key to behaviour.

anna-freud.line: Mapped out the ego's defence mechanisms and founded child psychoanalysis.
anna-freud.vs: Feuded with Melanie Klein over how children should be treated.

winnicott.line: Children need a "good enough" mother. Perfection isn't required. Without room to be spontaneous, a child builds a compliant false self.

horney.line: Neurosis grows in the gap between the real self and the idealized self we feel we have to be.
horney.vs: Dismissed Freud's account of female psychology as male bias.

lacan.line: Desire is always the desire of the Other. The self forms in a mirror, as a unity we see before we feel it.
lacan.vs: Critics say he wrote obscurely on purpose and that his ideas can't be tested.

erikson.line: Saw identity developing across eight life stages, each built around a crisis. He coined "identity crisis".

laing.line: Held that madness can be an understandable response to an unlivable situation, often a family one.
laing.vs: Mainstream psychiatry didn't accept his account of schizophrenia.

may.line: Brought existentialism into therapy. Anxiety is the price of freedom, and apathy is what you get when you refuse to pay it.

yalom.line: Inner conflict comes from four givens: death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness.

rogers.line: People grow when they receive unconditional positive regard. Conditional love teaches us to disown parts of ourselves.
rogers.vs: Behaviourists thought his claims were too vague to test.

maslow.line: Proposed a hierarchy of needs that ends in self-actualization. Later he added self-transcendence on top.
maslow.vs: The empirical support for a strict ordering of needs is weak.

james.line: Founded American psychology. Emotion is our perception of bodily change. Truth is what works in experience.

ainsworth.line: Her Strange Situation test picked out secure, anxious and avoidant attachment in infants.

harlow.line: Infant monkeys chose a soft cloth mother over a wire one that fed them. The bond came from comfort. Food didn't build it.
harlow.vs: People now see his experiments as ethically indefensible.

piaget.line: Children aren't small adults. They build understanding through distinct stages of reasoning.
piaget.vs: Later research found children capable far earlier than he thought.

asch.line: Many people denied the clear evidence of their own eyes to agree with a unanimous group.
asch.vs: He pointed out that most answers were still independent.

zimbardo.line: Ran the Stanford Prison Experiment and claimed that roles can turn ordinary people cruel.
zimbardo.vs: Recordings show the guards were coached, which undercuts the conclusion.

tajfel.line: Even trivial group labels make people favour their own side. Part of identity is group membership.

cialdini.line: Six principles of influence, among them reciprocity and social proof, explain why we say yes.

haidt.line: Moral judgments are fast intuitions. Reasoning mostly turns up afterwards as their lawyer.
haidt.vs: Critics say his moral foundations are culturally narrow.

baumeister.line: Studied belonging, self-control and threatened egotism. His ego-depletion theory has largely failed to replicate.

keltner.line: People are given power for empathy and collaboration, and power then erodes exactly those qualities.

tversky.line: With Kahneman, traced the heuristics behind human judgment and built prospect theory.

bandura.line: We learn by watching others, and what we attempt depends on how capable we believe we are.
bandura.vs: Challenged pure behaviourism by putting thought back into learning.

gilbert.line: We're bad at predicting what will make us happy, and good at adapting to what doesn't.

taleb.line: We underrate rare, extreme events and over-explain the past. Some things gain from disorder.

csikszentmihalyi.line: Happiness often shows up as flow, full absorption in a challenge that matches your skill.

damasio.line: Patients who lost emotion also lost good judgment. Feeling turns out to be part of reason.

sapolsky.line: Behaviour has causes at every timescale, from neurons to evolution. He concludes that free will doesn't exist.
sapolsky.vs: Philosophers say his conclusion goes further than his evidence.

sacks.line: Wrote case studies of how brain damage exposes the hidden machinery of the self.

ekman.line: Argued that a few basic emotions show up in universal facial expressions.
ekman.vs: Lisa Feldman Barrett leads the push against universality.

panksepp.line: Mapped seven primal emotional systems in mammalian brains, among them SEEKING, FEAR and PANIC.

dennett.line: Consciousness isn't a single inner theatre. The sense of a hard problem is itself something the brain produces.
dennett.vs: Chalmers and Nagel say he explains consciousness away.

herman.line: Described complex trauma after prolonged captivity or abuse, and a recovery that moves in stages: safety, remembrance, reconnection.

husserl.line: Founded phenomenology. Describe experience as it appears before you explain it away.

merleau-ponty.line: We are our bodies, and perception is lived rather than computed.

levinas.line: Ethics starts with the face of another person, who makes a claim on you before any theory does.
levinas.vs: Pushed back against Heidegger's focus on being over responsibility.

buber.line: We relate to others either as an It, an object to use, or as a Thou, a presence to meet.

weil.line: Attention is the rarest form of generosity. Affliction crushes the soul in a way ordinary suffering doesn't.

tillich.line: Courage means affirming yourself in spite of the anxiety of death, meaninglessness and guilt.

adorno.line: The culture industry manufactures our desires, then calls them free choices.

marcuse.line: Consumer society creates false needs, and "one-dimensional" people who can't imagine alternatives.

habermas.line: Legitimacy comes out of communication free of domination, where the better argument wins.
habermas.vs: Argued that Foucault leaves no ground for criticizing power.

derrida.line: Meaning is never fully present, and every text depends on what it excludes. He called the method deconstruction.
derrida.vs: Critics, Searle among them, found it evasive.

deleuze.line: Desire produces things. It isn't a lack. Society organizes and captures it.
deleuze.vs: Opposed head-on the psychoanalytic idea of desire as lack.

baudrillard.line: Images and signs have replaced the reality they once pointed to. That's the hyperreal.

han.line: Modern people exploit themselves and call it freedom. Then they burn out.

debord.line: Social life has turned into a spectacle. Relationships between people now run through images.

rawls.line: Pick the principles of justice from behind a veil of ignorance, with no idea which position you'll end up in.
rawls.vs: Nozick objected that it trampled individual rights.

popper.line: A theory counts as scientific only if it could be proven false. He aimed that test at Freud and Marx.

berlin.line: Separated negative liberty (freedom from interference) from positive liberty (self-mastery), and was wary of the second.

murdoch.line: Moral life is mostly attention: the slow work of seeing other people justly instead of through the ego.

williams.line: Showed how luck shapes our moral standing, and how moral theory can crush the things that make a life worth living.

taylor.line: The modern self rests on an ideal of authenticity, and that ideal can decay into narcissism.

macintyre.line: Modern moral argument never settles, because we inherited scraps of older traditions without their context.

nussbaum.line: Emotions are judgments about what matters. A good life is open to luck, and that vulnerability is part of its value.

parfit.line: Personal identity matters less than we think. Once he saw that, death scared him less.

frankfurt.line: A person is someone who has desires about their desires. Bullshit, unlike lying, is indifference to truth.

singer.line: If you can prevent great suffering at little cost, you should. Distance makes no difference.

wittgenstein.line: Meaning is use. Many philosophical problems are confusions that language creates.
wittgenstein.vs: He rejected much of his own early work.

weber.line: Modern life shuts us in an "iron cage" of rational efficiency, with the enchantment drained out.

durkheim.line: Even suicide has social causes. Where norms weaken, people suffer from anomie.

goffman.line: Social life is performance. We manage impressions front-stage and relax back-stage.

bourdieu.line: Taste is social rank in disguise. Cultural capital hands down privilege as reliably as money does.

campbell.line: Myths from different cultures share one pattern, the hero's journey: departure, ordeal, return.
campbell.vs: Scholars say he flattened the real differences between myths.

graeber.line: Many jobs are pointless even to the people doing them, and that pointlessness is itself a source of suffering.

harari.line: Humans dominate because we cooperate around shared fictions: money, nations, laws, gods.
harari.vs: Historians fault him for sweeping generalizations.

de-botton.line: Brings philosophy to ordinary life: status anxiety, love, work and consolation.

zizek.line: Uses Lacan to read ideology. We often know a belief is false and act on it anyway.

mcgilchrist.line: Argues the two brain hemispheres are two ways of attending, and that modern life has handed power to the narrow, grasping one. As neuroscience he's contested. As a diagnosis of attention, he's hard to dismiss.
mcgilchrist.vs: Most neuroscientists think the left/right story is far too simple. He answers that it's about attention, not tasks.
mcgilchrist.tag: Modern life attends to the parts and misses the whole.

fisher.line: Treated depression and anxiety as social facts and refused to file them under private failure. His idea of capitalist realism names the feeling that no alternative can even be imagined.
fisher.vs: He argued with the self-help view that distress is personal chemistry, to be fixed alone.
fisher.tag: Private misery, he said, is a public question.

metzinger.line: Holds that there is no self, only a model of a self that the brain builds and can't see as a model. We live inside it, so it feels like us.
metzinger.vs: Where Descartes found a thinking thing, Metzinger found a transparent simulation.
metzinger.tag: The self is a model that can't see itself as one.

seth.line: Describes perception as controlled hallucination: the brain predicts the world, then corrects itself against the senses. For him, consciousness is rooted in being a living body, not in computation.
seth.vs: He doubts that a sufficiently clever machine would be conscious.
seth.tag: Perception is a best guess, kept in check by the world.

turkle.line: Spent decades studying how we relate to machines and, through them, to each other. What she found: we expect more from technology and less from one another.
turkle.vs: Against techno-optimists who treat connection as the same as conversation.
turkle.tag: Asks what connection costs when it's always on.

phillips.line: Writes about the lives we don't lead: boredom, missing out, tickling, kissing. He treats psychoanalysis as a literary, playful practice, not a medical one.
phillips.vs: Freud searched for hidden causes. Phillips asks what we're avoiding wanting.
phillips.tag: Psychoanalysis as a way of attending to the unlived.

benjamin.line: Argues that desire needs mutual recognition: to be a self, you have to be seen by another who is also a self. Domination starts when one side is no longer allowed to be a subject.
benjamin.vs: Pushes against drive theory. The core need is recognition, not discharge.
benjamin.tag: Domination starts where mutual recognition breaks down.

rosa.line: Argues that modern life speeds up just to stay in place, and that the cost is a world that no longer answers us. His remedy is resonance: moments when something touches you and responds.
rosa.vs: Against the view that more options and faster time are simply progress.
rosa.tag: Acceleration without resonance leaves us busy and unreached.

scarry.line: Showed that pain destroys language and unmakes the world of the person in it, which is why torture works. Her later work on beauty runs the other way: it makes us want to be fair.
scarry.vs: Against the idea that suffering can simply be told. It resists expression.
scarry.tag: Pain unmakes the world. Beauty asks us to repair it.

bauman.line: Described modern life as liquid: jobs, relationships and identities that can't hold a shape. Freedom has grown, and so has the burden of choosing alone.
bauman.vs: Durkheim feared too little freedom. Bauman feared too little ground.
bauman.tag: Modern life is liquid and nothing is built to last.

fanon.line: A psychiatrist who saw colonial violence as a wound in the mind as well as in the state. He wrote about being seen first as a category and only second as a person.
fanon.vs: Against the idea that racism is only an attitude. He said it shapes the body and the self.
fanon.tag: What colonialism does to the inside of a person.

hooks.line: Argued that love is an action, a mix of care, respect and honesty, and that domination in any form rules it out. She wrote plainly so more people could use the ideas.
hooks.vs: Against the view that love is a feeling that simply arrives.
hooks.tag: Love is something you do. It doesn't just happen to you.

butler.line: Argues that gender is something done over and over rather than something one simply is, and that our lives are shaped by norms we didn't choose. Later work asks whose lives get mourned.
butler.vs: Against the view that identity is natural and settled.
butler.tag: Identity is made through repetition, and could be repeated differently.

midgley.line: A plain-speaking philosopher who insisted that humans are animals and that science needs philosophy to stay honest about its own myths. She went after scientism and the idea of the lone rational self.
midgley.vs: Against the Selfish Gene view that human nature is ruled by gene-level egoism.
midgley.tag: Humans are animals, and science runs on myths too.

illouz.line: Studies how capitalism shapes love: how we choose, compare and suffer. She says our modern freedom to choose has made love more uncertain, not easier.
illouz.vs: Against the romantic view that love sits outside economics.
illouz.tag: Why having more choice made love harder.

neff.line: A researcher who defined self-compassion as kindness toward oneself, a sense of common humanity and mindful awareness. She argues it motivates better than self-criticism.
neff.vs: Against the belief that being hard on yourself is what keeps you going.
neff.tag: Kindness toward yourself is a skill, not an indulgence.

lear.line: Reads Freud and Aristotle together to ask how a person can face a world in which their way of life has ended. Irony and hope are his tools for being more honest about what we can become.
lear.vs: Freud sought cure. Lear seeks the possibility of a good life after collapse.
lear.tag: How to hope when your world ends.

sontag.line: Wrote about how we see: photographs, illness and the metaphors that crowd around suffering. Her instinct was to strip the metaphor away and look at the thing itself.
sontag.vs: Against interpretation that swaps experience for commentary.
sontag.tag: Attention to what we see, and what we do with it.

canetti.line: Studied crowds, power and death as one subject. He saw power as the wish to survive others, and refused to accept death as natural.
canetti.vs: Against the view that death can be made peace with. He never made it.
canetti.tag: Power is the wish to outlive others.

milosz.line: Examined how intelligent people take on an ideology to avoid disorder. His Captive Mind describes the mental tricks by which a person submits and calls it freedom.
milosz.vs: Against the idea that only the naive get captured. The clever, he said, are most at risk.
milosz.tag: How clever people talk themselves into submission.

cioran.line: A writer of despair as discipline: insomnia, futility, the burden of being born. His pessimism is oddly consoling because it's so honest.
cioran.vs: Against Camus: he didn't choose to imagine Sisyphus happy.
cioran.tag: A philosophy of insomnia, honestly lived.

sloterdijk.line: Reads human life as a project of building shelters, from the womb to the globe. His later work argues that people are made by the exercises they repeat.
sloterdijk.vs: Against the picture of the free-floating autonomous mind.
sloterdijk.tag: Humans are shaped by the spaces and routines they build.

amery.line: Wrote about torture and the loss of trust in the world, and defended resentment as a moral stance, not a flaw. His refusal to forgive is argued, not just felt.
amery.vs: Against the view that forgiveness is always the higher response.
amery.tag: Why some injuries should not be forgiven.

levi.line: A chemist who survived Auschwitz and wrote with precise restraint about what the camps did to moral judgment. He coined the grey zone, where victims and complicity blur.
levi.vs: Against the story that evil is easy to spot and stands apart from us.
levi.tag: Moral judgment in the grey zone.

appiah.line: Argues that identities are made partly by other people, and that moral progress often comes from a change in honour rather than from new arguments. His cosmopolitanism asks for obligations without uniformity.
appiah.vs: Against both strict nationalism and thin universalism.
appiah.tag: Identity is made with others, and so is moral change.

mcwilliams.line: Wrote the clearest map of personality structure in clinical psychoanalysis, treating character as an organised way of coping rather than a diagnosis.
mcwilliams.vs: DSM lists symptoms. She asks what the person is protecting.
mcwilliams.tag: Character is a way of coping that once made sense.

gopnik.line: Shows that babies and young children learn like scientists, with more imagination than adults. She suggests childhood is a protected time for exploration, not preparation.
gopnik.vs: Against the view that children are unfinished adults.

ahmed.line: Writes about how emotions, happiness and complaint move between people and shape who is welcome. Her work asks who is expected to be happy, and at whose expense.
ahmed.vs: Against the idea that happiness is simply a personal goal.
ahmed.tag: Happiness is a promise that tells people how to behave.

srinivasan.line: Asks whether desire can be political and what fairness means in who we find attractive. She holds that we can criticise preferences without punishing people for them.
srinivasan.vs: Against the view that desire is private and beyond question.

anscombe.line: Argued that modern moral philosophy had lost its footing, and that concepts like intention and action had to be understood before ethics could move on. Wittgenstein's student and translator.
anscombe.vs: Against consequentialism, and against reducing action to causes in the head.
anscombe.tag: Ethics has to begin with what an action is.

tomasello.line: Compared young children with apes to show that the difference is shared intention: humans want to do things together. Morality grows out of that cooperation.
tomasello.vs: Against the picture of humans as basically competitive.
tomasello.tag: Humans are the species that does things together.

hagglund.line: Argues that mortality gives life its value: an eternal life would leave nothing to care about. He calls this secular faith, caring about what can be lost.
hagglund.vs: Against religious consolation, and against Stoic detachment.
hagglund.tag: Finitude is what makes anything matter.

zahavi.line: A phenomenologist who argues that the self is the first-person character of experience, rather than an inner thing. He links empathy, shame and being with others to the structure of consciousness.
zahavi.vs: Against Metzinger. He says the self is no illusion, it's the form experience takes.
zahavi.tag: The self is how experience is lived, not a thing inside.

zuboff.line: Named surveillance capitalism: an economy that treats human experience as raw material for prediction. Her warning: behaviour is being engineered as well as observed.
zuboff.vs: Against the claim that free services are free.
zuboff.tag: What happens when experience becomes raw material.

young.line: Argued that injustice is often a matter of structures, not just individuals, and that responsibility can be shared without guilt. She wrote on oppression's five faces.
young.vs: Against the view that justice is only fair distribution.
young.tag: Injustice is built into structures, and so is responsibility.

pessoa.line: Wrote as dozens of invented selves, each with its own style and biography. His Book of Disquiet is the diary of someone who studies his own non-life so closely that it becomes a kind of life.
pessoa.vs: Sartre says we are what we choose. Pessoa asks what remains when we choose nothing and keep watching.
pessoa.tag: Lived as many selves and kept the minutes.

gilligan.line: In a Different Voice challenged the stage theory of moral development, which had been built largely on boys' answers, and described an ethics of care and responsiveness alongside the ethics of rights. The claim that the split is gendered has been disputed. The point that holds up: care is a moral framework, and shouldn't be mistaken for a failure of one.
gilligan.vs: Kohlberg ranked reasoning from abstract justice as the highest stage. Gilligan argued that reasoning from relationship and responsibility is a different mature way of thinking about right and wrong.
gilligan.tag: Asked whose experience moral theory was built on.

chodorow.line: Used object-relations psychoanalysis to argue that who does the early parenting shapes how people come to feel self and other, so social arrangements reproduce themselves psychologically. Contested, partly because it generalises from one family form, but a clear case of psychology and sociology explaining each other.
chodorow.vs: Freud put the formative drama in the triangle of child, mother and father. Chodorow looked earlier, at the first bond with the person who does the caring.
chodorow.tag: Showed how family arrangements are reproduced inside the mind.

davis.line: Studied philosophy with Herbert Marcuse and Theodor Adorno and became a leading theorist of how race, class and gender intersect. Argues that prisons are a social habit rather than a necessity. Her abolitionist position is contested. The question underneath it, what a society does with harm and who bears the cost, is not.
davis.vs: Marcuse located liberation in a break with the one-dimensional society. Davis located it in concrete organising and in rethinking institutions.
davis.tag: Asked what a society's punishments say about its idea of freedom.

woolf.line: Argued in A Room of One's Own that the conditions of a life, money and a door that locks, decide what a mind can produce. In her novels she wrote consciousness as a moving, interrupted stream, not a tidy story.
woolf.vs: Freud theorised the inner life in case histories. Woolf rendered it in language, from inside.
woolf.tag: Showed that thought needs a room, money and time.

kubler-ross.line: Swiss-American psychiatrist who listened to dying patients and described five common responses: denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. The stages were never meant as a fixed sequence, and grief research since hasn't found one. What holds up is that she asked the dying, and heard them.
kubler-ross.vs: Becker saw the denial of death as the engine of culture. Kübler-Ross treated denial as one human response among several.
kubler-ross.tag: Made dying a subject people could talk about.

kristeva.line: Bulgarian-French thinker who described abjection: the revulsion at what threatens the boundary between self and not-self, such as a corpse or waste. Interpretive and dense, but it names a feeling many people recognise and rarely explain.
kristeva.vs: Lacan placed the making of the subject in language. Kristeva added the pre-linguistic body and the early relation to the mother.
kristeva.tag: Looked at what a self must push away in order to exist.

douglas.line: Argued in Purity and Danger that ideas of pollution are about order: dirt is matter out of place, so a group's taboos show where its boundaries are and what it fears.
douglas.vs: Durkheim saw the sacred as society worshipping itself. Douglas read purity rules as a classification system that exposes what a group can't tolerate.
douglas.tag: Read dirt as a map of a society's anxieties.

hochschild.line: Coined "emotional labor": the effort of producing a feeling as part of a job, like the flight attendant's warmth. Later work on the "deep story" asks what felt narrative sits underneath a political view.
hochschild.vs: Goffman described impression management as an everyday skill. Hochschild asked what it costs when your wages depend on it.
hochschild.tag: Named the work of feeling on demand.

loftus.line: Her experiments showed that the wording of a question can change what people remember, and that false memories can be implanted. They changed how courts treat eyewitnesses. Her role in the repressed-memory debates is still controversial, but the core finding has been replicated many times.
loftus.vs: Freud treated memory as something recoverable under analysis. Loftus showed that recall is reconstructed each time and can be altered by what comes after.
loftus.tag: Showed that memory is rebuilt, and can be contaminated.

berlant.line: Cruel optimism names an attachment to something that gets in the way of what you want, such as a fantasy of the good life that your actual conditions make harder to reach. Dense academic prose, but the idea travels well.
berlant.vs: Maslow pictured fulfilment as a climb. Berlant asked what happens when the ladder itself is the problem.
berlant.tag: Described hope that gets in its own way.

ambedkar.line: Trained in economics at Columbia and the LSE, and as a lawyer. Argued that caste is no mere division of labour. It divides the labourers themselves, in grades, so every group has someone below it and a stake in the order. Chaired the committee that drafted India's constitution.
ambedkar.vs: Marx read society through class struggle. Ambedkar argued that in India caste cut across class and had to be taken apart in its own right.
ambedkar.tag: Showed how hierarchy hardens into common sense.

tagore.line: Nobel-winning poet who criticised nationalism as a machine that makes people efficient and morally smaller, and wanted education to widen sympathy rather than sort for examinations.
tagore.vs: Gandhi's politics leaned on mass mobilisation. Tagore feared mass movements could replace thinking with conformity.
tagore.tag: Warned what nationalism asks people to give up.

sen.line: Argues that development and well-being should be judged by capabilities, the real freedoms people have, rather than by income, and that we can recognise injustice without a blueprint of a perfect society.
sen.vs: Rawls built justice from an ideal social contract. Sen asked which actual change would make things less unjust.
sen.tag: Asked what people are free to do and be.

nandy.line: Trained as a clinical psychologist. He argued that colonialism worked on minds as much as on territory, rewarding rulers and ruled alike for treating the "mature" as better than the "childlike", and that cultures keep resources to answer it.
nandy.vs: Fanon stressed the violence of colonial rule and the need for a break. Nandy stressed how its values were absorbed and what cultural resources could answer them.
nandy.tag: Showed colonialism working on the mind.

kakar.line: Indian psychoanalyst who studied how childhood, family and culture shape the self in India, and which of psychoanalysis's claims are universal and which local.
kakar.vs: Freud's model grew out of the nuclear family of Vienna. Kakar looked at joint-family childhoods, where the mother-child bond and extended kin loom larger.
kakar.tag: Asked which parts of psychoanalysis travel.

spivak.line: Translated Derrida into English and became a leading postcolonial theorist. Her question "Can the subaltern speak?" asks whether the conditions for being heard even exist, and what happens when intellectuals speak on behalf of others.
spivak.vs: Foucault and Deleuze suggested the oppressed can speak for themselves if allowed. Spivak asked whether the conditions for being heard existed at all.
spivak.tag: Asked who gets to be heard, and who speaks for them.

chakrabarty.line: Argued in Provincializing Europe that concepts like modernity and the political present themselves as universal while having a particular origin, so historians have to use them and question them at once.
chakrabarty.vs: Marx's stages of capitalism were meant as a universal story. Chakrabarty asked whose histories fit that frame.
chakrabarty.tag: Questioned whose history counts as universal.

chatterjee.line: Argued that anticolonial nationalism did not copy the Western nation. It claimed a spiritual "inner" domain while competing in the material "outer". Later work on "political society" looks at how the poor negotiate with states outside formal citizenship.
chatterjee.vs: Benedict Anderson argued nationalism travelled as a model to be copied. Chatterjee asked what was left to imagine for those who received the model.
chatterjee.tag: Asked what is left to imagine once the models are taken.

ramanujan.line: In "Is There an Indian Way of Thinking?" he argued that Indian thought tends to be context-sensitive rather than context-free: what is right depends on who you are, to whom, and when. He called it a tendency, and was careful to say it wasn't an essence.
ramanujan.vs: Kantian ethics asks for rules that would hold for anyone. Ramanujan described a tradition where the right answer depends on who you are and whom you are with.
ramanujan.tag: Asked whether ethics must be the same for everyone.

nishida.line: Founded the Kyoto School. In An Inquiry into the Good he started from "pure experience", the moment before we divide the world into knower and known, drawing on William James, German philosophy and his own Zen practice.
nishida.vs: Descartes began with a thinking subject. Nishida began with experience before the subject-object split.
nishida.tag: Looked for experience before the split into subject and object.

watsuji.line: Argued that the human being (ningen) is both an individual and something between others (aidagara). The self forms in relations, and climate and place shape how we live. He criticised Heidegger's Being and Time for treating existence as time with no society or space.
watsuji.vs: Heidegger's Dasein is individual and temporal. Watsuji added the social and the spatial: people exist between each other.
watsuji.tag: Said a person exists between people.

kuki.line: Studied in Europe, partly under Heidegger. In The Structure of Iki he analysed a Japanese ideal of style built from allure, pride and resignation: erotic tension kept alive by never quite closing.
kuki.vs: Western romantic ideals pursue union. Iki values the tension of near-possession.
kuki.tag: Described desire kept alive at a distance.

doi.line: Japanese psychiatrist who described amae, the wish to be indulged by someone close, as a key to Japanese relationships, while arguing the feeling is universal even where there's no word for it. Often criticised for generalising about a nation.
doi.vs: Western developmental theory prizes independence. Doi asked whether being able to depend on others is a good in adult life.
doi.tag: Gave a name to the wish to be indulged.

fei.line: Studied under Malinowski at the LSE. In From the Soil he described Chinese rural society as a "differential mode of association": relationships spread outward from each person like ripples, with obligation shrinking with distance, unlike organisations bound like sticks in a bundle.
fei.vs: Durkheim saw society as solidarity within a group. Fei saw networks centred on individuals.
fei.tag: Described society as ripples, not bundles.

luxun.line: The leading modern Chinese writer. In The True Story of Ah Q he satirised "spiritual victory": the habit of turning every humiliation into an imagined triumph. He saw it as both a national habit and a human one.
luxun.vs: Freud read self-deception as repression. Lu Xun made it a comic social habit anyone can recognise.

alatas.line: Malaysian sociologist who showed in The Myth of the Lazy Native how colonial writers built an image of idleness to justify rule, and how it outlived empire. Also wrote on corruption.
alatas.vs: Said's Orientalism examined the West's image of the East. Alatas had already traced one image to its economic function.
alatas.tag: Traced how a stereotype was made to do work.

anderson.line: A Southeast Asia specialist who argued that nations are "imagined communities": people who will never meet feel bound together through shared print, language and time. He was clear that "imagined" does not mean false.
anderson.vs: Marx treated nationalism as a distraction from class. Anderson treated it as an attachment people will die for.
anderson.tag: Took belonging to a nation seriously as a feeling.

said.line: Argued in Orientalism that Western scholarship and art constructed "the Orient" in ways that served domination. Critics dispute its scope. The central point, that descriptions of other people are exercises of power, stuck.
said.vs: Foucault tied knowledge to power in prisons and clinics. Said carried the idea to empire.
said.tag: Showed that describing others is a way of ruling them.

freire.line: Described "banking" education, in which learners are treated as empty accounts, and argued that people begin to change their situation when they can name it themselves.
freire.vs: Dewey grounded education in experience and democracy. Freire insisted it is political and tied to conditions of oppression.
freire.tag: Argued that learning to name the world is how it changes.

ibn-khaldun.line: North African historian who described asabiyyah, group solidarity, as the force that builds states and fades as comfort grows. A secular, analytic account of rise and decline, written six centuries ago.
ibn-khaldun.vs: Marx saw history moving through class conflict. Ibn Khaldun saw cycles driven by cohesion and its erosion.
ibn-khaldun.tag: Saw group feeling build and decay states.

anzaldua.line: In Borderlands/La Frontera she wrote about living between cultures, languages and genders, and about a "mestiza consciousness" that tolerates contradiction instead of choosing a side.
anzaldua.vs: Du Bois described two warring ideals in one body. Anzaldúa described a third space that holds ambiguity without resolving it.
anzaldua.tag: Described living between worlds as a way of seeing.

paz.line: Mexican Nobel laureate whose The Labyrinth of Solitude reads Mexican identity through solitude, the mask and the festival that briefly breaks both.
paz.vs: Sartre located the loneliness of freedom in the individual. Paz saw a whole people carrying it, and sometimes breaking it open in festival.
paz.tag: Read a nation's character as solitude and masks.

dubois.line: Helped found empirical sociology in the US and described "double consciousness": the sense of looking at yourself through the eyes of a society that holds you in contempt.
dubois.vs: Mead described the self as built from the view of others. Du Bois asked what that does when the others' view is hostile.
dubois.tag: Named the experience of seeing yourself through others' eyes.

stendhal.line: Wrote On Love as a field study of his own heartbreak, and gave the process of falling in love a name, crystallisation: the lover adorns the beloved with perfections until the real person disappears.
stendhal.vs: Freud would later trace such idealisation to early attachments. Stendhal simply watched it happen and took notes.
stendhal.tag: Watched love cover a person in crystals.

tharoor.line: Indian writer and politician whose popular histories argue that British rule drained India economically and that its civilising mission was a story told afterwards. His critics say he understates what was already failing before the Raj.
tharoor.vs: Where many accounts weigh empire's gains against its costs, Tharoor insists the ledger was never fairly kept.

amrita-pritam.line: Punjabi poet and novelist who wrote about Partition, women's bodies and love that refuses permission. Pinjar and her memoir Raseedi Ticket treat a woman's inner life as the main subject rather than the background.
amrita-pritam.vs: Her contemporaries often wrote Partition as men's politics. Pritam wrote it from inside the women it was done to.
amrita-pritam.tag: Wrote love that grows in the earth, not in a pot.

shafak.line: Turkish British novelist who writes about belonging, exile and the stories that nations tell and bury. She argues that polarisation shrinks a person's sense of complexity, and that fiction trains us to hold several truths at once.
shafak.vs: Where some defend identity as a fixed ground, Shafak defends the person who belongs to more than one place.

john-williams.line: American novelist and teacher whose Stoner went almost unnoticed on publication and was rediscovered decades later. It follows an ordinary life, a quiet dignity and a love of work, without consolation or melodrama.
john-williams.vs: Heroic novels reward effort with outcomes. Williams asks what an unrewarded life is still worth.
john-williams.tag: Wrote the quiet life without pity.

bergson.line: Argued that lived time, duration, is felt as a flowing whole and cannot be cut into measurable instants without losing what it is. His claim that science spatialises time shaped Proust, James and later phenomenology.
bergson.vs: Physics treats time as a line of equal moments. Bergson says the clock measures space, not experience.
bergson.tag: Said the clock misses what time feels like.

rilke.line: Austrian German poet whose letters to a young would-be writer counsel patience, solitude and living the questions. He treats love as two solitudes that protect and greet each other, not a merger.
rilke.vs: Romantic myths promise fusion. Rilke asks for two whole people keeping watch over each other's solitude.
rilke.tag: Told a young poet to live the questions.

gibran.line: Lebanese American poet and artist whose The Prophet, in short sermons on love, work, pain and freedom, became one of the most read books of the twentieth century. Its tone is gentle and aphoristic, which critics find vague and readers find consoling.
gibran.vs: Philosophers argue for positions. Gibran offers images and trusts the reader to recognise them.
gibran.tag: Gave plain sermons on love, work and sorrow.

james-allen.line: English writer whose short book As a Man Thinketh argues that character and circumstance follow from habitual thought. It is a forerunner of modern self-help, and its claim runs stronger than the evidence allows.
james-allen.vs: Cognitive therapy treats thoughts as one cause among several. Allen treats them as the root of nearly everything.
james-allen.tag: Said thought hardens into habit, then circumstance.

krishnamurti.line: Indian-born speaker who refused the role of guru and told audiences that truth is a pathless land. He argued that authorities, methods and belief systems prevent people from seeing for themselves.
krishnamurti.vs: Most spiritual teachers offer a path. Krishnamurti said the offer of a path is the obstacle.

morrison.line: American Nobel-winning novelist who read the canon for what it avoids. In Playing in the Dark she argues that an invented Africanist presence shapes white American literature even where Black characters hardly appear.
morrison.vs: Standard criticism asks what a text says. Morrison asks what the text is built to avoid saying.
morrison.tag: Read American literature for its silences.

slater.line: American sociologist who argued in The Pursuit of Loneliness that competition, individualism and the wish for control leave people isolated while promising freedom. His view of the counterculture was equally critical.
slater.vs: Most critiques of conformity praise the individual. Slater suggests individualism may be what makes people easy to rule.

pirsig.line: American author whose Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance mixes a road trip with an argument about Quality, the thing that classical and romantic ways of knowing both claim and neither can define.
pirsig.vs: Philosophers usually split fact from value. Pirsig tries to start from value and derive the split.
pirsig.tag: Tried to define quality on a motorcycle trip.

coyle.line: American author who studies high-performing groups and reports that their success rests less on talent than on small signals of safety, vulnerability and shared purpose. His evidence is mostly case studies, so the claims are suggestive rather than proven.
coyle.vs: Management advice often ranks skill first. Coyle ranks belonging first.
coyle.tag: Looked for what makes groups trust.

epicurus.line: Greek philosopher who taught that the aim of life is untroubled pleasure, which he found in modest desires, friendship and freedom from fear of gods and death. Little of his writing survives; most comes from three letters and a list of doctrines.
epicurus.vs: The Stoics train the will against pain. Epicurus lowers the demand until pain has less to bite on.
epicurus.tag: Taught that fear is the real pain.

lorde.line: American poet and essayist who wrote about race, gender, sexuality and illness. She argued that difference is a source of strength and that silence protects no one.
lorde.vs: Many movements ask people to put one identity first. Lorde asked them to bring all of it.

alexievich.line: Belarusian Nobel laureate who writes books built from hundreds of interviews, letting ordinary people tell the Soviet century in their own voices. Her method trades a single author's argument for a chorus.
alexievich.vs: Historians usually record events and leaders. Alexievich records what it felt like to live through them.
alexievich.tag: Wrote history as a chorus of voices.

callard.line: American philosopher who studies how a person can come to value something they do not yet understand. Her concept of proleptic reasons describes becoming a new kind of person by acting like one before you are.
callard.vs: Most accounts of choice assume your values are already set. Callard asks how you get new ones.
callard.tag: Asked how anyone learns to want better.

montaigne.line: French essayist who invented the essay as a way of thinking by trying things out, with himself as the main subject. He distrusted certainty and wrote about custom, death, friendship and the body with unusual frankness.
montaigne.vs: Philosophers tend to write systems. Montaigne wrote a self, and found it would not hold still.
montaigne.tag: Invented the essay to study himself.

ortega.line: Spanish philosopher who coined the formula I am myself and my circumstance. In The Revolt of the Masses he feared that a mass of self-satisfied people who recognise no standard above themselves would end liberal civilisation.
ortega.vs: Many thinkers blame elites for decline. Ortega blamed the comfort of the average person.
ortega.tag: Wrote that I am myself and my circumstance.

marcel.line: French philosopher who separated problems, which can be solved from outside, from mysteries, which one is inside of. He placed presence, fidelity and hope at the centre of existence and distrusted turning people into things to have.
marcel.vs: Sartre sees others as a threat to freedom. Marcel sees them as the place where freedom becomes real.

baldwin.line: American writer whose essays examine race, love and the self-deception of a country that wants innocence. He argued that white Americans were as imprisoned by the lie of race as the people it was used against.
baldwin.vs: Many arguments about race treat one side as the problem. Baldwin insisted both sides were hurt.
baldwin.tag: Wrote that denial costs the denier too.

stevenson.line: American lawyer who founded the Equal Justice Initiative to defend people condemned to death or sentenced harshly as children. He argues that proximity to the suffering of others is what changes a person's sense of justice.
stevenson.vs: Debates about punishment usually stay abstract. Stevenson insists on the case in front of you.

cs-lewis.line: British scholar and Christian apologist who argued in The Abolition of Man that rejecting any objective standard of value leaves only the power of those who condition others. His defence of a shared moral law, the Tao, is disputed by secular and religious critics alike.
cs-lewis.vs: Modern ethics often treats values as preferences. Lewis argued that if values are only preferences, someone will set yours.
cs-lewis.tag: Warned of power over people with nature as its tool.

langer.line: Harvard psychologist who defines mindfulness as actively noticing new things, not as a meditative state. Her studies, such as one on counterclockwise living in older adults, suggest that mindlessness and rigid categories shape what people think they can do.
langer.vs: Eastern-inspired mindfulness stresses stillness. Langer's version stresses noticing and doubting categories.
langer.tag: Defined mindfulness as noticing new things.

chanakya.line: Traditionally credited as the author of the Arthashastra, an Indian treatise on statecraft, economy, spycraft and war. Its authorship and dating are debated by scholars, and the quotations popular online are often attributed to him loosely.
chanakya.vs: Machiavelli comes much later and is often called cynical. The Arthashastra is as hard-headed but also covers welfare, taxes and law.
chanakya.tag: Taught statecraft as a discipline of interests.

solzhenitsyn.line: Russian writer who survived the Soviet camp system and documented it in The Gulag Archipelago. He argued that the line between good and evil runs through every human heart, not between classes or nations.
solzhenitsyn.vs: Ideologies place evil in an enemy group. Solzhenitsyn placed it in everyone and said that is why it can be resisted.
solzhenitsyn.tag: Said the line between good and evil runs through each heart.

david-foster-wallace.line: American novelist and essayist who wrote about attention, entertainment and loneliness. In a well-known commencement speech he argued that the real freedom in adult life is deciding what to pay attention to.
david-foster-wallace.vs: Self-help treats attention as a skill. Wallace treats it as a moral choice made many times a day.
david-foster-wallace.tag: Treated attention as a moral choice.

books.thesis: A dream is a disguised wish, and decoding the disguise opens a way into the unconscious.
books.summary:
Dreams seem like nonsense, yet Freud found that the dreamer's own associations lead from them back to things the dreamer cares about. The book asks what a dream is for and why it looks so strange. His answer is that a dream is a disguised attempt to fulfil a wish the waking mind would not accept in plain form.

He builds the case from dreams, many of them his own, and from a close look at how a dream gets made. Condensation and displacement hide the meaning, so the story the dreamer remembers is only a surface. Along the way the book sets out the first full model of an unconscious mind. Later researchers dispute that every dream is a wish, but reading dreams as personal material has lasted.
ideas: A dream is a disguised wish, even when it seems anxious or dull. Freud claims the wish is often one the dreamer would reject awake, so it has to arrive in altered form.

The dream we remember is only a surface, and its meaning sits behind it. Freud calls the remembered story the manifest content and the hidden meaning the latent content, and interpretation moves from the first to the second.
One dream image can stand for several thoughts at once. Freud calls this condensation, and it means a single figure or scene can carry far more than it first appears to.

The real concern in a dream can be pushed onto something trivial. In displacement, emotional weight moves to a minor detail, so the dream seems to dwell on the unimportant while the worry stays out of sight.

Freud interprets a dream by following the dreamer's own associations. In free association the dreamer reports whatever comes to mind about each element in turn, and the chain of thoughts leads away from the image toward its source.
Dreams borrow material from the previous day's small events. Freud calls these day residue, and they give the unconscious wish something ordinary to attach itself to.
Oedipus and Hamlet still move audiences because, Freud argues, they stage a wish found in many people. He offers this as an early statement of the idea he later made central.
Freud's own dream of Irma's injection is the model case for his method. He analyses it line by line and reads it as a wish to be cleared of blame for a patient's poor recovery.

Dreams show ideas as pictures because abstract thoughts have to be put into images. Freud calls this requirement considerations of representability, and it is why thoughts turn up as scenes, puns and visual stand-ins.

The dream we tell is already an edited copy. Secondary revision is the waking mind's tidying of a dream into a coherent story as it is recalled, so the version we report sits further from the raw material.

books.thesis: Slips, forgetting and small mistakes have motives. They are not random noise.
books.summary:
A name that will not come, a word said by mistake, a lost object: most people shrug these off. Freud asks whether such lapses are just noise. He argues that they usually have a reason, and that the reason is often something the person would rather not admit.

The case is built from a long run of examples, many from his own life and from people he knew. Each is treated like a tiny symptom with a cause that can be traced. The larger point is that the line between healthy and troubled minds is thin, because the same mechanisms run in both. Critics say Freud finds motives too easily and is hard to disprove, but the book made slips of the tongue a common subject of conversation.
ideas: Forgetting a familiar name can have a motive. Freud's own example is failing to recall the painter Signorelli, which he traces through a chain of associations to thoughts about death and sexuality.
A slip of the tongue can say what the speaker meant to hold back. Freud collects cases where a mistaken word carries the thought the speaker was suppressing.
Freud denies that slips are only accidents of sound. He argues that two intentions collide, and the suppressed one briefly wins out in what comes from the mouth.
A lost or broken object can be a quiet way of acting on a feeling. The book gives examples of things dropped or mislaid by people who had reason to resent them.
We tend to forget what we do not quite want to do. Freud reads forgotten intentions, such as a letter never posted, as signs of reluctance.
A childhood memory with odd detail may be a screen memory. Freud suggests that such an ordinary scene stands in for something more charged and less easily recalled.
Freud argues that these errors are normal and common in healthy people. This narrows the gap between everyday life and the neuroses he treated.

A harmless-looking lapse can lead to a concealed concern. Freud analyses a young man who cannot recall the word aliquis in a line of Virgil, and the chain of associations ends in a private worry about a woman he knew.
A slip can state a preference outright. Freud cites a chairman who opened a meeting by declaring it closed, and reads the slip as what the speaker would rather have been doing.

Not every slip is meaningful, and Freud admits it. He grants that some have simple mechanical causes, such as similar sounds or fatigue, but critics still say his readings are hard to test, since almost any error can be given a hidden motive after the fact.

books.thesis: People keep repeating what hurts them, which suggests something in the mind runs against pleasure.
books.summary:
Freud had long held that the mind works to avoid pain and find pleasure. This short book asks why that cannot be the whole story. People relive painful events in dreams and in their relationships, and they seem driven to do it. Freud calls this the compulsion to repeat and tries to explain what could lie behind it.

The argument is openly speculative, and Freud says so. He moves from war trauma and a child's game to a large proposal about drives, including one that pulls the organism back toward an earlier state, the death drive. Many readers find that idea hard to accept and many analysts have dropped it, while the observation about repetition has stayed useful. The biggest claim is left as a hypothesis, not a result.
ideas: Traumatic dreams contradicted Freud's own theory. Soldiers with traumatic neuroses kept dreaming of the event that injured them, which did not fit the claim that dreams fulfil wishes, and Freud takes it as a puzzle.
Repetition after trauma may be an attempt to master the shock after the fact. Freud says the mind needs a protective shield against overwhelming stimulation, and trauma breaks through it.
A toddler's game shows how repetition can turn loss into control. Freud describes a child throwing a reel away and pulling it back, with sounds he took to mean gone and there.
Transference is repetition inside the consulting room. Patients repeat old patterns with the analyst instead of remembering them, and Freud saw this as a form of the same compulsion.
What looks like bad fate may come from within the person. Some people seem to live through the same bad outcome again and again, and Freud suggests the cause lies inside them.
Freud proposes that drives are conservative, aiming to restore an earlier state. Followed to its end, this leads him to suggest a drive toward death.
Freud sets the death drive against Eros, the drive that binds things together, and admits the idea is speculation. He says he is unsure how far he believes it.

Some behaviour defies both pleasure and reality. Freud says the pleasure principle is checked in practice by the reality principle, which delays satisfaction when the world demands it, and the puzzle of the book is what falls outside both.
Freud takes over the term Nirvana principle for the mind's tendency to reduce excitation to zero. This supports his claim that the drives aim at rest, not at pleasure as such.
Freud explains Eros with a myth, and says so. He turns to Plato's Symposium, in which beings were split in two and each half seeks the other, and offers it as an image and not as proof.

books.thesis: Civilization demands that we renounce aggression and desire, so unhappiness is built into it.
books.summary:
Freud asks why people who have built so much, from medicine to cities, are still unhappy. His starting point is that the pleasure principle is blocked on every side: by the body, by nature and by other people. Society makes life safer, but only by demanding that individuals give up part of what they want.

The argument leans on his later view of drives. Aggression is a real and permanent part of human nature, so civilization has to turn it back on the self. The result is guilt, which Freud describes as the price of living together. He offers no cure and ends on a doubtful note about whether love can hold off destruction. His picture of aggression is contested, and many see his account of guilt as the book's most lasting contribution.
ideas: Freud traces the oceanic feeling of oneness with the world back to infancy. A friend reported the feeling to him, but Freud says he cannot find it in himself and treats it as a leftover of early life.
Suffering comes from three directions, and Freud says the last is often the hardest. They are our own bodies, the external world and our relations with other people.
Civilization trades some sexual and aggressive satisfaction for safety. Freud argues that much of our unhappiness comes from this bargain.
Freud finds the commandment to love your neighbour as yourself unrealistic. People are not gentle creatures, he says, and are often tempted to use and hurt each other.
Groups bond more easily when they have outsiders to dislike. Freud calls this the narcissism of small differences.
Guilt is aggression turned back on the self. Freud says it settles in the superego, which watches over the ego like a garrison in a conquered city.
Nothing in psychic life is lost, Freud argues. He compares the mind to Rome, where every earlier layer of the city remains in some form.
No single path to happiness works for everyone. Freud lists powerful distractions, substitute satisfactions and intoxicants as the ways people bear suffering, and argues that each helps only in part.
Freud calls the sense of guilt the most important problem in the development of civilization. He says the price of progress is a loss of happiness through a heightened sense of guilt.
He doubts that abolishing private property would end aggression, since he thinks hostility existed long before property did. The remark is aimed at the communist programme of his day.

books.t: The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence
books.thesis: Repression, projection, reaction formation and more: a systematic map of how the ego defends itself.
books.summary:
Anna Freud argued that analysts had spent too long on the unconscious and too little on the ego, the part of the mind that manages conflict. She asks how people protect themselves from feelings and impulses that threaten them. Her answer is a set of defences, each with its own character.

The book works as a catalogue. It describes each defence, shows how it operates and ties it to cases from child and adult analysis. Later chapters apply the ideas to puberty, when old conflicts return with new force. Some critics say the list is arbitrary and the boundaries between defences blur. Even so, the book gave clinicians a shared vocabulary, and terms such as reaction formation and identification with the aggressor are still in use.
ideas: The ego deserves study alongside the unconscious. Anna Freud argues that an analyst who watches only for hidden drives will miss how the person is defending against them.

Anna Freud lists ten defences and says the list is open. They are regression, repression, reaction formation, isolation, undoing, projection, introjection, turning against the self, reversal and sublimation, and she notes that others could be added.
Reaction formation turns a feeling into its opposite. A person harbouring hostile wishes may become unusually gentle or polite as a way of keeping the wish out of sight.
Projection lets us disown an impulse by seeing it in other people. We then treat them as the hostile or desiring ones and feel free of the trait.
A child can cope with fear by becoming the frightening figure. In identification with the aggressor, the child copies a threatening figure's manner and sometimes turns it on others.
Altruistic surrender is giving that serves the giver. A person lives out their own wishes through someone else, helping in ways that satisfy a hidden need.
Adolescence is a period of intense defensive activity. Anna Freud describes asceticism and intellectualisation as ways teenagers deal with the pressure of newly strong drives.
The analyst should not side with the drives against the ego. Anna Freud asks for a position equidistant from the id, the ego and the superego, giving each its due.
A patient's habitual defences show up inside the analysis itself. Anna Freud calls this transference of defence, and treats it as material to study as much as an obstacle to remove.

The fear behind a defence shapes which defence the ego chooses. She sorts the motives into three kinds of anxiety: fear of the superego, fear of the external world and fear of the strength of the drives.

books.thesis: Jung's late account of his inner life, told with Aniela Jaffé, and a good way into his ideas.
books.summary:
Jung worked on this late in life with his associate Aniela Jaffé, and it is not a standard autobiography. He says the outer events of his life matter less to him than his inner experience. The book asks what it is like to live with an unconscious that keeps pressing forward with images, dreams and visions.

It moves through childhood, his years as a psychiatrist, the break with Freud, a long period of inner confrontation, and the building of his tower at Bollingen. Much of it is experience, not argument. Some readers find that moving and others find it vague. It also leaves open how much of Jung's later theory came from clinical work and how much from his own visions. For many readers it is the easiest route into his thinking.
ideas: Jung treats his inner life as the real record of his life. He opens by saying his life is a story of the unconscious realising itself, with outer events as the background.
A childhood dream stayed with Jung for decades. In it he saw an underground chamber and a strange figure on a throne, and he wrote that it shaped his later thinking.
Jung's break with Freud came from a disagreement about the unconscious. He objected especially to Freud's stress on sexuality, describes the split as painful, and tells it from his own side.

Jung's later ideas came out of a crisis. After the break he went through years of intense inner imagery and nearly lost his footing, and he says engaging with the images became the source of his later ideas.
Building the tower at Bollingen gave shape to Jung's inner state. He built it in stages, and he describes the building and carving as part of that work.
A serious illness in later life changed how Jung felt about death. He gives an account of visions from it that he took seriously.
Jung sees a person's task as becoming who they are. He writes that this work takes the whole of a life.
The book is Jung's account of his inner life, not a conventional autobiography. It was recorded and shaped with the help of Aniela Jaffe, and Jung insisted it say little about outward facts.

Jung describes living as two personalities. No. 1 is the schoolboy and ordinary man, No. 2 an older and timeless presence, and he treats the dialogue between them as a thread running through his life.

A visit to Taos Pueblo let Jung see Western habits from outside. A chief told him that white people seemed mad because they think with their heads, and Jung records that this made him see those habits for the first time from outside.

books.thesis: Jung's introduction for general readers: archetypes, dreams, the shadow and individuation.
books.summary:
Jung wrote the opening chapter for readers with no training in psychology, and colleagues added chapters to complete the book. It was among his last pieces of writing. The question is how the unconscious speaks to us. His answer is that it speaks in symbols, above all in dreams.

The book argues by example and explanation. Jung introduces archetypes as shared patterns in human imagination, and describes the shadow, the anima and animus, and the Self. Individuation is the long process of coming to terms with these figures. His colleagues apply the ideas to myth, art and the lives of ordinary people. Archetypes are hard to test, and the book reads more as a guide to Jung's view than as evidence for it.
ideas: A symbol points to something that cannot be fully stated in words. Jung distinguishes it from a sign, which stands for a known thing.
Dreams should be read in the context of the dreamer's own life. Jung calls them a main route to the unconscious and rejects a fixed dictionary of meanings.

Some images recur across cultures because the tendency to form them is inherited. Jung calls these tendencies archetypes, such as the wise old man or the mother, and says they show up in myth and dreams.
The shadow is not simply evil. Jung says it holds the parts of ourselves we reject, and that facing it is a basic step in knowing yourself.
The anima and animus cut both ways. Jung describes them as inner figures of the opposite sex in a person's psyche, and treats them as guides to the unconscious and also as sources of projection.
Individuation is a lifelong process with no end point. Jung describes it as becoming a whole person by integrating conscious and unconscious material.
Modern people have lost touch with the symbols that earlier cultures lived with. Jung suggests that dreams are one way those symbols return.
The Self is the archetype of wholeness and the centre of the psyche as a whole. Jung says it often appears in dreams and art as a circle or mandala, and sometimes as a figure of fourfold order.
Dreams compensate for a one-sided waking attitude. A person who is too rigid in waking life may meet different qualities in dreams.
Jung's alternative to the dream dictionary is amplification. It means enlarging a dream image by comparing it with myths, folk tales and other parallels.

books.thesis: Mass society crushes the individual. Self-knowledge, the shadow included, is the defence.
books.summary:
This short Cold War book asks what happens to the individual in a mass society. Jung sees states, parties and organisations as forces that teach people to think of themselves as units in a crowd. He argues that this makes people easier to manipulate and more dangerous, because no one feels personally responsible.

His answer is self-knowledge. A person who has looked honestly at their own shadow is less likely to project evil onto enemies and less likely to be swept into a collective movement. Jung also gives religion a role as a counterweight to the state, since it ties a person to something beyond politics. The tone is urgent and warning. Some of it now reads as dated, but the worry about conformity and projection is still clear.
ideas: An average describes no real person, and mass society forgets this. Jung argues that treating people as statistics, and seeing yourself as a unit in a group, weakens personal judgement.
Real change can only start in the individual. Jung says groups and states are made of individuals who each hold a share of the problem.
Much of the evil we see in others is partly our own, pushed outward. Jung argues that withdrawing such projections is a practical political task.
Religion can give a person an inner relation to something larger than the state. Whatever one thinks of its claims, Jung worries that losing this leaves people open to the state's demands.
Shared belief can spread like an epidemic. Jung argues that these psychic epidemics can seize whole populations and are hard to resist without some self-knowledge.
A denied shadow is not removed. Jung says it has to be recognised to be dealt with, and otherwise it tends to turn up in how we judge others.
The gap between rational outlook and inner life is a public danger. Jung thinks modern people live with this gap, and he sees it as a source of danger beyond the private.
Jung locates the danger of nuclear weapons in the human psyche. The book is written against the Cold War, and he argues that the psyche that would use them deserves more study than it receives.

The modern state has taken over the place religion once held. Jung says it asks for loyalty and gives a person little inner ground to stand on, which leaves the individual easy to absorb into the mass.

Self-knowledge is the only real safeguard, in Jung's view, and knowing people in general does not help us know one particular person. A person who has met their own inner opposites is, he says, harder to carry along with a slogan.

books.t: Modern Man in Search of a Soul
books.thesis: Modern people have lost the myths that held meaning in place, and they suffer for it.
books.summary:
These essays from the 1930s ask why so many educated people feel their lives lack direction. Jung's answer is that modern life has stripped away the religious and mythic frameworks that gave people a sense of place. His patients, he says, often came with problems that were less about symptoms than about meaning.

The essays range across dream analysis, the aims of therapy, the stages of a human life, and the relation of psychology to art. Jung also sets his approach apart from Freud's. He proposes that the second half of life has its own task, which cannot be borrowed from the first. His remarks on religion and psychology are not always rigorous, but the questions he raises about meaning are still discussed.
ideas: Many of Jung's older patients suffered from a loss of meaning, not from a clear illness. He says helping them required attention to their outlook on life.
A dream's surface differs from its function. Jung describes using dreams in therapy and says they often compensate for the attitude of the conscious mind.
Life has two halves with different tasks. Jung argues the first is about establishing oneself in the world, while the second calls for turning inward and asking what it was all for.
People take spiritual troubles to the doctor because the old institutions no longer answer them. Jung compares the psychotherapist with the priest on this point.
A work of art grows from a collective source, one essay argues. The artist is partly a channel for something beyond personal life.
Jung separates his view from Freud's. He says he cannot reduce all psychic life to sexuality and wants to take the religious side of experience seriously.
Jung calls on modern people to take their own inner life seriously. He says it should not be handed over to ready-made creeds or to purely rational explanations.

Treatment has four stages, and the last cannot be forced. In the essay on problems of modern psychotherapy Jung names confession, elucidation, education and transformation, and says transformation is rare and cannot be reached by technique alone.
The modern person is cut off from tradition. Jung defines this person as standing at the edge of time, and suggests the position brings a pride in being new and a hidden loneliness.

The therapist is part of the treatment. Jung holds that the two personalities meet and both may be changed, and that a therapist who has not faced his own problems cannot lead a patient further than he has gone himself.

books.thesis: A short, clear guide to Jung's shadow and to what disowning it costs you.
books.summary:
Robert Johnson, a Jungian analyst, wrote this as a short, practical introduction to one of Jung's best-known ideas. It starts from a plain observation: everyone has traits they hide, even from themselves. The book asks what becomes of those traits once they are pushed out of awareness, and answers that they do not disappear.

Johnson explains that as children we split off parts of ourselves to fit in with family and culture. What is split off becomes the shadow, which returns in outbursts, in projections onto others and in odd bits of behaviour. Taking it back is difficult but worthwhile, he suggests, and he proposes simple symbolic acts as one way to do it. The book is short on evidence and long on illustration, so it works best as an orientation to Jung.
ideas: The shadow is not only dark. Johnson defines it as the part of us we have refused to accept, and stresses that some of what we hide is admirable.

Childhood teaches us to hide parts of ourselves, and the person ends up living only half of what they are. A child learns which traits are welcome and which are not, and the unwelcome ones are pushed out of sight.
What is cast off does not vanish. Johnson describes it as gathering energy out of sight and then returning in sudden rage, accidents or mood swings.
Strong dislike of someone is often a hint about something we have not accepted in ourselves. Johnson says we tend to see our own hidden traits in other people.
The golden shadow holds our unclaimed strengths. Johnson points to talents we refuse to claim and instead see in people we admire.
Taking back the shadow takes humility. Johnson argues it means seeing that we are neither as good nor as bad as we pretend.
Insight alone does not settle the shadow. Johnson recommends small ritual and symbolic acts, along with imaginative work, because purely rational insight tends not to be enough.
Nations and groups have a shadow too. Johnson says societies project it onto enemies in times of conflict, which he treats as the large-scale form of the personal habit of blaming others.
Stevenson's Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde is Johnson's picture of a shadow that is shut away and then breaks out with force. A respectable surface, the tale shows, tends to be bought at the cost of denial.
The aim is neither to act out the shadow nor to push it down again. Johnson describes a third course of holding the tension and letting it be known, so that its energy can be put to some use.

books.t: The Drama of the Gifted Child
books.thesis: A child who must meet a parent's needs hides their own and loses touch with their true feelings.
books.summary:
Alice Miller, a Swiss psychoanalyst, looks at what happens to a sensitive child whose parent needs the child to behave in a particular way. Such children, she observes, learn quickly what is wanted and supply it, and in doing so lose contact with what they feel. They grow up capable, often admired and empty.

The book draws on her work with patients who were successful but depressed or driven. She argues that grandiosity and depression are two faces of one problem, a self-worth that depends on performing. Recovery, in her view, means feeling the pain of what was missed and mourning it. Critics question how much rests on clinical impressions and how hard she is on parents, but many readers recognise the pattern she describes.
ideas: Giftedness, for Miller, is a child's skill at reading a parent's needs. A child who senses that a parent needs something from them will often supply it.
The child hides whatever threatens the parent's love, and eventually cannot feel it. Anger and need are suppressed to keep that love, and over time the child loses access to them.
Grandiosity and depression are linked in Miller's account. The person who feels special when achieving can fall into emptiness when achievement fails.
The pattern passes down the generations unseen. Many parents were treated this way themselves, and they repeat it without being aware of it.
Self-esteem built on being useful or successful stays fragile. It depends on constant performance and never on being accepted as one is.
Therapists can repeat the problem. If they require the patient to be a good patient, Miller argues, the analyst has to let the patient's real feelings appear instead.
Understanding the story is not enough to heal. Healing, in Miller's account, requires feeling the original pain and grieving what was lost.
The person who has hidden their needs often treats weakness with contempt, in themselves and in others. Miller says the contempt repeats how the child's own neediness was once met.
Miller suggests that many people who become therapists were gifted children in her sense. Their sensitivity to other people's needs is real, but it can also be a way of avoiding their own.
Adults who never had a mirror may look for one in a partner or a child. They ask for the admiration and attention they missed, which Miller sees as a quiet way the pattern is handed down.

books.thesis: Creativity and a sense of being real grow in a space of play that a good-enough environment makes possible.
books.summary:
Donald Winnicott was a paediatrician and psychoanalyst, and this book gathers his late thinking on play. He asks where creative life comes from and what makes a person feel real instead of merely compliant. His answer begins with how infants and parents interact, long before words.

The argument is built around a space between inner and outer worlds, which he calls potential space. A baby moves into it with a favoured object, and later with play, art and culture. A parent who is good enough, meaning reliable but not perfect, lets that space open. Therapy is described as two people playing together. The writing is gentle and often hard to pin down, so expect suggestion more than strict argument.
ideas: Transitional objects sit between the inner and outer worlds. A favourite blanket or soft toy belongs wholly to neither, and Winnicott sees it as a first step toward culture.
Playing is where creative living starts. It takes place in a potential space between self and world, and Winnicott insists it is more than a pastime.

Small, manageable failures by a parent are part of good parenting. A good-enough parent adapts closely at first and then fails in small ways, which helps the child tell what is inside from what is outside.
The mother's face works as a first mirror. If a baby sees itself reflected, it feels real, and if it sees only the mother's mood, it learns to adapt.

A compliant false self can leave a person feeling unreal. Winnicott contrasts a true self with a false self that complies with others' demands, and says the feeling of unreality comes when the false self dominates.
Surviving attack makes the other person real. In the use of an object, the child attacks the parent in fantasy and finds that the parent survives, which lets the other become real and separate.
Therapy happens where two people's playing overlaps. Winnicott says the therapist's job is to make play possible, not to deliver clever interpretations.

A healthy start includes illusion before disillusion. Winnicott describes the mother giving the baby a first illusion of omnipotence by offering the breast just when the baby is ready to imagine it, then gradually disillusioning the baby, which he treats as healthy and necessary.
Fantasying is not play. Winnicott separates it from dreaming and playing, calling it a cut-off, repetitive state that does not feed life, while play is creative and connected to the world.

Art and religion belong in the same space as play. Winnicott places cultural experience in the potential space and treats it as a continuation of how a child first finds meaning between inner and outer worlds.

books.thesis: Envy attacks what is good because it is good. Gratitude is the slow antidote.
books.summary:
Melanie Klein asks what early emotional life is like and what goes wrong when it goes badly. She proposes that envy, a wish to spoil what someone else has, appears from the start of life and is aimed at the good thing itself. A baby who has received good care can still envy it, because it belongs to someone else.
