The argument rests on her work with children and on inference about infancy. She contrasts envy with greed and jealousy, and describes how envy undermines a person's ability to take in help. Gratitude, the capacity to enjoy good things without spoiling them, builds slowly and works against it. Many critics doubt that infants can feel such things, and others find her descriptions of adult attitudes more convincing than her account of infancy.
ideas: Klein proposes that envy is present from birth, directed first at the mother's breast as the source of nourishment. Many analysts question whether infants can experience envy in this form.
Envy attacks what is good because it is good. That makes it different from hatred of something harmful, and it explains why help can sometimes make people angry.
Klein separates envy from greed and from jealousy. Greed wants to take all there is, jealousy involves a rival and a third person, and envy is about spoiling.
Envy can wreck the capacity to learn from or be helped by others. Accepting good means admitting one lacks it.
Patients sometimes get worse when the analyst does useful work. Klein reads this as envy of the analyst's ability to help.
Gratitude is the main counterweight to envy. Klein defines it as the ability to feel the goodness of what one has received and enjoy it.
Strong early envy leaves lasting marks on character. Klein argues it brings difficulty in trusting good experiences and in feeling secure.

Envy is harmful because it spoils the good object. Klein's picture of early life divides the mother's breast into a good one and a bad one, and the baby takes the good object in as an inner source of security.
Defences against envy protect a person from feeling how much they need what they envy. Klein lists idealisation, devaluing what is good and stirring up envy in others.
Klein also sees envy of creativity, such as the mother's power to feed and bear children. She links it to later hostility to anyone who is seen as productive or fertile.

books.thesis: The "tyranny of the should": we wear ourselves out trying to become an idealised self.
books.summary:
Karen Horney was a psychoanalyst who broke with Freud on several points. Here she asks why people with talent and opportunity so often fail to grow. Her reply is that they set up an idealised image of who they ought to be and spend their energy trying to meet it. The real self is neglected and ends up alienated.

The idealised image produces what she calls the tyranny of the should, a constant set of demands the person makes on themselves. When these cannot be met, self-hatred follows. She also describes three broad ways of coping: expansive, self-effacing and resigned. Horney thinks the road to health runs through the real self, though she is less specific about how people get there, and later readers have found her diagnoses more useful than her cures.
ideas: People build an idealised self-image, often without knowing it. It may be glorious or saintly, and it replaces the effort to be who one is.
The tyranny of the should is a list of inner demands about how one must feel and act. Horney says these demands are experienced as obligations, not as wishes.
The search for glory covers a deeper insecurity. Horney describes it as a drive to be perfect and to rise above ordinary limits.
Neurotic pride makes a person defensive about any perceived flaw. It attaches itself to the idealised self, is easily hurt, and can make people more rigid.
Self-hatred arises when the real self cannot match the ideal. The person may turn this hatred on themselves or externalise it onto others.
People settle inner conflict in three different ways. The expansive type seeks mastery, the self-effacing type seeks love, and the resigned type withdraws from the struggle.
Healthy growth moves toward the real self, with its actual feelings and limits. Horney contrasts this with trying to live up to a picture.

Neurotic claims leave the person feeling wronged. They are the demands a person feels entitled to make on others and on life because of the idealised self, and when they go unmet the person often cannot see their own part in it.

Externalisation means experiencing inner processes as if they happened outside. A person may blame others for their own self-contempt or feel that the world is hateful when they are hateful to themselves.

Alienation from self is the main cost of the idealised self. Horney describes it as losing touch with one's own feelings, wishes and beliefs as the true source of one's life, and sees it as the thing therapy must undo.

books.thesis: Narcissism has its own line of development, and its disorders come from unmet needs for mirroring.
books.summary:
Heinz Kohut was a Chicago analyst whose patients did not fit the usual categories. They were not in conflict over drives. They felt empty, fragile or unreal, and they reacted badly to slights. The book asks how narcissism develops and what goes wrong when it does not develop well.

Kohut argues that narcissism has its own developmental line and is not a stage to be left behind. A child needs to be mirrored, and also needs someone to admire and lean on. When those needs go unmet, the self stays fragile. In treatment, patients form characteristic transferences, and the analyst's task is empathic understanding. Critics say Kohut's break with Freud went too far, while supporters credit him with making room for patients who had been hard to treat.
ideas: Narcissism is not simply a defect. Kohut treats it as a developmental line that matures into healthy self-esteem, ambition and ideals if the right conditions are met.
A child needs a caregiver who responds with delight and approval to its achievements. Kohut calls this mirroring, and says its lack leaves the self weak.
Children also need someone to look up to. The idealised parent figure gives calm and strength, which the child gradually takes in as its own.
A selfobject is a person experienced as part of one's own self-regulation. Kohut uses the term for someone who is not experienced as a separate person.
Patients with narcissistic difficulties develop a mirror transference and an idealising transference. Kohut says these should be understood and not rushed away.
Empathy is Kohut's main method of observation. He holds that psychological facts are known by putting oneself inside another person's experience.
Small failures of empathy can build the self, if they can be worked through. The person takes over the functions the caregiver used to provide, which Kohut calls transmuting internalisation.

Kohut argues that patients with narcissistic disorders can be treated by classical analysis, against Freud's view that such patients could not form a useful transference. The key was to treat the two narcissistic transferences as genuine and not as resistance.
Narcissism can be transformed into mature forms. Kohut names creativity, empathy, humour, wisdom and an acceptance of one's own transience as outcomes of healthy development.
The analyst's own narcissistic needs can get in the way of the patient's transference. Kohut asks the analyst to tolerate being admired or devalued without defending against either.

books.thesis: Collected papers, including the mirror stage, where the self first forms as an image seen from outside.
books.summary:
Écrits collects Lacan's papers and talks from several decades, assembled in 1966. It asks what Freud meant, and what the self is if it forms by looking outward. Lacan calls for a return to Freud and reads him through linguistics and philosophy rather than biology or ego psychology.

The book is known for its difficulty. Lacan writes in an allusive, sometimes playful style and assumes a great deal of learning. The main strands are the mirror stage, the claim that the unconscious is structured like a language, and the interplay of what he calls the Imaginary, the Symbolic and the Real. Admirers see a deep rereading of psychoanalysis, while critics accuse him of obscurity. Approach it with a guide and with patience.
ideas: The first sense of an I rests on an outside image, partly a misrecognition. In the mirror stage an uncoordinated infant sees a whole image of itself and greets it with delight.
Lacan argues that the unconscious is structured like a language. Symptoms and slips work like words that stand for other words, and so they can be read.
For Lacan the signifier matters more than what it signifies. He takes the term from linguistics, and meaning arises from the chain of signifiers, not from a direct link to things.
Lacan sorts experience into three orders: the Imaginary, the Symbolic and the Real. The Symbolic is the world of language and law that structures a person's place among others.
A signifier can steer the people who handle it, whatever they intend. Lacan shows this in the opening seminar on Poe's story The Purloined Letter.
Desire is the desire of the Other. We want what we think others want, and we want to be wanted, so desire never settles on a final object.
Lacan rejects the ego psychology of his time, which aimed to strengthen the ego. He holds that the ego is an imaginary construct and not a reliable ally.
Speech can be empty or full. In the Rome Discourse, empty speech circles round what the patient says, while full speech is where a patient first hears something true about their own desire.
The Name-of-the-Father gives a child a place in the symbolic order and sets limits on desire. Lacan argues that when this signifier is foreclosed, psychosis can result.

Critics such as Sokal and Bricmont say Lacan's use of mathematical terms and topology is loose and that his style hides weak arguments. His defenders reply that the difficulty is part of how the texts ask to be read.

books.thesis: Madness can be an understandable strategy for a self that does not feel safe in the world.
books.summary:
R. D. Laing, a Scottish psychiatrist, set out to understand people diagnosed with schizophrenia from the inside. The book asks what madness looks like if we assume it makes sense. Laing proposes that a person who lacks a basic sense of being safe in the world, which he calls ontological insecurity, may withdraw and divide, and that the resulting behaviour is a strategy for survival.

He takes an existential and phenomenological approach, describing how a person experiences their own body, other people and their own identity. Case descriptions show how a patient's speech becomes intelligible once taken seriously. Later readers have criticised Laing for downplaying the biology of psychosis, and he himself moved further from conventional psychiatry. It remains a landmark in the effort to listen.
ideas: Psychotic speech and behaviour can be understood as meaningful. Laing thinks the clinician's task is to grasp how the world looks to the patient.
Ontological security is a firm sense of oneself as real and continuous. Laing says someone who lacks it experiences ordinary life as a threat to their existence.
A person can live as an embodied or an unembodied self. Embodied means at home in the body, unembodied means watching life from a detached position, and Laing links the second to schizoid experience.
A false-self system protects the person and also isolates them. Laing describes a compliant outside while the real self stays hidden and untouched.
The insecure person fears closeness in three ways, which Laing calls engulfment, implosion and petrification. Each is a fear that closeness or being seen will destroy the self.
Distance meant to protect the self can empty it. The schizoid person often keeps others away, and Laing says this can leave the self depleted and unreal.
Purely clinical language misses the person. Laing is critical of terms that describe the patient as a collection of symptoms and not as a person in a situation.

Laing describes the patient before diagnosing. He uses an existential-phenomenological method, drawing on Kierkegaard, Sartre and Binswanger, to describe the patient's way of being in the world from the inside.
For the insecure person, concealment feels like safety. Being seen or understood can feel like a threat, so relationships become a matter of defending the self.
Later critics say Laing paid too little attention to biology and came close to romanticising madness. The book itself is more careful, but this was the direction his later work took.

books.thesis: Identity is built across eight life stages, each with its own crisis.
books.summary:
Erik Erikson was an analyst trained in Vienna who spent his career in America. This book asks how a person acquires a sense of who they are, and how that sense depends on both the inner life and the society around them. He takes Freud's interest in childhood and widens it to include culture and history.

The central proposal is a scheme of eight stages across the whole life, each organised around a crisis between two outcomes. Erikson supports it with studies of two Native American peoples, case material, and an essay on how young people in Germany came to follow Hitler. Critics find the stages too neat and too tied to his own society, but the idea of an identity crisis has entered everyday language.
ideas: Erikson describes eight stages of life, from infancy to old age. Each stage poses a crisis, and the way it is handled shapes the later ones.
Infancy sets trust against mistrust. A baby who is reliably cared for gets a basic confidence that the world and other people can be depended on.
Harsh handling of a toddler can leave lasting shame. Toddlers face autonomy against shame and doubt as they begin to do things for themselves, and the shame attaches to their own wishes.
School age brings industry against inferiority. A child wants to make things and master skills, and failing at this can lead to a feeling of being inadequate.
Adolescence centres on identity against role confusion. Young people try out roles and loyalties, and Erikson uses the term identity crisis for the strain of this search.
Child-rearing practices fit the demands of each culture, Erikson argues, so psychology must take culture seriously. He draws on his work with the Sioux and the Yurok.

Adulthood and old age bring their own crises. Generativity is set against stagnation in adulthood and integrity against despair in old age, and the final crisis is whether a person can accept the life they had.

Development follows a ground plan. Erikson's epigenetic principle holds that each part has its time of special ascendancy, each stage builds on the one before, and a missed stage can be partly repaired later.
A leader's story can speak to a society's unresolved childhood conflicts. Erikson makes this case through studies of Hitler's imagery and German youth, and of Maxim Gorky's early life.

Erikson read children's play as a sign of their bodily sense of themselves. In a play study, children aged ten to twelve arranged toy scenes and he found regular differences in how boys and girls used space, an interpretation later critics have found dated.

books.thesis: People act toward goals, above all to overcome felt inferiority and to find a place among others.
books.summary:
Alfred Adler worked with Freud early on, then broke away to build his own school. This book is a set of lectures for a general audience. It asks why people act as they do, and it answers by looking forward. Behaviour makes sense once we see the goal a person is moving toward, even if they would not name it.

All children begin with a feeling of inferiority, he argues, because they are small and dependent. They compensate by striving for competence, and the way each person does so becomes a style of life. A healthy style includes concern for others, which Adler calls community feeling. Critics say his ideas can be vague and hard to test. His influence is wide, though, and many later therapies carry traces of his thinking.
ideas: Adler explains behaviour by the goal it serves, not only by its past causes. A person's actions fit together once you see what they are aiming at.
Feeling inferior is normal. All children feel inferior because they are small in a world of larger people, and Adler treats this feeling as a spur to development and not as a sickness.
An inferiority complex arises when the feeling becomes too heavy to handle. The person may then seek superiority by showing off or by retreating into symptoms.
Each person forms a style of life in early childhood. It is a pattern of how they approach tasks and other people, and Adler says it stays fairly consistent through adult life.
Community feeling is the main mark of a healthy person. Adler defines it as the sense of belonging with others and wanting to contribute.
Character traits such as vanity, envy and shyness are tools, not fixed givens. Adler says they can be understood by asking what the person gains.
Pampering and neglect both distort a child's style of life. Adler says this is because both kinds of child have missed the experience of cooperating with others.

Striving for superiority, or perfection, is the basic movement of mental life. Adler describes it as a drive to rise from a felt minus to a felt plus, and it can be healthy or damaging depending on its direction.
Private intelligence is the mark of a troubled style of life. Adler sets common sense against it, since a person who follows private intelligence uses a logic that only makes sense to themselves.
Adler rejects a sharp split between conscious and unconscious. He treats the person as an undivided whole, which is the meaning of the name Individual Psychology.

books.thesis: Adlerian psychology told as a dialogue. Freedom means accepting that some people will not like you.
books.summary:
This Japanese bestseller presents Alfred Adler's ideas as a conversation between a philosopher and a sceptical young man over several nights. The question is whether people can change, and what freedom costs. The philosopher says they can, and that most of what holds us back is our own choice, even though it does not feel that way.

The dialogue form lets the young man push back on each claim. They work through the denial of trauma as a cause, the separation of tasks, and the role of community feeling. Readers either find the argument bracing or think it blames people too much for their own suffering. It is a popular rendering, not a scholarly study, so it simplifies Adler and adds its own emphasis.
ideas: The past does not determine the present. The philosopher argues that we use past events to serve our current goals, an approach Adler called teleology.
All problems are interpersonal on this view. Feeling inferior or ashamed always involves a comparison with other people.
Conflict starts when people interfere with each other's tasks. The separation of tasks says whose task a matter is depends on who bears its final consequences.
Both praise and rebuke rank people, and ranking creates dependence. The book prefers encouragement that treats others as equals.
Being disliked by some people is a sign that you are living according to your own views. The authors say seeking everyone's approval costs you your freedom.
Community feeling is reached by contribution, not by getting recognition. The book says it means seeing others as companions, not competitors.
Life is not a path toward a future goal. The book urges people to live earnestly in the present moment, with each moment lived in full.
The dialogue form tests the ideas against ordinary doubts. The book is a conversation between a philosopher and a sceptical youth over five nights, and the youth voices the reader's objections.
Relationships are horizontal and not vertical. People are equal though not the same, and the authors argue that treating others as above or below us lies behind much anxiety and resentment.
Self-acceptance comes first among the book's three steps, followed by trust in others and contribution to others. Self-acceptance means working with what one has, and not wishing to be someone else.

books.thesis: Much of who we are lives in an adaptive unconscious, out of reach of introspection.
books.summary:
Timothy Wilson, a social psychologist, asks how well we can know our own minds. He argues that much of mental life goes on outside consciousness, in a system he calls the adaptive unconscious. It judges, evaluates and sets goals quickly, and it does not tell us.

The evidence comes from decades of experiments showing that people often cannot report the real causes of their choices. They give reasons that sound sensible but are guesses. Wilson's unconscious is more practical than Freud's: a useful system, not a store of hidden wishes. He also argues that to know ourselves we may need to watch our behaviour as we would watch a stranger's. Some of the research cited has been challenged in later replication efforts.
ideas: Much of mental life runs fast and outside awareness. Wilson proposes an adaptive unconscious that handles much of what we perceive, judge and decide.
Wilson's unconscious is not Freud's. It is not a place for repressed wishes but more like an efficient set of tools that we cannot inspect.
People are often wrong about why they did something. In experiments, they offer reasons that sound plausible but do not match what influenced them.
Introspection gives us a story about ourselves, not direct access. We build the story from what seems reasonable and from our theories about how people work.
Explicit and implicit attitudes can differ. A person can sincerely say they hold one view while their quick reactions show another.
We construct a self-narrative that we find believable and flattering. Wilson argues the story shapes how we see ourselves, even if it is not accurate.
Watching what we do may teach us more than looking inward. Wilson suggests that our behaviour and how others react to us are better evidence about ourselves.
Feelings we take as direct sometimes come from watching ourselves. Self-perception theory holds that we often work out our own attitudes by observing what we do, much as an outsider would.
Analysing our reasons can lead us away from our real preferences. In a well-known study, people asked to list reasons for liking posters chose ones they later liked less.
We forecast our own feelings poorly. People overstate how strongly and how long events will affect them, which Wilson treats as another sign that we know our own minds less well than we think.

books.thesis: We deceive ourselves so we can deceive others better, and we pay for it in bad decisions.
books.summary:
Robert Trivers, an evolutionary biologist, asks why people lie to themselves when the truth would serve them better. His proposal is that self-deception exists because it helps us deceive other people. A person who believes their own story gives off fewer signs of lying, and so is more convincing.

The book ranges across biology, psychology and history. Trivers looks at deception among animals, at the way people inflate their own virtues, and at the costs of biased thinking in marriage, organisations and war. He also considers how the mind keeps the truth available somewhere while hiding it from awareness. The evolutionary logic is neat but hard to test, and some critics say the book stretches the idea to cover too much.
ideas: Self-deception evolved to help us deceive others, Trivers argues. If you believe your own claim, you show fewer cues of lying, and the claim becomes more persuasive.
Deception is an ordinary strategy in nature. Trivers points to animals that mimic others and organisms that hide their true condition.
People see themselves as better than average and as more in control than they are. Trivers treats these inflated views as typical self-deception.
We find faults in others while overlooking the same faults in ourselves. Trivers argues that this bias shapes conflicts between individuals and between groups.
Self-deception has costs. A mind that does not see the truth can make bad decisions, and Trivers discusses how it contributes to errors in organisations and in war.
Close relationships can run on two flattering self-portraits. In marriage, each partner may keep up a good picture of themselves and a critical picture of the other, which fuels conflict.
The mind may store accurate information in one place while the conscious self holds a different version. Trivers suggests this split lets us act on the truth without admitting it.

Self-deception can arise at several stages of handling information. Trivers calls this biased information flow: we may avoid information, encode it in a slanted way, remember it selectively or reason badly about it.

Organisations can play down warnings when accepting them would be costly. Trivers gives the Challenger and Columbia shuttle disasters as examples, arguing that those in charge had reason to discount the warnings.

False national and historical narratives let groups think well of themselves. Trivers argues these accounts spread in much the same way as individual self-deception, and can have serious consequences.

books.thesis: Much behaviour, from charity to education, runs on hidden status motives we do not admit.
books.summary:
People say they give to charity to help others, go to school to learn, and see doctors to get better. Kevin Simler and Robin Hanson argue that these noble explanations do not quite fit. Other motives, often about status and impressing others, do part of the work, and we are built not to notice.

They test the idea across everyday activities, using evolutionary psychology and economics. The brain, on their account, works like an organisation with a press secretary who gives the public story while other parts pursue other goals. Critics say the book explains too much with one mechanism and that its evidence is uneven. It is best read as a provocation about hidden motives, not as settled science.
ideas: We hide our motives from ourselves because that helps us hide them from others. The elephant in the title is the set of motives we do not discuss.
The mind has a press secretary. It produces flattering reasons for our actions, while other parts of the brain pursue less admirable aims we are not told about.
Visible charity is shaped by how it looks to others. The authors argue that people often show off by being useful and generous, and that giving is not driven only by its effects.
Education may serve to signal qualities such as intelligence and conformity to employers, as well as to teach. The authors point to how many people want the credential more than the lessons.
Much medical spending shows care instead of delivering benefit. The authors argue that people want to be seen to care, and so they favour the visible effort.
Conversation, laughter and art display quality to others. The authors suggest we enjoy them partly because they make us look good.
Hidden motives are not necessarily bad. The authors suggest that seeing them clearly could help us design institutions that work better.

Political behaviour is largely about showing loyalty to a group. Voting and arguing serve as signals of belonging, which would explain why people care more about taking a side than about policy results.
We are good at hiding our own norm violations from ourselves and at noticing other people's. The authors argue that norms are enforced in public but often broken in private.

The signalling account is hard to test, critics say, since almost any behaviour can be given a signalling explanation after the fact. The authors accept that motives are mixed and that the stated reason is often partly true.

books.thesis: Split-brain research and the interpreter suggest the self is a story the brain tells after the fact.
books.summary:
Michael Gazzaniga, a neuroscientist who helped found the study of split-brain patients, asks whether we are in charge of our own actions or whether the brain works things out and tells us afterward. He answers that the sense of a single controlling self is something the brain constructs from many parts working at once.

The argument rests on his experiments with patients whose brain hemispheres had been surgically separated. In these cases the left hemisphere invents explanations for actions it did not originate, which he calls the interpreter. Gazzaniga then turns to free will and law. He holds that the brain is deterministic but that people remain responsible, because responsibility arises in social interaction and not within one skull. Philosophers still dispute whether this answer works.
ideas: A single unified mind is not as basic as it feels. In split-brain patients, Gazzaniga says, the two hemispheres can act on different information.
The interpreter generates explanations for our behaviour. It is a system in the left hemisphere that will produce a plausible story even when it has no access to the real cause.

A patient will believe a reason invented after the fact, with no sense of making it up. In Gazzaniga's experiments, a patient did something prompted to the right hemisphere, and the left invented a reason.
The feeling of one self in charge is built on top of many modules. Gazzaniga describes the brain as made of many specialised modules working in parallel.
A deterministic brain does not make free will meaningless, Gazzaniga argues. He accepts that the brain is a physical system and that its workings are determined, but rejects that conclusion.
Responsibility is a social matter. Gazzaniga says it exists in the interactions between people and not inside any single brain, so it survives even if the brain is deterministic.
Brain science should be used with care in law. Gazzaniga argues that knowing about a person's brain does not by itself tell us whether to excuse them.

Mind and brain are best explained at different levels. Gazzaniga argues for emergence, in which a higher level of organisation has properties that cannot be read off from the parts, and compares it to traffic, which cannot be understood by studying one car.
Explanation-making also shows in patients with brain injuries. Those who deny or explain away problems such as paralysis show, in Gazzaniga's view, the same process as in his split-brain studies.

Brain activity that precedes a reported decision does not remove responsibility. Gazzaniga argues these experiments show the brain working before the interpreter speaks, and do not show that people are not responsible.

books.thesis: Identity is an internal life story, and its plot and tone shape how we live.
books.summary:
Dan McAdams, a personality psychologist, asks what it means to have an identity. His proposal is that from late adolescence on, people build an internal story of their lives that gives them unity and purpose. He calls it a personal myth and suggests that its plot and tone shape how people live.

McAdams draws on Erikson's theory of identity and on personality research. He describes the parts a life story has, including imagery, theme, tone and characters. He also notes that stories are shaped by culture and by the needs of different life stages. Critics ask how much of a person the story they tell can capture, and whether such stories are accurate. McAdams treats them as meaningful whether or not they are strictly true.
ideas: Identity is an internalised and evolving life story, McAdams holds. The story gives a person a sense of unity and purpose over time.
A personal myth is not a false story. McAdams uses the word for a story that carries meaning and shapes a life.
The life story begins to form in adolescence. McAdams says that is when people first can think about their lives as a whole and ask who they are.
A life story has recognisable features. McAdams names an overall tone, recurring images, a theme and an ideological setting of beliefs and values.
Certain scenes give a life story its shape. McAdams calls them nuclear episodes, such as peaks, turning points and low points.
Idealised personifications of the self organise how a person plays roles. McAdams calls them imagoes, such as the healer or the warrior.
Agency and communion recur as the two broad themes of life stories. One is about power and achievement, and the other about love and connection.
McAdams builds on Erikson. He treats identity as the task of adolescence and early adulthood, and sees the life story as the form identity takes once a person can place themselves in time.
No one invents a life story from nothing. A personal myth draws on the stories a culture makes available, such as familiar plots and figures, so identity is both personal and shared.
A good life story hangs together but still has room to change. McAdams proposes criteria for judging one: coherence, openness, credibility, differentiation and reconciliation.

books.thesis: Most of what your brain does happens without you. Consciousness is a small part of it.
books.summary:
David Eagleman, a neuroscientist, asks how much of what goes on in the brain is available to the person it belongs to. His answer is little. Most processing happens without awareness, and consciousness sees only a small part of it.

He supports the point with examples from perception, illusions, sport and brain damage. He also proposes that the brain is a team of rivals, with different systems competing and cooperating. This has consequences for blame and punishment, since a person's choices rest on factors they did not choose. Eagleman argues for a more forward-looking approach in law. Critics say the practical conclusions go beyond what the science supports.
ideas: Most of what the brain does is out of reach of awareness. Eagleman compares consciousness to the tip of an iceberg, with most of the activity out of sight.
Perception is built by the brain and is not a direct view of the world. Eagleman uses visual illusions as evidence that what we see is a construction.
Behaviour comes from competing systems, not a single will. Eagleman describes the brain as a team of rivals, with different systems that disagree.
Skilled actions happen faster than conscious thought. In catching a ball or hitting in baseball, Eagleman says, we are mostly told about the action afterward.
Brain damage and disease can change a person's behaviour and character. Eagleman discusses a man with a tumour who committed violence, to ask what this means for responsibility.
A Ulysses contract is a commitment made in a calm state to bind one's later self. Eagleman uses it to show how the rational and impulsive parts of us can cooperate.
Law should focus less on blame and more on predicting and reducing future harm. Eagleman argues this because people's choices rest on factors outside their control.
Expert skill can run on knowledge its owner cannot report. Eagleman cites chicken sexers, who learn to sort chicks by sex without being able to say how they do it.
Character and choice are sensitive to brain chemistry. Eagleman cites Parkinson's patients who took certain dopamine drugs and developed compulsive gambling.
Prejudice does not need conscious endorsement to operate. Eagleman describes in-group bias as built into the brain, shaping how strongly we respond to other people.

books.thesis: The unified self is something the brain constructs. It is useful, but it is not what it seems.
books.summary:
Bruce Hood, a developmental psychologist, asks whether the sense of being one continuous self is accurate. He argues that it is not. The feeling of a unified I is built by the brain from many processes, memories and social influences, and it can come apart under certain conditions.

Hood goes through evidence from psychology, neuroscience and philosophy, including Hume's remark that he could find no self when he looked inward. He stresses that the self is shaped by other people and by the stories we tell. Calling it an illusion does not mean it is useless: Hood calls it a helpful construction that we need in order to live. Critics point out that an illusion needs someone to be fooled, a puzzle the argument only partly addresses.
ideas: The self is a construction of the brain. Hood argues there is no single place where it sits, and the feeling of unity is built from many processes.
Hume looked inward and found only particular perceptions, never a self. Hood recalls this report and treats it as an early version of his own view.
Other people shape the self. Our beliefs, habits and sense of who we are come in large part from the groups we belong to.
Memory is reconstructive. The past that supports our sense of continuity is rebuilt each time we recall it, and so it is open to error.
The sense of choosing is not direct evidence of being in control. Hood draws on studies suggesting we often act first and construct a reason afterward.
We tell stories about ourselves to hold the pieces together. Hood says these narratives give coherence to a self that would otherwise feel scattered.
The illusion is a useful one, Hood says. Knowing it is constructed may change how we think about blame, ambition and personal identity.

A sense of a bodily self appears early. In the rouge test a mark is put on a child's face and the child is watched for whether they touch it in a mirror, and passing at around eighteen months is taken to show it.
Ideas of the self differ across cultures. Western ideas of an independent, bounded self are not universal, which supports Hood's claim that the self is built from experience.
Disorders and injuries show that the self can break apart. Hood treats split-brain cases and dissociative states as clues that unity is something the brain makes and not something it starts with.

books.thesis: The bond to a caregiver is a biological system in its own right, not a by-product of feeding.
books.summary:
John Bowlby was a British psychiatrist trained in psychoanalysis, and this is the first volume of his trilogy Attachment and Loss. He asks why infants cling to their caregivers and become distressed on separation. The prevailing view held that babies attach because they are fed. Bowlby argued that the bond is its own biological system, with survival value.

He draws on ethology, animal studies and observations of children separated from their parents. Crying, following and clinging are treated as an instinctive system that keeps the young close to protection. The theory has been refined since, and some critics note that it can underplay cultural variation. The book is dense and technical, but it set out ideas that shaped later work on childhood and love.
ideas: Attachment does not come from feeding. Bowlby rejects the idea that babies become attached merely because the caregiver feeds them, and argues that the bond serves protection and comes from its own system.
Crying, smiling, clinging and following keep the infant close to a caregiver. Bowlby treats these as attachment behaviour, which works especially when the infant is frightened or tired.
Attachment has an evolutionary basis. Bowlby drew on ethology, including studies of imprinting in animals, to argue that it should be studied as behaviour in its natural setting.
Attachment works like a control system. The child monitors the caregiver's nearness and acts to restore it when the distance grows too great.
A secure bond is what lets a child explore. Bowlby describes exploration and attachment as linked, with the child venturing out and then returning for comfort.
Separation brings protest, then despair, then detachment. Bowlby argues that this sequence shows how strong and how real the bond is.
The bond develops in phases over the first years. It moves from general responsiveness to people toward a preference for particular figures.
Infants usually attach most strongly to one main figure, which Bowlby calls monotropy. He does not mean that other attachments are absent, only that one usually stands first.

Attachment answers the dangers of the environment of evolutionary adaptedness. Bowlby introduces this term for the setting in which human behaviour took its shape, and the main danger there was being left alone and exposed.
Filmed observations of young children in hospital made the effects of separation hard to dismiss. Bowlby draws on James Robertson's films to show the stages of protest and despair.

books.thesis: Late lectures that sum up attachment theory for clinicians and parents.
books.summary:
These are lectures Bowlby gave late in his career, presenting attachment theory in a form meant for clinicians and parents. The question behind them is how early relationships shape later life, and how that knowledge can help in therapy and in raising children. The central image is a parent who acts as a secure base from which a child explores.

Bowlby describes patterns of attachment, links them to how parents behave, and argues that they tend to persist into adult relationships. He applies the ideas to family problems and to the work of therapists, who can offer a similar base to their patients. Critics say the evidence for long-term continuity is more mixed than the lectures suggest. The tone is plain, and the book is far easier to read than his first volumes.
ideas: A secure base is a figure the child can leave from and return to. Bowlby says a child who has one explores and learns more freely, because the way back is safe.
Bowlby argues that therapy works when the therapist becomes a secure base for the patient. From that footing, the patient can look at painful memories and feelings that once felt too risky.
Sensitive, responsive parenting is the main influence on later well-being that Bowlby names. Parents who read a child's signals and answer them tend to raise secure children.
Bowlby describes anxious and avoidant patterns of attachment, drawing on Mary Ainsworth's research. Each is a way of coping that a child learned from an unreliable caregiver.
Early experience builds internal working models of self and others, Bowlby suggests. These models set what a person expects from later relationships.
How a parent was treated as a child affects how they treat their own children. Bowlby uses this to explain how patterns of care repeat across generations.
Attachment needs do not end when childhood does. Bowlby holds that the wish for close bonds is normal at every age and is nothing adults need to outgrow.

Compulsive self-reliance and compulsive care-giving are the two disordered patterns Bowlby singles out. The first person insists on needing no one, and the second gives care to others as a way of getting it.
Bowlby holds that real events, such as threats of abandonment, explain later disturbance better than fantasy does. This was a deliberate break from psychoanalytic views that stressed inner fantasy.
School refusal often arises, as Bowlby reads it, from anxiety about leaving the parent or about what may happen at home. He points to the parent's own anxiety as a common factor.

books.thesis: Names limerence, the obsessive, uncertain state most people call being in love.
books.summary:
Psychologist Dorothy Tennov coined the term limerence for the state most people call being in love, in the sense of being obsessed with another person. She asks what it is like from the inside and how common it is. Her description is plain and unromantic. It centres on intrusive thinking about the person, a craving to be loved back, and a mix of hope and dread.

The book draws on interviews and questionnaires she collected, and she lets people speak in their own words. She distinguishes limerence from sexual attraction and from the calmer affection of a long relationship. Not everyone, she found, experiences it, which she saw as a real difference between people. Her methods were informal, but many readers recognise her portrait of longing.
ideas: Limerence is Tennov's name for the involuntary state of being in love with someone. It brings constant thoughts of the other person and a strong wish that they return the feeling.
Intrusive thinking is the central feature of limerence. The limerent person keeps returning to the other in thought, and the thoughts feel hard to stop.
Limerence needs uncertainty to survive. A little hope keeps it going, and Tennov says a love that is certain tends to feel different.
Joy and fear sit together in limerence. The person swings between elation at a sign of interest and misery at a sign of rejection.
Tennov borrows Stendhal's crystallisation to describe how the limerent person comes to see the other as nearly flawless. Small gestures then read as meaningful.
Limerence is separate from sexual desire and from affection. A person can feel one without the others, and the three can pull in different directions.
Some people report never having experienced limerence, and Tennov counts this as a real difference between people. She does not read it as a failure to love.
Tennov calls the target of limerence the limerent object. The limerent person watches that object closely for signs and treats each small gesture as significant.
Tennov gives limerence a typical duration of about eighteen months to three years. It can end when reciprocation turns into another kind of bond, through fading, or through lasting loss.
Limerence has bodily signs, including trembling, weakness, an aching in the chest and shyness near the other person. Tennov counts these as part of the state itself and not as side effects.

books.thesis: Love is a skill and an activity. You do not simply fall into it.
books.summary:
Erich Fromm, a psychoanalyst and social thinker, argues that most people treat love as a matter of being lovable and finding the right object. He asks why we do so little to learn the skill of loving. Love, he says, is an activity that takes discipline, concentration, patience and practice, like any art.

He starts from the human need to overcome the anxiety of separateness, then describes different kinds of love: parent for child, brotherly love, erotic love, self-love and love of God. He also criticises modern capitalist society for turning people into things to be exchanged. Some readers find his picture of mature love idealistic, and some find it dated in places. The book is short and still widely read.
ideas: Fromm says love is an art that demands knowledge and effort. Most people treat it as luck, a matter of finding the right person, and so they never learn it.
Fromm roots love in the need to overcome separateness. Being cut off from others is the deepest human anxiety, and love is the mature answer to it.
Mature love has four elements: care, responsibility, respect and knowledge. Fromm argues that without all four, what we feel is something less.
Fromm separates mature love from symbiotic union, where two people merge and lose their independence. In mature love each person stays whole while being close.
Self-love is not selfishness, in Fromm's account. He argues that respect for a person includes oneself, so someone unable to love themselves cannot love others.
Fromm criticises a market-oriented society in which people see themselves and each other as goods to be exchanged. Love is hard to practise in that setting.
Brotherly, motherly and erotic love are different forms, yet Fromm says they share the same basic elements.

Love is an orientation of character and not a relation to a single object, Fromm says. A person who loves one other and stays indifferent to the world has, in his view, a symbiotic attachment and not love.
Practising love, like any art, needs discipline, concentration and patience. Fromm thinks these qualities are rare in a culture that prizes speed and comfort.
Fromm treats the love of God as following a person's development. He sees religion moving from a mother-centred to a father-centred picture and then to a more mature one.

books.thesis: Intimacy and desire need different conditions, and a long relationship has to hold both.
books.summary:
Esther Perel, a Belgian-born couples therapist, asks why desire so often fades in long relationships even when love is strong. Her observation is that the qualities that make a home safe, such as closeness, predictability and care, can work against erotic excitement, which seems to need distance and mystery.

She draws on her practice and on conversations with couples. Instead of offering a technique, she argues that security and adventure are both human needs and that a couple has to hold both. Desire, she says, often needs a space of one's own, a touch of the unknown and room for imagination. Her points can be hard to generalise, and her examples come from a limited range of clients.
ideas: Intimacy and desire work on different principles, Perel argues. Love seeks closeness and certainty, while desire thrives on distance, novelty and the sense of something not yet possessed.
People need both security and adventure. A relationship that offers only one feels stifling or unstable, so a couple has to live with the tension between them.
Too much care can dampen desire. When one partner becomes the caretaker, the erotic charge can slip, because it is hard to want someone you are responsible for.
Desire often needs a gap between two people. Perel says that seeing your partner as an independent person can bring it back.
Erotic life depends on fantasy and imagination. Perel argues that people need permission to have an inner erotic life, even when it is not shared with a partner.
Couples often treat sex as a gauge of the relationship's health. Perel argues that this pressure makes desire harder.
Eroticism plays with risk and uncertainty, in Perel's view. Committed couples may have to make room for these on purpose.
Erotic intelligence is Perel's term for the ability to bring imagination, play and attention to desire. She treats it as a skill couples can develop and not as a gift some people lack.
Total transparency is not always good for a couple, Perel says. Mystery and privacy keep some distance between partners, and that distance can feed desire.
Egalitarian marriage, with its stress on fairness and negotiation, can flatten erotic tension. Perel argues that power, difference and play do something for desire that equality alone does not.

books.thesis: Infidelity is often less about the partner than about a longing for another version of yourself.
books.summary:
Esther Perel follows her earlier book with an examination of infidelity. She asks why people stray even when they are not unhappy at home, and what the betrayal does to those involved. Her observation from years of practice is that an affair is often less about the partner than about a part of the self the person feels they have lost.

The book draws on case stories and interviews, with details changed. She defines an affair by three elements: secrecy, an emotional connection and a sexual element. She also considers how today's expectation that one person will be everything has raised the stakes. Perel is interested in what couples can build afterward, which sometimes means ending and sometimes a stronger partnership. Some readers think she is too forgiving, and others find her account balanced.
ideas: Perel defines an affair by three elements: secrecy, emotional connection and sexual alchemy. She says all three must be present for it to count.
Many people who cheat say they are not leaving their partner. Perel's reading is that they are looking for a version of themselves they miss, and the other person is its mirror.
Modern couples expect one partner to supply security, passion and friendship at once. Perel argues this expectation is historically new and sets intimate relationships up to fail.
For the betrayed partner, the deepest injury is often finding that their picture of the relationship was false. The lies can hurt as much as the sex.
Affairs can answer deadness as much as unhappiness. Perel notes that people sometimes look outside the marriage to feel alive, even when the marriage is stable.
Couples can recover from an affair, Perel says, and some use the crisis to rebuild. It does not always work, and she argues that either staying or leaving can be a reasonable choice.
Views of infidelity differ across cultures and eras. Perel notes that today's focus on honesty and romantic fulfilment shapes how we judge it.
Perel links the growing number of affairs among women to changes in women's independence and expectations. She does not treat these affairs as a mirror image of the male pattern.
Technology has changed how affairs begin and how they are found. Perel points to messaging and dating sites, which widened the room for secrecy and contact and also the means of exposure.
In recovery, Perel asks the partner who strayed to answer questions and acknowledge the hurt. In time the couple may build a shared account of what happened, which she treats as a step toward trust.

books.thesis: Couples fight in predictable attachment patterns, and repair by reaching for each other.
books.summary:
Sue Johnson, a clinical psychologist, developed Emotionally Focused Therapy for couples, and this book presents it to a general audience. She asks why couples get stuck in the same fights and how they get out. Her answer is that adult partners are attachment figures to each other, so a conflict is often a protest about whether the other person is there when needed.

She names the patterns of conflict demon dialogues, then guides readers through seven conversations meant to move a couple from distance to connection. The underlying idea is that vulnerable reaching, as opposed to blame, renews a bond. The approach does not fit every couple, and the research backing is stronger for some groups than others. The tone is clear and practical.
ideas: Adult partners are attachment figures to each other, Johnson says. Many arguments come from fear that the other person is not reliably available.
Johnson names three demon dialogues. In Find the Bad Guy both partners blame, in the Protest Polka one pursues and the other withdraws, and in Freeze and Flee both shut down.
Pursue and withdraw is one of the most common patterns. One partner protests to get a response, the other retreats to avoid conflict, and each makes the other worse.

Johnson reduces a couple's fights to three questions, summed up as A.R.E.: accessibility, responsiveness and engagement. Partners are asking whether you are there, whether you will respond, and whether they matter to you.
Anger and criticism sit on top of softer feelings such as fear and hurt. The therapy aims to help people say those feelings directly.
A past injury, such as a betrayal or a moment of abandonment, can leave a lasting wound. The book offers a conversation for forgiving injuries that helps partners repair it.
The seven conversations are meant to be done together. They are designed to move a couple from distance toward emotional closeness.
Effective dependency is the ability to turn to a partner and be turned to in return. Johnson argues that this kind of dependence supports independence and does not weaken it.
Emotionally Focused Therapy, which Johnson developed, is presented as built on evidence and not only on clinical impression. She cites research reporting that most couples who complete it improve.
Touch and sex are expressions of the attachment bond. Johnson describes how sex can serve a search for closeness or an escape from it, and says emotional safety shapes lovemaking.

books.thesis: A popular guide to adult attachment styles and the ways they collide.
books.summary:
Psychiatrist Amir Levine and psychologist Rachel Heller wrote this popular book to apply attachment research to adult dating and partnership. They ask why some people feel at ease in close relationships while others feel anxious or crowded, and why certain pairs repeatedly hurt each other. The answer is attachment style, a pattern in how people handle closeness.

The authors describe three styles, anxious, avoidant and secure, and give signs to help readers identify their own and their partner's. They argue that anxious and avoidant partners often fall into a painful cycle. Their advice is to understand your own style, and to seek a secure partner or become more secure. The styles are simplified into categories, and people are more flexible than the book may suggest. It is easy to read.
ideas: Levine and Heller sort adults into three attachment styles: anxious, avoidant and secure. Each style describes how a person responds to closeness and to the risk of losing someone.
Anxious people crave closeness and worry about rejection. They tend to read small signals as signs that a partner is pulling away.
Avoidant people value independence and feel uneasy when a partner gets close. They often keep some distance and may pull back as intimacy grows.
Secure people are comfortable with both closeness and independence. The authors say they communicate directly and respond well to a partner's needs.
The anxious-avoidant trap is a pairing where the anxious partner's need for reassurance triggers the avoidant partner's withdrawal, which in turn heightens the anxiety.
Two habits feed the trap. Anxious people use protest behaviours to get a partner's attention, and avoidant people use deactivating strategies to keep feelings at bay.
The authors suggest attachment style can shift. A relationship with a secure partner may help, and so can learning to state needs clearly.
The authors estimate that around half of adults are secure, with the rest divided mainly between anxious and avoidant. A small remainder fits a fourth pattern.
The fourth pattern, anxious-avoidant, combines a wish for closeness with a fear of it. People with this style may swing between pursuing and pulling away.
The authors recommend effective communication: saying what you need plainly, without blame and without games. They say it is the quickest way to find out whether a partner can respond.

books.thesis: A love affair taken apart with philosophy, from idealisation through to disillusion.
books.summary:
Alain de Botton's first book is a novel built as an essay. A narrator meets a woman named Chloe on a flight from Paris to London, and the story follows the relationship from first attraction to its end. At each turn he stops to think about what is happening, with the help of philosophers. Underneath is a puzzle: why a love that feels so special can seem so ordinary once examined.

The book pairs small scenes with short bursts of reflection. It looks at idealisation, the fear of seeming needy, what we want from being known by someone, and how love can slide into doubt. Critics have found its tone arch and its characters thin, while others enjoy the wit. It offers no advice, but it treats ordinary courtship as worth close attention.
ideas: Falling in love makes ordinary events charged. The narrator meets Chloe on a flight, and the early days are told with close attention to small details.
Idealising the other is part of falling in love, and de Botton treats it as both pleasing and risky. We attach hopes to a person we hardly know.
The narrator wonders how he can love someone he has just met. The book asks whether he loves Chloe or a picture he has made of her.
Wanting to be loved is a strain, and de Botton shows it in detail. The narrator reads any sign of interest or coolness at length, and he knows how silly this seems.
Early love feels like fate, as if the two people were made for each other. De Botton looks at how this belief is both thrilling and a poor guide.
De Botton sets real philosophers beside small romantic moments. Abstract thought is tested against a private event and in turn lights it up.
Disillusion arrives as the relationship matures. The book treats it as an expected result of seeing the other person more clearly and not simply as a failure.
The romantic fallacy is de Botton's name for the belief that beauty means goodness. The narrator assumes Chloe must be wise and kind because she is lovely, and finds this hard to hold.
The book is a novel with a philosophical commentary running through short chapters. De Botton uses the story to illustrate ideas and not merely to tell it.
After the relationship ends, the narrator tries to explain why. De Botton shows that the explanation is built after the event, and that the real causes were small and mixed.

books.thesis: After falling in love comes the long, unromantic work of staying.
books.summary:
De Botton's later novel picks up where love stories usually stop. It follows a couple, Rabih and Kirsten, from their first meeting through marriage, children and the strains of ordinary life. The question is what happens after the romance, and what it takes to stay with someone. His answer is that love, in the long run, is a skill and a series of small acts.

Short essays interrupt the narrative to comment on the couple's troubles, and they set out his view that Romanticism has given people unrealistic ideas about love. He argues that frustration and disappointment are normal, and that compatibility is something couples build over time. The tone is wry and gentle. Critics say the characters mostly serve to illustrate his ideas, but many readers find the situations familiar.
ideas: The long middle of a relationship is the real subject of love, de Botton says. The book follows Rabih and Kirsten through marriage, children and dull routine.
Romanticism taught us to expect effortless love, de Botton argues. When difficulty appears we assume something is wrong, when it is a normal part of any partnership.
Compatibility emerges from working through differences. De Botton presents it as an achievement of the couple and not a quality they have at the start.
The couple's quarrels often start from small matters. De Botton shows how a trivial complaint can stand in for a larger sense of being unappreciated.
Each partner carries a damaged side from childhood, and the book suggests these sides collide in a marriage.
The pull of an affair or of another person is treated as a response to ordinary frustration. The book also stresses the cost of acting on it.
Love is learned, de Botton suggests. Understanding and forgiving a partner is a skill that has to be practised.
Sulking is a recurring problem in the book. One partner expects the other to guess what is wrong, and the failure to say so openly leaves both feeling misunderstood.
The Romantic view assumes a true partner will understand us without explanation, de Botton says. He traces this wish to the way a parent first met a baby's needs without being told.
Short essay passages interrupt the narrative to comment on the couple. This lets de Botton step back and name a pattern while Rabih and Kirsten are still living it.

books.thesis: Love is a practice of care, respect and responsibility, not a feeling we passively receive.
books.summary:
Everyone talks about love, hooks says, and almost nobody practises it well. The word gets stretched to cover neglect, control and even abuse, and that muddle keeps people from loving well. Her book sets out to say what love is.

Her answer is that love is an action. She borrows M. Scott Peck's definition, the will to nurture one's own or another's growth, and holds that love and abuse cannot exist together. Honesty and commitment are its base. She then follows the idea into community, spirituality and the way patriarchy teaches men to suppress feeling and women to give care without receiving it. The tone is personal and direct, and she draws on her own experience. Some readers want more evidence than she gives.
ideas: Hooks argues that love is a verb. It is something we do through care, commitment, respect, trust and honesty and not a feeling that arrives on its own.
Hooks takes from M. Scott Peck the definition of love as the will to nurture growth. She says this makes love a matter of choice.
Love and abuse cannot exist together, hooks says. If a person is harming or controlling us, it is not love, however much feeling is involved.
Honesty is the base of love. hooks argues that lying and secrecy, even in the name of kindness, wear away trust.
Our culture is confused about love, hooks says. It treats love as a commodity or a source of excitement, so people lack a clear model.
Patriarchy harms love by teaching boys to suppress feeling and girls to give care without receiving it. hooks says change is needed from both sexes.
Hooks links love to community and justice. She argues that a society built on domination cannot teach people to love.
A love ethic means love guides how we live with others and not only in private. hooks draws on Martin Luther King Jr and his idea of the beloved community.
Many people learn in childhood to confuse love with control or punishment. A parent who hurts a child in the name of love teaches that care and harm can go together.
Hooks says love has a spiritual side and that seeking it can be a way to approach the divine. She sees spiritual practice as a help in staying with love when it is hard.

books.a: Thomas Lewis, Fari Amini and Richard Lannon
books.thesis: Our nervous systems regulate each other, which makes love partly a physiological bond.
books.summary:
Three psychiatrists, Thomas Lewis, Fari Amini and Richard Lannon, take on two puzzles: why relationships shape us so and why therapy works. They say Western culture has the picture wrong. It treats emotion as the junior partner of reason and the person as a self-sufficient unit.

Their claim is that the human nervous system is open. Close relationships help set heart rate, mood and stress, which they call limbic regulation, and early care leaves lasting patterns that later relationships can revise. Therapy works mainly through the relationship itself, they argue, and not through insight. They lean on the triune brain model, which many neuroscientists now call too simple, and some claims outrun the evidence. The central point about connection holds up better than the anatomy.
ideas: The human nervous system is open, the authors argue, so relationships help regulate heart rate, mood and stress. A person alone is a different thing from a person with others.
Limbic resonance is the authors' term for two mammals attuning to each other's emotional states. They suggest it is the basis of empathy and closeness.
Limbic regulation is how a close relationship steadies the body. A calm companion can help calm us, and an upset one can unsettle us.
Limbic revision is the idea that relationships can change emotional patterns laid down early in life. The authors use it to explain what happens in psychotherapy.
The authors rely on the triune brain model, with its reptilian, limbic and cortical layers. Many neuroscientists now think this model is too crude.
Early care leaves a lasting pattern in the infant's brain. The authors cite studies of infants deprived of contact to show how much love affects development.
Western culture overvalues reason and neglects emotional life, the authors say. Its habit of treating the self as independent hides how much we rely on others.
Implicit memory is early emotional learning that works without words. The authors use it to explain why old patterns of feeling persist even when a person knows better.
The main work of psychotherapy is the relationship itself and not the insights offered, they argue. A therapist who can attune to the patient helps change the patient's emotional patterns.
Self-sufficiency runs against our biology, the authors say. People are built to be regulated by others, and a culture that prizes the lone individual works against this.

books.t: The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work
books.thesis: Couples last on friendship and small daily gestures, and four habits predict breakup.
books.summary:
Some marriages last and some fall apart, and from outside the difference is hard to see. John Gottman spent decades watching couples talk in a research lab, then followed them for years to see who stayed together. With Nan Silver, he asks what the stable couples do differently and whether it can be taught.

The answer is less dramatic than most advice. Happy couples do not avoid conflict. They keep a friendship underneath it, know their partner's inner world, answer small bids for attention and repair a fight before it hardens. He names four patterns that predicted divorce, the Four Horsemen: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling. Critics note that the samples were limited and that prediction is not a cure.
ideas: The Four Horsemen are criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling, and couples who split tended to show them in arguments. Gottman found contempt the most damaging.
A love map is detailed knowledge of your partner's inner world, including worries, hopes and daily details. Couples who keep updating it cope better with stress and change.
Fondness and admiration work as an antidote to contempt. Couples who still hold a respectful story about each other weather conflict better than those who have rewritten the past.
Turning toward means answering the small bids a partner makes, like a remark about the news or a sigh. Gottman says these ordinary exchanges build trust.
Husbands who resist their wives' input are at more risk of splitting, Gottman says. He treats willingness to share power as a sign of a stable marriage.
A harsh startup predicts a bad ending. Gottman advises raising a complaint gently and describing the issue without blame, because conversations usually end the way their first minutes begin.
Many conflicts never get solved because they come from lasting differences in personality. Gottman suggests discussing them with humor and curiosity and looking for the dream beneath each position.
Repair attempts are efforts to calm an argument as it unfolds, such as a joke, an apology or a touch. Gottman finds that stable couples make them and that their partners accept them.
Flooding is being overwhelmed by physiological arousal in a fight, with a racing heart and a loss of clear thought. Gottman advises a break of at least twenty minutes to calm down before continuing.
The last principle is creating shared meaning through rituals, roles, goals and symbols the couple holds in common. Gottman says couples with a shared sense of purpose withstand conflict better.

books.thesis: We meet the world in two ways, as things to use or as presences to encounter.
books.summary:
Martin Buber starts from how we stand toward the world. Sometimes we treat a person or a tree as a thing with features, something to use, measure or understand. Other times we meet it whole, and something happens between us that neither side owns. He asks which stance makes a human life, and what is lost when the first crowds out the second.

He argues in a compressed, almost scriptural style. The two stances are I-It and I-Thou. I-It is necessary for ordinary life and no fault in itself. I-Thou takes the whole being, cannot be produced on demand, and cannot last, since every Thou settles back into an It. Buber finds the source of all such meeting in an eternal Thou, which he calls God. Readers disagree on how to take this, and on whether the book is philosophy, theology or poetry.
ideas: Buber says a person speaks two basic words, I-It and I-Thou. I-It describes experience and use, I-Thou describes meeting, and the I is different in each, so the self is not fixed.
I-It is necessary for ordinary life and is no fault in itself. In this mode the other is a bundle of qualities placed in space and time.
I-Thou happens with the whole being and cannot be done halfway. Buber describes it as mutual and immediate, with no goal or technique standing between the two.
No Thou can be held onto. Every I-Thou meeting fades and the other becomes an It again, which Buber treats as the sad but ordinary rhythm of life.
Buber places relation in three spheres: nature, other people and spiritual beings. A tree can be met as a Thou in a moment of real attention.
Grace and will both play a part in meeting. We cannot seek a Thou directly, yet we must be ready, so Buber's advice is openness with no scheme to get anything.
Every particular Thou points to the eternal Thou, which Buber links to God as the one who is never an It. He suggests prayer is a kind of address.
The between is where meeting happens, for Buber. The relation belongs to neither person alone but to the space that opens when both are present.
Love is not a feeling one has but something that happens between I and Thou, Buber says. Feelings are possessed, while love is the responsibility of one person for another.
Buber writes in aphorisms because he means the book to be undergone and not only studied. It comes in three parts and reads more like an address than an argument.

books.thesis: Romantic love runs on the brain's reward systems, which is why it can feel like addiction.
books.summary:
People fall for one person and not another, and it feels like something that happens to them. Helen Fisher, an anthropologist, takes this to the brain. She asks whether romantic love is an emotion, a drive or something nearer a craving, and what the answer means for heartbreak and for long relationships.

Her evidence is brain scans of people newly in love, cross-cultural surveys and animal work. She proposes three linked systems, lust, attraction and attachment, which can run partly apart. Her striking claim is that romantic attraction is a drive like hunger, tied to dopamine and reward circuits, and that rejection can make it stronger. The book is lively and sometimes speculative, and critics say brain activity maps onto love less cleanly than the title promises.
ideas: Fisher reports that scans of people intensely in love show activity in dopamine-rich reward areas, including one near the brainstem.
Fisher proposes three brain systems for mating: lust, romantic attraction and attachment. They can run apart, which might explain deep attachment to one person alongside lust for another.
Romantic love is a drive and not simply an emotion, Fisher argues. Like hunger or thirst, it has a goal, can be focused on one person and can last.
Lovers show intrusive thinking, craving, mood swings and a focus on one person. Fisher notes that these resemble features of addiction and links them to reward chemistry.
Romantic love appears in nearly every culture Fisher surveyed, in songs, poems and stories. She reads that spread as evidence that it is a human universal and not a Western invention.
Rejection can make attraction stronger. Fisher says obstacles and abandonment push the reward system harder, which she offers as one reason people keep chasing someone who has left.
Attraction is built to last for a limited time, Fisher suggests, while attachment can carry a couple through child rearing and beyond.

Fisher's scans singled out the ventral tegmental area and the caudate nucleus, parts of the brain tied to reward and motivation. She reads these as signs of a motivation system and not of a feeling alone.
Lowered serotonin is Fisher's likely basis for the obsessive thinking of new love. She also raises concern that antidepressants that raise serotonin may dull romantic feelings.

Fisher discusses what shapes who we fall for, including timing, familiarity, mystery and early experience. She suggests we carry an unconscious pattern of what we find attractive, formed long before we meet anyone.

books.thesis: Growth starts by accepting that life is difficult, and love is the will to help another grow.
books.summary:
M. Scott Peck was a psychiatrist who noticed that his patients often wanted relief without change. His book opens with a plain sentence, life is difficult, and works out what follows if we accept that instead of resenting it. It mixes case stories, moral argument and some religion, written for ordinary readers.

Peck argues that growth takes discipline, which he breaks into delaying gratification, accepting responsibility, dedication to truth and balance. He defines love as the will to extend oneself for another person's spiritual growth, and separates it from falling in love, which he calls a temporary collapse of ego boundaries. Late in the book he turns to grace and religion. Critics find the tone moralizing and the case material thin as evidence.
ideas: Life is difficult, Peck says, and the pain starts to ease once we stop expecting it to be otherwise. Complaining about the difficulty makes it heavier.
Delaying gratification means facing the painful part of a task first so the rest can be enjoyed. Peck treats it as the base of every other discipline.
Accepting responsibility means admitting a problem is yours to solve. Peck contrasts neurotics, who take too much blame, with character disorders, who take too little.
Dedication to truth requires constant testing of your own map of reality. Peck argues we avoid this because revising the map hurts, and that avoidance is a root of mental illness.
Peck defines love as the will to extend oneself to nurture another person's growth. He says it is an act of will and not a feeling.
Falling in love is, in Peck's view, a temporary collapse of ego boundaries driven by instinct. It can start a relationship but it is not love in his sense.
Laziness is named as a form of original sin, the pull toward ease that fights growth. Peck sets against it grace, a force he says helps us grow without being earned.
Balancing is Peck's fourth tool of discipline. It includes the flexibility to give up one thing for another and bracketing, which means holding back a strong feeling long enough to act well.
Peck separates love from dependency. A dependent person wants to be taken care of and calls it love, while real love looks to the growth of the other.

Peck's claims about grace and evil rest on religious belief and go beyond what clinical evidence can support. Some readers object to this mixing of psychiatry with faith, and the case stories alone cannot carry them.

books.thesis: Great novelists saw that desire is borrowed from a mediator, and the hero's romantic lie is that it is his own.
ideas: Desire is triangular, Girard claims. We want an object because a model wants it, so the model stays in the picture and the thing wanted is secondary.
Don Quixote picks knight-errantry by imitating the legendary Amadis. Girard uses him as the clearest early case of a hero whose wishes are borrowed from a mediator.
External mediation means the model is far away and cannot be a rival. A fictional hero or a distant king can be imitated with little conflict and little shame.
Internal mediation means the model is close enough to compete. As model and imitator draw nearer, desire turns into rivalry, obsession and resentment.
The romantic lie is the belief that our wants are our own. Girard says modern heroes cling to it, and the novelistic truth is its exposure.
Snobbery, vanity and jealousy are forms of imitation rivalry. Girard reads Proust's social climbers and Stendhal's proud men as people who want what others seem to want.
Many great novels end with the hero recognising the lie, a conversion that comes late. In Dostoevsky, this sometimes costs the hero everything.

Metaphysical desire is Girard's name for the later stage of triangular desire. The object matters less and less while the mediator becomes the real aim, and the desiring person wishes to be like the model.
Emma Bovary and Stendhal's vain men show imitation in different settings. Emma takes her wants from romances she has read, while Stendhal's men act for the eyes of a rival.
Dostoevsky's Underground Man is Girard's extreme case of internal mediation. He is drawn to the people who humiliate him, and his hatred and admiration are mixed together.
books.surprise: Girard argues the novels themselves record their authors' conversion: they only see mimetic desire after renouncing their own.
books.crit: The theory explains everything it touches, which makes it hard to falsify.
books.summary:
