ideas: Enlightenment aims to dispel myth but becomes a new myth of domination, the authors claim. The effort to control nature slides into control of people.
Instrumental reason treats thought as the calculation of means. The world, including other people, becomes material to be measured and used.
Odysseus bound to the mast, with his rowers' ears stopped with wax, shows an early form of the self. It survives by self-control and cunning, at the price of renunciation.
The culture industry delivers film, radio and magazines in standardized form. Amusement becomes an extension of work and prepares people for more of the same.
Mass culture offers pseudo-individuality. Small variations on a pattern feel like choice and keep the pattern in place.
They treat antisemitism as a product of mass society, not only an inherited prejudice. In their account it is an outlet for frustration and rage at difference.
Written in fragments, the book offers no clear route of escape. Critics such as Habermas say its critique of reason is too total to allow any.
In an excursus on Sade and Kant, the authors argue that formal reason cut off from substantive ends can serve any purpose, including cruelty.

They distinguish false projection from reflective thought. In false projection the persecutor places inner hostility onto a victim, while reflective thought returns the world to the self, and antisemitism is their example of the first.
Two German Jewish exiles in California wrote the book during the Second World War. It first circulated in 1944 as Philosophical Fragments and was published in 1947.

books.t: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life
books.thesis: Everyday encounters work like theatre: we perform roles and manage the impressions others form.
books.summary:
Erving Goffman asks how everyday encounters work, and answers in the language of theatre. People present a version of themselves, and others read it and respond. He wants to know what keeps interaction running smoothly, and how we manage the impressions we give off, whether we mean to or not.

Drawing on observation, including fieldwork in a hotel on a Shetland island, he introduces front, front stage, backstage, team and the definition of the situation. Interaction depends on shared agreement about what is going on, slips cause embarrassment, and audiences often cooperate to save the performer's face. He does not say that everything is fake. By the end he suggests the self is partly an effect of performance, not something hidden behind it. Critics find the picture cynical, and Goffman treats the theatre comparison as scaffolding to drop once it has done its work.
ideas: People manage impressions, using words, clothes, manner and setting to shape how they appear. They also give off impressions they do not intend.
The front is the expressive equipment a person uses to define the situation for the audience. It includes setting, appearance and manner.
Front stage is where a performance is given to an audience. Backstage is where performers relax and drop the act, such as a restaurant kitchen out of customers' sight.
Performances are often team efforts. Members cover for one another, share secrets and protect the impression the team is trying to give.
Performers tend to present idealized versions of themselves that fit the values of their society. They hide behaviour that does not fit.
Audiences help sustain a performance through tact. They ignore slips and play along, because exposing the performer would embarrass everyone.
Goffman ends by suggesting that the self is an effect of a successful performance, not a hidden thing beneath it.
Discrepant roles hold secrets that threaten the team's performance. Goffman lists the informer who pretends to be a team member, the shill, the spotter and the go-between.
Performers can be sincere, believing in their own act, or cynical, using it to manage the audience. Goffman notes that people can move between the two.
Goffman's examples draw on fieldwork in a Shetland Isle community, including a hotel. He adds writing on service workers and other settings.

books.thesis: Stigma is a relationship of expectations, not a trait, and people manage a spoiled identity within it.
books.summary:
Erving Goffman looks at people who carry a trait that leads others to disqualify them from full acceptance, leaving what he calls a spoiled identity. He asks how people with visible or hidden marks handle ordinary encounters, and how those without such marks respond.

He draws on memoirs, case histories and published accounts of people with disabilities, disfigurement, mental illness, criminal records and minority status. He separates the discredited, whose difference shows, from the discreditable, whose difference can be hidden, and describes covering, passing and careful control of information. The wise are sympathetic outsiders, and the own share the stigma. His central point is that stigma sits in a relationship of expectations, not in the trait itself, and that anyone can be on either side at some time. The book is short and observational, and describes more than it prescribes.
ideas: Stigma is a language of relationships, not of attributes, Goffman insists. It is a trait that is discrediting in a particular social setting.
Goffman names three kinds of stigma: abominations of the body, blemishes of individual character, and tribal stigma of race, nation or religion.
The discredited person's difference is known or visible. The discreditable person's difference is hidden, so they must decide whether and when to reveal it.
Passing means hiding a stigma to be taken as normal. Covering means playing it down so that it intrudes less in interaction.
Information control is a constant task for the discreditable. They manage who knows what and weigh the costs of disclosure against concealment.
The wise are people who are not stigmatized but understand the situation and are accepted by those who are. The own are others who share the stigma.
Normal and stigmatized are roles within interactions, not kinds of people. Goffman notes that everyone has some trait that could be judged this way.
Stigma opens where virtual and actual social identity do not match. Virtual social identity is the character we assume of a person, and actual social identity is the attributes they have.
Courtesy stigma is the discredit that spreads to people close to the stigmatized. Family members, for example, share some of the difficulty.
Stigma symbols draw attention to a flaw. Disidentifiers, such as a style of dress, are used to suggest a person is something other than what the stigma implies.

books.thesis: Total institutions strip people of their identities and then remake them.
books.summary:
In the mid-1950s Erving Goffman spent about a year at a large public mental hospital in Washington, observing patients as an assistant to the recreation staff. He asks what life inside a total institution does to a person. Such a place holds many people, cut off from wider society, in an enclosed and formally administered life.

His examples include prisons, barracks, monasteries and asylums. He describes the mortification of the self at admission, when belongings, names and routines are taken away, and the privilege system of small rewards. He also describes the underlife, the secondary adjustments through which inmates keep some selfhood. Much of what looks like symptom, he argues, is a response to institutional treatment. Critics note that it rests on one hospital and one observer, and may underrate the reality of illness.
ideas: A total institution is a place of residence and work where many people, cut off from the wider society, lead an enclosed, formally administered round of life. Prisons, barracks and asylums all fit.
Mortification of the self happens at admission. Possessions and clothes are taken, the person is given a number, and old roles are stripped away.
A wide gap separates staff and inmates. Each side holds stereotypes of the other, and information and decisions flow one way.
A privilege system of small rewards and punishments, such as access to a ward or a yard, shapes behaviour. It makes obedience pay.
Underlife and secondary adjustments are the unofficial ways inmates get around rules and keep a sense of self. Examples are hidden items and private rituals.
The moral career of the mental patient runs through stages from becoming a patient to life inside. Each stage reshapes how the person sees themselves.
Goffman suggests that a lot of what is read as symptom is shaped by the institution. The patient's reaction to confinement plays a part too.
Goffman did the fieldwork over a year in the mid 1950s at St Elizabeths Hospital in Washington. He worked there as an assistant to the athletic director.

He sorts total institutions into five kinds. They hold people thought incapable and harmless, people incapable and a threat, people dangerous to the community, work-based settings, and retreats such as monasteries.
Inmates adapt in several named ways: situational withdrawal, the intransigent line, colonization, conversion, and playing it cool.

books.thesis: Taste in food, art and music is not a private gift. It marks social class and helps reproduce it.
books.summary:
Pierre Bourdieu asks whether taste is a private, natural gift or something tied to social position. Using surveys carried out in France in the 1960s, he maps preferences in music, art, food, clothing, sport and furnishing across occupation and education, and asks what they reveal about class.

He introduces cultural capital, habitus and field. The upper classes, he argues, hold the advantage in what counts as legitimate taste, learned early at home and in school and then felt as natural. A working-class taste of necessity favors the practical and filling, while bourgeois taste values form, restraint and distance from need. Taste therefore classifies the person who displays it and helps pass advantage on. Critics say the data are tied to one country and period and the theory is too deterministic, and later work on cultural omnivores complicates the picture.
ideas: Taste classifies the classifier. Choices of music, food or decor mark where a person stands and reveal social position to others who read the signs.
Habitus is the set of durable dispositions people absorb from family and class. It guides perception and choice without conscious thought.
Cultural capital is knowledge, ease and credentials in legitimate culture. Families pass it on, and schools tend to reward it as if it were natural talent.
Bourdieu maps social space by the volume of capital a person has and by the balance between economic and cultural capital. That balance shapes lifestyle.
The taste of necessity favours the practical and filling. The taste of luxury favours form over function, because those freed from need can put style first.
Kant's pure aesthetic, a disinterested contemplation of art, is itself a product of privilege, Bourdieu argues. It depends on distance from necessity.
The data come from France in the 1960s, which limits how far the findings travel. Later work on cultural omnivores finds people of high status enjoying a wider mix.
Taste is first of all distaste, Bourdieu says, meaning the disgust provoked by other people's tastes. Class boundaries are drawn partly by what each group rejects.
The petite bourgeoisie shows cultural goodwill, a striving and anxious effort to acquire legitimate culture. The dominant class displays ease, as if its taste came naturally.
Symbolic violence is the way dominated groups accept the legitimacy of the dominant taste and judge themselves by it. Inequality then works through misrecognition rather than open force.

books.t: The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
books.thesis: Calvinist anxiety over salvation helped build the modern compulsion to work and save.
books.summary:
Max Weber asks why modern capitalism, with its discipline, steady work and habit of earning money as an end in itself, first took hold in parts of northern Europe with a strong Protestant presence. Greed and trade existed everywhere. What struck him as unusual was the sense of duty attached to earning.

His argument is that Calvinist ideas, especially predestination, produced anxiety about whether one was saved. Success in a worldly calling became a sign of grace, and an ascetic ethic of hard work and restrained spending led to saving and reinvestment. In time religion faded and left an economic order that people must serve, the iron cage. Weber treats religion as one factor and does not claim to replace economic explanations. Historians dispute his evidence and the link between Protestantism and capitalist growth, and the debate has not settled.
ideas: The spirit of capitalism treats earning more as a duty and a goal in itself. Weber uses Benjamin Franklin's maxims on thrift and industry as an example.
The idea of a calling comes from Luther's view that worldly work is a task assigned by God. It gives ordinary labour moral weight.
Calvinist predestination held that God had already decided who is saved. Believers could not know their fate, and that produced intense anxiety.
Worldly asceticism combined hard, methodical work with restrained spending, so profit was reinvested and not enjoyed. Weber saw this as a driver of capitalism.
Several Protestant movements shared an ascetic outlook in daily life, Weber argues. He looks at Pietism, Methodism and the Baptist sects as well as Calvinism.
The iron cage is a rationalized economic order that outlives the religious motives that built it. People keep working because the system requires it.
Weber insists that he is not replacing a materialist account with a spiritual one. Historians continue to dispute the evidence and the strength of the link.
Protestantism disenchanted the world, in Weber's account, by stripping away magic and sacraments as means of salvation. That left the believer to prove himself through conduct.
Traditionalism is what the capitalist spirit had to overcome. Weber's example is workers who earned less when piece rates went up, because they only wanted to earn what they were used to.
Weber ends with the remark that the modern order produces specialists without spirit and sensualists without heart. He offers it as a warning about where rationalization leads.

books.thesis: Suicide rates follow social bonds, rising with too little or too much integration and regulation.
books.summary:
Suicide seems the most private of acts. Émile Durkheim asks whether it has social causes. He compares rates across countries, religions, marital statuses and periods, and finds that they are stable within a society and vary in regular ways. The question is what social facts could explain such patterns.

He proposes four types: egoistic suicide, from too little integration into groups; altruistic, from too much; anomic, from too little regulation of desires; and fatalistic, from oppressive regulation, which he treats briefly. He finds higher rates among Protestants than Catholics and links anomic suicide to sudden economic change. The book also helped establish sociology as a discipline with its own subject matter. Critics point to unreliable official statistics, the risk of reading individual causes from group data, and his treatment of religion.
ideas: Suicide rates are steady within a society and differ between groups. Durkheim takes this as a sign of social forces that psychology alone cannot explain.
Egoistic suicide comes from weak integration. People without strong ties to family, religion or community lack something to anchor them.
Altruistic suicide comes from excessive integration. Individuals are so bound to a group that they give up their lives for it, as in some military settings.
Anomic suicide arises when the regulation of desires breaks down. Durkheim links it to sudden economic booms and crashes that unsettle people's expectations.
Fatalistic suicide, which Durkheim treats only in a footnote, comes from excessive regulation. His examples are people whose future is blocked and whose lives are tightly controlled.
Protestants showed higher suicide rates than Catholics in the data Durkheim used. He attributed this to Protestantism's weaker communal integration.
Official statistics of the time were unreliable, and group-level patterns do not prove individual causes, as critics note. The book nonetheless established sociological method.
Suicide is a social fact, Durkheim holds, to be explained by other social facts. He rules out individual explanations such as mental illness, race, climate and imitation as accounts of the rates.
Marriage and family life protect against suicide, Durkheim finds. Married men and parents have lower rates, while divorce is linked with higher rates, especially among men.
Rates of suicide fall during wars and national crises. Durkheim explains this by the way shared events strengthen social integration.

books.thesis: Even among the comfortable, lower social rank goes with worse health and earlier death.
books.summary:
Michael Marmot, an epidemiologist, asks why people lower on the social ladder get sicker and die sooner, even in wealthy countries with health care and stable jobs. He starts from the Whitehall studies of British civil servants, where death rates rose steadily as one moved down the grades of employment.

The pattern is a gradient, not a divide between poor and prosperous: each step down goes with worse health. Standard risk factors such as smoking and diet explain only part of it. A key idea is control. Low autonomy at work and in life, and limited social participation, seem to matter, probably through chronic stress. Marmot argues for policy that reduces inequality and invests in early childhood and working conditions. Critics raise questions about causation and confounding, and the policy translation is debated.
ideas: In the Whitehall studies, civil servants in lower employment grades had higher mortality than those in higher grades. All of them had steady jobs and access to health care.
The pattern is a gradient, with health worsening at each step down the ladder. It appears even among people far from poverty, so it is not only about material deprivation.
Standard risk factors such as smoking, blood pressure and diet explain only part of the gradient. This pushed Marmot to look at social and psychological causes.
Low control at work, meaning high demands with little say, was linked to higher risk of heart disease in the Whitehall research.
Autonomy and social participation are central to health, Marmot stresses. That means having a say in one's life and being involved with others.
Early childhood matters. Conditions in the first years of life shape health and opportunities later on, and Marmot says early investment pays.
Reducing inequality is a health policy, Marmot argues. Critics ask how far the findings show cause and how well they translate into policy.
Marmot considers whether illness lowers status instead of the other way round. He argues that the evidence points mainly to social position affecting health.
Chronic stress is his proposed pathway. Stress hormones and effects on the heart and immune system link a low sense of control to disease.
Marmot discusses the sharp rise in mortality among men in Russia and Eastern Europe in the 1990s. He offers it as an example of how social upheaval and loss of control can affect health.

books.thesis: Much of human life is a set of status games, and we rarely admit we are playing them.
books.summary:
Storr treats status as a basic human need and asks how the hunger for it shapes our sense of who we are, what we believe and how we judge others. Families, workplaces, online communities and ideologies each run their own game, with its own rules, players and prizes, and people move between them without noticing.

He names three kinds: dominance games won by force or fear, virtue games won by showing moral worth, and success games won by skill. The brain, he argues, edits our lives into a story with ourselves as hero, and group beliefs often work as badges of belonging more than claims about the world. Playing is unavoidable, so he advises noticing which game you are in and preferring games that benefit others too. Critics say explaining so much through status risks being unfalsifiable.
ideas: Status is a basic human need. We are sensitive to how others rank us, and loss of standing hurts, so people go to great lengths to avoid it.
Storr names three kinds of game. Dominance games are won by force or intimidation, virtue games by displaying moral worth, and success games by skill and achievement.
Each game has its own rules, players and prizes, and people move between them without noticing. Knowing which game is on explains behaviour that otherwise looks irrational.
The brain is a storyteller that edits our life into a narrative with ourselves as hero. This helps us hold a stable self and defend our status.
Group beliefs often work as badges of belonging. Holding the right view signals loyalty and earns standing, a pattern Storr sees in cults and in political movements.
Social media turns status into a visible scoreboard of likes and followers. This intensifies the games and rewards displays of virtue and outrage.
Storr advises noticing which game you are playing and choosing games that benefit others as well. Opting out entirely is not possible.
Status is not wealth. It is the respect and influence that others grant, felt as a matter of how one is seen, which is why losing it can hurt more than losing money.
In virtue games, rank is lifted by condemning those who break the group's moral code. Public displays of outrage and shaming therefore bring rewards.
The hunger for status is an old social adaptation shared with other primates, Storr argues. It shapes both our worst behaviour and many of our most admired achievements.

books.thesis: Worry about our standing hurts even the comfortable, and philosophy and art can ease it.
books.summary:
De Botton asks why worry about our standing hurts so much, even when we are comfortable. He defines status anxiety as the fear that we are failing to meet society's ideals of success and may lose dignity and respect as a result. The first part looks for causes: lovelessness, the demand for esteem, rising expectations, snobbery and the belief that success is earned by merit.

The second part offers remedies drawn from philosophy, art, politics, Christianity and bohemia. He writes as an essayist, with humour and examples from painters and philosophers, and does not promise a cure. The response is closer to consolation, ways of seeing that loosen the grip of other people's opinions. Critics say the remedies are gentle and personal and say little about structural inequality.
ideas: Status anxiety can hurt even people who are comfortable, because it is a fear of failing society's ideals of success. De Botton defines it as the worry that we will lose the dignity and respect of others.
Part of the hunger for status is a hunger for love. De Botton argues that we seek rank partly to win the attention and affection we feel we lack, because respect brings a kind of love.
A neighbour's success stings more than a king's. Envy is strongest toward people near us, because we compare ourselves with those we see as similar.
Meritocracy makes low rank hurt more. If position is believed to reflect worth, a low place feels like a verdict on the person and not a stroke of bad luck.
Philosophy helps by asking whose opinions deserve our concern. Socrates and the Stoics suggest we should weigh the judgment of others against truth instead of simply fearing it.
Art can widen our sense of what counts as worthy. Tragedy and realist painting treat ordinary and suffering people with dignity.
Bohemia answers status anxiety by rejecting the dominant measures of success and building communities with their own values. De Botton notes that this remedy comes with its own risks.
Snobbery makes a person's value seem to hang on a job title. In de Botton's account it is the habit of judging worth by rank or occupation.
Rising expectations feed the anxiety. As modern societies tell people they are equal and can rise, people set their hopes higher and feel greater disappointment when they do not.
Christianity is another remedy de Botton discusses. It taught the vanity of worldly rank and the humility of every person before God.

books.thesis: People gain power through empathy and generosity, then lose those qualities once they hold it.
books.summary:
Keltner asks how people gain power and why they lose it. Drawing on his research and others' on groups, he finds that power usually goes to those who improve the lives of others, through empathy, generosity and cooperation. Holding power then tends to wear those same qualities away, leaving people impulsive, self-focused and less able to read others.

He treats the Machiavellian picture of power as force and manipulation as a poor fit for influence in ordinary groups. Power is granted by others and kept by continuing to serve them. Its abuse, he suggests, often comes from the experience of power itself, which lowers empathy. The book draws on studies of teasing, touch and laughter and ends with practices such as gratitude and generosity. Some social priming studies in the wider field have struggled to replicate, so some experimental claims deserve care.
ideas: Power, for Keltner, is the capacity to make a difference in other people's lives. He stresses that it can be gained and kept through giving as well as through force.
In many groups, the people who rise are the enthusiastic, kind and attentive ones. They are not the most dominant or aggressive.
The power paradox is that the qualities that win power, such as empathy and generosity, tend to decline once a person holds it.
Holding power makes people more impulsive and self-focused. They also become less accurate at reading other people's emotions and less able to take their perspective.
Small gestures build trust, and Keltner uses studies of playful teasing, laughter and touch to show it. People with power sometimes lose these habits.
Keltner treats the Machiavellian view of power as a poor fit for everyday influence. Force and manipulation matter less, he argues, than the consent of others.
Practising gratitude, generosity and humility is Keltner's suggested way to hold onto empathy. Some priming studies behind similar claims have been hard to replicate, so this deserves care.
In the cookie experiment, power loosened manners. Three students worked together with one assigned to lead, and the leaders were more likely to take the extra cookie and eat messily.
Rank among primates, Keltner points out, often depends on building coalitions, sharing and making peace. Research he cites suggests that bullying alone does not secure it.
Power does most damage when it is unchecked. Keltner argues that accountability and reminders of one's own vulnerability help keep empathy alive.

books.thesis: Many workers privately think their jobs are pointless, and Graeber argues the harm of that is real.
books.summary:
A short essay by Graeber in 2013 brought a flood of letters from people saying their own jobs were pointless. The book asks why, in a society that praises work, so many workers feel their jobs accomplish nothing, and why such jobs persist. He defines a bullshit job as paid work so pointless that even the person doing it cannot justify it.

He sorts the testimonies into five types: flunkies, goons, duct tapers, box tickers and taskmasters. The harm, he argues, is psychological: shame, depression and a loss of any sense of making a difference. He explains the jobs through managerial hierarchy, politics and a moral belief that paid work is a virtue, not through market efficiency, and floats universal basic income as a way out. Critics note that the argument leans on self-reports of a subjective feeling, and some economists dispute the scale he claims.
ideas: A bullshit job is paid work so pointless that even the worker cannot justify it. In Graeber's definition, the worker feels they must pretend it has a purpose.

The testimonies Graeber collected sort bullshit jobs into five types. Flunkies make others look important, goons play an aggressive role, duct tapers patch problems, box tickers let an organisation seem to be doing something, and taskmasters supervise people who need no supervising.
Graeber's evidence starts with readers' own words. The idea began as a 2013 essay in an online magazine, which drew so many replies describing pointless work that he expanded it into a book.
The harm is psychological, and Graeber calls it a kind of spiritual violence. People paid to do nothing useful often feel ashamed, depressed or trapped.
Graeber sees an inverse link between social value and pay. Bullshit jobs are often well paid, while essential work such as care and teaching is low paid.
Market efficiency, Graeber doubts, can explain these jobs. He points instead to managerial feudalism, in which firms hire retainers to display rank.
Paid work is treated as a virtue, and Graeber says this moral belief sustains bullshit jobs. He proposes universal basic income as one way to loosen it.
Keynes predicted that technology would let people work fifteen hours a week by the end of the twentieth century. Graeber starts from that prediction and asks why it did not happen.
Bullshit jobs differ from shit jobs. The latter are useful but poorly paid and often degrading, while bullshit jobs are pointless but may be comfortable.
Graeber backs his thesis with survey data as well as testimony. A YouGov poll he cites found that about 37 percent of British workers thought their job made no meaningful contribution to the world.

books.thesis: Debt is older than money, and Graeber argues it has always been a moral idea as well as an economic one.
books.summary:
Graeber challenges the textbook story in which barter came first, then money, and only later credit. He says anthropologists have found no societies that ran on barter, and that credit and debt came before coins. The book asks what debt is and how an economic relation became a moral idea.

Over five thousand years, from Mesopotamia through the Axial Age and medieval religion to modern empires, he traces alternating eras of credit money and metal coin. He proposes three moral foundations of social life: everyday communism, exchange and hierarchy. Debt turns human relationships into impersonal exchange, and the rule that debts must always be paid is a moral claim often tied to violence. Historians and economists dispute many of his claims, and some chapters are speculative. What lasts is the suggestion that the moral language of debt hides its political uses.
ideas: Barter did not come first. Economics textbooks say money grew out of barter, but Graeber argues that anthropology has found no society that ran mainly on direct swaps.
Debt is older than coin. Temples in ancient Mesopotamia kept credit accounts on tablets long before coined money appeared.
Graeber finds three moral principles beneath social life: everyday communism, exchange and hierarchy. Each, he says, shapes how people understand obligation.
The rule that debts must always be paid is a moral claim, and Graeber argues it has often been used to justify violence and servitude.
Ancient Near Eastern rulers periodically cancelled debts. These jubilees kept indebtedness from tearing societies apart.
Coinage spread alongside armies and slavery, in Graeber's account. He ties precious metal to the paying of soldiers and the trade in captives.
Debt can slide into servitude when people pledge themselves or family members against a loan. Graeber argues this pattern recurs across history.
In human economies, money does not mainly buy and sell goods. Among groups such as the Tiv, Graeber describes it as a way to create and rearrange relations between people, such as marriages.
History alternates, Graeber proposes, between ages of virtual credit money and ages of bullion. Coin and metal dominate in periods of war and plunder.
Graeber relates the Axial Age, roughly 800 BCE to 600 CE, to coinage, war and the rise of the major world religions. He calls debt a promise corrupted by math and violence.

books.thesis: Early humans tried many social arrangements, so inequality was not the unavoidable price of progress.
books.summary:
Graeber and Wengrow challenge the standard story in which humans moved from small egalitarian bands to farming, cities and states, with inequality as the price of progress. They ask why we assume that large societies must have rulers and hierarchy.

Drawing on archaeology and anthropology, they argue that early societies experimented. Some groups changed their political arrangements with the seasons, some built large settlements without evident kings, and farming spread slowly and unevenly. They also argue that Indigenous critiques of European society shaped Enlightenment thought, and propose that people have lost three basic freedoms: to move away, to disobey and to reshape social relations. Specialists dispute parts of the evidence, and critics say the authors choose examples that suit them.
ideas: The standard story of human history, with Rousseau's lost innocence and Hobbes's brutal origins, is a one-way ladder. The authors argue the evidence does not fit it.
Some early societies changed their social structure with the seasons. Groups such as certain Indigenous peoples shifted between looser and more hierarchical arrangements through the year.
Scale does not require hierarchy, the authors argue. Large early settlements, such as sites in Ukraine and the city of Teotihuacan, show no clear signs of kings.
Farming arrived slowly and unevenly, not as a single revolution. Some groups tried it, left it, or mixed it with other ways of living.

Indigenous critics shaped European ideas about freedom, the authors argue. Thinkers such as Kandiaronk criticised European society, and these critiques helped form Enlightenment ideas about freedom and equality.
The authors propose three basic freedoms that societies have allowed or taken away. These are the freedom to move away, to disobey orders, and to reshape social relations.
Specialists dispute parts of the evidence and the authors' choice of cases. The book works better as a provocation than as a settled account.
Schismogenesis explains why neighbouring societies might deliberately choose different ways of life. It is the process by which they define themselves in opposition to each other.
Domination has three separate sources in the authors' account: control of violence, control of information and personal charisma. Societies can have one without the others.

Early cities need not have had rulers. The authors describe cities such as those in Mesopotamia and the Mesoamerican polity of Tlaxcala as governed by councils or assemblies, which challenges the idea that cities require rulers.

books.thesis: Humans came to rule the planet because enough of them could believe the same shared fictions.
books.summary:
Sapiens covers our species from the cognitive revolution tens of thousands of years ago to the present. Harari asks why one ape among several human species ended up running the planet. His answer starts with something odd about us. We can believe in things nobody has touched, such as nations, gods, corporations and money, and when enough people share a story, strangers can cooperate at huge scale.

The argument runs through three revolutions, the cognitive, the agricultural and the scientific, with empire and money tying them together. Harari keeps asking whether each step made individuals happier and often suggests it did not, calling farming a trap. The last chapters turn to biotechnology and the chance that sapiens will redesign itself. Specialists dispute some of his claims, and critics say the sweep forces simplification. The book leaves open what we should want to become.
ideas: Flexible language let sapiens do more than share facts about the world. Harari proposes that it allowed gossip about each other and descriptions of things that do not exist, which made cooperation in large groups possible.
Gods, nations, corporations and money exist because enough people believe in them. Harari calls these shared fictions, and they let millions of strangers act together.
Harari calls the agricultural revolution history's biggest fraud. Wheat tamed people as much as the reverse, and most farmers worked harder and ate worse than foragers.
Hierarchies such as caste and race are presented as natural, but Harari argues they are imagined orders. Shared belief, habit and force keep them going.
Money, Harari says, is the most universal system of mutual trust. It lets people who share no gods or customs still trade with each other.
The scientific revolution starts with admitting ignorance. Harari ties it closely to European empires and capital, which paid for exploration and research.
Harari doubts that history made people happier. Material gains do not clearly bring contentment, and the book ends on bioengineering that might replace sapiens itself.

The Cognitive Revolution, around 70,000 years ago, is when Harari says sapiens began to use language in new ways. He links their spread to the extinction of large animals in Australia and the Americas.
Comforts turn into necessities, which Harari calls the luxury trap. The ones farming brought became things people then worked harder to keep.
Harari names three great unifiers: money, empires and universal religions. Together they brought the world's peoples into larger shared systems.

books.thesis: Once algorithms know us better than we know ourselves, humanism's trust in human feelings is in doubt.
books.summary:
Harari begins from the claim that famine, plague and war, once treated as fate, have mostly become problems of management. He guesses humanity will go after immortality, lasting happiness and upgraded abilities, a bid for godlike powers. The deeper question is authority. Modern humanism treats human feelings as the final guide, and the book asks what happens to that trust once algorithms can read us better than we read ourselves.

He argues by sketching scenarios and says he offers possibilities, not prophecies. Drawing on biology and neuroscience, he doubts that free will works the way liberal thought assumes. He describes an emerging faith in data flow, which he calls Dataism, and worries about people who lose economic value to machines. The book gives no instructions. It ends on whether intelligence can separate from consciousness, and what we would still value if it did.
ideas: Famine, plague and war have become problems of management rather than fate, Harari says. The human agenda therefore shifts toward immortality, happiness and enhanced abilities.
Humanism replaced God as the source of authority. The voter, customer and viewer are supposed to know best, and personal feeling becomes the final guide.
Biology and neuroscience undermine the liberal idea of free will, Harari argues. They describe us as complex biochemical algorithms and not free agents.
Harari separates the experiencing self from the narrating self, drawing on research like Kahneman's. The storyteller, he notes, often makes our decisions.
Dataism is Harari's name for an emerging creed that treats the universe as data flows. It judges anything by its contribution to processing information.
Artificial intelligence could create a useless class of people who lack economic or military value. Harari treats this as a political danger.
If algorithms come to know us better than we know ourselves, we may hand over choices about careers, partners and votes. Harari frames this as a scenario, not a forecast.
Humanism comes in three forms, Harari says: liberal, socialist and evolutionary. They differ on whether the individual, the collective or the species is the source of meaning.
Harari describes the modern bargain as a covenant. Humans give up meaning in exchange for power, trusting science and growth to make up for the loss of a cosmic plan.
The industrial treatment of animals serves as a warning. Harari uses it to suggest how a more capable intelligence might treat humans who lose their economic value.

books.thesis: In a crowd, people lose personal responsibility and become suggestible, as one collective mind.
books.summary:
Published in 1895, The Crowd tries to explain what happens to people when they gather in large numbers. Le Bon watched strikes, revolutions and mass politics in France and asked why ordinary individuals act so differently together than alone. His answer is that a crowd forms a kind of collective mind, in which people lose personal responsibility and become suggestible, emotional and quick to follow.

He argues through assertion and example more than evidence. Anonymity, contagion and suggestion are his mechanisms, and he says crowds think in images and respond to leaders who repeat bold claims with confidence. He feared for civilization in what he called the age of crowds, and the book influenced later writers on propaganda. Critics call it dated, snobbish about the lower classes and short on proof, and later research has found crowds far more varied than he allowed.
ideas: A crowd, Le Bon claims, forms a collective mind. People together think and feel differently from how any one of them would alone.
Anonymity removes restraint. Numbers give the individual a feeling of invincible power, and the restraint that comes from being identifiable and accountable drops away.
Feelings and acts spread through a crowd by contagion. Le Bon says a person will give up personal interest for the collective one.
Le Bon compares the crowd member to a hypnotised subject. The conscious personality fades, and the person acts on impulse and suggestion.
Crowds think in images, not arguments. Vivid, exaggerated and simple statements move them far better than reasoning does.
Leaders sway crowds through affirmation, repetition and contagion. Le Bon adds prestige, a kind of authority that is felt and rarely examined.
Le Bon saw his age as the era of crowds and feared for civilization. Critics call this alarmist and class-biased, and note that later studies found crowds less uniform.

Crowds come in different kinds, Le Bon says. He sorts them into heterogeneous ones, such as street crowds and juries, and homogeneous ones, such as sects, castes and classes, with leaders and moods that suit each.
Crowds hold convictions in an absolute, almost religious way. Le Bon says this makes them intolerant, authoritarian and impatient of doubt.
The Crowd influenced later thinkers, and Freud engaged with it in Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego. Le Bon's ideas on race are now widely rejected.

books.thesis: Mass movements attract people who want to escape a self they find spoiled or unbearable.
books.summary:
Eric Hoffer was a self-taught longshoreman, and The True Believer is his attempt to explain what draws people into mass movements. He asks why such different causes, religious, nationalist or revolutionary, seem to gather the same sort of follower. His answer is that movements attract the frustrated, people who want to escape a self they find spoiled.

Hoffer writes in short, aphoristic chapters and relies on observation and history, not formal study. Joiners, he says, trade individual identity for the group, find pride in a holy cause, and are held together by hatred of a common enemy. Doctrine matters less than intensity of faith, so a fanatic can move from one movement to its opposite. He also sketches how movements pass from thinkers to fanatics to administrators. Critics say he generalizes too boldly on thin evidence.
ideas: Mass movements draw the frustrated, Hoffer holds. Their lives feel spoiled, and they want to be rid of a self they cannot bear.
Movements with opposite creeds attract similar temperaments. That explains why a convert can switch from one fanatical cause to another with little change in manner.
Self-renunciation is what a movement offers most. Joiners give up individual identity for the group and gain pride and purpose they could not find through their own efforts.
Hatred acts as glue. Hoffer says movements can do without a god but not without a devil, since a common enemy keeps followers united.
Doctrine works best when it cannot be tested. Hoffer says faith needs to be shielded from facts, so obscure and unprovable teaching serves a movement well.

Movements pass through a sequence of leaders. Hoffer describes men of words preparing the ground, fanatics carrying the movement forward, and practical administrators eventually taking over and consolidating it.
Action holds a movement together, Hoffer suggests, which is why followers are kept busy with marches, causes and campaigns. Critics say his sweeping claims outrun his evidence.
Hoffer wrote from observation, not from an academic post. He was a self-taught San Francisco longshoreman, and the book rests on his reading and experience.
Many kinds of people join movements, and Hoffer says they share one feeling. His list includes the poor, misfits, the bored, the ambitious, minorities and sinners, all frustrated with themselves.
Strong movements use many unifying agents at once. Hoffer names hatred, imitation, persuasion, coercion, leadership and action.

books.thesis: American civic and social ties have frayed since the 1960s, and Putnam argues this has real costs.
books.summary:
Bowling Alone starts with a small observation. More Americans bowl than before, but fewer bowl in leagues. Putnam uses it to ask whether Americans have drifted away from the clubs, congregations, unions and neighbourhood ties that once held communities together. Decades of survey data show civic and social participation falling from the 1960s onward.

His key term is social capital, the networks and norms of trust that help people cooperate. He puts much of the blame on generational change and television, with time pressure and suburban sprawl as further factors. He then links the decline to costs for schools, safety, health and democracy, and ends with a call for renewal. Critics ask whether he undercounts new kinds of association, including online ones, and how firmly the costs can be tied to the decline.
ideas: Putnam's central term, social capital, names the networks and norms of trust that let people cooperate for shared goals. A community can build it up or run it down.
More Americans bowl than before, yet fewer bowl in leagues. Putnam uses solo bowling as a small symbol of fading group life.
Putnam documents declines from the 1960s onward in membership of civic groups, PTAs, unions and congregations. He finds the same drop in informal habits such as hosting dinners or visiting friends.
Healthy communities need two kinds of social capital. Putnam separates bonding capital, within similar groups, from bridging capital, across differences.
Generational change and television carry most of the blame in Putnam's account. Busy schedules, commuting and suburban sprawl take smaller shares.
Putnam links higher social capital to better schools, safer neighbourhoods, better health and more responsive government. Critics say causation is hard to show.
The closing chapters call for civic renewal and look to the early twentieth century as a precedent. Critics ask whether the internet changes the picture.
A long civic generation, born roughly between 1910 and 1940, was unusually active in community life. Putnam says its gradual replacement by less engaged cohorts is a main cause of the decline.
The argument grew out of Putnam's earlier study of Italian regions, Making Democracy Work. That study found that regions with stronger civic traditions had better governments and economies.
Generalized reciprocity is the core of a trusting community, Putnam says. It means helping now without expecting an immediate return, because you trust that others will help you in time.

books.thesis: Modern life has become a spectacle, a social relation between people mediated by images.
books.summary:
The Society of the Spectacle is a short book of 221 numbered theses by Guy Debord, a leader of the Situationist movement. He asks what happens to social life when images and commodities stand between people. The spectacle, in his usage, is more than television or advertising. It is a social relation among people mediated by images, in which living gives way to watching.

Debord writes in dense aphorisms, borrowing from Hegel and Marx and extending Marx's commodity fetishism to all of modern life. Consumers become passive spectators, separated from each other even as the same images seem to unite them. The book offers no program in the usual sense, pointing instead to Situationist tactics such as turning existing images against themselves. Readers disagree on whether it is a precise theory or a mood, and its density is part of its reputation.
ideas: The spectacle is not a pile of images. Debord says it is a social relation between people, mediated by images.
What was once directly lived has turned into representation. Life gives way to watching, and watching comes to stand in for acting.
Debord extends Marx's commodity fetishism to all of social life. The commodity has taken over so fully that people mainly contemplate it.
The spectacle separates people while appearing to unite them. The more we contemplate the images offered to us, the less we live our own lives.
The spectacle speaks in a one-way monologue. What appears is declared good, and the only response demanded is passive acceptance.
Consumer society runs on a repeating, pseudo-cyclical time of work, weekends and holidays, Debord says. This rhythm hides the sense of history.
Detournement is the Situationist tactic of taking existing images and texts and turning them against their original message. The book itself reuses lines from earlier writers.
The book argues in fragments, not in steps. It is made up of 221 numbered theses in nine chapters, written in aphorisms in the style of Hegel and Marx.

Debord separates two kinds of spectacle. The concentrated spectacle belongs to totalitarian regimes with a single leader, and the diffuse spectacle of abundant commodities belongs to Western societies.
Workers' councils are Debord's alternative. In his chapter on the proletariat, he favours people controlling their own conditions of life instead of watching them.

books.thesis: Signs no longer point to reality. They replace it, leaving copies with no originals behind them.
books.summary:
Simulacra and Simulation is a set of essays in which Baudrillard asks what remains of the real when copies multiply and models come first. His claim is that modern life is increasingly lived in the hyperreal, a space made of representations with no original behind them. Signs and images no longer point to reality. They replace it.

Baudrillard works by provocation and example more than sustained proof. He lays out stages in the life of an image, from reflecting reality, to masking its absence, to bearing no relation to it at all. His illustrations are Disneyland, Watergate and Borges's fable of the map. The tone is gnomic, and the book is often quoted for its title idea and rarely read through. Critics say it offers a mood more than an argument, with little way to test its claims. Supporters say it names a real feature of media saturated life.
ideas: Baudrillard sketches four phases of the image. It first reflects reality, then distorts it, then hides that reality is absent, and finally becomes a pure simulacrum.
The map now comes before the territory. Baudrillard retells the fable of the map that covers the territory, then says models today generate the real.
Copies without originals can seem more real than reality. The hyperreal, in Baudrillard's term, is cleaner and more coherent than the real thing.
Disneyland is presented as imaginary so that the rest of America can look real. In Baudrillard's reading, that rest is just as simulated.
Baudrillard reads Watergate as a scandal whose exposure hid the fact that political life is already staged. It helped persuade people that moral order otherwise exists.
Simulating differs from pretending. Someone who feigns an illness can be found out, but one who produces its symptoms blurs the line between real and false.
The book's claims are hard to test, and critics call it more provocation than argument. Admirers say it names a genuine feature of media saturated life.
Anthropology needs a preserved primitive to prove its own reality, Baudrillard argues. He discusses the Tasaday, a group said to have been found untouched in the Philippines.
Real life and its televised version merge in the American television series about the Loud family, in Baudrillard's reading. The family becomes a model of itself.
The Beaubourg effect, named for the Pompidou Centre in Paris, is Baudrillard's image for a cultural institution that absorbs and neutralizes the masses it claims to serve.

books.thesis: We no longer need a master: we exploit ourselves in the name of freedom, and exhaustion follows.
books.summary:
The Burnout Society is a short essay by Byung-Chul Han on the sickness of an age that no longer needs to be told what to do. He asks why depression, attention disorders and burnout have become typical complaints, in place of the infections and repression of earlier eras. His answer is a shift from a society of commands and prohibitions to a society of achievement, whose slogan is that we can do anything.

In such a world the person becomes both exploiter and exploited. With no master to blame, failure turns inward as exhaustion and self reproach. He sets this against the older order described by Foucault. He holds that deep boredom and contemplation have been lost to constant stimulation and multitasking, and that some kinds of tiredness might be worth recovering. The essay is compressed and assertive rather than empirical, and some find it too sweeping.
ideas: The disciplinary society of prohibitions and commands has been replaced by an achievement society, Han says. Its driving belief is that we can do anything.
The achievement subject is both exploiter and exploited. With no outside master to resist, failure is felt as personal fault, and exhaustion follows.
The typical illnesses of our time are neural, Han argues. Depression, attention deficit and burnout replace infections, and he calls the cause a violence of positivity.
Too much openness leaves nothing to push back against. With so many stimuli, options and information, Han says, the immune model of defence against an outside enemy no longer fits.
Multitasking is a regression, in Han's view. It resembles the divided attention of an animal watching for threats, while deep attention is a cultural achievement we are losing.
Han defends deep boredom and idleness as conditions for contemplation and creativity. A culture that never pauses, he says, loses the ability to see.
Han contrasts an isolating, exhausting tiredness with a shared, inspiring one, an idea he borrows from Peter Handke. Whether this is a real remedy is left open.
Depression is tied to a self that must keep producing, Han argues. He draws on Alain Ehrenberg's idea of the weariness of the self and links it to optimizing oneself without end.
Han argues that modern life has made activity absolute. He engages Arendt's contrast between the vita activa and the vita contemplativa and says the contemplative side has been lost.

The disappearance of otherness leaves a society of sameness, Han says. Otherness is the negativity of what is foreign and resists us, and without it more of the same is the only thing that can happen.

books.thesis: Societies contain mimetic violence by uniting against one scapegoat, then honour it as sacred.
books.summary:
Violence and the Sacred asks why religion everywhere seems tied to sacrifice and ritual killing. Girard starts from desire. We learn what to want by copying others, so rivals end up wanting the same things and becoming alike. He asks how communities survive when that copying produces escalating conflict and endless vengeance.

His proposal is that societies resolve such crises by turning on a single victim. The group's tension is discharged on the scapegoat, and peace returns. The victim is then honoured as sacred, since the killing seemed to save everyone. Ritual sacrifice repeats the event in controlled form, and myths hide the original violence. Many anthropologists reject his evidence, and critics say the theory explains everything and so cannot be checked. Others find it unusually good at describing how groups pick targets.
ideas: Imitation, more than the worth of an object, drives desire, Girard says. We want what others want, and that pushes people into rivalry.
Rivals become doubles. As they copy each other, differences between them blur, and Girard says this sameness escalates conflict instead of calming it.
Left alone, violence can destroy a community. It is contagious and vengeance has no natural stopping point, so retaliation spirals.
The scapegoat mechanism ends the spiral by having the group turn unanimously on one victim. Tension drains away, and the victim is blamed first and then treated as sacred.
Ritual sacrifice repeats the founding act in controlled form. It uses a surrogate victim who cannot be avenged, so violence is spent and order renewed.
The sacred is violence in disguise, Girard says. The gods who terrify also protect, because the same mechanism produces both the threat and the peace.
Judicial systems replace sacrifice by giving vengeance to an institution. Girard's readings of tragedy and myth are contested, and critics call the theory hard to falsify.
Girard reads Oedipus the King as a story of a plague and a crisis in which differences collapse. Oedipus is cast out as the community's scapegoat.
The sacrificial crisis is Girard's term for the breakdown of ritual order. Differences are lost and sacrifice no longer works to contain violence.
Girard thinks earlier theories of myth and ritual missed violence. He faults Freud's Totem and Taboo, the Oedipus complex and Levi-Strauss's structuralism for overlooking mimetic rivalry.

books.thesis: Texts written by persecutors can be read so that the innocence of their victims shows through.
books.summary:
The Scapegoat extends Girard's earlier work by looking closely at texts written by persecutors. He asks how accounts of crimes, plagues and monstrous outsiders can be read so that the victim's innocence shows through. His model case is a medieval account of the Black Death in which Jews were blamed, a story told from the crowd's side.

Girard argues that persecution texts share recurring features, and that the persecutors usually believe what they write. Myths, he says, tell the story from the crowd's side, while the Gospels tell it from the victim's side and so expose the mechanism. He claims this exposure weakens the scapegoat effect in modern societies. That Christian reading is the most contested part. Many scholars doubt the Gospels are unique in this way, and critics say he flattens differences between texts. His method of reading accusations with suspicion has been widely borrowed.
ideas: A persecutor's text hides the innocence of its victims, and Girard shows how to read past it. His model case is a medieval account of the Black Death in which Jews are blamed.
Persecution stories share four recurring features. Girard lists a social crisis, accusations of crimes that dissolve distinctions, signs that mark the victim, and collective violence.
Persecutors usually sincerely believe the victim is guilty. Girard treats that conviction as part of the mechanism and not a lie told afterward.
Myths tell the story from the crowd's side, and the Gospels tell it from the victim's side. In Girard's reading, myths keep the victim guilty while the Gospels reveal innocence.
Peter's denial in the Passion story shows how a crowd pulls a person into joining against a victim. Girard reads it as an example of that pull.
Once victims' innocence is widely recognised, scapegoating works less well. Girard thinks this leaves modern societies with fewer ways to contain violence.
The claim that the Gospels are unique in siding with victims is contested. Critics note that other traditions also show sympathy for the persecuted.
Unanimity makes an accusation look self-evident. If everyone agrees, Girard argues, the victim must seem guilty.
Girard reads the saying about Satan casting out Satan as a description of the scapegoat mechanism. Disorder is driven out by turning on a single victim.
Persecutors do not see themselves as persecutors. Girard links this to the Gospel line that they know not what they do.

books.thesis: Under capitalism, workers are alienated from their product, their work, other people and their human nature.
books.summary:
The young Marx wrote these notebooks in Paris, and they were not published until the 1930s. He asks what happens to a person whose work belongs to someone else. His answer is alienation. Under capitalism the worker is cut off from what he makes, from the activity of making it, from other people, and from what Marx calls species-being, the human capacity for free, conscious production.

Marx argues by criticizing the political economists, who treat private property as a given, and by borrowing and reworking Hegel. He claims private property is the result of alienated labour, not its cause, and treats money as a force that inverts human qualities. The text is unfinished and fragmentary, and its passages on communism are sketchy. Scholars still argue about whether its humanist themes continue in his later work or were left behind.
ideas: The more the worker produces, the poorer he becomes, Marx says. His product confronts him as an alien power in the world of things he has made.
Work under capitalism is external to the worker and forced. People feel at home only outside work, so work becomes a loss of self instead of an expression of it.

Alienated labour strips people of what Marx calls species-being. This is the human capacity to produce freely and consciously and to shape nature, and alienated labour reduces it to a means of survival.
Alienation in work becomes alienation from other people. If the product and the activity belong to another person, that person controls the worker's life.
Private property is the result of alienated labour, Marx argues, reversing the political economists. He treats it as something to be explained instead of assumed.
Money inverts human qualities, Marx argues, citing Shakespeare's Timon and Goethe's Faust. It can buy what one is not, so it turns ugliness or cowardice into their opposites.
Scholars still debate whether the young Marx of these manuscripts stands apart from the later economist. The notebooks stayed unpublished until the 1930s.
Marx criticizes Hegel's Phenomenology in the final manuscript. He says Hegel understood labour as the self creating itself, but only as abstract mental labour.
Crude communism is universalized envy, Marx says. It wants to level everyone by turning private property into common property and has not yet understood what property means.
Under the wage system the worker is reduced to a commodity, Marx says. His fate depends on demand, and he sinks to the level of a thing that must be kept alive to work.

books.thesis: Among rich countries, wider income gaps go with worse social outcomes, though the statistics are disputed.
books.summary:
The Spirit Level begins with a puzzle. Among rich countries, average income tells us little about how a society does on health and social problems. Wilkinson and Pickett say the size of the gap between rich and poor does. They gather data on life expectancy, violence, imprisonment, mental illness, teenage births and trust, and compare countries and American states.

They argue that more unequal societies do worse on nearly all of these measures, and that the effect reaches beyond the poor to most of the population. Their proposed mechanism is status anxiety, the stress of being judged and ranked. The book was influential in policy debates and was also attacked. Critics say the countries were selected, that correlation is not cause, and that results weaken with other data. The authors have answered these points, and the dispute continues.
ideas: Average income tells us little about social outcomes among rich countries, while the gap between top and bottom tracks them closely.
The authors combine measures such as life expectancy, obesity, mental illness, violence and imprisonment into an index. They compare it with inequality across countries.
The same pattern is reported among US states. The authors offer this as a check that the result is not an accident of which countries were chosen.
Status anxiety is their proposed mechanism. Where differences are larger, people feel judged more, and chronic social stress harms health and behaviour.
The effects are said to reach beyond the poor. Even well-off people in unequal societies are reported to do worse on several measures than counterparts in equal ones.
Trust and community life are weaker in unequal societies. The authors link this to the social strain that wider gaps create.
Critics say the countries were selected, that correlation is not cause, and that results weaken with other data. The authors dispute these objections.
Equality can be reached by different routes. The book notes that Japan has small pre-tax income gaps and Sweden relies more on taxes and benefits, and both do well on the index.
More inequality goes with lower social mobility, the authors report. Where you start matters more, which they link to the idea of the American Dream.
Research on social evaluative threat supports the claim that inequality works through social stress. It shows that stress hormones rise when people feel judged or looked down on.

books.thesis: Prejudice is an inflexible generalization about a group, and contact can reduce it under the right conditions.
books.summary:
The Nature of Prejudice is Allport's classic attempt to understand how people come to dislike others for belonging to a group. He asks how prejudice forms in the individual, how society keeps it alive, and what can be done about it. He defines it as antipathy based on a faulty and inflexible generalization, one that holds even when the facts say otherwise.

Sorting people into categories is a normal habit of thought, Allport argues, and prejudice is an exaggerated, rigid form of it. He warns against any single explanation and describes a ladder of rejection from careless talk to violence. His most cited idea is that contact between groups can reduce prejudice when certain conditions hold. Later research has largely supported a version of this, though critics note the conditions are hard to meet in real life.
ideas: Allport defines prejudice as antipathy resting on a faulty and inflexible generalization. It may be felt or expressed, and is directed at a group or at an individual because of membership in it.
Prejudice is a rigid, exaggerated version of an ordinary habit. The mind works with categories, and Allport says this helps us cope with a complicated world.
Preferring the in-group does not require hating the out-group. Allport suggests loyalty to what we know usually comes first, and hostility is a further step.
Rejection has degrees. Allport describes a ladder from antilocution, which is hostile talk, through avoidance and discrimination to physical attack and extermination.
Contact between groups lessens prejudice only under conditions. The groups need equal status, shared goals and cooperation, and the support of authorities or custom.
Personality plays a part. Allport notes that people who need rigid certainties and clear categories are more likely to hold strong prejudices.
No single cause explains prejudice. Allport reviews historical, economic, social and psychological causes and warns against explaining it by any one of them.
Scapegoating is linked to frustration and displaced aggression. In Allport's discussion, hostility that cannot reach its true source is turned on a weaker group.
Persecuted groups react in ways that can be mistaken for their nature. In a chapter on traits due to victimization, Allport covers withdrawal, obsessive concern, in-group solidarity and clowning.
Prejudgment becomes prejudice only when it is not reversible on exposure to new knowledge. For Allport, the test is whether a person can change their mind.

books.thesis: Moral instincts serve the tribe, so settling disputes between tribes takes slower, deliberate thinking.
books.summary:
Moral Tribes asks why people who each think they are decent can still disagree, and sometimes fight. Greene argues that our moral instincts evolved to help us cooperate within groups, which solves the problem of Me versus Us. They do much less well on Us versus Them, where each tribe's intuitions feel obviously right to its own members.

Drawing on psychology and brain imaging, including trolley problem studies, Greene describes two modes of thought, one fast and automatic and one slow and deliberate. For disputes between tribes he proposes using the manual mode to find a common currency, and argues that utilitarian reasoning, which he calls deep pragmatism, can serve. Many philosophers object that he treats intuitions too lightly and that utilitarianism yields results most people will not accept. The book is a clear statement of a contested position.
ideas: Morality evolved to solve Me versus Us. Greene says it settled the tension between selfish and group interests by making people cooperative inside their own groups.
The tragedy of commonsense morality is that the instincts that make us cooperate within a tribe leave us unable to settle disputes between tribes.
Greene compares the mind to a camera. It has automatic settings for speed and a manual mode for flexibility, and moral thinking has both, which can disagree.
People accept switching a track in trolley cases but resist pushing a man off a footbridge. Greene links the difference to emotional responses seen in brain imaging.
Appeals to rights and moral intuition are often used as weapons, Greene says. They let each side feel righteous while rationalizing its own tribe's position.
Between tribes we need a common currency, and Greene proposes happiness, weighed impartially, as the shared standard. He calls this approach deep pragmatism.
Critics reply that Greene dismisses intuitions too quickly. They also say utilitarian reasoning can lead to conclusions most people reject.
Me versus Us is framed with the tragedy of the commons, the parable of herders sharing a pasture. Greene calls Us versus Them the problem that morality does not solve by itself.
Our feelings are strong for a child in front of us and weak for children far away. Greene uses Peter Singer's drowning child and related cases to press this gap.

Our automatic settings are reliable for familiar problems, such as dealing with kin and neighbours, Greene argues. They are unreliable for unfamiliar ones such as distant strangers or new technologies.

books.thesis: Humans are animals who know they will die, and much of character and culture defends against that knowledge.
ideas: The human predicament is a dual nature, in Becker's account. We have a symbolic self that can imagine forever and a body that decays, and living with that gap is hard.
Personality is a defence, in Becker's idea of character armour. It is a structure built early to avoid terror, narrowing a person so that life feels manageable.
Becker revises Freud by putting the fear of death at the root of repression. Ordinary normal life then looks like a kind of managed denial.
Heroism is an immortality project. We want to matter on a cosmic scale and to be more than an animal that will be forgotten.
Culture supplies the hero system. It offers scripts and rewards through which people can feel that their lives count beyond death.
Love hands the burden of meaning to another person. Through transference, a partner is asked to be the answer to everything, and Becker says no one can bear that.
Becker leaves the problem open. Because illusions seem unavoidable, he points toward faith in something larger than the self, and admits that is not a proof.
The creative person tries to fashion a lasting work from limits, Becker says. He draws on Otto Rank, who held that the neurotic refuses the loan of life to avoid the debt that comes with it.
Creatureliness is the horror of being an animal with a body that decays. Following Kierkegaard, Becker sees human beings as gods who excrete and die.
The Denial of Death had a long afterlife in experimental psychology. It won a Pulitzer Prize shortly after Becker's death in 1974, and it later became the basis for terror management theory.
books.surprise: Becker reads Freud through Kierkegaard. Neurosis isn't just repression; it's a refusal of the full truth of the human condition, and so is "normal" adjustment.
books.crit: Totalizing: almost everything becomes death denial. The experimental programme it inspired (TMT) has struggled with replication.
books.summary:
The Denial of Death argues that human beings are unusual animals. We know we will die, and we also have a self that imagines living forever. Becker asks how a mind can carry that gap and still get through a day. His answer is that much of what we call character, culture and ambition is built to keep the terror of death out of view.

Becker draws on Freud, Otto Rank and Kierkegaard, and revises Freud by putting the fear of death, not sex, at the root of repression. We protect ourselves through personality, heroic projects and love, he says, and none of these fully works. The book won wide readership and shaped later research in terror management. Critics find the sweep too large and the evidence mostly interpretive. It offers no cure, only a hope that a person might live with fewer illusions, perhaps through faith in something larger.

books.thesis: Much human evil comes from ordinary people trying to deny death and win immortality.
books.summary:
Escape from Evil follows The Denial of Death and asks where human evil comes from. Becker's thesis is that much of it grows out of ordinary people trying to deny death and win some kind of immortality. He asks why humans have been so willing to hurt and kill each other for causes that feel holy.

Every culture, he argues, is a hero system that offers ways to feel one's life counts. Rival systems threaten each other, because another culture's existence suggests ours may not be the real route to permanence. We then project our fear and guilt onto victims and try to destroy them. He draws on Otto Rank and Norman O. Brown. He gives little program for change, only the hope that seeing the motive might loosen its hold. Critics find the claims broad and speculative, and some doubt a single motive can explain so much.
ideas: Much human evil comes from ordinary people seeking to secure immortality, Becker argues. He disputes that it mainly flows from a simple instinct to aggress.
Each culture works as an immortality system. It gives its members heroic roles and a sense that their lives will count beyond death.
Rival hero systems threaten each other, so war can be a contest over whose version of heroism is real. Another culture's existence suggests that ours may be false.
Scapegoating lets people unload their guilt and mortality onto others. Destroying the victim feels like cleansing, so evil can be done in the name of good.
Money is a symbol of immortality, following Norman O. Brown. Accumulation becomes a way of denying that one will die.
Contempt keeps the creaturely at a distance. Becker follows others in saying that unease about our animal bodies gets projected onto groups seen as dirty or lowly.
Becker closes without a program. He suggests only that seeing the motive may loosen its hold, and he is unsure we can live without victims.
Becker finished the book as he was dying of cancer. It appeared posthumously in 1975 as a kind of sequel to The Denial of Death.
Guilt for being alive demands payment, Becker argues, following Rank. People try to pay with a sacrifice, so other people become the price of their own immortality.
Modern ideologies take over the religious job of offering immortality, Becker holds. Nationalism and revolutionary politics can therefore become holy wars.

books.thesis: The drive to find meaning is primary in human life, and meaning can be found even in unchangeable suffering.
ideas: Frankl treats prisoners' reactions as psychological patterns that came in stages. He describes shock on arrival, then apathy, then a bitter disillusion after liberation.
The last human freedom is choosing your attitude. Circumstances can be taken from a person, and Frankl says the choice of one's response remains.
Frankl claims meaning is a more basic motive than pleasure or power. He sets the will to meaning against Freud's will to pleasure and Adler's will to power.
Meaning can be found in three places: work or deeds, love, and the stance taken toward unavoidable suffering. Frankl says avoidable suffering should be avoided.
Happiness cannot be pursued directly. Frankl says it ensues, as a side effect of living for something beyond oneself.
The existential vacuum is Frankl's name for a sense of emptiness that shows up as boredom. He calls it a mark of modern life.
Prisoners with a task or a person to live for seemed to endure better. Frankl ties this to Nietzsche's remark about having a why to live.
Logotherapy's techniques aim to break fixation. The second part of the book sets out paradoxical intention and dereflection, which help people stop fixing on a symptom or on themselves.

Frankl closes with tragic optimism, the capacity to say yes to life despite pain, guilt and death. It works by turning suffering into achievement, guilt into change and transience into responsible action.
Freedom must be balanced by responsibility, Frankl argues. He suggests the Statue of Liberty on the East Coast be supplemented by a Statue of Responsibility on the West Coast.
books.surprise: Frankl is unsentimental about fellow prisoners. He writes that the best did not return, and that survival often depended on luck and ruthlessness.
books.crit: It can be read as implying that meaning helped people survive, when survival was overwhelmingly a matter of chance.
books.summary:
Man's Search for Meaning has two parts: Frankl's account of surviving Nazi camps, and an outline of logotherapy, the approach to psychology he developed. He asks what keeps people going when almost everything has been taken. His answer is that the drive to find meaning is primary in human life, and that a person can find it even in suffering that cannot be changed.

Frankl writes in a plain, observational voice and offers his own experience and that of fellow prisoners as evidence. He set the will to meaning against Freud's pleasure and Adler's power, and says meaning can come through work, love, or the stance we take toward unavoidable suffering. Critics point out that it rests on one man's observations, not a systematic study, and some worry it can make suffering sound useful. Frankl is careful to say suffering has meaning only when it cannot be avoided.

books.thesis: The absurd is the clash between our longing for meaning and a silent world, and Camus answers it with revolt.
ideas: Whether life is worth living is the one serious philosophical problem, Camus says. Everything else comes after it.
