The absurd lives in the meeting of two things. It arises from the confrontation between human longing for meaning and a silent universe, and in neither alone.
Camus calls a leap to a meaning that is not there philosophical suicide. He accuses thinkers such as Kierkegaard, Jaspers and Husserl of making it.
Revolt, freedom and passion are the three consequences Camus draws from the absurd. He means by them living without appeal to anything beyond this life.
Each absurd hero lives fully inside limits. The seducer, the actor, the conqueror and the artist do so without hoping for something beyond them.
Quantity of experience matters more than quality for the absurd person, Camus says. Without a higher measure, the aim is to live as much as possible.
The book ends by asking us to imagine Sisyphus happy. Camus says the struggle itself is enough to fill a heart.
Camus reads Kafka as a play between the absurd and a hope. In the appendix he argues that Kafka's work holds both, and treats the hope as a leap.
Kirilov in Dostoevsky's The Possessed is Camus's case of logical suicide. He kills himself to prove his freedom, and Camus disagrees with the conclusion.
Suicide would end the absurd by removing one of its two sides. So the absurd person, Camus argues, rejects it and keeps the confrontation alive.
books.surprise: Camus's main targets aren't nihilists. They're the existentialists, whom he accuses of escaping into hope.
books.crit: Some philosophers find the argument more lyrical than rigorous; Sartre thought Camus avoided politics.
books.summary:
The Myth of Sisyphus opens with a blunt claim. Whether life is worth living is, Camus says, the one serious philosophical question. He asks what to do when human longing for meaning meets a world that gives no answer. That collision is the absurd, and it lives in the meeting of the two, not in either alone.

Camus sees two cheap exits. One is suicide. The other is what he calls philosophical suicide, a leap into faith or a system that promises meaning the world does not supply. He rejects both and proposes revolt, which means living with the absurd and refusing to look away. He sketches absurd figures such as the seducer, the actor, the conqueror and the artist, and closes on Sisyphus pushing his rock, whom we are told to imagine happy. Critics ask whether revolt is a real answer or only a mood, and some say Camus misreads the thinkers he criticizes.

books.thesis: Revolt affirms a value shared by everyone, and it destroys itself when it justifies murder.
books.summary:
The Rebel takes up where The Myth of Sisyphus left off. Camus asks whether anything rules out murder in an absurd world, what revolt means, and whether it can be kept from sliding into killing in the name of revolution. He starts with the rebel who says no, and argues that the no also carries a yes to some value the rebel believes belongs to everyone.

He traces the history of revolt through metaphysical rebellion, against creation itself, and historical rebellion, against rulers, taking in Sade, Ivan Karamazov, Nietzsche, Marx and the terror of the French and Russian revolutions. His claim is that revolt loses itself when it justifies murder for a future end. He argues instead for limits and a Mediterranean sense of measure. The book led to a public break with Sartre and the Left, and critics still disagree on whether his alternative is practical or only a moral stance.
ideas: Revolt is more than refusal. The rebel says no, but in saying it also affirms a value he takes to be shared by everyone.
Camus turns Descartes into a formula of solidarity: I rebel, therefore we exist. Revolt takes for granted a common human dignity.
Metaphysical rebellion is revolt against the human condition and creation itself. Camus follows it through Sade, the Romantics, Ivan Karamazov and Nietzsche.
Historical revolutions betray the revolt that began them, Camus argues, when they justify killing for a future end. He points to the French Terror and Soviet Russia.
Revolt implies a limit. Because it starts from an affirmation of human worth, it cannot consistently justify unlimited murder.
Camus appeals to a Mediterranean idea of measure. He sets it against ideologies that treat history as an absolute to which people can be sacrificed.
The book led to a public break with Sartre and his circle. The dispute over whether Camus weakened the left continues.
Revolt and ressentiment differ, Camus says. Revolt gives and affirms a value, while ressentiment is the bitter product of long powerlessness and only poisons.

Camus praises the Russian terrorists of 1905, such as Kaliayev, who accepted that killing is a crime and paid for it with their own lives. He sets them against later revolutionaries who treated murder as routine.
Art is also a form of revolt, Camus argues. The artist says no to the world as given and rebuilds it with a unity and style that reality lacks.

books.thesis: Consciousness is a kind of nothingness and therefore free, and bad faith is how we deny that freedom.
books.summary:
Being and Nothingness is Sartre's large attempt to describe what it is to be conscious. He asks how a being that can question, imagine and deny relates to the solid world of things. His answer is that consciousness is a kind of nothingness, always lacking and never fixed, and that this makes it free. No human nature settles in advance what a person must do.

Sartre argues through detailed scenes, such as a waiter acting out his role and the shame of being watched through a keyhole. Freedom brings anguish, and bad faith names the ways we deny it, by pretending to be mere things or to have no choice. Other people appear as a threat to our freedom, and love is a doomed attempt to possess another consciousness. The book is long and difficult, and critics question whether his picture of relations is too bleak.
ideas: Sartre separates two kinds of being. Being-in-itself is solid and complete like a stone, and being-for-itself is consciousness, defined by what it lacks.
Consciousness brings nothingness into the world. We can see an absence, such as a friend who is not in the cafe where we expected to find him.
Anguish is the awareness of our own freedom with nothing to lean on. Sartre compares it to vertigo on a narrow path, where the fear is of our own possible act.
Bad faith is lying to oneself about one's freedom. His example is a waiter who plays at being a waiter as if it were his fixed nature.
We are always both facticity, the given facts of our situation, and transcendence, our projection beyond them. Bad faith tries to live as only one.
Another person's gaze turns me into an object. Sartre calls this the Look and uses the shame of being caught peeping through a keyhole to show it.
Relations with others tend toward conflict, Sartre says. He treats love as a project to possess another's freedom, which cannot succeed, and critics find this account too bleak.
Human beings want to be both in-itself and for-itself, solid like a thing yet conscious. Sartre calls this the project of being God, concludes it is impossible and calls man a useless passion.

Bad faith can be a refusal to decide what something means. In Sartre's example of a woman on a first date, she leaves her hand in her companion's hand and treats it as neither giving nor withdrawing it.
Sartre replaces Freud's unconscious drives with existential psychoanalysis. It looks for a person's fundamental project, the original choice of self behind particular desires.

books.thesis: Existence precedes essence, so we have no fixed nature and answer for what we make of ourselves.
books.summary:
Existentialism Is a Humanism began as a public lecture in Paris in 1945 and was published the next year. Sartre was answering critics, Catholics who saw despair in his work and Communists who saw self-absorbed idleness. He states in plain terms that existence comes before essence. A human being has no fixed nature, and we become what we do and choose.

A paper knife is made for a purpose, he says, but people have no maker whose purpose defines them. From this he draws abandonment, anguish and despair as the mood of a world without ready made values. In choosing for ourselves we also say how people ought to be, so we answer to everyone. A student torn between his mother and the Resistance shows the point: no rule can decide for him. Sartre later distanced himself from the lecture's simplifications, but it remains the most readable door into his thought.
ideas: Existence comes before essence. With a paper knife, the maker's idea comes first, but people have no maker, so we define ourselves through what we do.
Each choice carries responsibility for all humanity, Sartre says. In choosing for myself I also choose an image of what a person ought to be.
Anguish is the awareness of that responsibility. Sartre likens it to a military leader who knows his decisions will cost others their lives.
Abandonment means there is no God to supply values and nothing written in the sky. We are left with our choices and their consequences.
Despair, for Sartre, means acting without counting on hopes beyond our control. We rely only on what lies within our power to do.
No moral theory settles a real dilemma. Sartre's student must choose between caring for his mother and joining the Free French, and has to invent his own answer.
Existentialism is a humanism because humans are always still in the making. Sartre does not mean humanity is to be worshipped, and he later expressed regret about the lecture.
The lecture answers two kinds of critic. Communists said existentialism was quietist and gloomy, and Christians said it was subjective and left no firm ground for morals.

A universal human condition survives without a fixed human nature. Sartre denies the latter, since there is no God to have conceived one, but allows the limits of being in the world that every person must face.
A person is nothing other than the sum of his actions, Sartre says. The coward makes himself a coward by what he does and could have chosen otherwise, so temperament or circumstance gives no excuse.

books.thesis: We are both free and situated, and willing our own freedom means willing the freedom of others.
books.summary:
The Ethics of Ambiguity was Beauvoir's first book of moral philosophy, written just after the war. She asks how to act when human life is irreducibly ambiguous. We are free subjects who make meaning, and also objects in the world with bodies, limits and a death. Ethics, she argues, should begin there, not try to escape one side of ourselves.

Beauvoir builds on Sartre but disagrees with him in places. Her central claim is that freedom wills itself and, in doing so, must also will the freedom of others. She describes failed ways of facing freedom through character types: the serious man, the sub-man, the nihilist and the adventurer. She treats oppression as a real limit on what some people can choose. Critics debate whether her answer on violence against oppressors is settled or left uneasy. She seems content to leave it uneasy.
ideas: Ethics must start from ambiguity, Beauvoir says. We are both free subjects and objects in the world, and that tension is the human condition.
To will oneself free is also to will others free. Freedom must will itself, and my freedom needs other people's to have any meaning.
The serious man gives up his freedom by treating values as given from outside and absolute. He takes them to be things to obey.
Beauvoir sketches several failed ways of facing freedom. The sub-man, the nihilist, the adventurer and the passionate man each avoid part of the human situation.
Some adults retreat into the world of childhood to avoid choice. Children live among ready made values and are not asked to justify them.
Freedom is real but situated. People kept in conditions where choosing is hard cannot simply be told that they are free anyway.
Violence against oppressors may sometimes be unavoidable, Beauvoir grants. She treats it as a tragic cost and not as a clean solution.
Freedom cannot be sacrificed for any value that depends on it, Beauvoir holds, since it is the source from which all values spring. This is her ground for refusing to let ends justify any means.
Systems that dissolve the individual into History or the universal fail, Beauvoir argues. Each person's separate existence and death is a fact that cannot be argued away.
Philosophers have tended to deny ambiguity, the book opens by noting. Beauvoir says the attempt to escape it, by calling man pure spirit or pure thing, produces much of the evil in the world.

books.thesis: Woman has been defined as man's Other, and one is not born a woman but becomes one.
books.summary:
The Second Sex is Beauvoir's long study of what it has meant to be a woman. She asks why women have been treated as secondary, and how a person comes to live as one. Her starting point is that man is taken as the human norm and woman as his Other, defined in relation to him. The famous line says that one is not born a woman but becomes one.

The first part examines biology, psychoanalysis and historical materialism and finds that none fully explains women's position, then reads the myths of the Eternal Feminine in literature. The second follows women's lived experience through childhood, puberty, marriage, motherhood and old age. Beauvoir argues that economic independence is needed for liberation, though not enough alone. Some claims are criticized as dated or drawn from a narrow class of women, but the book set the terms for much later feminist thought.
ideas: One is made a woman by upbringing and social pressure, not simply born one. Beauvoir's best known line points to gender as learned over a lifetime.
Man is treated as the subject and the norm, while woman is the Other. She is described in relation to him and rarely allowed to define herself.
No single explanation accounts for women's subordination. Beauvoir tests biology, psychoanalysis and historical materialism in turn, and finds that each helps but none is enough on its own.
Male writers fix woman in an image. Beauvoir reads myths of the Eternal Feminine in which she is cast as mystery, nature or muse.
Girls are taught to see themselves as objects for others to look at. Beauvoir traces how puberty and menstruation can sharpen this self-consciousness.
Marriage and domestic life tie women to repetitive work, Beauvoir criticizes. They trap women in immanence while men pursue projects.
Economic independence is needed for liberation, Beauvoir argues, though it is not enough alone. The hope is relations between people who see each other as equals.

Women lack a shared history or solidarity of their own, Beauvoir says, because they are dispersed among men. They live with them in homes and classes, which is why their case differs from that of other oppressed groups.

Love as self-abandonment is the subject of the chapter on the woman in love. She makes herself an object for a man's sake, and Beauvoir hopes instead for a love of two free people who recognise each other as equals.

Male writers use woman as a mirror for the male hero, Beauvoir says, and she names Montherlant, D. H. Lawrence and Breton. The first English translation by Parshley was abridged, which long limited how the book was read in English.

books.thesis: Heidegger asks what it means to be, and describes us as thrown into a world, lost in the They, facing death.
books.summary:
Being and Time asks a question Heidegger thinks philosophy has forgotten: what does it mean to be? He starts with the one being that can ask it, which he calls Dasein, roughly the human way of existing. Rather than treating us as minds looking at objects, he describes us as always already in a world, involved with tools and other people, and living in time.

Heidegger works by close description of ordinary life. We are thrown into circumstances we did not choose, and mostly live as the They do, following what one does. Anxiety and awareness of our own death can pull us out of that and open the chance of authenticity. The book is famously hard, its vocabulary is new, and it was never finished, since the planned second half did not appear. Heidegger's later involvement with the Nazi party has also complicated how readers receive it.
ideas: Heidegger says philosophy has forgotten the question of what it means to be. He starts with the one being that can ask it, which he calls Dasein, roughly the human way of existing.
Tools show that we are in the world before we ever look at it. A hammer is ready to hand while we use it, and only shows up as an object when it breaks.
Thrownness means we begin in a time, place, family and language we did not choose. We have to live from there.
The They, the anonymous everyone, supplies the habits, opinions and tastes we follow in daily life. Doing what one does spares us the burden of deciding.
Anxiety differs from fear because it has no object. It reveals the world as without support, and that pulls us out of the comfort of the They.
Death is always one's own and cannot be handed to anyone else. Facing it, Heidegger says, can make a person's life authentic.
Care is the structure of Dasein, and Heidegger argues that its meaning is time. The announced second half never appeared, so the book remains unfinished.
Daily life drifts into idle talk, curiosity and ambiguity, and Heidegger calls this tendency fallenness. We repeat what is said, chase novelty and cannot tell real understanding from its show.
Moods disclose how the world matters to us before we think about it. Heidegger calls this attunement, and a mood is a way the situation is disclosed, not a private colouring of inner states.
The call of conscience carries no content and no moral instruction, Heidegger insists. It summons Dasein out of the They toward its own potential, and resoluteness is the answer.

books.thesis: Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac shows a faith that suspends ethics and defies understanding.
books.summary:
Fear and Trembling is written under the pseudonym Johannes de Silentio and takes up the story of Abraham and Isaac. Kierkegaard asks what it would mean to obey a command to sacrifice your own son, and why we praise Abraham instead of treating him as a murderer. The narrator admits he cannot understand Abraham and approaches him with awe, from the outside.

The book retells the story several ways, then sets Abraham beside tragic heroes such as Agamemnon, who sacrifice a child but stay within what a community can understand. Abraham cannot explain himself, so he is silent. Kierkegaard calls what he does a teleological suspension of the ethical, and describes faith as believing by virtue of the absurd. Readers dispute what this means. Critics ask whether the argument could excuse any killing done on a claimed divine order, and the book does not settle that worry.
ideas: The narrator, Johannes de Silentio, admits he cannot understand Abraham. He writes as an admirer who stands in awe from outside faith.
Retelling the Genesis story in several versions makes it strange again. Partly, the book shows how easily familiar tellings smooth away the horror.
The knight of faith looks like an ordinary citizen. Like the knight of infinite resignation, he gives up what he loves, but he then believes he will get it back.
Faith by virtue of the absurd means Abraham believed he would receive Isaac back in this life. Everything made that impossible, and he believed anyway.
Agamemnon stays within ethics when he sacrifices his child, because the community can understand his cause. Abraham has no such public reason, and that separates him from the tragic hero.
Kierkegaard calls Abraham's case a teleological suspension of the ethical. The individual stands in a relation to God that outranks the universal.
Abraham's silence follows from his position, since he cannot make himself understood. Critics ask if this defence could excuse any murder, and the book does not settle it.

Three Problemata give the book its structure. They ask whether there is a teleological suspension of the ethical, whether there is an absolute duty to God, and whether Abraham's silence toward Sarah, Eliezer and Isaac can be defended ethically.

Kierkegaard attacks the Hegelian view that the ethical is the universal. On that view the individual is justified only by fitting into it, while Abraham, he says, stands as the single individual in an absolute relation to the absolute.
Kierkegaard complains that his age wants to go beyond faith, treating it as a first step to leave behind. For him faith is the hardest task, and no one finishes with it.

books.thesis: Two ways to live, the aesthetic and the ethical, are each written from the inside, with no clear verdict.
books.summary:
Either/Or is Kierkegaard's first major book, published under a pseudonymous editor who claims to have found two sets of papers in a secondhand desk. One set is by a young man called A, who lives for aesthetic interest and pleasure. The other is by Judge William, an older married man who defends the ethical life of commitment and duty. The title poses the question of which way to live.

Kierkegaard does not argue in his own voice. Each life is written from the inside, so the reader meets A's wit and melancholy and the Judge's warmth and moral earnestness. A's pages include the Diary of the Seducer and an essay on rotating the crops against boredom. The Judge replies in long letters on marriage and on choosing oneself. The book gives no clear verdict, and its closing sermon points beyond both. Many see it as setting up his later religious stage, though that reading is debated.
ideas: Kierkegaard hides behind an editor. Victor Eremita claims to have found the papers of two men, A and Judge William, in a desk, which lets Kierkegaard avoid speaking in his own voice.
A fights boredom by varying how he approaches things, not where he goes. His essay on rotating the crops sets out this method for keeping interest and pleasure alive.
The Diary of the Seducer shows pursuit turned into a cold art. Johannes the seducer manipulates a young woman, and the story exposes the cruelty of the aesthetic life.
The aesthetic life carries its own despair. A's opening aphorisms show a bored and melancholy writer behind the wit.
Judge William argues that marriage keeps romantic love alive by giving it duration and commitment. Left as a fleeting mood, he says, love would fade.
For the Judge, ethical choice is the choice of oneself. It means becoming a self with a history and responsibilities, and not only picking among options.
Neither life is declared the winner. A closing sermon points past both, and many readers take it as pointing toward a religious stage, though that reading is debated.
Don Giovanni is best expressed in music, the Mozart essay argues. He is sensuous desire in general and not an individual character. The essay sits in the section on the immediate erotic stages.
The unhappiest man is always absent from himself. In A's speech he lives in hope or memory and never in the present, and A suggests this is a mark of the aesthetic life.
The closing sermon, the Ultimatum, holds that in relation to God we are always in the wrong. This points past Judge William's ethics toward a different kind of seriousness.

books.thesis: Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom, a response to possibility itself and not to any object.
books.summary:
The Concept of Anxiety is a short, dense book published under the name Vigilius Haufniensis. Kierkegaard asks what anxiety is and how it connects to freedom and sin. He starts from the story of Adam and inherited sin, but his real subject is the moment before a choice. Anxiety differs from fear because it has no object. It is anxiety about possibility itself.

His image is vertigo. A person looking into an abyss feels dizzy not only because of the drop but because of their own freedom to jump, and he calls anxiety the dizziness of freedom. Sin enters, he says, through a leap that psychology cannot fully explain. The style is technical, and readers disagree about how much of the book is theology and how much psychology. It is influential partly because it treats anxiety as a sign of human possibility.
ideas: Anxiety has no object, which separates it from fear. Kierkegaard calls it the anxiety of possibility, the sense that anything could happen.
Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom. Looking into an abyss makes us dizzy because of our own freedom to jump, as well as because of the drop.
Anxiety is present in innocence, before any sin has taken place. In the story of Adam, the prohibition awakens the possibility of freedom.
Sin enters through a qualitative leap that psychology cannot fully explain. Kierkegaard says that explaining it away and denying it are both mistakes.
Anxiety attracts and repels at once. Kierkegaard calls it a sympathetic antipathy and an antipathetic sympathy.
Anxiety is a teacher. Whoever has learned to be anxious in the right way, Kierkegaard says, has learned the ultimate, because it teaches us about our freedom.
The demonic is shut-upness, the condition of a person who closes himself off from the good. He refuses to be opened out, from fear.

The book frames itself as psychology about a dogmatic problem. Its subtitle calls it a simple psychological deliberation on the dogmatic issue of hereditary sin, and the pseudonym Vigilius Haufniensis means the watchman of Copenhagen.
The human being is a synthesis of soul and body held together by spirit. Anxiety arises when spirit tries to posit that synthesis and meets its own freedom.
Adam is both himself and the race, Kierkegaard says of hereditary sin. Each individual repeats the beginning of sin for himself, so no one is merely a product of Adam's fall.

books.thesis: Despair is a failure to be a self, and most people are in it without knowing.
books.summary:
The Sickness unto Death is written under the pseudonym Anti-Climacus. It asks what a self is and why so many people are in despair without realizing it. Kierkegaard defines the self as a relation that relates itself to itself, grounded in something beyond it. Despair is a failure of that relation. It is called a sickness unto death because one cannot die of it.

Kierkegaard describes despair through pairs such as the finite and infinite, and possibility and necessity, and the many ways a person can go wrong. Despair can be unconscious, as in the cheerful, busy person, or defiant, as in the person who wants to be a self on his own terms. The cure is faith, in which the self rests transparently in the power that established it. Readers disagree over how much the book depends on Christian belief, though the diagnosis of self-evasion can be read without it.
ideas: The self is a relation that relates itself to itself, and Kierkegaard says it is grounded in another power. Despair is a misrelation within it.
Despair is called a sickness unto death because one cannot die of it. The torment is that the self cannot be used up and ended.
Each way the self can go wrong produces its own despair. The misrelation can show up in pairs such as the finite and the infinite, or possibility and necessity.
Unconscious despair is the most common kind. A cheerful, busy person who thinks he is fine may be in the deepest despair, simply because he has no idea.
Defiant despair wants to be a self entirely on its own terms. Weak despair wants to be rid of the self altogether.
Kierkegaard distinguishes despair over the earthly, despair of the eternal and despair about one's own sin. The sequence intensifies as the person becomes more aware.
The cure is given as a formula. When the self relates to itself and wills to be itself, it rests transparently in the power that established it, and Kierkegaard calls this faith.

Anti-Climacus is presented by Kierkegaard as a higher Christian standard than his earlier Johannes Climacus. The subtitle calls the book a Christian psychological exposition for upbuilding and awakening.
The opposite of sin is faith, not virtue. In the second part, despair is shown to be sin, meaning living before God while refusing to rest in him.
More self-awareness brings deeper despair. The more a person knows of what a self is, the more intense the despair, and the farther he is from the unconscious kind.

books.thesis: With God dead, Zarathustra offers the overman, eternal recurrence and a yes to life.
books.summary:
Thus Spoke Zarathustra is Nietzsche's most poetic book, written as a kind of mock scripture. A prophet comes down from ten years in the mountains to teach that God is dead and that people should live toward something beyond themselves. Under it runs the question of what to do with life once the old sources of meaning lose their authority.

Nietzsche answers through speeches, parables and songs, not argument. Zarathustra offers the overman as a goal, warns against the last man who wants only comfort, and tells of the camel, the lion and the child as stages of the spirit. The most testing idea is eternal recurrence, the thought of living this life again without end. Readers still argue about what the overman means, and political movements Nietzsche would have despised have misused the book. Some find its style exhilarating, others overheated and hard to pin down.
ideas: Zarathustra's first message falls flat. He comes down from ten years alone and tells a town that God is dead, but the crowd, waiting for a tightrope walker, is not much interested.
The overman is offered as a goal. Humanity is something to be overcome, as the ape is to the human.
The last man is the comfortable, small, blinking figure who says he has found happiness. Nietzsche presents him as a warning about contentment without aspiration.
The three metamorphoses describe stages of the spirit. It begins as a camel that bears burdens, becomes a lion that says no, and ends as a child that begins again and creates new values.
Zarathustra asks his hearers to remain faithful to the earth. He warns that otherworldly hopes teach people to despise the body and this life.
Eternal recurrence works as a test of one's attitude to life. It asks whether you could will to live this life again, and so whether you can say yes to your existence.
The meaning of the overman stays disputed because the book is parable and poem. Readers still disagree about what exactly Nietzsche meant.
In the speech on the despisers of the body, Zarathustra says he is body entirely, and that soul is only a word for something about the body. The body is a great reason, wiser than the thinker.
Eternal recurrence is put to the reader as an image in the vision and the riddle. Zarathustra shows a dwarf a gateway called Moment, from which two paths run back and forward.
The book parodies the Bible, with parables, sermons and a prophet with disciples. The form lets Nietzsche mock the voice of religion while teaching something opposed to it.

books.thesis: Philosophers' systems are confessions of their drives, and Nietzsche reads them as symptoms.
books.summary:
Beyond Good and Evil is a collection of aphorisms and short essays in which Nietzsche turns his suspicion on philosophers. They claim to pursue cold, impartial truth, yet their systems tend to defend moral prejudices they inherited. He asks why we want truth at all, and what drives lie behind the arguments of thinkers who say they have none.

His method is to read a philosophy as a symptom of the person who wrote it. He questions Descartes's confidence in an I that thinks, treats knowledge as seeing from many perspectives, and proposes the will to power as a hypothesis for psychology and life. He contrasts noble morality with slave morality and calls for free spirits who test their own convictions. The book is playful and uneven, and some passages offend readers. It builds no system, and Nietzsche seems to prefer leaving the reader unsettled.
ideas: Philosophers claim to pursue cold truth while defending inherited prejudices, Nietzsche says. He asks the odd question of why we want truth in the first place.
Every great philosophy, he says, is the personal confession of its author. It is a kind of involuntary memoir, with moral intentions hidden inside it.
He challenges Descartes's "I think." A thought comes when it wants and not when I want, so Descartes assumes more than he has shown.
Truth is perspectival. Knowing means looking from many angles, and the falseness of a judgment is no objection to it if it helps preserve and promote life.
The will to power is offered as an experimental hypothesis, not as settled doctrine. Nietzsche tests it as an account of psychology and of life.
Master morality starts from self-affirmation. Slave morality starts from the reaction of the weak and values humility and pity.
Nietzsche calls for free spirits and philosophers of the future. They treat their own convictions with suspicion and are willing to experiment.
The Stoic ideal of living according to nature draws his mockery. Nature is indifferent and wasteful, he says, and the Stoics read their own values into it and then claim to have found them there.
Fighting monsters carries a risk, the aphorism on the abyss warns. Whoever does so should take care not to become a monster, and when you gaze long into an abyss the abyss gazes into you.
In Peoples and Fatherlands he ridicules the nationalism of his day and hopes for good Europeans. He thinks the future lies in a mixing of peoples and not in a stiffening of national pride.

books.thesis: Morality has a history, and Nietzsche traces much of it to the ressentiment of the powerless.
books.summary:
On the Genealogy of Morality is made of three essays asking where our moral ideas came from. Nietzsche's wager is that morality has a history, and that tracing it may reveal origins we would not call noble. He asks what good and evil, guilt and conscience, and the ideals of self-denial did for the people who invented them.

The first essay contrasts the noble good and bad with the later good and evil, and links the latter to the ressentiment of the powerless. The second derives guilt from the idea of debt, and bad conscience from instincts turned inward. The third asks what ascetic ideals mean, and suggests priests gave suffering a purpose, so that people would rather will nothing than not will at all. Scholars debate whether this is history or polemic. Nietzsche himself says we need a critique of moral values, and that task still seems unfinished.
ideas: Moral values have a history, Nietzsche says, and tracing it may show origins that are unflattering. We tend to assume pure ones.
He contrasts two moral outlooks. A noble good and bad begins from the self-affirmation of the strong, while a later good and evil begins from reaction.
The slave revolt in morality comes from ressentiment. Those who cannot act turn their imagination to revenge, and call their powerlessness a virtue.
Guilt, Nietzsche suggests, grows out of debt. The German word for guilt is close to the word for debts, and punishment began as repayment.
Bad conscience is instinct turned inward. When society closes in, humans learn to suffer from themselves and from their own cruelty.
Ascetic ideals give suffering a meaning, and that is their strength. Nietzsche says humans would rather will nothingness than not will at all, and priests exploit this need.
Nietzsche asks for a critique of moral values and wants to know their worth. Scholars debate whether the genealogy is real history or a pointed polemic.

The second essay describes breeding an animal with the right to make promises. This needs active forgetting, a power that keeps the mind clear, and ends in the sovereign individual who answers for himself.
Science, Nietzsche argues in the third essay, is the latest form of the ascetic ideal. It still believes in truth as unconditionally valuable.
Knowing is a kind of perspectival seeing. The more eyes we can use for one matter, the more complete our idea of it will be, and there is no view from nowhere.

books.thesis: Nietzsche's aphorisms, where the madman announces that God is dead and eternal recurrence first appears.
books.summary:
The Gay Science is a collection of aphorisms, poems and short essays, first published in 1882 and expanded in 1887. The title names a knowledge that is light, joyful and close to poetry. It is where Nietzsche first announces that God is dead and first poses eternal recurrence.

In the scene of the madman, a man runs into a marketplace with a lantern and tells the crowd they have killed God. They do not believe, so they laugh, and he says he has come too early. Nietzsche suggests the consequences are not yet felt. Elsewhere he asks us to love fate, give style to our character and doubt how much consciousness matters. The book is varied rather than systematic, often called his warmest. Some readers take its lightness as a serious philosophical position.
ideas: The madman comes too early. He runs into a marketplace with a lantern and says we have killed God, and the crowd, who do not believe, only laughs.
The death of God is presented as a cultural event. The beliefs that held up morality are losing their footing, and the consequences have not yet been felt.
Eternal recurrence appears as a demon's proposal. The demon asks whether you would welcome living your life again, exactly as it was, for ever.
Amor fati, the love of fate, means saying yes even to what cannot be changed. Nietzsche wants to see what is necessary in things as beautiful.
The gay science is knowledge held with lightness and joy. The book mixes aphorisms, verse and songs, and treats thinking as an art as well as a task.
Consciousness is overrated, Nietzsche argues. It developed for the sake of communication, and so it tends to flatten experience into what can be shared.
Character can be given a style. Nietzsche says to shape strengths and weaknesses into a unified plan, so that even faults become part of a pleasing whole.
Book Five reads the death of God as an opening. In We Fearless Ones, added in 1887 with a new preface and an appendix of songs, he says the horizon seems open again, and the sea lies open.
Polytheism has a great advantage, Nietzsche says. It lets an individual create his own ideal and give himself his own laws, while monotheism he calls the rigid rule of a single normal human type.
His cheerfulness is something won after illness, not a simple temperament. The title echoes the Provencal gai saber of the troubadours, and the book carries verses and a closing set of songs.

books.t: The World as Will and Representation
books.thesis: Reality is blind striving, so life swings between pain and boredom, with brief relief in art and compassion.
books.summary:
The book opens with the claim that the world is my representation: we know only how things appear to a subject. Schopenhauer builds on Kant, then asks what lies behind appearances. His answer is that we can know it from inside, through our own body and its urges. Underneath everything is will, a blind striving with no purpose or end.

Because will never rests, wanting never ends. Satisfaction is brief, and life swings between pain and boredom. Relief comes only in moments, mainly through art (music above all) and through compassion, which recognizes the same will in others. The deepest relief is denial of the will, as practised by saints and ascetics. Critics note the tension between his pessimism and his comfortable life, and doubt that will explains as much as he claimed.
ideas: The book opens with the claim that the world is my representation. We know things only as they appear to a subject, and Schopenhauer extends Kant on this point.
The will is the thing in itself. We know it from inside through our bodily urges, and the same blind force runs through all of nature.
Because will has no final aim, wanting never ends. Satisfaction is brief and lack is lasting, so life swings between pain and boredom.
Aesthetic contemplation briefly lets us forget the will, since we lose ourselves in disinterested attention. The relief is real, but it does not last.
Music has a special place among the arts. Schopenhauer treats it as a direct expression of the will itself, which he says explains its power over us.
Compassion is the basis of ethics. Seeing another's suffering is recognising that the same will is at work in them as in me.
The deepest relief is the denial of the will, practised by saints and ascetics. Critics note the tension with his own comfortable life.

Our representations are tied together by the principle of sufficient reason, but the will lies outside it. Schopenhauer had set out the principle in an earlier work, and it covers causes, reasons and motives.
Schopenhauer denies free will in the usual sense. Our acts follow necessarily from our character and motives, though he allows that the will itself is free because it is not subject to causes.

Individuation is an appearance, a veil of Maya borrowed from Indian thought. Seeing past it makes one feel for others as for oneself. He also argues that suicide is no denial of the will, since it destroys only the body.

books.thesis: Late essays in which Schopenhauer asks how to live reasonably well, given how bleak he thinks life is.
books.summary:
Parerga and Paralipomena is a two volume collection of essays and fragments that Schopenhauer published late. The title means roughly appendices and omissions, extending his main philosophy. The question running through them is practical. They look for a way to live reasonably well, given his view of life. This book, not his major work, made him famous.

The essays range from Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life to pieces on suffering, solitude, religion, reading and writing. Schopenhauer argues that happiness depends more on what a person is than on what one has or how one is seen. He also tells the parable of the porcupines, who cannot bear to be too close or too far apart. Some pieces, notably his essay on women, are widely seen as prejudice rather than argument. Readers take what they like and leave the rest.
ideas: The appendices made his name. Parerga and Paralipomena means appendices and omissions, and this 1851 collection finally brought Schopenhauer the fame he had waited for.
Happiness depends more on what one is than on what one has or how one appears to others. This is the argument of the Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life.
Pain is the positive reality and pleasure only its absence, he argues. A good life is therefore mostly one in which suffering is kept small.
The porcupines huddle for warmth and prick one another with their quills, and learn a moderate distance. Schopenhauer says that is how people should treat each other.
Solitude suits those with much within themselves. The more a person has inside, he argues, the less he needs others, and the less others can touch him.
His pieces on reading and writing urge people to think for themselves and read less. He also warns against the pull of whatever is newest.
His essay on women is widely criticized as prejudice dressed as argument. It is a reminder that wisdom literature carries its author's blind spots.
University philosophy, he says in his essay on it, bends thought to the professors' jobs and the state. He aims much of the scorn at Hegel, whose prose he calls nonsense used to impress.

In a speculation on the apparent intention in the fate of the individual, Schopenhauer suggests that a life may be arranged like a novel by a hidden hand. He offers this as a conjecture, not as proof.
Against Leibniz, he calls this the worst of all possible worlds, meaning that a slightly worse one could not continue to exist. Optimism, he thinks, is a bitter mockery of human suffering.

books.thesis: Courage is self-affirmation in spite of anxiety about death, meaninglessness and guilt.
books.summary:
Tillich asks what courage is and what it requires. His definition is that courage is self-affirmation in spite of non-being: the possibility of ending, emptiness or condemnation. Anxiety, as he uses the word, is the awareness of that threat. Unlike fear, it has no particular object.

He names three forms of anxiety: of fate and death, of emptiness and meaninglessness, and of guilt and condemnation. He suggests each dominated a different age. He also separates the courage to be as a part, finding oneself in a group, from the courage to be as oneself, standing alone. Both risk loss. His answer is theological: a God above the God of ordinary belief, who survives doubt. Critics find this vague, and some secular readers set the theology aside and keep the analysis of courage and anxiety.
ideas: Tillich defines courage as self-affirmation in spite of what threatens being. Everything in the definition turns on the phrase in spite of.
Anxiety is the awareness of non-being. Unlike fear, it has no definite object, and that makes it hard to meet directly.
Tillich names three forms of anxiety: of fate and death, of emptiness and meaninglessness, and of guilt and condemnation. He suggests each marked a different age.
Neurotic anxiety tries to avoid non-being by avoiding being. The self shrinks into a small area where it feels safe.
Courage takes two forms, the courage to be a part, finding oneself within a group, and the courage to be oneself. Tillich says each carries its own risk of losing the self.
He treats certain existentialist writers as showing the courage to face meaninglessness. They take despair seriously instead of covering it.
Tillich points to a God above the God of theism, the ground of being, that survives doubt. Critics find this vague, and secular readers often leave it aside.
Courage answers a polarity of individualization and participation. The self must be itself while belonging to a world, and courage can fail by losing either side.

Each age, on Tillich's reading, has its own dominant courage. He reads Stoicism as the ancient courage to be oneself in the face of death and fate, medieval Christianity as answering anxiety of guilt, and the modern age as answering anxiety of meaninglessness.
Justification by faith, translated religiously, becomes accepting acceptance. One has courage to be when one accepts being accepted in spite of being unacceptable.

books.thesis: Anxiety is more than a symptom. It is a condition of being free.
books.summary:
The Meaning of Anxiety grew out of Rollo May's doctoral work. He asks what anxiety is and why it seemed to be spreading in his time. His answer is that anxiety is the response to a threat to values a person holds essential to their existence as a self. That is why it feels different from fear of a specific harm.

May surveys Kierkegaard, Freud, Kurt Goldstein and Harry Stack Sullivan and finds each partial. He leans most on Kierkegaard's link between anxiety and freedom. He separates normal anxiety, which is proportionate and can be faced, from neurotic anxiety, which is out of proportion and involves repression. He ties anxiety to competition and weakened shared values. Therapy, he says, cannot promise an end to anxiety. It can help a person bear it and use it.
ideas: Anxiety is a response to a threat to values the person holds essential to their existence as a self. That is why it differs from fear of a specific harm.
May finds every earlier account partial. He surveys Kierkegaard, Freud, Goldstein and Sullivan, among others, and leans most heavily on Kierkegaard.
From Kierkegaard he takes the link between anxiety and freedom. Anxiety goes with possibility, and a person who grows must move through it.
Normal anxiety is proportionate to the threat and can be faced constructively. Neurotic anxiety is out of proportion, involves repression, and blocks growth.
Anxiety belongs to its time, May argues. He cites competitiveness and the loosening of shared values in modern Western society as reasons it was spreading.
Facing anxiety allows a person to grow, while avoiding it narrows life. New freedom tends to arrive with some measure of anxiety.
Therapy cannot promise to end anxiety. May says its job is to help a person bear it and make use of it.

The book began as a dissertation written during illness. May wrote it while recovering from tuberculosis in a sanatorium, where he read Kierkegaard, and it became his doctoral dissertation at Columbia, with Paul Tillich as advisor.

Goldstein's brain-injured patients show what being overwhelmed looks like. In the catastrophic reaction, a person overwhelmed by a task falls into a disordered state, and May treats it as anxiety when a person's world is shaken.

Freud's later theory is closer to the truth, May thinks. Freud moved from anxiety as transformed libido to anxiety as a signal of danger to the ego, but May says the later version still lacks a view of the self.

books.thesis: People have more freedom than ever, yet many feel numb and unable to commit. May blames apathy.
books.summary:
People now have more freedom than before, especially sexual freedom, yet many report feeling numb, empty and unable to commit. May asks what has gone wrong with love and will. He suggests the answer is apathy, a defence against feeling too much. He draws on therapy, literature and philosophy.

May separates sex from eros, the drive toward union and creation, and says our culture has reduced eros to technique. He describes the daimonic, a natural power that can take over a whole person. Denied, it is destructive. Integrated, it is creative. He also separates wish from will and argues that each fails without the other. Care is the root of both. Critics call the book wide-ranging and loose, and some claims work better as observations than as proof.
ideas: May starts from apathy. In an age of sexual openness many people feel numb, and he reads that numbness as a defence against feeling too much.
Eros is the drive toward union and creation, while sex is a physiological need. May says the culture reduced eros to technique and so lost its force.
The daimonic is any natural power, such as sex, anger or eros, that can take over the whole person. Denied, it erupts, and integrated, it can become creative.
A wish is imagining a possible act, while will is organising oneself toward it. May argues that each is empty without the other.
Intentionality is the structure that gives experience its meaning. May treats it as the bridge between wish and will.
Care is the root of both love and will. Without it, people become either detached from what happens or unable to act on their wishes.
Pseudo-innocence is the claim to be harmless. May says it is used to avoid owning one's power and its effects on others.
A mature love contains all four Greek kinds of love, May holds: sex, eros, philia and agape. He says modern culture has flattened them into sex.
He criticises the new puritanism of technique, where sex becomes performance and measurement, as seen in the work of Kinsey and of Masters and Johnson. Feeling is lost when function is the only goal.
Violence grows from impotence and from the need to feel significant, May argues. When a person cannot affect the world, the daimonic can take over in destructive form.

books.thesis: A therapy textbook built on four facts of life: death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness.
books.summary:
Yalom's textbook starts from the givens of human life. He asks whether psychological conflict comes only from repressed drives, or also from our confrontation with certain facts of existence. He names four ultimate concerns, death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness, and organizes the book around them.

Each concern, he argues, sets the awareness of a given against our wish to avoid it, and many symptoms are ways of managing that conflict. He draws on Kierkegaard, Sartre and Frankl, with clinical examples from his own practice. He describes therapy as a real encounter between two mortal people, more than a technique. Critics ask how well the framework can be tested, and some find the book long and uneven. It has been widely used in training.
ideas: Yalom proposes that psychological conflict comes from confronting the givens of existence, and not only from repressed drives. The four he names are death, freedom, isolation and meaninglessness.
Death anxiety often shows up in disguise. Yalom describes two main defences, a belief in one's personal specialness and a belief in an ultimate rescuer.
Confronting mortality can also awaken a person. Yalom reports that those who face death sometimes shift their priorities and live more fully.
Freedom means we are responsible for our own lives, with nothing outside us to give them structure. Yalom draws on Sartre and May here.
Isolation comes in three kinds: interpersonal, within oneself, and existential. Relationships can ease the last but cannot remove it.
We seem to need meaning in a universe that supplies none. Yalom suggests that meaning tends to follow engagement with life more than direct pursuit.
The therapist is a fellow mortal and not a detached expert, so the relationship itself is central to the work. Critics ask how testable the framework is.

Cosmic meaning and terrestrial meaning are different things, Yalom says. The first is a scheme laid on the universe, the second is found in purposes inside a life, and he thinks people can live well with the second even without the first.
Patients dodge responsibility, for instance by seeing themselves as victims of forces they did not choose. Therapy aims to show them their own part in creating their situation.
Boundary situations can break through everyday routine. Following Jaspers, Yalom points to a death or a diagnosis as events that push a person to reconsider how to live.

books.thesis: A late, personal book arguing that facing the fear of death loosens its hold and changes how we live.
books.summary:
After decades as a therapist, Yalom believes the fear of death often lies behind other complaints, and that most of us spend our lives trying not to look at it. The title borrows La Rochefoucauld's remark that neither the sun nor death can be looked at steadily. The book is an attempt to look anyway.

Yalom mixes stories from his practice with candid notes on his own aging and fears. He describes awakening experiences, where a brush with mortality changes how a person lives, and rippling, the idea that our influence carries on through others. He brings in Epicurus and the thought experiment of eternal recurrence as aids. The advice is modest. Critics find it uneven or too reassuring, and it is not a treatise.
ideas: Yalom believes death anxiety often hides beneath other complaints. After decades of practice he sees it as common and usually unspoken.
Awakening experiences are moments, often after loss or illness, when awareness of mortality changes a person's priorities. Sometimes the shift in how they live is permanent.
Rippling is the idea that our influence passes outward through other people. It is a kind of survival that does not depend on personal immortality.
Epicurus held that nonexistence after death is like nonexistence before birth. Yalom admits the argument comforts some people far more than others.
Unlived life feeds the fear of death. Yalom suggests that the more of it a person carries, the greater the fear, so living more fully may lessen it.
Eternal recurrence serves as a test. Imagine living your life again exactly as it was, and notice the regrets that appear.
The title borrows La Rochefoucauld's remark that neither sun nor death can be looked at steadily. The book looks anyway, mixing case stories with Yalom's own fears.
The defences of personal specialness and an ultimate rescuer can fail. Yalom revisits both and shows how each can break down when a person meets real loss.
Yalom credits Ernest Becker's The Denial of Death as a major influence. He takes Becker's claim that fear of death shapes our lives and applies it in the consulting room.
Isolation with the fear makes it worse. Yalom suggests that talking openly about death, in therapy or in groups, makes it less frightening.

books.thesis: Medicine is good at fixing bodies and poor at helping people decide what matters at the end of life.
books.summary:
Atul Gawande is a surgeon whose training taught him to fix bodies and said almost nothing about how people age and die. The book asks what a good end of life looks like once medicine can no longer cure. It asks what doctors, families and institutions get wrong when they treat old age as a problem to solve.

Gawande visits nursing homes, assisted living, hospice and his own father's illness. He argues that safety and survival have crowded out autonomy, meaning the chance to keep living by one's own priorities. Clinicians, he suggests, should ask patients what they fear, what they hope for and what trade-offs they would accept, then help them act on the answers. It leaves open how to weigh a longer life against a better one when patients, families and doctors disagree.
ideas: Gawande's medical training prepared him to rescue patients and left him unready to talk with people who could not be rescued. He came to see this gap as built into the profession.
Nursing homes often put safety and routine ahead of what residents want. A long life can end up with little say over meals, schedules or possessions.
Physician Bill Thomas brought plants, dogs, cats and birds into a nursing home where he worked. The book reports that residents became livelier and needed fewer drugs.
Keren Brown Wilson's assisted living idea started from giving frail people their own rooms with doors that lock and keys of their own. Privacy and choice can survive dependence.
Gawande describes three kinds of doctor, those who decide for patients, those who only hand over information, and those who help patients work out what they want. He favours the last kind.

Hospice and palliative care did not always shorten life. The book reports that seriously ill patients who accepted them sometimes lived as long as, or longer than, those who kept pursuing aggressive treatment.
A useful end-of-life conversation asks what the patient understands, what they fear and hope for, what they would give up, and what outcome they could not accept.
Gawande contrasts the modern institutional treatment of old age with his grandfather in rural India. The old man was cared for at home by his family and held status for his age.
His own father, a surgeon with a spinal tumour, brought the questions home. The family had to work out what he valued before deciding which risks were worth taking.
A young pregnant woman with terminal lung cancer keeps hoping for more treatment. Her case shows how hard it is for patients and doctors to move from fighting disease to caring for comfort.

books.thesis: Her interviews with dying patients gave us the five stages, which research does not support as a sequence.
books.summary:
In the 1960s Elisabeth Kübler-Ross, a Swiss-born psychiatrist working in Chicago, began sitting with terminally ill patients and asking what dying was like. Hospitals mostly avoided the subject, and patients were often not told how ill they were. The book asks what dying people experience and what the living, especially medical staff, can do for them.

From interviews and seminars, in the patients' own words, she describes denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance as reactions she kept seeing, with hope running through them. She urged doctors and nurses to listen rather than deflect. Later research has not found that people move through these reactions in order, and she herself said they were not meant as rigid steps. Many readers now value it most for the permission it gave to talk with the dying.
ideas: Avoiding the dying protected the staff more than the patients, she argued. Patients in hospitals were often avoided or kept in the dark, which spared others their own discomfort with death.
Her method was simple. She invited terminally ill patients to talk about their situation, often in front of students, and she treated their accounts as the main source of knowledge.
Denial comes first for many patients. Shock and disbelief at a terminal diagnosis act as a temporary buffer, and she saw it as a defence to respect rather than to break.
Anger shows up as the question of why this is happening to me. It often lands on nurses and relatives, who she said should try to understand it.
Bargaining is the attempt to postpone the end in exchange for good behaviour or promises. Depression follows as grief for what has already been lost and what is still to be lost.
Acceptance, in her account, is not happiness. It is a quiet, nearly feelingless stage in which patients are tired, want fewer visitors, and have made some peace with what is coming.
The stages were observations, not a schedule. Later studies have not found that people pass through them in order, and Kübler-Ross warned against treating them as fixed steps.
Hope persists through all the stages, she writes, even in patients who accept death. She advises staff not to take hope away, since it gives meaning to suffering.
Families of dying patients go through similar reactions and need support of their own. She asks staff to include relatives in conversations and not treat them as bystanders.
The work began with a seminar at the Chicago hospital where she taught, after theology students asked for help understanding crisis in human life. Her interviews with the dying became its material.

books.a: Sheldon Solomon, Jeff Greenberg and Tom Pyszczynski
books.thesis: Fear of death, the authors argue, drives culture, belief and status. It is their own theory, argued by them.
books.summary:
The title borrows from William James. Following Ernest Becker, the book asks why humans do so much that looks unrelated to survival, such as building monuments and chasing status. Its answer is Terror Management Theory. We are animals who know we will die, and the authors say the resulting dread shapes much of culture.

Solomon, Greenberg and Pyszczynski lay out Becker's argument, then add experiments. In a typical study, people reminded of their own death grow more attached to their worldview and harder on those who reject it. They link this to religion, self-esteem, prejudice and politics. Because the theory's founders wrote it, the book reads as a case for the theory rather than a neutral survey. Critics ask whether death is special, or whether any threat to meaning would produce the same reactions.
ideas: Following Becker, the authors say humans combine animal bodies with minds that can picture their own death. This pairing produces a terror that must be managed somehow.
Cultures supply protection by offering a worldview that gives life meaning and a way to count as lasting. The permanence can be literal, as in afterlives, or symbolic, as in legacy, nation or family.
Self-esteem works as a buffer. Feeling that one is a valuable person within a worldview that gives life sense is presented as the main way individuals calm their death anxiety.
People distance themselves from their animal nature, the authors argue. This helps explain disgust at bodily functions and unease about the physical side of sex, since bodies remind us we will decay.

In mortality salience experiments, participants asked to think about their own death often judged people who share their beliefs more kindly and critics of their group more harshly than control participants did.
A rival worldview threatens the one that shields us, so the authors tie death anxiety to prejudice, conflict and war. Groups can treat different beliefs as a danger to life.

The theory has critics. Some researchers question whether death is special or whether any threat to meaning produces similar reactions, and some mortality salience results have struggled in replication attempts.
The title comes from William James, who spoke of the worm at the core of our usual happiness. The authors take it to mean that awareness of death underlies ordinary life.
In one study, municipal judges reminded of death set a much higher bond for an alleged prostitute than judges who were not. The authors read it as defence of cultural values.

The authors argue that after the September 11 attacks, reminders of death helped raise support for George W. Bush. They cite experiments in which such reminders increased preference for a strong leader.

books.thesis: Existentialism told through the lives, loves, quarrels and politics of the people who made it.
books.summary:
Sarah Bakewell tells the story of existentialism through its makers, among them Sartre, Beauvoir, Heidegger, Husserl, Camus and Merleau-Ponty. She asks what a philosophy of freedom, authenticity and responsibility looks like when lived by real people with jealousies, lovers and bad decisions.

She weaves biography with plain explanation of the ideas. The story opens with an apricot cocktail in a Paris bar. It moves through Husserl's call to return to the things themselves and Heidegger's account of being in the world, then follows Sartre and Beauvoir's partnership and the quarrels that ended friendships. She does not hide Heidegger's embrace of the Nazis, and she leaves open how far a philosophy can be separated from its author.
ideas: The story opens with an apricot cocktail, over which Raymond Aron told Sartre that phenomenology could make philosophy out of an ordinary drink. Sartre reportedly reacted with excitement.
Husserl's phenomenology asked philosophers to go back to the things themselves, describing experience as it appears before explaining it. This method shaped nearly everyone in the book.
Heidegger argued that we meet the world first as a place of tools and tasks we are involved in, not as detached observers looking at objects.
Heidegger joined the Nazi party in 1933. Bakewell shows how that sits uneasily with his thought and leaves readers to decide how to read him.
Sartre claimed that existence comes before essence and that people are condemned to be free. Pretending we have no choice is bad faith, a form of self-deception.
In The Second Sex, Beauvoir applied existentialist ideas to women's situation. She argued that womanhood is shaped by society and history instead of being fixed by nature.
Camus broke with Sartre in the early 1950s over politics and the Soviet Union. He also rejected the label existentialist for himself.
Merleau-Ponty appears as the thinker of the body. In his account, perception is not a mental act but something we do as embodied beings immersed in the world.
In 1935 Sartre took mescaline, and for some time afterward he felt followed by lobsters and other creatures. Bakewell says the episode shaped his sense of the dark side of consciousness.
After the war existentialism became a fashion in Saint-Germain, with cellar clubs, jazz, Juliette Greco and Boris Vian's parodies. Sartre and Beauvoir found themselves cast as celebrities.

books.thesis: Life is short, no productivity method can change that, and accepting it brings relief.
books.summary:
An average human life lasts around four thousand weeks. Burkeman starts from that number and asks why so many people feel overwhelmed despite having more time-saving tools than any earlier generation. His question is what to do with a life that is short and in which we cannot do everything.

He argues that productivity advice treats time as a resource to be mastered, which assumes that with enough efficiency we could fit it all in. We cannot, so every yes closes off other possibilities. Drawing on Stoics, Buddhist teachers, Heidegger and modern psychology, he suggests accepting limits, choosing what to neglect, and taking relief from how little one life matters on a cosmic scale. Critics note that the advice suits people who already have some control over their hours.
ideas: Four thousand weeks is roughly an eighty-year life. Burkeman uses the number to make finitude concrete and to remove the fantasy that there is plenty of time later.
Efficiency creates a trap. Clearing tasks faster tends to bring more of them, so reaching the bottom of the inbox simply makes you the person who gets more work.
Staying busy has become a badge of importance. Burkeman argues the to-do list will never end, so peace has to come from accepting that and not from finishing.
Every choice costs other choices. He recommends the joy of missing out in place of the fear of missing out, since a full life requires giving things up on purpose.
Treating time as a tool to be used makes the present a means to some future that never quite arrives. That empties out the time people have.
Because neglect is unavoidable, he suggests deciding in advance which important things to do badly or skip.
Cosmic insignificance therapy is his name for the relief of seeing that one's life matters little in the grand scheme. It can lower the pressure to make every week count.
Burkeman suggests paying yourself first with time. Put the most important work first in the day or week, and accept that other things will be done less well or not at all.
Rest should be valued for itself and not used to recharge for more work. Treating leisure as a means to productivity, he says, keeps us in the same frame of mind.
He recommends limiting work in progress to a few projects and finishing before starting new ones. A small number of open tasks keeps the sense of a finite life from being buried.

books.thesis: The more we chase security, the more anxious we get. Meaning is found by attending to the present.
books.summary:
Watts wrote this short book in 1951 and subtitled it A Message for an Age of Anxiety. He asks why people who are safer and more comfortable than their ancestors still feel anxious, and why the harder we try to secure ourselves, the less secure we feel.

It is a set of essays, not a tight argument. Watts draws on Buddhism, Taoism and Christian mysticism and returns to one point. The mind grabs at the future and the past, which exist only as thought, and so misses the one place where experience happens. Pleasure and pain, life and death come bundled together, and trying to keep only half of each produces tension. His remedy is to stop resisting impermanence and attend to what is here now. Critics find him loose and more persuasive than rigorous.
ideas: The desire for security and the feeling of insecurity are the same thing, Watts says. The anxious grasping for safety is what produces the sense of being unsafe.
Faith and belief are different for Watts. Faith is an open mind willing to meet whatever turns out to be true, while belief is clinging to a fixed idea for comfort.
Pleasure and pain are bound together. Efforts to keep one and banish the other tend to create more tension than they remove.
Memory and anticipation take place in the present as thoughts. People often live in these mental pictures of past and future instead of in the experience in front of them.
We confuse symbols with the things they stand for. Watts's examples are money mistaken for wealth, and reading the menu and calling it dinner.
The present moment is the only point at which anything is experienced. Watts treats attention to it as the practical answer to worry about what comes next.
For Watts the sense of a separate self standing apart from experience is an illusion. The thinker and the thought, the feeler and the feeling, are one process.
Watts describes his time as an age of anxiety. He says medicine and religion are tried as ways to buy security, and that the more they promise it, the more people worry.
Music is his analogy for life. We play a piece for the playing and do not hurry to the last note, and life should be treated the same way, without reducing it to a goal.
To try to hold on to life is like trying to grasp water, which runs away the tighter the fist closes. Living well means moving with the flow and not fixing it.

books.thesis: Private notes from a Roman emperor on controlling what he can, accepting what he cannot, and acting well.
books.summary:
Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180. The notes later called Meditations were written in Greek for his own use, often on military campaign, and he never meant them for readers. They ask how a person with great duties can act well, stay steady and treat others fairly while facing loss, annoyance and death.

It is a series of reminders, not a treatise, and the same points return in new forms. He follows Stoic ideas. Our judgments and actions are up to us. Other people's behaviour, our bodies, our reputations and the events around us are not. The universe is orderly, and everything passes. Scholars debate how systematic the notes are. Some readers worry the advice tips into resignation. Others read it as a training manual by someone who knew he often failed to follow it.
ideas: The notes were written to himself, in twelve books, with no known audience. They read like exercises meant to correct his own tendencies and moods.
Each morning he prepares himself for difficult people. He will meet meddling, ungrateful and arrogant people, he reminds himself, and they act out of ignorance of what is good and bad.
Distress comes from how we judge events, and judgment is something he can change. His task is to separate what is up to him from what is not.
The view from above shrinks worries to their proper size. He pictures the Earth and its crowds from a great height, so that ambition and quarrels look small.
Fame does not last. Those who praise you will die and so will those who remember them, which he offers as a reason to stop craving reputation.
An obstacle to action becomes material for action. What stands in the way can be turned into the way, which is his advice for setbacks.
Humans are made to cooperate, like hands or feet. Acting against other people goes against our own nature and treats a shared community as if it were not there.
Book One is a ledger of gratitude. It lists debts to those who shaped him, from his grandfather and mother to teachers and the emperor Antoninus, and records the habits he learned from each.
He often says the universe is either providence or atoms, and that the right response is much the same either way. Either we belong to a rational whole, or there is nothing to fear in dissolution.
The past and future are not ours to lose, and only the present can be taken from us. He tells himself to retreat into his own mind, the inner citadel, where nothing external can reach.

books.thesis: Seneca's letters to a friend on time, death and friendship, and on living by reason.
books.summary:
Seneca was a Roman statesman and, for a time, tutor and adviser to Nero. In his last years he wrote 124 letters to his friend Lucilius, a provincial official in Sicily. They are usually read in selection. The letters ask how to live by reason when time is short, fortune is unreliable and a ruler can order your death.

Each letter is brief and practical, built around one theme, such as using time, choosing friends, facing poverty, fearing death or reading wisely. Seneca borrows freely from Epicurus and presents himself as a learner who has not reached the Stoic ideal of the wise person. Critics have long pointed to the gap between his praise of simple living and his great wealth. Nero eventually ordered him to kill himself, in 65, which gives the letters on death a grim backdrop.
ideas: The first letter urges Lucilius to claim his time for himself. People guard money carefully and waste hours as if they cost nothing.
Seneca recommends reading a few authors thoroughly rather than many authors lightly. A mind that wanders through many books settles into none of them.
On friendship, he advises thinking carefully before choosing a friend and then trusting completely. He treats shared life with a friend as one of the great goods.
Practising hardship weakens the fear of loss. He suggests living for a few days on poor food and rough clothes, so that the fear of losing wealth loses some of its hold.
Death is not a single event ahead of us. Each day uses up part of life, so we are dying all along and have no reason to dread only the last step.
Travelling will not cure restlessness. A person who is unhappy at home carries the same mind abroad, and the work has to be done on oneself.
Seneca argues that enslaved people are human beings and should be treated with decency. Critics note that he lived in wealth supported by that system.

In the letter on crowds, Seneca warns that mixing with them leaves one more greedy, cruel and inhuman. He describes the games where gladiators were killed and says he came home worse for having watched.
Quoting Cleanthes, he says fate leads the willing and drags the unwilling. The Stoic path is to want what happens, so that necessity feels like choice.
In the letter on suicide, he holds that a person may leave life when it can no longer be lived well. He treats the freedom to die as a final guard against being forced to live in disgrace.

books.thesis: Personal identity is not what matters, and once you see that, ethics and death look different.
books.summary:
Parfit asks what a person is and whether the answer changes how we should live. Everyday views about self-interest, identity and morality seem to assume something we may be unable to find when we look closely.

The book has four parts, on self-defeating theories, rationality and time, personal identity and future generations. Parfit argues for reductionism: a person's existence just consists in physical and psychological facts, with no further deep fact such as a soul. Thought experiments such as teletransportation and split brains are meant to show that what matters is continuity of memory and character, not strict identity. He said this made death seem less bad. The last part turns to population ethics and a conclusion he disliked and could not escape. Critics resist his reductionism.
ideas: Some theories of self-interest and morality can be self-defeating, Parfit argues. Everyone following them can leave everyone worse off, as in prisoner's dilemma cases.
Being nearer in time is no rational ground for caring more about an experience. Parfit questions the common bias toward whatever is coming over what has passed.
In the teletransporter case you are scanned, destroyed on Earth and rebuilt on Mars from the scan. Parfit uses it to test whether the person who wakes up is you.
Reductionism holds that persons exist through bodily and psychological continuity. There is no extra fact, such as a soul or Cartesian ego, that makes identity deeper than those links.
The fission case shows that identity cannot be what matters. Each half of your brain is placed in a different body, and both people continue your life.
Accepting this view felt to Parfit like leaving a glass tunnel. His own life seemed less separate from others, and death felt less bad.

Parfit never found a satisfying way out of the Repugnant Conclusion. Certain reasonable-looking assumptions imply that a vast population with lives barely worth living could be better than a smaller happy one.

What matters in survival is Relation R, Parfit proposes, meaning psychological connectedness and continuity with the right kind of cause. Identity is not what matters, and this relation comes in degrees.

A policy can change which people come to exist, which is the non-identity problem. If a depletion policy gives rise to different people than conservation would, it is hard to say anyone has been harmed.

In the section on mistakes in moral mathematics, Parfit argues that acts can do harm together without harming anyone alone. In the case of the harmless torturers, each small shock is unnoticeable but the sum is agony.

books.thesis: An Epicurean poem arguing that the world is atoms and void, and that death is nothing to fear.
books.summary:
