Lucretius wrote this Latin poem in six books to explain the philosophy of Epicurus to a Roman audience. It asks what the world is made of and what follows for how people should feel about gods and death. Its stated aim is to free readers from fears he thought rested on ignorance.

The argument begins with atoms and empty space. Nothing comes from nothing, and nothing returns to nothing. The soul is material and disperses at death, so there is no afterlife to dread. The gods exist but take no interest in us, and thunder and disease have natural causes. Lucretius compares his verse to honey on the rim of a cup of bitter medicine. The poem seems unfinished and ends with a plague. Modern readers disagree on whether his arguments against fearing death work, since death may still deprive us of good things.
ideas: Lucretius says he is putting hard doctrine into sweet verse, like honey on the rim of a cup of bitter medicine, so that readers will take it in.
Nothing comes from nothing and nothing is destroyed into nothing. Things are made and unmade by matter rearranging, which is why the world renews itself without a creator.
Everything is made of invisible atoms moving in empty space. Differences in shape and arrangement explain the many properties of the things we see.
Atoms sometimes swerve unpredictably. Lucretius uses this idea to break strict necessity and leave room for free will.
The mind and soul are material, made of fine atoms that spread out when the body dies. Nothing remains to suffer after death.
We feel no distress about the endless time before we were born, and Lucretius says the same calm should apply to the time after we are gone.
The poem opens with Agamemnon sacrificing his daughter Iphigenia, offered as an example of the evil that religion can inspire. Lucretius insists the gods live untroubled and do not meddle.

Book Two opens with the line that it is sweet to watch from shore the struggle of a ship in a storm. Lucretius says it is sweet to see from what troubles you are free, and he uses the image to praise philosophic calm.
Book Four takes love apart. He argues that passion for a single person is a kind of illusion and an affliction, and advises taking the physical side lightly instead of becoming bound to one lover.
The poem ends with the plague of Athens, described in grim detail. Many readers have found it an odd ending and have debated whether it was meant to be finished.

books.thesis: Modern moral language is a heap of fragments, and virtue needs practices, community and tradition.
books.summary:
MacIntyre opens with a thought experiment. After a catastrophe, science is wiped out, and later generations keep scraps of its vocabulary without the understanding that gave them sense. He says modern morality is in that condition. The book asks why moral arguments today seem endless.

He traces the story from Aristotle's ethics of virtue through the Enlightenment attempts to ground morality in reason alone. Those attempts failed, he argues, leaving a culture where moral claims often work as expressions of preference. His proposal is to recover virtue by understanding it through practices, the shape of a whole life as a story, and the traditions that carry such stories. Critics call this nostalgic and worry it leads to relativism. It is unclear whether tradition-based ethics can work in a pluralist society.
ideas: MacIntyre imagines a world where science is destroyed and only fragments of its language survive. He claims our moral vocabulary has lost its original context in just that way.
Emotivism is the view that moral judgments only express feelings or preferences. MacIntyre says people use moral language that way while pretending to appeal to impersonal standards.
The Enlightenment project of justifying morality by reason alone, in Kant, Hume and others, failed in his view. It discarded the idea of a human purpose that gave moral rules point.
He puts the choice as Nietzsche or Aristotle. Either morality is a mask for the will to power, or we should return to a purpose-based ethics of the virtues.
A practice is a cooperative human activity with its own standards of excellence, such as chess or farming. The virtues are the qualities needed to achieve the goods internal to it.
A human life has a narrative unity, MacIntyre says. We are characters in a story with a quest, and we make sense of actions by seeing where they fit in that story.
Moral reasoning happens inside traditions carried by communities. The book ends by hoping for another, different, St Benedict to help local communities sustain civility.

Internal goods can only be had by taking part in a practice, while external goods are things such as money or fame. In MacIntyre's example of teaching a child chess by offering sweets, the child must come to value excellence itself.
Three social characters embody emotivism: the Aesthete, the Manager and the Therapist. Each treats ends as given and asks only how to get what one wants.

Rival moral arguments in modern debates on justice, war and abortion are interminable, he holds, because they use premises that cannot be weighed against each other. The disagreement is deep, not merely about facts.

books.thesis: People change morally through attention: the slow work of seeing others justly, against the ego.
books.summary:
This short book collects three essays by Iris Murdoch, written when moral philosophy pictured the self as a will making clear choices. She asks how people change morally, and suspects the answer lies in what happens before any choice is made.

Her answer is attention. Moral work is the slow, continuous effort to see other people and the world justly, against the pull of an ego that spins comforting stories. Her examples are a mother-in-law who revises her opinion of her daughter-in-law without doing or saying anything, and a hovering kestrel that pulls her out of her own worries. Goodness, for Murdoch, is real and draws us. It cannot be reduced to our wishes or decisions. The essays give no method for becoming good and leave open how far the Good can be defended without religion.
ideas: Murdoch criticises the picture of a lonely will choosing between options. It overrates the moment of decision, she says, and neglects the vision that shapes what choices look possible.
The moral life is continuous. What matters happens in how we look at people and situations over time, long before we face a decision.
In her example, a mother-in-law sees her son's wife as vulgar, then looks again and sees her as fresh and spontaneous. All the change takes place inside her.
Attention is the main moral skill. Murdoch borrows the term from Simone Weil and describes it as a just and loving gaze directed at an individual reality.
The selfish ego is a fantasy machine that builds flattering stories and distorts what we see. Clear sight of others takes constant effort.
A hovering kestrel makes her forget her own anxious preoccupations. She uses the moment to show how nature and art can draw us out of the self.
The Good is real and attracts us like a centre of gravity. It cannot be defined away as a human invention, even though we lack a clear picture of it.
Unselfing is her word for what happens when great art or nature pulls us out of our small concerns. She sees it as training in moral perception, not mere pleasure.

Love is the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real. It is the main discipline of moral attention, and it works against the ego's urge to turn others into figures in its own story.
Taking up Plato's image of the sun as the Good, she argues that moral progress is a movement toward perfection. Perfection is known only dimly and still guides us as a standard.

books.thesis: Some of what we are blamed or praised for comes down to luck, and moral theory struggles to admit it.
books.summary:
These essays, published between 1973 and 1981, share a worry about ethical theory that aims at purity. The title essay asks how much of what we are praised or blamed for depends on matters outside our control. It asks why moral philosophy pretends otherwise.

Williams argues through examples. Gauguin leaves his family to paint in Tahiti, and whether he was justified depends on whether the painting succeeds, which he could not know beforehand. A lorry driver who is not at fault runs over a child and feels a regret that no bystander shares. Williams uses such cases to attack the Kantian hope that morality is shielded from luck. He also argues that utilitarian and Kantian demands can alienate people from the projects that give life a point. He offers no neat replacement.
ideas: Williams distrusts ethical theory that tries to make morality neat and shielded from the accidents of life. That suspicion holds together essays written between 1973 and 1981.
The Kantian hope that moral worth depends only on the will is a comforting fantasy, Williams argues. It promises immunity from luck, and he thinks no such immunity exists.
Gauguin's choice to leave his family for Tahiti can only be judged by how it turns out. Williams says it is justified partly if he becomes a great painter, which no one could know beforehand.
A blameless lorry driver who runs over a child feels agent-regret, which an onlooker does not. Williams describes it as a special regret for what he did, even though he was not at fault.

Some moral deliberation is itself a failing, and Williams calls it one thought too many. A man who can save only one of two people, one of them his wife, should not stop to check whether saving her is permissible.
Morality that demands impartial sacrifice can alienate people from their own commitments. Integrity, the loyalty to projects that make life worth living, then gets treated as mere self-indulgence.
A person has a reason to act only if it connects with something already in their motivations. Williams argues this in the essay on internal and external reasons.
Nagel's reply to Williams is the usual starting point for the debate on moral luck. Nagel adds a taxonomy that includes luck in results, circumstance, constitution and cause.

Necessity can be found inside deliberation and not only imposed from outside. In the essay on practical necessity, Williams uses Luther's 'I can do no other' to show that a person can feel some options are not open to them without being forced.

When moral claims conflict, the claim that loses leaves a remainder. Regret and a sense of what was owed are not mistakes, Williams argues in the essay on ethical consistency, so ethics is not a tidy system.

books.t: Ethics and the Limits of Philosophy
books.thesis: Moral theories cannot deliver the foundation they promise, which is no reason to stop thinking about ethics.
books.summary:
Williams starts from the Socratic question of how one should live and asks whether moral philosophy can answer it by theory. He doubts that the main contenders, utilitarianism and Kantianism, can deliver what they promise: a reasoned foundation that any rational person must accept.

He distinguishes ethics from what he calls the morality system, a narrow scheme built around obligation, blame and voluntariness. Real ethical life is broader and uses thick concepts such as cruelty, courage and gratitude, which mix description with evaluation. He worries that theory can wreck the ethical confidence it hopes to justify. The book does not give up on reflection. It treats philosophy as a way to understand and criticise our ethical lives, and leaves open how to reason without a neutral standpoint.
ideas: Ethics starts from the Socratic question of how one should live. Williams says this is wider and messier than the question of what a person's duty is in some narrow case.
The morality system is a peculiar institution, in Williams's phrase, and it misrepresents much of what matters in ethical life. It centres on obligation, blame and guilt.
Thick ethical concepts such as coward, brutal and grateful describe and evaluate at once. They belong to particular communities, and Williams thinks they can still carry real knowledge.
Reflection can destroy ethical knowledge. Theory can undermine confident habits while giving nothing equally dependable in their place.
Williams calls it relativism of distance when he says it makes little sense to praise or condemn societies that are too remote to be real options for us.

Theory cannot prove its own foundations, because there is no Archimedean point. Williams means that no neutral place exists outside our ethical life, and he doubts utilitarianism or Kantianism can supply one.
The Greeks treated character, luck and shame more honestly than modern morality does. Williams gives particular credit to Aristotle and the tragedians.

Science might converge on an absolute conception of the world, but ethical thought has no such convergence to hope for. Williams uses this contrast to mark the limit of the comparison between the two.
Aristotle's hope of deriving an ethics from a theory of human nature looks doubtful to Williams. Even if we knew our nature, it would not settle how to live among competing ways of life.
Philosophy has a more modest role than laying a foundation. It should help us understand and criticise our ethical life from within, Williams says, and not build a base for it from outside.

books.thesis: Fair principles are the ones you would choose without knowing your place in society.
books.summary:
Rawls asks what principles should govern the basic institutions of a society of free and equal people. He wants an alternative to utilitarianism, which he thinks allows some people's basic claims to be traded away for a larger total of happiness. His answer is called justice as fairness.

His method is the original position: imagine representatives choosing principles for society behind a veil of ignorance, not knowing their class, talents, race or even their view of the good life. They would pick two principles: equal basic liberties for everyone, and inequalities allowed only if they come with fair equality of opportunity and benefit the least well off. Critics varied: Nozick defended strong property rights, communitarians questioned the picture of the self, and feminists asked about the family. Rawls later revised his view.
ideas: Justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought. A law or arrangement that is unjust must be reformed, Rawls says, however efficient it is.
Utilitarianism fails to take seriously the separateness of persons. Rawls objects that it can justify sacrificing some people's basic interests for a greater sum of advantage to others.

Fair principles come from a choice made without bargaining power. In the original position, people choose principles of justice together in a hypothetical situation set up so that fairness decides the result.
The veil of ignorance blocks self-serving principles by hiding who you are. Behind it nobody knows their class, talents, social position or conception of the good.
Liberty cannot be traded for economic gain, because the first principle takes priority over the second. It gives everyone an equal set of basic liberties.
The difference principle allows social and economic inequalities only when they work to the benefit of the least advantaged. Offices must also be open under fair equality of opportunity.
Rawls expects people behind the veil to protect themselves against the worst position. Harsanyi replies that this reasoning is too cautious and that expected utility is a better guide.

Justice applies to the basic structure of society and not to every individual choice. That structure is how major institutions assign rights, duties and shares of social benefits, and Rawls leaves individual conduct and private associations to other principles.

Rawls justifies his method by fit, through reflective equilibrium. Principles and considered judgments are adjusted against each other until they match, and the original position earns trust by how well it matches our firm convictions.

Rawls measures advantage with an index of primary goods, such as rights, liberties, opportunities, income and the social bases of self-respect. Any rational person is assumed to want these whatever else they want.

books.thesis: Taylor traces where the modern self came from and what moral sources it still draws on.
books.summary:
Taylor traces how people in the modern West came to understand themselves as having inner depths, as owing respect to all humans, and as entitled to affirm ordinary life. He asks where this identity came from and what moral sources it still draws on, whether or not we admit it.

He proceeds historically, through Plato, Augustine's turn inward, Descartes, Montaigne, the Romantics and modern writers. His central claim is that having an identity means having an orientation in moral space, a sense of what is worth doing and being, which a purely naturalistic picture of the person cannot capture. Some readers find the story too confident and too shaped by Taylor's Catholic sympathies. He admits these sources are contested, and the book leaves open whether they can last without the religious background that first fed them.
ideas: Identity is an orientation in moral space. Knowing who I am means knowing where I stand on questions of what is good and worth doing.
Strong evaluation ranks desires as higher or lower, and as worthy or base. It does not merely register which desire is stronger.
Some goods, which Taylor calls hypergoods, rank above others and give a framework for judging the rest. People usually hold such frameworks without stating them.
Augustine shifted attention inward, finding the path to God inside the self. Taylor treats this as an early step toward the modern sense of inner depth.
Descartes and Locke brought a disengaged, objectifying stance toward the self. In it we stand back and remake ourselves by control and method.
The Reformation and later movements affirmed ordinary life, work and family as places of real value. This overturned older ideas that the highest life lay in contemplation or war.
Romantic expressivism made inner nature a source of moral direction. It held that each person has an original way of being human, which prepared the modern ideal of authenticity.
Frameworks are inescapable, Taylor argues. A person with no orientation toward the good would not be free but in an identity crisis, unable to tell what matters or who they are.

Life goods, the things we value, differ from constitutive goods, the sources that make them worth valuing. These moral sources can empower us, and a loss of faith in them leaves ideals hard to sustain.
Modernist writers such as Joyce, Eliot and Pound use epiphanies, moments in which a deeper meaning shows itself. Taylor reads these as a late form of the Romantic search for sources inside the self.

books.thesis: Authenticity is a real ideal, but without something beyond the self to answer to, it shrinks into narcissism.
books.summary:
Taylor asks whether the modern emphasis on self-fulfilment is a sign of decline or holds an ideal worth saving. He wants to stand between those who mock it as narcissism and those who simply celebrate it.

He names three malaises of modernity: a narrowing individualism, the dominance of instrumental reason, and a drift toward soft despotism in politics. Against critics, he argues that authenticity is a real moral ideal, which grew from thinkers like Rousseau and Herder: each person has their own way of being human to live out. But the ideal needs something beyond the self. Choices matter only against horizons of significance, and identity is formed in dialogue with others. Without that background, authenticity shrinks into self-absorption.
ideas: Individualism brings real gains in freedom to choose one's own life, but Taylor says it can also narrow people's concern. It can leave them less interested in others and in larger purposes.

Authenticity is a moral ideal with its own demands, and both critics and defenders of modern culture miss this. Critics see narcissism, defenders see liberation, and Taylor says neither sees the ideal.
The modern ideal of authenticity has a source in Herder's idea that each person has an original way of being human. Each has a measure of their own to live up to.
No one can work out an identity alone. The dialogical self takes shape in conversation with significant others, which is why recognition matters.
Choices count only against horizons of significance. These are a background of things that matter independently of my choosing them, such as history, nature, community and the demands of others.
Soft relativism undermines itself. The claim that everyone has a right to their own values rests on the value of self-choice, which is itself a value beyond what anyone chooses.
Following Tocqueville, Taylor warns of soft despotism. People absorbed in private lives leave decisions to a distant administrative power that treats them gently and gives them little say.

Modernity has three malaises, in Taylor's account: individualism, the primacy of instrumental reason, and the loss of freedom through soft despotism. The book tries to take them seriously without wishing for the past.
When instrumental reason dominates, technology and cost-benefit thinking crowd out other ways of valuing things. Taylor defines it as the kind of rationality that seeks the best means to a given end.

Taylor's method is retrieval, which means finding the moral ideal behind a degraded practice and not simply praising or condemning it. The book began as the 1991 Massey Lectures and was published in Canada as The Malaise of Modernity.

books.thesis: Belief went from nearly unavoidable to one option among many, and Taylor asks what that did to meaning.
books.summary:
Around 1500 in Latin Christendom it was almost impossible not to believe in God. Today belief is one option among many, and often a contested one. His long book asks how that change came about and what it has done to the way people find meaning.

He rejects what he calls subtraction stories, in which science removes religion and leaves humanism as what remains. Humanism, he says, was itself an invention. His account follows the shift from the porous self, open to spirits and powers, to the buffered self, and the rise of disciplined reform from the Reformation onward. The result is the immanent frame, a way of understanding the world that can be read as open or closed to the transcendent. People live under cross-pressures between belief and unbelief. Critics say his story centres on Latin Christianity.
ideas: Secularity has three senses, and Taylor cares most about the third. The first is public spaces emptied of God, the second is declining belief and practice, and the third is a condition where belief is contestable.

Humanism was an invention and not simply what remains when religion is removed. Subtraction stories say that when science and religion part, humanism is left over, and Taylor says it was a real new option.

The shift from the porous self to the buffered self changes what experience feels like. The porous self is open to spirits, demons and forces outside the mind, and the buffered self is protected from them.
Reform movements starting before and during the Reformation pushed people to remake themselves and society by discipline. Taylor treats this push as one driver of disenchantment.
The immanent frame is the natural and social order understood without reference to anything transcendent. It can be lived as closed or as open to something beyond.
People feel cross-pressures, tugged between belief and unbelief. The number of positions available keeps growing, which Taylor calls the nova effect.
People sense a place of fullness, where things come together, and disenchantment brings a feeling of flatness. They respond to that flatness in many different ways.

The link between religion and society has passed through three stages. In the paleo-Durkheimian stage church and state are bound together, in the neo-Durkheimian belonging runs through a denomination, and in the post-Durkheimian spirituality is individual.
A Great Disembedding came to see people as individuals with rights and not as members of fixed orders. This change in the social imaginary made a moral order of mutual benefit seem natural.
The 1960s began an age of authenticity, Taylor thinks, in which each person is encouraged to find their own way. Religion survives, but as one option among many and often on the terms of the self.

books.thesis: How far a good life depends on luck, as Nussbaum reads it in Greek tragedy and philosophy.
books.summary:
Nussbaum asks how much of a good human life is at the mercy of luck. She asks whether a person can flourish whatever happens, or whether flourishing depends on friends, health, politics and chance. She reads Greek tragedy and philosophy side by side.

She reads Plato as trying to make goodness secure against fortune by setting reason above love and need. Aristotle, she argues, allows a more exposed kind of good life, in which friendship, political activity and responsiveness to particular situations matter and can be damaged. The tragedians, especially in Agamemnon and Hecuba, show conflicts between real values and characters broken by events. She suggests vulnerable goods are valuable partly because they can be lost. Scholars dispute her readings of Plato in particular. The book does not settle whether a life open to loss is worth the price.
ideas: A good life depends on things outside our control, and Nussbaum asks how far. She names friends, health, political circumstances and sheer chance.
Even a right choice can leave real moral remainder. In Agamemnon the king must choose between sacrificing his daughter and abandoning the fleet, and Nussbaum says his anguish shows this.
Hecuba shows a person of good character broken by catastrophe. Nussbaum uses it to suggest that virtue can be damaged by what happens to us.
Plato's early dialogues try to make goodness invulnerable. Nussbaum presents their hope that a science of measurement could remove luck from ethics as that attempt.
Nussbaum reads the Symposium as urging us to leave behind love of particular persons. She takes the speech of Alcibiades as a reminder of what that ascent would cost.
For Aristotle, practical wisdom responds to the situation instead of applying fixed rules. A good life needs friends, resources and a trained perception of particular cases.
Vulnerability is part of the value of friendship, love and civic life. Nussbaum says the fragile goods of a human life are like a plant, unlike a jewel.
Antigone shows a conflict between two real claims, family piety and civic duty, and Creon fails by seeing only one. Nussbaum thinks the play shows that a good person can be forced into wrongdoing.

The Phaedrus marks a change of view by Plato, Nussbaum argues. He now allows that madness and passion can be sources of the greatest goods, and the self-sufficient reason of the middle dialogues is partly given up.
A good life can be undone by bad luck. Nussbaum notes that Aristotle says Priam's disasters can damage his happiness, though a good person will bear it nobly and not become wretched.

books.thesis: Emotions are intelligent judgments about what we value, not blind surges that reason must restrain.
books.summary:
Nussbaum asks what emotions are and what part they should play in ethical and political life. Her answer, given in the subtitle The Intelligence of Emotions, is that they are judgments about things that matter to our flourishing, not blind surges that reason must hold in check.

The book begins with her grief at her mother's death, which she uses to show that emotion recognises the importance of another person. She builds on the Stoics but rejects their wish to stamp emotions out, saying emotions reveal how needy and vulnerable we are. She draws on developmental psychology, literature and music, including Proust, Dante and Mahler, to explore love, disgust, shame and compassion. Just societies, she argues, need cultivated public emotions. Critics ask whether she makes emotions too cognitive, and whether compassion fits with impartial justice.
ideas: Grief can be a way of seeing someone's value and not an irrational upset. Nussbaum opens with her grief after her mother's death to argue this.
Emotions are evaluative judgments about things outside our control that matter to our flourishing. That makes them closer to thoughts than to mere feelings.
Emotions expose how needy we are. We grieve, fear and hope because we depend on people and things we cannot command, and Nussbaum thinks a mature view should accept this.
Adult emotions carry the history of infancy. Drawing on developmental psychology, Nussbaum points to helplessness, dependence and early experiences of shame and disgust.

The ascent of love is a Platonic and Christian ladder from particular persons toward something higher. Nussbaum examines it through Plato, Augustine and Dante, and she is wary of leaving individuals behind.
Compassion needs three judgments: that the suffering is serious, that it was not deserved, and that I could meet something similar. The third makes the other person part of my world.
Societies need public emotions such as compassion, since just institutions depend on citizens who feel for others. Nussbaum argues these can be cultivated through art, education and law.
Nussbaum starts from the Stoic view that emotions are judgments of value. She accepts that account but rejects the Stoic aim of removing emotions, since they track what we care about.
Music can express emotional patterns without words, Nussbaum argues, and she takes Mahler's Third Symphony as a case. This widens her account beyond what can be stated in propositions.
Narrative is a good way to learn how emotions work because it shows their history. Nussbaum reads novels like Proust's In Search of Lost Time as studies of love, jealousy and memory.

books.thesis: Before any theory, the face of another person addresses me and makes me responsible.
books.summary:
Levinas asks what comes before knowing, before theory and before any system of thought. His answer is the encounter with another person. He argues that Western philosophy has tended to reduce everything, other people included, to something the thinker can grasp and absorb. He calls this totality.

Against it, he describes the face of the other as something that exceeds every concept I form, and he calls this infinity. The face is an expression that addresses me and makes a demand, and the first thing it says is that I may not kill. My responsibility is asymmetrical: I owe it without expecting anything back. Ethics therefore comes before ontology, the study of being. The book is dense, moves between phenomenology and Jewish thought, and is hard going. It leaves open how a face-to-face relation becomes justice among many people.
ideas: Western philosophy tends to reduce everything to a single system of the Same, which Levinas calls totality. Other people become objects of knowledge or use.
Before the other person appears, the self lives in enjoyment and dwelling, at home in the world. The encounter interrupts that self-contentment.
The other person exceeds any idea I form of them. Levinas calls this infinity, since the other can never be contained in a concept.
The face is an expression that addresses me and not an object I look at. It calls for a response and cannot be mastered.
The first word of the face is that I may not kill. Levinas treats this as the origin of ethical obligation, whether or not it is heard.
My responsibility for the other is asymmetrical, and it is not a contract. I am responsible for them without waiting for them to be responsible for me.
Ethics is first philosophy, because the relation to the other comes before knowledge and before being. The rest of philosophy depends on it.
Taking ontology as first philosophy makes philosophy a philosophy of power, Levinas says in the opening section. He ties this to war, the state in which beings are reduced to roles in a whole.
Levinas sets Abraham against Ulysses. Ulysses returns home and keeps to the Same, while Abraham leaves his country for an unknown land and answers a call.
Fecundity, the relation to a child, is a way of being beyond oneself. Levinas says it opens a time that continues after one's own death, without making the child a mere extension of the parent.

books.thesis: Fragments on attention, affliction and decreation, on how the ego drags the soul down and grace lifts it.
books.summary:
This is a selection from Simone Weil's notebooks, arranged by her friend Gustave Thibon and published in 1947, four years after her death. It is made of fragments, not chapters. Its question is how a person can turn toward the good when the ego and the pull of nature keep dragging the soul down, as gravity drags a stone.

Weil answers in short entries on attention, affliction, the void and what she calls decreation. Grace comes from outside and lifts us. We cannot earn it, only make room for it. She mixes Christian mysticism with Plato, Greek tragedy and Indian texts. Thibon selected and ordered the entries and shaped the result to his own religious view, so scholars treat the arrangement with caution. The book cannot be read as a system, and it leaves open how a reader without her faith might use it.
ideas: Self-interest and the ego pull the soul downward as reliably as physical laws, and Weil calls this gravity. Grace comes from beyond.
Attention is the rarest kind of generosity. Weil defines it as turning toward what is real without forcing it, and saw it as the substance of prayer.
Affliction differs from suffering. It joins physical pain, social humiliation and a sense of being crushed, and it can destroy a person's feeling of being someone.
False comfort blocks grace, so Weil says we should accept the void and not fill it with imaginary consolations. The openness that grace needs is closed by them.
Decreation means undoing the self's claim to be the centre of things. Weil asks for the ego to be given up so that something real can take its place.
Beauty is a trace of the good in the material world. It holds our attention without any wish to possess it.
Real evil is monotonous and dull, while imaginary evil is varied and exciting. Weil says the reverse holds for good, since imaginary good is boring and real good is always new and surprising.
The book is a sequence of aphorisms and not a systematic treatise, and Thibon shaped it. He assembled it from notebooks Weil left with him in 1942, and it was published after her death.
God's absence from the world is a sign of love and not of neglect. In Weil's account, creation is an act of withdrawal, and God lets the world exist by retreating.
False good often comes dressed as the social. Weil uses Plato's Great Beast for the collective force that gives out opinion and approval, and says real goodness must resist its pull.

books.thesis: Berlin's essays, including the split between negative and positive freedom and a warning about the second.
books.summary:
Berlin's 1969 collection has four essays: on twentieth century political ideas, historical inevitability, Mill, and the famous Two Concepts of Liberty. The question running through them is what freedom means, and why people have done terrible things in its name.

Berlin separates negative liberty, being left alone by others, from positive liberty, being one's own master. He treats both as legitimate but warns that positive liberty can be bent into a doctrine that some rational elite knows people's true selves and may force them to be free. Behind this lies value pluralism, his belief that human goods are many and can conflict without a hidden harmony. Critics, including MacCallum, argue the distinction is too sharp, since freedom always involves an agent, an obstacle and a goal.
ideas: The idea that history follows laws that excuse individuals would dissolve praise, blame and moral responsibility. Berlin attacks it in Historical Inevitability.
Negative liberty is the area in which a person can act without being obstructed by others. Berlin treats it as the core of what most liberals value.
Positive liberty is the wish to be one's own master, a subject and not an object. It means steering one's life by one's own purposes.
Positive liberty turns dangerous when it splits the self into a real, rational self and an ordinary one. That split can justify coercing people for their own good.
Harmony among human goods is a dangerous fantasy. Value pluralism says that goods such as liberty, equality and justice are many and sometimes conflict, so some loss is unavoidable.
Berlin reads Mill as defending liberty because people are fallible and differ in the ends they pursue. A society therefore needs room for experiments in living.
Critics like MacCallum say Berlin's two categories blur, because there is one concept of freedom. It always involves an agent, an obstacle and a goal.

The two concepts are historical strands and not a strict logical split, Berlin clarifies in the introduction added in 1969. Two Concepts of Liberty began as his inaugural lecture at Oxford in 1958, and the volume answers critics.
Liberty is liberty and not equality, justice or culture. Poverty may make freedom worthless to a person, Berlin says, but it does not make it absent, and the two should not be confused.

Retreating to the inner citadel gains freedom by changing the self, and Berlin thinks it can be a way of giving up. A person escapes coercion by shrinking what he wants, which is a form of positive liberty.

books.thesis: The bullshitter does not care whether what he says is true, which Frankfurt calls worse than lying.
books.summary:
Frankfurt wrote this essay in the 1980s and published it as a small book in 2005. He observes that there is a great deal of bullshit around and little theory of what it is. The book asks what bullshit is and how it differs from lying.

His central claim is that the liar and the bullshitter stand in different relations to truth. The liar knows the truth and works to hide it, so he is still tied to it. The bullshitter does not care whether what he says is true, only what impression it makes. For this reason Frankfurt calls bullshit a worse enemy of truth than lying. He suggests it flourishes when people feel obliged to speak on matters they know little about, and when scepticism about objectivity leads people to prize sincerity instead. Critics say his line between liar and bullshitter is too tidy.
ideas: Bullshit is everywhere, yet there is almost no theory of it. Frankfurt sets out to say what it is.
Bullshit is a kind of pretence short of lying, especially about one's own thoughts, feelings and attitudes. Frankfurt reaches this by way of the idea of humbug.
A liar needs to care about the truth in order to avoid it, whereas the bullshitter has no concern with it either way.
Bullshit arises when circumstances demand speech beyond one's knowledge. People feel obliged to give opinions on every subject.
Wittgenstein caught Fania Pascal speaking beyond what she knew. She told him she felt like a dog that had been run over, and he replied that she did not know what that felt like.
Doubt about objectivity pushes people toward sincerity, and Frankfurt calls that bullshit as well. Those who doubt that any account of reality can be correct fall back on being true to oneself.
A bullshitter's statements may even be true by accident. What matters is that they were picked for their effect and not for their accuracy, which is why they erode the habit of caring.
Frankfurt's essay waited nearly twenty years for its wide audience. It first appeared in 1986 in the journal Raritan, and its sales as a small book in 2005 surprised many people.
Bullshit is a greater enemy of truth than lies. The liar still respects the truth enough to hide it, while the bullshitter loosens the hold of any distinction between true and false.

The bull session is speech that is unserious by shared agreement. People speak freely, trying out ideas without committing to them, and everyone understands the talk is not meant as a serious statement of belief.

books.thesis: Our final reasons for acting come from what we love, and love creates the value it responds to.
books.summary:
Frankfurt asks where our reasons for acting finally come from. Moral rules, self-interest and reason itself all seem to run out at some point. He suggests that what we care about and love provides the last ground. The book is a short set of essays.

He defines love as a disinterested concern for the existence and good of the beloved. He reverses the usual order of explanation: love does not respond to the value of what we love but creates it. Parents love their children without having chosen to, and that is his model case. He also writes of volitional necessity, the fact that some things we simply cannot bring ourselves to do, and ties identity to what we cannot help caring about. Critics ask whether this makes love's authority arbitrary, and whether it can account for love of unworthy objects.
ideas: Reasons for action come to an end somewhere, and Frankfurt places the end in what we care about. Practical reason cannot be the final foundation of action.
Love is a disinterested concern for the existence of the beloved and for what is good for them. It is not a means to some benefit for ourselves.
Love creates the value of the beloved and does not respond to value that was already there. Frankfurt reverses the common picture.
A parent's love for a child is Frankfurt's main example. The child has not earned it by merit, and the parent did not choose it after weighing reasons.
Volitional necessity marks the limits of the will. There are things we cannot bring ourselves to do, and these limits show what we love and who we are.
Meaning comes from wholehearted care for something and not from an external standard. What a person cares about determines the shape of their life.
Critics ask whether love can ground reasons if it can attach to unworthy objects. The book gives only a partial answer.
Love is of a particular person and not of a list of qualities. The beloved cannot be swapped for someone with the same traits, and this particularity is part of why love gives reasons.
What binds us most is what we cannot bring ourselves to will against, not what reason alone commands. Frankfurt contrasts this volitional necessity with the rational necessity of Kant.
Wholeheartedness, being free of inner conflict about what one cares about, marks a good life. Frankfurt ties it to a kind of self-love that means caring about one's own ends.

books.t: The Open Society and Its Enemies
books.thesis: Certainty about utopia ends in tyranny, while open societies can criticise and correct their mistakes.
books.summary:
Popper wrote this in New Zealand during the Second World War and called it his contribution to the war effort. It asks what ideas helped make totalitarianism possible and what kind of society can resist it. Its two volumes take on Plato, then Hegel and Marx.

Popper argues that these thinkers share historicism, the belief that history follows laws that let us predict where it must go. That belief, he says, licenses leaders to override individuals for the sake of a promised future. He opposes utopian social engineering with piecemeal reform that can be tested and reversed. An open society is one where citizens can criticise policy and replace rulers without bloodshed. Many classicists and Hegel scholars say he caricatures his targets. How an open society defends itself without losing what it defends stays open.
ideas: Popper called the book his war effort. He wrote it in New Zealand during the Second World War as a response to the rise of fascism and communism.

Closed and open societies differ in how they treat custom. In a closed society customs are fixed and sacred, while in an open one individuals face personal decisions and can criticise their institutions.
Popper reads Plato's Republic as a blueprint for a closed society, with rule by philosopher-kings, censorship and fixed classes. Many classicists say this is unfair.
Historicism is mistaken and dangerous, Popper argues. It is the belief that history follows laws we can discover and use to predict the future.
Utopian engineering aims to rebuild society according to a blueprint, and it tends to require authority and the silencing of dissent. Piecemeal reform fixes specific problems and can be reversed.
Democracy is defined less by who rules than by whether a people can remove a government without violence.
Unlimited tolerance can destroy itself. This is the paradox of tolerance, and it means a society may have to defend itself against the intolerant.

Popper attacks Marx's method while crediting his motive. He treats Hegel as a defender of the authoritarian state and Marx as a historicist whose prophecies could not be tested, yet he grants Marx a sincere humanitarian motive.
Political action should aim to reduce avoidable suffering and not to maximise happiness. Popper says the first goal is clearer, less open to abuse and easier to agree on.
Leaving the sheltered life of the tribe brings what Popper calls the strain of civilization. It is the unease of having to take responsibility for one's own choices.

books.thesis: Meaning is use, and philosophical confusion comes from taking words out of the settings where they work.
books.summary:
Wittgenstein's late book, published after his death in 1953, asks how words come to mean anything, what it is to follow a rule, and why philosophical problems are so hard to leave alone. It begins by quoting Augustine on how a child learns language, as if every word were a name for an object.

Wittgenstein gives numbered remarks, examples and imagined scenes. He introduces language-games, family resemblance, the argument about rule-following and the argument against a private language. His view of philosophy is therapeutic: confusion arises when language is taken out of the contexts where it does its work, and the aim is to show where the confusion began. Interpreters disagree sharply about his conclusions, especially on rules, where Kripke's reading is influential and disputed.
ideas: Augustine's picture, in which words name objects and sentences combine names, describes only a small part of what we do with language. Wittgenstein opens the book by quoting it.
Words get their meaning from the activities in which they are used. Wittgenstein's language-games, such as builders calling for slabs and blocks, show this.
For a large class of cases, the meaning of a word is its use in the language. To understand a word is to know how it is used.
Concepts such as game share no single feature that all instances have, only overlapping similarities like members of a family. Many everyday concepts work the same way.
A rule cannot interpret itself. Following one depends on shared practice and agreement in how people go on, not on an inner act of grasping.
The beetle in the box shows how a private thing drops out of meaning. If each person had something private they called a beetle, it could play no role in the meaning of the word.
Philosophy aims to show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle. Problems arise when language goes on holiday, and the remedy is to see how words are used.

A word for a purely private sensation would have no check on correct use. Whatever seems right to the speaker would be right, and that removes any sense of being right or wrong, which is the private language argument.
Pointing at something does not settle a word's meaning by itself, since the same gesture can be taken in many ways. Ostensive definition already assumes a background of shared training.
Noticing an aspect is neither plain seeing nor plain interpretation. In the later part Wittgenstein uses the duck-rabbit figure to show this under the heading of seeing-as.

books.thesis: Language pictures the world, and what lies beyond what can be clearly said must be passed over in silence.
books.summary:
Wittgenstein's first book was published in 1921 and written partly during his First World War service. It asks how language can represent the world and what limits that places on what can be said. It begins with the sentence that the world is all that is the case.

The core idea is the picture theory. A proposition pictures a possible state of affairs by sharing its logical form. What cannot be said, such as logical form itself, ethics, aesthetics and the mystical, can only be shown. Near the end, Wittgenstein says that anyone who understands him will see his own propositions as nonsense and will throw away the ladder after climbing it. Interpreters disagree sharply over whether this means there are unsayable truths or whether the book aims to show that supposed truths are plain nonsense. He later rejected much of it.
ideas: The world is the totality of facts, not of things. The book opens by saying that the world is all that is the case.
A proposition represents by sharing logical form with the situation it describes, as a map or model does. This is the picture theory.
All sayable language can be broken down into simple propositions about how things stand. Compound propositions are truth-functions of elementary ones.
Some things can be shown but not said. Logical form is visible in the way language works, yet any attempt to state it produces nonsense.
The limits of my language mean the limits of my world, a line that has been read as pointing toward a kind of solipsism.
Ethics, value and the mystical lie outside what can be said. Wittgenstein describes the feeling of the world as a limited whole as something that cannot be put into propositions.
The book calls its own propositions nonsensical, a ladder to be thrown away after climbing. It ends by saying that whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.
The decimal numbering gives the text a form that mirrors its structure. There are seven main propositions, and the sub-propositions mark how much logical weight each carries.
Logic has no subject matter of its own. Tautologies and contradictions say nothing about the world, and Wittgenstein holds that the propositions of logic are tautologies.
Names in elementary propositions refer to simple objects, which form the unchanging substance of the world. Wittgenstein never gives an example of one.

books.thesis: We perceive through a lived body, not through sensations assembled by a detached mind.
books.summary:
Merleau-Ponty asks how perception works and what kind of being does the perceiving. He rejects two dominant pictures. Empiricism builds perception from bits of sensation. Intellectualism says the mind constructs it through judgment. He starts instead from the experience of a body living in a world.

His central claim is that the body is the subject of perception. We do not have a body the way we have a coat. We are our bodies, and they give us a practical grip on the world before any reflection. He supports this with cases from psychology and neurology, such as phantom limbs and the patient Schneider, whose injury shows a gap between concrete and abstract movement. Perception is always from a viewpoint, so things show only some sides. The book is dense and demanding, and readers disagree over how fully it escapes the mind and body split.
ideas: Perception is where knowledge starts, and science builds on the world as we live it. Merleau-Ponty asks us to return to that lived experience.
Both empiricism and intellectualism misdescribe the experience of seeing a whole object. Empiricism assembles perception from separate sensations and intellectualism says judgment constructs it.
The lived body is the subject of perception. I am my body and do not merely own it like a coat, and it gives me a way of having a world.
The body schema is a practical, pre-reflective sense of where my body is and what it can do. It lets me reach for a cup without measuring.

The patient Schneider could perform concrete movements, such as scratching a mosquito bite, but not abstract ones like pointing on command. Merleau-Ponty takes this to show that action has its own kind of understanding.

A phantom limb resists both bodily and mental explanation. The person keeps feeling a missing limb as part of their habitual world, and Merleau-Ponty says neither a purely bodily nor a purely mental account explains this.
Incompleteness belongs to how real things appear. Perception always has a point of view, so objects show only some sides and carry a horizon of more to see.
Consciousness is first of all not an 'I think' but an 'I can'. This is motor intentionality: the body is directed toward the world in action before any thought about it.
We perceive structured wholes, a figure against a ground, and not collections of atomic sensations. Merleau-Ponty draws on Gestalt psychology for this.
Speech is a kind of gesture, and thought completes itself in being expressed. Meaning is therefore not a private idea that language merely labels.

books.thesis: Bracket your assumptions about the world, then describe experience as it is given.
books.summary:
Husserl's Ideas I (1913) asks how philosophy could become a rigorous science of experience. He wants to start from what is given in consciousness, not from theories about the world.

The method begins with the natural attitude, our default belief that the world is simply there. The epoché suspends that belief so experience itself can be studied. Consciousness is always consciousness of something, which he calls intentionality, and he separates the act of experiencing from the object as experienced. Varying examples in imagination, he says, lets us grasp essences. The book ends in transcendental idealism, where the world gets its sense from consciousness. Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty took the method elsewhere and rejected that turn, and it is still debated whether the bracketing can be carried out.
ideas: Husserl starts by describing the natural attitude, our ordinary stance in which we treat the world as simply there and take its existence for granted.
Whatever presents itself in intuition, as it is given, is a legitimate source of knowledge within the limits in which it is given. Husserl calls this the principle of all principles.
Essences are reached by varying an example in imagination to see what cannot change. Husserl calls this eidetic reduction.
The epoché brackets our belief that the world exists without denying it. This lets experience be examined on its own terms.
Consciousness is always consciousness of something. Husserl calls this intentionality, and the object may be real, remembered or imagined.
Husserl separates noesis, the act of perceiving or judging, from noema, the object as it is experienced. This lets him describe experience without settling what exists outside it.
The reduction leads to pure consciousness, and Husserl argues that the world's sense depends on it. This transcendental idealism is what Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty rejected.
Husserl opposes psychologism, the view that the laws of logic are just facts about how minds happen to work. He wants philosophy to become a rigorous science without presuppositions.
Phenomenology is an eidetic science of consciousness and not an empirical one. Husserl separates sciences of fact from eidetic sciences of essence, such as geometry.

Physical things are given only through changing perspectival profiles, which Husserl calls adumbrations, while consciousness is given directly. He therefore treats consciousness as absolute and the world as relative to it.

books.thesis: Desire produces reality; psychoanalysis and capitalism both try to capture it.
books.summary:
Deleuze, a philosopher, and Guattari, a psychoanalyst, wrote this first volume of Capitalism and Schizophrenia after 1968. They ask what desire is and why people so often come to want their own repression. They aim at Freudian psychoanalysis and the power capitalism supports.

Their central move is to treat desire as productive, not as a response to lack. Desire makes connections, flows and things, which they call desiring-machines. Psychoanalysis, they say, locks the unconscious inside the family triangle of mother, father and child. Capitalism frees flows of money and labour, then recaptures them. They praise the schizophrenic process as a way of breaking through, apart from the suffering of hospital patients. Their alternative is schizoanalysis, and its politics stay open. Critics find the style obscure and the view of madness romantic.
ideas: Desire is productive, and treating it as a lack to be filled is a mistake that suits those in power, the authors say. Desire makes connections, flows and new things.
Desiring-machines are the authors' image for desire at work. They are always connecting to something else, as a mouth connects to a breast or a hand to a tool.
Psychoanalysis domesticates desire into a private drama. The authors accuse it of reducing the unconscious to the family triangle of mother, father and child.
The question of why people fight for their servitude as if it were their salvation drives the book. Following Spinoza and Reich, the authors apply it to fascism.
The body without organs is a surface on which desire is recorded. The phrase comes from Artaud, and the body resists being organised into a fixed hierarchy of functions.
Capitalism decodes older social codes and frees flows of money and labour, then re-captures them. In the authors' view it works only by constantly approaching its own limits.

Schizoanalysis is the authors' alternative to psychoanalysis. They praise the schizophrenic process as a breakthrough while separating it from the clinical patient, a distinction critics find romantic.
The unconscious works through three syntheses: connective, disjunctive and conjunctive. These are the ways desire joins, divides and distributes its elements.
History falls into three social machines, the primitive territorial one, the despotic one and the capitalist one. Each has its own way of coding and managing flows of desire.
Foucault's preface calls the book an introduction to the non-fascist life. The authors set a paranoid, fascist pole of investment against a schizophrenic, revolutionary one.

books.thesis: Western thought ranks speech above writing, and its own texts undo that ranking.
books.summary:
Derrida asks why Western thought has placed speech above writing, treating the spoken word as close to thought and writing as a pale copy. He calls this phonocentrism, part of a wider logocentrism that looks for a source of meaning that is fully present.

He reads Saussure, Lévi-Strauss and Rousseau to show that each calls writing secondary while relying on features that belong to writing. He introduces différance, the idea that meaning comes from differences between signs and from endless deferral, and the trace, the mark of what a sign differs from. He also describes the supplement, which both adds to a thing and replaces it. His line that there is nothing outside the text is often taken to mean only words exist. Defenders say it means no reading can step outside context. Critics such as Searle found the argument obscure and exaggerated.
ideas: Western thought has long treated spoken presence as the source of meaning and writing as a secondary copy of speech. Derrida calls this habit logocentrism.
Saussure treats writing as external to language, yet his account of language relies on differences between signs, Derrida argues. He says that feature belongs to writing.
A supplement both adds to something and substitutes for it, so the original was never complete. Derrida draws this from Rousseau, who treats writing as a dangerous supplement to speech.
Lévi-Strauss describes writing among the Nambikwara as a violence brought by outsiders. Derrida replies that this view idealises speech and overlooks forms of violence that predate writing.
Différance names both difference and deferral. A sign gets its meaning from how it differs from other signs, and that meaning is never fully settled.
No meaning is purely present, because every sign carries a trace of the others it differs from. There is no unmarked origin to find.
The line 'there is nothing outside the text' is easily misread as saying only books exist. Defenders say it means no reading can step outside context.
Writing in the narrow sense is not a late addition to speech. Archi-writing, Derrida's name for a general structure of marks and traces, makes both speech and ordinary writing possible.
The privilege given to phonetic writing is ethnocentric, Derrida argues. Western thinkers have misread non-phonetic scripts such as Chinese as less developed.

The theory of the supplement is worked out in a close reading of Rousseau's Essay on the Origin of Languages. That reading is the second half of the book, which follows a survey of the logocentric tradition.

books.thesis: One principle, equal consideration of interests, pushed consistently through hard cases.
books.summary:
Peter Singer asks how we should act on animals, abortion, euthanasia, poverty and the environment if we follow an argument wherever it leads and do not lean on tradition.

His tool is one principle: like interests count equally, whoever has them. He argues that this puts animal suffering on the moral map, and that favouring human interests only because they are human is speciesism, comparable to racism. What makes killing wrong, he holds, depends on features such as self-awareness and plans for the future, which leads him to controversial conclusions about disabled newborns. He also argues that people in wealthy countries must give far more to the poor. Disability activists protested strongly, and other philosophers dispute his utilitarian reasoning. The book leaves open how far consistency should override moral intuition.
ideas: Equal consideration of interests does not mean equal treatment. Similar interests count the same whoever has them, whatever their race, sex or species.
Speciesism is an unjustified prejudice, Singer argues, like racism and sexism. It means giving less weight to an animal's interests purely because of its species.
Killing persons wrongs them in ways that killing beings without self-awareness may not. Persons, in Singer's sense, are self-aware beings who see themselves as existing over time.
Singer rejects the sanctity of human life as a basis for ethics. He argues that a newborn's severe disability can be morally relevant to decisions, a claim that remains highly controversial.
Voluntary euthanasia should be permitted in some circumstances, Singer argues, because people have a right to make decisions about their own death. He adds that safeguards against abuse are needed.
Ordinary affluence becomes morally demanding under the drowning child analogy. If we would ruin our shoes to save a child, we should also give to relieve distant suffering.
Singer's consistency has a cost, according to his critics. Disability activists protested his views, and some philosophers say he discards strong moral intuitions that should count as evidence.
Singer defends preference utilitarianism, which weighs the satisfaction of interests and preferences of all affected beings and not only their pleasure and pain.
Factory farming is hard to defend once equal consideration is applied to food. Singer argues that the suffering it causes outweighs the minor benefit of human taste.
Birth is not a morally decisive line on abortion, Singer argues. Moral weight depends on capacities such as sentience and self-awareness, a position that many readers reject.

books.thesis: Six philosophers as advisers on unpopularity, poverty, frustration, inadequacy, heartbreak and hardship.
books.summary:
Alain de Botton asks whether philosophy can console us for everyday troubles. He pairs six thinkers with six problems, in order: Socrates and unpopularity, Epicurus and not having enough money, Seneca and frustration, Montaigne and inadequacy, Schopenhauer and a broken heart, Nietzsche and difficulty.

His premise is that philosophy began as a guide to living well and that the academic kind has drifted from that job. Each chapter mixes short biography, plain explanation and everyday scenes, and reads the philosopher as an adviser. Socrates says to follow reason over the crowd, Epicurus that friends and freedom matter more than luxury, and Seneca that we should adjust our expectations. Professional philosophers have often dismissed the book as popular and tidy. It does not try to settle disputes between the thinkers.
ideas: Philosophy began as a practical guide to living well, De Botton argues. Much academic philosophy has moved away from helping people with their troubles.
Logic should decide a matter, not majority opinion, and De Botton makes Socrates the guide for unpopularity. Socrates accepted a death sentence rather than abandon his reasoning.
Happiness needs friends, freedom and time for thought, none of which depend on luxury. De Botton cites Epicurus on money.
Anger and disappointment grow from false expectations. De Botton matches Seneca with frustration, and the remedy is to remember how much of life is outside our control.
Even the great sit on their own behinds, and this eases shame. De Botton makes Montaigne the guide for inadequacy, easing shame about the body and the mind.
Pessimism can console a broken heart. De Botton offers Schopenhauer's reminder that suffering is common and part of life, which helps us feel less singled out.
Hardship is a condition of growth, and what looks like an obstacle may be necessary to achievement. De Botton makes Nietzsche the voice for difficulty.
The book is easy to read but light on argument. It is aimed at general readers and builds each chapter around a vivid scene or image from a philosopher's life.
Epicurus separates natural and necessary desires from vain ones. De Botton uses this to question advertising that presents luxury as the route to happiness.
Offering quotations from six thinkers as remedies turns philosophy into self-help, critics note. It also passes over the disagreements between them.

books.thesis: One question, how to live, answered twenty ways through Montaigne's life and essays.
books.summary:
Sarah Bakewell takes the life of Michel de Montaigne and asks one question of it, how to live. She gives twenty answers, one per chapter, each built on a way of living Montaigne tried or described.

The structure follows the man. Montaigne withdrew to his tower library around the age of thirty-eight and began writing essays about himself and everything else. He mourned his friend La Boétie, nearly died after a riding accident, served as mayor of Bordeaux during plague and religious war, and kept asking what he knew. Bakewell draws out answers such as paying attention, questioning everything and guarding a private space inside public life. She also traces how readers over the centuries found themselves in the essays. None of the answers is final, and the book does not claim Montaigne had the last word.
ideas: Bakewell answers one question, how to live, with twenty attempts, and none is meant to be final.
Montaigne's essays began in retreat. He withdrew to his tower library at about thirty-eight, after his father's death, and began writing the essays that made him famous.
Grief for La Boétie shaped Montaigne's thinking about friendship. Bakewell shows how the loss, when La Boétie died, fed into his writing on friendship and grief.
Nearly dying can be peaceful. After being thrown from his horse and nearly killed, Montaigne found the experience calm, which fed into his view that we should not worry about death.
One answer is to read a lot and forget most of what you read. Montaigne said he had a poor memory, and he treated it as a lesson in thinking for oneself.
Montaigne's scepticism was part of his curiosity and not a pose, in Bakewell's presentation. His motto, usually given as 'What do I know', expressed a habit of doubt.
Public life calls for a back shop, a private inner room. Montaigne recommends keeping one while serving as mayor of Bordeaux during plague and war.
People call barbarous whatever is not their own custom, Montaigne suggests in the essay on cannibals. Bakewell uses it to show his early taste for comparing cultures with an open mind.
Montaigne said that he was himself the matter of his book. Bakewell shows how his essays became a self-portrait that wanders from topic to topic without a plan.
Illness was one of Montaigne's teachers, Bakewell suggests. His travels through Italy and Germany to take spa waters for kidney stones show his curiosity about other customs and about the body.

books.thesis: Give people genuineness, acceptance and empathy, and they move toward their own growth.
books.summary:
Carl Rogers collected these papers under the subtitle A Therapist's View of Psychotherapy. They ask what helps people change in therapy and what kind of person emerges when someone is freed to grow. He writes as a psychologist who came to trust his clients more than his theories.

His argument is that therapy works when the therapist offers three conditions: genuineness, unconditional positive regard and empathic understanding. With these, he says, clients drift away from facades and from what they feel they should be, toward trusting their own experience. He called the direction becoming a fully functioning person. Rogers was among the first to record sessions so they could be studied. Critics say his picture of human nature is too optimistic and the claims hard to test, and later work has debated whether these conditions are enough.
ideas: Client-centred therapy trusts the client's own capacity to find direction. The therapist follows instead of interpreting from above.
Congruence, or genuineness, means the therapist is real in the relationship rather than hiding behind a professional front.
Unconditional positive regard means accepting the client as they are, without judging or requiring them to earn approval.
Empathic understanding means sensing the client's inner world as if it were one's own, without losing the as-if quality.
Change in therapy shows as a shift in a person's relation to their feelings, from fixed and distant to flowing and owned. Rogers describes therapy as this process.
Many clients begin by hiding behind facades and asking who they are. Rogers describes them gradually dropping masks they felt they had to wear.
The fully functioning person is open to experience and trusts their own organism. Critics say this view is too optimistic about human nature.
Healthy change moves the locus of evaluation from outside the person to inside. Rogers means a shift from the approval of others to the person's own sense of what is right.
Rogers helped bring psychotherapy into the research laboratory. He was among the first to record therapy sessions and to study outcomes empirically.

The main barrier to communication is the tendency to evaluate, Rogers says in his essay on communication. He proposes that each side restate the other's view to the other's satisfaction before replying.

books.thesis: Psychology should study health and growth, not only illness.
books.summary:
Abraham Maslow asks why psychology spends so much effort on illness and so little on health. A field that studies only damaged people, he argues, distorts our picture of human nature. He wanted a psychology of growth and creativity, and the book is a landmark of what he called the third force.

He separates deficiency motivation, driven by needs we must fill, from growth motivation, which seeks fulfilment. He describes self-actualization, peak experiences of wonder and unity, and Being-values such as truth, beauty and goodness. His evidence came from case studies of people he judged unusually healthy. Critics note that he chose them by his own standards, that the sample was small, and that the framework reflects one culture. He insists that science should include values, and the book leaves open whether these ideas can be tested.
ideas: A psychology built on the study of the sick gives a distorted picture of human nature, Maslow argued. A fuller account needs to study healthy, creative and fulfilled people as well.
Growth motivation does not stop when a need is met. Deficiency motivation arises from needs that must be filled, such as safety, while growth motivation is the drive toward fulfilment.
Self-actualization is the tendency to become what one is capable of becoming. Maslow saw it as the mark of psychological health.
Peak experiences are brief moments of intense joy, wonder or unity that Maslow found many people report. He treated them as glimpses of healthy functioning.
Being-values such as truth, beauty, goodness and wholeness are what self-actualizing people tend to care about. Maslow treats them as real motives and not just preferences.
The evidence is thin, critics say, because Maslow chose his healthy subjects by his own judgment. That makes the conclusions subjective.
Healthy development depends on safety coming first. Every child faces a choice between safety and growth, and growth becomes attractive once safety needs are met enough.
Seeing a thing for its own sake differs from seeing it as a means to our needs. Maslow calls the first B-cognition and the second D-cognition.
Love that accepts the other without using them differs from love that arises from need. Maslow calls the first B-love and the second D-love.
Humanistic psychology is a third force beside behaviourism and Freudian psychoanalysis. Maslow presents it as studying the whole person and human potential.

books.thesis: Human needs rank by priority, and higher needs emerge only as lower ones are met.
books.summary:
This is the book where Maslow set out his hierarchy of needs, first sketched in a 1943 paper. He wanted a theory of motivation that treated the person as a whole, neither reduced to drives nor to responses to stimuli.

He describes physiological needs, safety, love and belonging, esteem and self-actualization. Lower needs tend to dominate until they are reasonably met, then higher ones come forward, and a satisfied need stops motivating. He studied people he considered self-actualizing, including historical figures such as Lincoln. Maslow says the order is flexible and has exceptions, and the familiar pyramid does not appear in the book. Others drew it later. Research has not strongly backed a strict order, and cultural studies suggest priorities vary.
ideas: A person who is starving finds that most other concerns shrink or disappear. Physiological needs such as hunger, thirst and sleep come first.
Safety needs cover order, predictability and protection from threat. They show most clearly in children and in times of disaster or insecurity.
Frustrated belonging is a major cause of poor adjustment, Maslow says. The need is for affection, friends and a place among others.
Esteem takes two forms, self-respect and the respect of others. Maslow connects it with confidence, achievement and a sense of being useful.
Self-actualization is the need to become what one is capable of being. Maslow studied people he judged to be examples, including Lincoln.
A satisfied need stops acting as a motivator. Lower needs tend to dominate until they are reasonably satisfied, after which higher needs emerge.
The familiar pyramid is not in the book. Maslow said the order is flexible with many exceptions, and later research has not strongly confirmed a strict sequence.
Curiosity is a basic human drive and not only a tool for survival. Beside the five levels, Maslow describes cognitive needs, the desire to know and understand.
Self-actualizing people share traits such as spontaneity, a focus on problems outside themselves, a need for privacy, autonomy, a democratic outlook and frequent peak experiences.
Maslow's percentages are illustration and not data. He suggests an average person is satisfied perhaps 85 percent in physiological needs but only about 10 percent in self-actualization.

books.t: Cognitive Therapy and the Emotional Disorders
books.thesis: Distorted interpretations keep depression and anxiety going, and they can be tested and changed.
books.summary:
Aaron Beck, trained as a psychoanalyst, noticed that his patients had streams of automatic thoughts running alongside what they said. This 1976 book asks what keeps depression and anxiety going, and answers that how people interpret events is central to how they feel and act.

Beck proposes that emotions follow from interpretations, and that people with emotional disorders show systematic distortions such as arbitrary inference, selective abstraction, overgeneralization, magnification and minimization. In depression he finds a negative view of the self, the world and the future. Therapy is a collaboration in which patient and therapist treat beliefs as hypotheses and test them against evidence. Later research gave it a large evidence base. Critics say it may overstate the causal role of thinking compared with biology and circumstances.
ideas: Thinking is the place to intervene, Beck concluded. As a psychoanalyst he noticed that patients reported streams of rapid, automatic thoughts.
Emotions follow from how a situation is interpreted and not from the situation alone. In the cognitive model, two people can react differently to the same event.
Depression rests on a self-feeding cognitive triad. It is a negative view of oneself, one's experiences and the future.
Thinking errors bias the reading of facts toward threat or loss. Beck lists arbitrary inference, selective abstraction, overgeneralization, and magnifying or minimizing events.
Anxiety comes from overestimating danger and underestimating one's ability to cope. A harmless situation can then feel overwhelming.
Collaborative empiricism treats beliefs as hypotheses to test and not as positions to argue away. Patient and therapist check them against evidence, with behavioural experiments.
Stable beliefs formed early, which Beck calls schemas, bias interpretation. Critics say the approach may overstate thinking's causal role compared with biology and circumstances.
Depression and anxiety differ in their content. Beck argues for content specificity, in which depression centres on themes of loss and defeat and anxiety on danger and threat.
Behavioural methods give depressed patients evidence against the belief that nothing can be done. Beck describes activity scheduling and graded task assignment, which counter inertia.
The Stoic idea that people are disturbed by their view of events and not by the events themselves runs behind Beck's model. He also acknowledges influences such as Albert Ellis and George Kelly.

books.thesis: Trauma from war, rape and captivity follows common patterns, and recovery runs in stages.
books.summary:
Judith Herman asks what links the damage done by combat, rape, domestic violence and political terror, and why knowledge about that damage keeps being lost. Psychiatry, she observes, has studied trauma in bursts and then forgotten it, and each revival followed a political movement: hysteria, shell shock, then the Vietnam veterans and the women's movement.

She argues that the aftermath looks similar whatever the cause. She describes the core symptoms, then argues that long captivity, in abusive homes or camps, produces a wider pattern than the standard diagnosis covers. Recovery, she says, has three stages: safety, remembrance and mourning, and reconnection with ordinary life. The stages overlap, and no one moves through them alone.
