Whether the wider pattern deserves its own diagnosis is still debated, but her staging remains a common clinical reference.
ideas: Psychiatry's interest in trauma follows a repeating cycle of study, denial and forgetting. Herman says it returns only when a social movement forces the subject open.

Trauma shows itself in three groups of symptoms. They are hyperarousal, in which the body stays on alert, intrusion, in which the event returns uninvited, and constriction, in which feeling and action shut down.
Prolonged abuse in a situation of control changes a person more broadly than a single frightening event does. Herman gives a violent home or a prison camp as examples.
Coercive control works the same way in domestic abuse and in political captivity. Herman compares the two and finds fear, isolation and the loss of any sense of choice in both.

Safety must come before uncovering the past. Recovery begins with safety, in the body and in the person's surroundings, and Herman argues that uncovering the past before safety exists tends to do harm.
Remembrance and mourning need a witness. In the second stage the survivor tells the story in full and grieves what was lost, with someone who can bear to hear it.
Healing happens in relationships. In the last stage, reconnection, survivors rebuild trust and a place among others, and group settings are often useful because they end isolation.
The standard picture of PTSD misses the damage of prolonged abuse, so Herman proposes complex post-traumatic stress disorder. The damage falls on identity and relationships.
The central conflict of trauma is what Herman calls the dialectic of trauma. It is the pull between the wish to deny horrible events and the wish to proclaim them aloud.
Bystanders are pushed to take a side, and siding with the perpetrator is tempting. The perpetrator asks only that people do nothing, while the victim asks them to share the burden.

books.thesis: Trauma is held in the body, and talk alone may not reach it.
books.summary:
Bessel van der Kolk worked with Vietnam veterans and abused children. He asks why trauma so often outlasts the event and why talking alone sometimes fails. His answer is in the title: the body holds what the mind cannot put into words, and survivors stay stuck reacting to a past that feels present.

The book mixes patient stories, brain imaging findings and his own clinical history. He argues that trauma disturbs the systems that sense danger and regulate the body, and he backs treatments that work through the body as well as speech, such as EMDR, yoga and neurofeedback. He also pushes for a wider diagnosis for traumatised children. Critics say he overstates what brain scans show and leans on small studies, and some of his preferred therapies have thinner evidence than the book suggests. It still changed how many general readers talk about trauma.
ideas: Traumatised people react to a harmless moment as if the original danger were back. Van der Kolk says the brain's alarm system keeps treating the past as the present, which leaves survivors responding to a threat that has ended.
During a flashback the thinking part of the brain goes quiet, and he says this is why survivors struggle to put what happened into words. He links the claim to imaging studies.
Many survivors lose the ability to sense their own bodies, so they cannot tell what they feel. Van der Kolk treats rebuilding that awareness as a first task of therapy.
Early neglect and abuse are common and tied to later illness and troubled lives. The book uses the large study of adverse childhood experiences to make this case.
Van der Kolk argues that children raised amid abuse show a pattern the standard adult diagnosis misses. He campaigned for a separate diagnosis, which the diagnostic manual declined to adopt.

The body needs a way to feel safe that talk cannot supply, so Van der Kolk backs EMDR, yoga, neurofeedback and theatre work. He describes these as treatments that work through the body as well as speech.
Critics say the book claims more certainty about brain mechanisms than the research supports. They add that its picture of trauma stored in the body is closer to metaphor than to a finding.
Safety with other people calms the stress response, in Van der Kolk's telling. He draws on Stephen Porges's polyvagal ideas for this, a theory that some researchers question.
Reason fails once the alarm system takes over, and he explains this with the triune brain model of reptilian, mammalian and thinking layers. The model is widely seen as outdated.
Traumatised people may freeze or stay passive when they could act to protect themselves. Van der Kolk explains this with animal studies of inescapable shock.

books.thesis: Ten therapy cases where patients meet death, freedom and isolation.
books.summary:
Irvin Yalom is an existential psychiatrist, and this book asks what happens in the consulting room when people run into the facts they most want to avoid: that they will die, that they are responsible for their own lives, and that each of us is finally alone. Ten stories, each built around one patient, show those facts surfacing through obsession, grief, weight and loneliness.

The book works by telling, not by building a system. Yalom writes as a fallible participant who admits irritation, doubt and mistakes, and he disguises his patients. His claim is that therapy is mostly an honest meeting between two people, and that real change often comes when someone stops fighting these givens and starts looking at them. Readers who want evidence will not find it. What they get is a vivid, sometimes self-critical account of one therapist's method.
ideas: Many everyday symptoms are an attempt to dodge one of three givens, Yalom claims: death, freedom and isolation. He organises his whole approach to therapy around them.
Death anxiety often hides behind other complaints. Patients bring up other troubles while their fear of ending sits underneath and shapes what they do.
Freedom is frightening because each person must author a life with no ready design. Yalom presents responsibility as a burden and reads much passivity as a way to avoid it.
In the title story, Yalom treats a woman's obsessive love for a former lover as something to work through, even to kill off, and not to indulge.
A therapist's honest feelings, including dislike and aversion, are useful clinical information. Yalom is open about his own reactions to patients and argues that they should be used.
The relationship between therapist and patient is the main tool. What happens between the two people in the room is treated as a live sample of how the patient lives.
Telling the cases as stories lets Yalom show therapy as a human encounter with uncertainty. He changes patients' names and details, so the book offers narrative and not data.
Meaninglessness joins death, freedom and isolation as a fourth ultimate concern. Yalom says people who lack a sense of purpose often show it as boredom or restlessness.
In the story of the woman he calls Fat Lady, Yalom describes his first revulsion toward an obese patient. Admitting that feeling to himself opened the work.
Anxiety is a response to the human situation, in Yalom's existential approach, and not a sign of buried urges. He draws on Nietzsche, Kierkegaard and Sartre and not on Freud's drive theory.

books.thesis: Decades of Yalom's practice as short pieces of advice, centred on the therapeutic relationship.
books.summary:
Irvin Yalom wrote this for younger therapists and, he says, for their patients too. It asks what helps in the room, and the answer is spread across dozens of short chapters, each a single piece of advice.

There is no single argument. Yalom offers rules of thumb and the reasoning behind them, drawn from his own sessions, and he is frank about where he thinks the field has gone wrong, including its drift toward manuals and quick fixes. The recurring view is that the relationship between therapist and patient does most of the healing and technique matters less. He admits that much of his advice may not suit a therapist of a different temperament. The short format makes it easy to read in pieces, and his existential outlook runs through every lesson.
ideas: The relationship between therapist and patient is the agent of change. Technique matters, but Yalom says it works mainly through the bond it supports.
The here and now of the session shows how the patient treats other people. Yalom urges therapists to attend to what is happening between the two of them.
Every patient needs a new therapy. Yalom warns against forcing everyone into one model or a manual.
A therapist who shares real feelings, in moderation, gives the patient permission to be honest too. Yalom argues for careful, honest self-disclosure.
Dreams reach what the patient has not yet said, which makes them useful material. Yalom recommends asking about them directly.
Diagnostic labels can narrow the therapist's view of the person sitting in the room, and Yalom is wary of leaning on them.
Therapists should have therapy themselves and look at their own fear of death. Unexamined anxieties leak into their work, he says.
The book reads like a notebook of working habits and not a theory. It is made of 85 short chapters, each a piece of advice for younger therapists.
Looking out of the patient's window means trying to see the world as the patient sees it. Yalom urges this and reminds therapists that they and their patients are fellow travellers.
A patient's belief that therapy can help is itself part of the cure. Yalom draws on his group therapy research to stress this instillation of hope.

books.thesis: A psychiatrist's memoir of her own bipolar illness, from inside and outside.
books.summary:
Kay Redfield Jamison studies mood disorders for a living, and in this memoir she describes living with manic-depressive illness since adolescence. The book asks what the illness is like from inside, and what it costs and gives a person who also treats it.

She reports more than she argues. Jamison describes the early highs, the crashes that followed, a suicide attempt, and the years she kept the diagnosis private for fear of her career. She writes about the lure of mania as well as its wreckage, and about how hard it is to keep taking medication when part of you misses the illness. Her conclusion is that lithium and psychotherapy together kept her alive and working, and that the love of others mattered as much. She is honest that she cannot simply say whether she would give the illness back.
ideas: Jamison found her first manic episode, as a teenager, intoxicating. Racing thoughts, boundless energy and confidence came first, and a crash followed.
Mania is not only wreckage, she admits, because it felt wonderful. Missing those highs makes it harder to stay on medication.
Jamison attempted suicide in her twenties and writes about it plainly. She uses it to show how depression can distort judgment.
For years she hid her illness from colleagues and kept her treatment quiet. She feared that disclosure would cost her licence and standing in psychiatry.
Lithium brought stability, but it came with side effects, and she resisted taking it, as many patients do. It is central to her account.
Medication alone was not enough for her. Psychotherapy gave her a place to make sense of the moods.
Steady relationships were part of her treatment and not an extra. She writes of the support of family, friends and her husband.
Jamison was a professor of psychiatry who studied mood disorders while living with one. Her account therefore carries both clinical knowledge and personal experience.
Untreated mania led to reckless spending, damaged relationships and risky behaviour. The wreckage left behind added shame to the illness.
Her long relationship with her own psychiatrist, shown as steady and humane, is the care she credits with keeping her alive.

books.thesis: An atlas of depression: personal, clinical, historical and political.
books.summary:
Andrew Solomon asks what depression is, where it comes from and why it has been so hard to understand and treat. He writes as a sufferer, drawing on his own breakdowns, and as a reporter who spent years interviewing patients, doctors and researchers. The book won the National Book Award for nonfiction.

It is built as an atlas. Chapters cover the experience itself, causes, treatments, suicide, addiction, poverty, history and politics. Solomon argues that depression is partly biology, partly circumstance and partly the stories a society tells, and that no single framework explains it. He is open about his own use of medication and therapy, and weighs other treatments with a mix of curiosity and doubt. His conclusion is cautious: depression is a common human condition, not a failure of will, and living with it often takes several kinds of help.
ideas: Solomon sees depression as the opposite of vitality more than of happiness. A person can lose the capacity to feel anything at all.
In his own breakdowns the illness arrived gradually. Ordinary tasks turned into things he could not do.
No single cause explains depression. Genes, brain chemistry, loss, stress and social conditions all feed in, and different people reach it by different routes.
Solomon gives each treatment a hearing, from medication and talking therapy to electroconvulsive therapy and alternatives. He does not pretend that any one works for everybody.
Suicide gets a chapter of its own and is treated as a real outcome of depression, not only a moral failing or an act of choice.
Poverty and social hardship shape depression as much as biology does, he notes. People in poor places seldom get care.
The way depression is named and judged changes with the age and the culture. Solomon reads it across history to show that the suffering recurs.
The title comes from the medieval idea of acedia, the noonday torpor that monks feared. Solomon uses it to link old accounts of despair with modern depression.
Depression is the flaw in love, in Solomon's phrase, the pain of being unable to care or connect. He calls it love's absence turned into a condition.
Many interviews with other sufferers keep his own story from standing for everyone's. They show how varied the illness is.

books.thesis: Severe depression described from inside, briefly and exactly.
books.summary:
William Styron wrote this short book after his own severe depression in 1985 and an essay he had already published about it. It asks a narrow question and answers it with care: what the illness feels like, and why ordinary language fails to describe it.

Styron argues that the word depression is too weak for what he went through, since it sounds like a low mood and not a storm in the mind. He describes the dread, the loss of the ability to read or write, the sense of being watched by his own despair, and the way suicide began to seem reasonable. He points to a possible trigger in giving up alcohol, and to the suicides of other writers. He admits he does not know why he recovered, and credits rest and the hospital. The book is brief and humble about what anyone can explain.
ideas: The word depression is too weak for what Styron went through. He thinks it sounds like a dip in mood and has no weight for the agony.
The pain is hard to compare with anything physical, and Styron calls it a drowning feeling. He says people who have not had it cannot easily imagine it.
The illness invades the work a person lives by. Styron lost the ability to concentrate, and his reading and writing fell away.
Giving up alcohol may have helped open the way for his collapse, he suggests, with caution. The onset followed his sudden decision to stop drinking.
Suicidal thinking grew in him as a calm kind of logic and not a moment of rage. He places his own near-miss alongside writers who died that way.
Recovery had no tidy medical account. Hospitalisation, rest and removal from his usual pressures were part of how it lifted, and he does not claim to know why.
People who have not been through depression should be slow to judge. Sufferers need patience, Styron argues, and not advice to pull themselves together.
The first clear sign came in Paris in 1985, on a trip to receive a literary prize. Styron's dread and disorientation showed there, and the book grew from an essay about it.
A sedative may have worsened his condition. Styron suspects Halcyon and uses this to warn that medications can interact with the illness in unpredictable ways.
On the night he nearly killed himself, a passage of Brahms from a film turned him back. He thought of his family and the life he would destroy, and checked himself into hospital.

books.t: Maybe You Should Talk to Someone
books.thesis: A therapist becomes a patient, and learns why people avoid what hurts.
books.summary:
After a sudden breakup, therapist Lori Gottlieb finds herself on the other side of the couch. The book asks why people avoid the thing that hurts and what changes when they stop. It follows her sessions with a therapist she calls Wendell, alongside several of her own patients, whose details she altered.

The argument runs through the cases. People arrive complaining about a partner or a boss, and the real trouble sits underneath. She finds she does the same, and that her own therapy teaches her what she tells patients. Among those she describes are a newly married young woman facing terminal illness, an older woman threatening suicide, and a difficult television writer. Her conclusion is that change needs honest looking and often a witness, and that therapists are as stuck as anyone. It is a memoir, so it offers observation, not evidence.
ideas: Gottlieb's breakup brings her to therapy, and she finds that the crisis she names is not what she is stuck on.
Patients often arrive asking someone else to change, a partner or a parent. Therapy turns slowly toward what they themselves can do.
Therapists have blind spots like anyone else. The book shows one in the patient's chair learning how it feels to be seen.
A young newlywed with terminal cancer shows how people face the end. In Gottlieb's account, presence can matter more than advice.
Despair can be stated as an ultimatum. An older woman says she will end her life on a coming birthday unless things improve.
People often hide behind a story about their lives. Gottlieb argues that the story protects them from grief or fear they have not allowed themselves to feel.
Good therapy is steady, honest company over time. Gottlieb resists the idea of a quick technique that fixes a life.
Her own therapist, Wendell, answers her questions and holds back advice. He treats her as she has treated others.
Following four patients across a year while describing her own therapy lets the reader see both sides of the room.
Change involves loss, Gottlieb suggests. Giving up an old way of coping means grieving what it once protected.

books.thesis: The Grant Study follows Harvard men to midlife and asks how their defences matured.
books.summary:
George Vaillant followed Harvard men chosen as college students around 1940, in what became the Grant Study. The book asks how they coped with adult strains, and whether the way they handled inner conflict predicted how their lives went.

The book reports on their careers, marriages, health and psychological troubles into middle age. It ranks their unconscious defences from immature, such as projection, to mature, such as humour, altruism and anticipation. Vaillant argues that defences change over adulthood and that the mature ones tend to go with better outcomes. He relies on interviews and his own clinical judgement, so some ratings are subjective. The sample was narrow, and critics doubt the findings carry over. His main point is that adults keep developing, and that how someone copes matters more than what happened to them.
ideas: The Grant Study followed Harvard students chosen in their college years. It tracked jobs, marriages, health and mental state to see what their lives looked like decades later.
Defence mechanisms are unconscious ways of managing anxiety and conflict, and Vaillant argues that they can be observed and rated from interviews.
Humour, altruism, suppression and anticipation sit at the mature end of his ranking, and projection sits at the immature end. Neurotic defences fall between.
Men who used more mature defences tended to do better at work, in love and in health. Heavy use of immature ones went with trouble.
Defences are not fixed. Vaillant reports that many men moved toward more mature ones over the years, so character keeps changing in adulthood.
Early promise predicted less than expected. Some men who looked well adjusted at first later struggled, and some who started poorly improved.
The group was male, white and from an elite college, so critics doubt the findings apply broadly. The ratings also relied on the judgement of the interviewers.
Vaillant groups defences into four levels. These are psychotic ones such as delusional projection, immature ones, neurotic ones such as intellectualisation and repression, and mature ones.
He links the men's lives to Erikson's stages, such as intimacy, career consolidation and generativity. They show how adult development unfolds.
Vaillant treats defences as ways of coping and not as pathology. Even immature ones protect a person from pain that would otherwise be unbearable.

books.thesis: After seventy-plus years, the Grant Study's strongest finding is that warm relationships predict flourishing.
books.summary:
Triumphs of Experience reports on the Harvard Grant Study after more than seventy years, with the men now old. George Vaillant, who directed the study for decades, asks what predicted a good life and a good old age, and tries to sort the strong findings from the weak ones.

His answer is plain. Warm relationships, in childhood and across adult life, predicted more than most other things, including wealth and early career success. Heavy drinking did serious damage to marriages and health. Mature defences and a capacity to learn from experience helped men recover from hard starts. He sets the Harvard men beside two other groups from the wider research, working-class Boston men and gifted women. The sample remains narrow, and measuring something like flourishing is debatable, but the pattern about close relationships has been widely repeated.
ideas: Warm relationships predicted flourishing in later life more reliably than income, status or early intelligence did. This is the study's central finding.
A loving childhood, especially a warm bond with a parent, was linked with better health, work and mood well into old age.
Alcohol abuse emerges as a major wrecker. It was tied to divorce, depression and early death, and Vaillant treats it as a leading cause of ruined lives.
A hard childhood did not settle a man's fate. Vaillant credits mature defences and the ability to take in warmth from others for the men who did well later.
To test whether the patterns held, Vaillant sets the Harvard men beside working-class Boston men and women of high ability. These are other groups in the long research on adult development.
Many men found new meaning late in life through generativity, caring for those who come after them. The book also covers retirement, ageing and the later stages of life.
The study cannot say what caused good outcomes, only what went with them. Critics also note that the sample was narrow, mostly white men from Harvard.
Vaillant sums the study up by saying that what matters in life is love. He reads the whole record of the men as support for that claim.
Satisfaction with relationships at midlife predicted health at eighty better than physical risk markers such as cholesterol, Vaillant reports.
Some men with troubled midlives became warm and engaged in old age. Vaillant offers this as evidence that development continues late in life.

books.thesis: Guilt and shame are different emotions, and they push behaviour in opposite directions.
books.summary:
June Tangney and Ronda Dearing ask a question that sounds like a quibble: are shame and guilt the same feeling, or do they send people different ways? Their book gathers years of research, using questionnaires that ask people how they would feel in everyday situations.

The distinction is that guilt concerns something you did, and shame concerns what you are. They report that guilt-proneness goes with empathy, apology and repair, while shame-proneness goes with anger, blaming others, withdrawal and psychological troubles including depression. They argue that shame is not the moral motivator it is often thought to be, and that guilt works better. The findings rest mostly on self-reports, and some critics think the two feelings overlap more in real life than the research allows. The book still moved the field toward separating them.
ideas: Guilt is about what you did, and shame is about what you are. Guilt says I did something bad, shame says I am bad, and that difference shapes what people do next.
Guilt-prone people tend to feel empathy for those they have hurt. They are more likely to apologise, make amends and try to put things right.
Shame-prone people are more likely to answer with anger and to blame others. They tend to see the fault as outside themselves.
Shame-proneness is linked with depression, anxiety and other psychological symptoms. Once shame is accounted for, guilt-proneness shows far less of such a link.
The researchers measured these tendencies with scenario questionnaires that ask how a person would react to a described situation. This method is also the main target of criticism.
Shame-prone people face greater risk of risky behaviour and addiction. The evidence is correlation and not proof of cause.
Shaming people in schools, prisons and families tends to make matters worse, the authors argue. Helping people feel guilt about acts may work better.
Shame and guilt are self-conscious emotions, which arise when we evaluate ourselves. The authors distinguish them from simple emotions such as fear or anger.
Parenting shapes the two tendencies. Explaining the consequences of harm tends to build guilt, and humiliating discipline tends to build shame.
Shame-prone people tend toward personal distress, a self-focused reaction to another's pain. They are less able to feel empathy directed at the other person.

books.thesis: Shame is an inborn emotion that forms in broken bonds and usually stays hidden.
books.summary:
Gershen Kaufman argues that shame is among the most important and least discussed emotions. His book asks why shame stays hidden, how it forms, and what it does to a person who carries a lot of it. He builds on Silvan Tomkins's affect theory, in which shame is inborn.

Kaufman says shame arises when the bond between a person and someone they depend on is broken. Repeated breaks can be internalised until shame becomes part of identity. People then defend against it with rage, contempt, perfectionism or withdrawal, and those defences hide the original feeling, often even from the person. He suggests that healing means repairing the bridge between people, through care and acceptance. The book is clinical and theoretical more than experimental, so its claims rest on case experience, and later researchers have tested parts of them.
ideas: Shame is an inborn emotion, in the line of Silvan Tomkins, and not a learned moral idea. Kaufman therefore treats it as central to everyday life.
Shame is triggered when the connection with another person, a parent or a friend, is suddenly broken.
Repeated shaming can be internalised. The person starts to feel shame without anyone present, and it becomes part of who they think they are.
Shame tends to hide itself. People often feel it as something else, which is why it is easy to overlook in daily life and in therapy.
People defend against shame with rage, contempt, perfectionism and the urge to control others. These defences often cause more harm than the shame itself.
A person bound by shame can feel ashamed of the shame itself. This makes a loop that is hard to break from the inside.
Healing comes from restoring the interpersonal bridge, Kaufman argues, so that the person feels accepted and connected again. The book leans on clinical experience for this.
In the shame-bound person, other feelings such as anger, fear and excitement have become tied to shame. The person feels ashamed of having them.
Following Tomkins, shame acts as a brake on interest or enjoyment. It appears when something wanted is blocked, which is why it shows in a lowered head and averted eyes.
Shame passes down in families, since parents who carry shame tend to shame their children. Patterns repeat across generations.

books.thesis: Learned helplessness as a first model of depression, later revised by Seligman himself.
books.summary:
Martin Seligman's Helplessness set out learned helplessness and proposed it as a model of depression. The book asks why some people and animals stop trying even when escape is possible, and whether that passivity can explain a human illness.

It starts from laboratory work in which dogs given shocks they could not control later failed to escape shocks they could have avoided. Seligman argues that what matters is experiencing events as uncontrollable, and that this learning carries over to new situations. He then compares the resulting passivity with features of depression and discusses development and death. The theory was soon revised. Researchers argued that how people explain bad events matters, which led to the attributional version. Later, Seligman and Maier reversed the story, saying passivity is the default and control is what gets learned.
ideas: The core experiments gave dogs shocks they could not stop. Many of them later failed to escape shocks that were easy to avoid.
Uncontrollability is the key factor, Seligman argues. What the animal learns is that its actions and outcomes are unrelated.
Helplessness spreads. After learning that nothing works in one setting, animals and people become slower to try in a different one.
Seligman sets out parallels with depression, including passivity, reluctance to start tasks and trouble believing that effort will pay off.
Early experience of control, or its absence, may shape children. The book also considers how helplessness might bear on health and death.
Seligman's own theory was later revised. Researchers argued that the way people explain bad events, as lasting and personal, decides who becomes helpless.
Seligman and Maier later proposed that passivity is the default response and that the brain has to learn that control is possible. This came decades after the book.
The key experiments used a triadic design. One group could stop the shock, a yoked group got the same shocks with no control, and a third got none, which isolated the effect of control.
Seligman describes helplessness as three deficits. A motivational one makes the animal stop trying, a cognitive one stops it learning that responding works, and an emotional one follows.
Prior experience of control can act as an immunisation. Animals that first learned to escape were less likely to become helpless later.

books.thesis: Human nature is real, shaped by evolution, and denying it has distorted science, art and politics.
books.summary:
Steven Pinker asks why so many thinkers have resisted the idea that people come with a built-in nature, and what that resistance has cost. He argues that human nature is real, shaped by evolution and visible in the brain.

He names three dogmas he wants retired: the blank slate itself, the noble savage and the ghost in the machine. Drawing on genetics, twin studies, neuroscience and cognitive science, he argues that minds have structure from the start. He says that denying this has warped debates in science, art and politics, and that knowing our nature helps us work with it. Critics say he attacks a straw opponent, since few serious scholars held that the mind is entirely blank, and that he overreads some evidence on sex and genes.
ideas: Pinker takes aim at three ideas: the blank slate, the noble savage and the ghost in the machine. He says each rests on faulty assumptions.
Personality and ability are partly heritable, twin and adoption studies show. Pinker argues from this that families and culture are not the only forces shaping children.
Human universals, features found in every known culture, are his evidence for a shared nature. It underlies the surface variety of customs.
People fear human nature because they link it with inequality, unchangeability, determinism and nihilism. Pinker says these fears rest on mistakes.
The mind is a set of evolved faculties, so learning depends on built-in structures. It is not poured into an empty container.
Average differences between the sexes may have biological roots, Pinker argues, a claim that critics dispute. He presents it with qualifications.
Critics say Pinker overstates his opponents, since few scholars have held that the mind is wholly blank. They add that his case for innateness sometimes goes beyond the data.
Political positions often rest on hidden assumptions about what people are like. Pinker uses Thomas Sowell's constrained and unconstrained visions of human nature to make the point.
Margaret Mead's work on Samoa is Pinker's case of anthropology that was too eager to find cultures without human nature. He cites Derek Freeman's criticisms of it.
Modernist and postmodern art lost its audience by rejecting the human taste for beauty, Pinker argues. He sees this as part of the same denial of nature.

books.t: The Better Angels of Our Nature
books.thesis: Violence has fallen across history, though statisticians and historians contest the evidence.
books.summary:
Steven Pinker asks whether violence has declined over the long run of history and, if so, why. His answer is yes: we may live in the most peaceful era of our species, though it rarely feels that way because we notice what makes the news.

The argument is organised around six trends, five inner demons and four better angels. Pinker draws on archaeology, homicide records and war statistics to claim that deaths from violence fell with the rise of states, commerce, literacy and the spread of rights. He credits empathy, self-control, moral norms and reason. The book drew heavy criticism. Statisticians say rare catastrophes make trends hard to read, and historians question his data on early societies and his treatment of recent wars. He accepts that the decline could reverse.
ideas: Violent deaths were a much larger share of all deaths in early societies than in modern ones. Pinker argues this from archaeological and historical evidence.
Settled states cut down the feuding and raiding of earlier life by monopolising force. Pinker calls this the Pacification Process.
Manners and self-restraint spread across Europe and made everyday violence less acceptable. Pinker calls this the Civilising Process, a term from Norbert Elias.
The Humanitarian Revolution ended practices such as judicial torture and public execution. New ideas about the worth of individuals took hold.
Pinker sets five inner demons against four better angels. The demons include predation, dominance, revenge and sadism, and the angels are empathy, self-control, a moral sense and reason.
The long peace after 1945 and the fall in wars between states are central to his case. He argues that great powers have grown less willing to fight.
Critics dispute his statistics, arguing that rare large wars make trends hard to read. Pinker himself concedes that the decline is not guaranteed to continue.
Fear of a first strike can lead each side to attack, in what Pinker calls the Hobbesian trap. He draws on Hobbes's three causes of quarrel: gain, safety and glory.
Pinker names five historical forces behind the decline: the Leviathan, gentle commerce, feminization, cosmopolitanism and the escalator of reason.
Rising measured intelligence, the Flynn effect, makes it easier to see violence from another's point of view. Pinker presents this as the escalator of reason, which favours more abstract thinking.

books.thesis: Selection works on genes, and bodies are their vehicles, which explains selfishness and some altruism.
books.summary:
Richard Dawkins asks what natural selection acts on, and why animals so often behave as if out for themselves or, sometimes, for others. His answer is the gene's eye view: genes are the units that get copied, and bodies are machines genes build to carry themselves on.

Selfish, he says, is a figure of speech, not a claim about motives. Genes that make copies of themselves become common, and that can explain aggression, parental care, cooperation among relatives and some apparent altruism. He uses kin selection and game theory to show how helping behaviour can spread, and a final chapter introduces the meme as a cultural replicator. Critics argue that selection also acts on individuals and groups, and that the gene's eye view is a way of seeing, not a separate theory. Dawkins closes by saying humans can, uniquely, rebel against their genes.
ideas: Dawkins puts the gene, not the organism or the species, at the centre. Genes are replicators, and bodies are survival machines that carry them.
Selfish describes what genes do and not what animals feel. Most of the animals he writes about have no intentions at all.
Kin selection explains why animals may help relatives. A gene that makes an animal help a sibling can spread because the sibling shares copies of it.
Using game theory, Dawkins shows how stable strategies such as cooperating only when others do can persist in a population. Mixed behaviour can also be an equilibrium.
Reciprocal altruism lets unrelated individuals benefit from trading favours. It works so long as cheaters can be recognised and not helped again.
The meme is a unit of cultural copying, such as a tune or an idea. It spreads from mind to mind much as genes spread through bodies.
Dawkins ends by saying that humans alone can understand the selfish replicators and choose to go against them. Critics find this hard to square with his own picture.
Good replicators are marked by longevity, fecundity and copying fidelity. Dawkins imagines a primeval soup in which the first replicators arose.
Parents and children can disagree about how much care to give, because each child is more related to itself than to its siblings. Dawkins treats this parent-offspring conflict as a result of genes.
An evolutionarily stable strategy can arise without any group planning. The hawk and dove example, with retaliator strategies added, shows how.

books.thesis: Evolutionary psychology applied to love, status and conscience, with Darwin's own life as the case study.
books.summary:
Robert Wright asks what evolution can tell us about how people love, climb in status, deceive themselves and decide what is right. The Moral Animal is a popular account of evolutionary psychology, and Charles Darwin's life runs through it as a case study.

Wright reasons that natural selection built the mind to serve the spread of genes, so our feelings about sex, family, friendship and conscience have reasons we do not see. He uses Darwin's marriage, ambitions and worries to show the theory at work in one real life. The moral sentiments, he argues, evolved partly to manage cooperation and reputation, and self-deception is part of the design. Critics call some explanations just-so stories that are hard to test. Wright says that understanding these pressures may help us resist them, and that the theory excuses no one.
ideas: Feelings such as love and guilt have evolutionary reasons even when we sense nothing of the kind. Wright says the mind is the product of natural selection.
Darwin's own life serves as a running example of how these pressures play out in one person. His cautious courtship, his marriage and his anxiety about status all appear.
Differences in what men and women seek in partners come from the cost of parental investment, Wright argues. Many critics find the argument too tidy.
Reciprocal altruism, helping others who will help you back, explains friendship, gratitude and anger at cheaters. It also explains why reputation matters so much to us.
Conscience and moral feeling are tools shaped by selection to regulate cooperation. Wright does not treat them as a window onto absolute right and wrong.
Self-deception is a design feature. We tend to see ourselves as better than we are because that makes it easier to convince others.
Critics say many of the explanations are just-so stories. Wright holds that understanding these urges gives us room to resist them.
Wright builds on the work of George Williams, William Hamilton and Robert Trivers. He presents them as the founders of the modern view of social behaviour.
Human mating is mildly polygynous, Wright argues. Men vary more than women in reproductive success and compete harder for mates and status.
Knowing where a moral feeling comes from does not tell us whether it is right, Wright says. He addresses this is-ought gap and cites studies of stepparent abuse by Daly and Wilson as a case.

books.thesis: Evolution built minds to mislead us, which Wright says matches the Buddhist diagnosis.
books.summary:
Robert Wright asks whether the Buddhist claim that ordinary experience misleads us has support from modern science. He argues that it does. Evolution shaped minds to chase pleasure and avoid threat, not to see clearly or be happy, which is why craving and anxiety keep pulling us around.

The book blends evolutionary psychology with accounts of meditation, including Wright's own retreat experience. He claims the mind is a set of semi-independent modules with no single self in charge, in line with the Buddhist teaching of not-self. Mindfulness, he says, lets us notice feelings as passing events and loosens their hold. He focuses on a modern, secular strand of Buddhism and sets aside rebirth and ritual. Critics say he leans on selective science and reads Buddhism through an evolutionary lens it never had. Wright admits he picks and chooses.
ideas: Natural selection built minds for gene survival and not for truth or contentment. Wright says our feelings about what matters are therefore often unreliable guides.
The Buddhist diagnosis is that suffering comes from craving and clinging. Wright links this to the way evolution keeps us wanting more.
Pleasure fades quickly by design, since lasting satisfaction would stop us seeking. This explains why getting what we want rarely makes us happy for long.
No single inner boss exists, because the mind is a set of modules that compete for control. Wright says this fits the Buddhist teaching of not-self.
Mindfulness meditation lets people watch feelings arise and pass without being swept along. Wright reports brain studies on this, with caution about how strong they are.
Wright's silent retreat gave him personal evidence. He says some of its effects supported the book's central claims.
Wright favours a secular, modern Buddhism and leaves out rebirth. Critics say this selection bends the tradition toward his argument.
Taking the red pill, the image from The Matrix, is Wright's picture of seeing through the illusions that evolution built into the mind.
Emptiness, as Wright explains it, is the way we project essences and value onto things. A thing seems to carry its goodness or badness within itself when the feeling comes from the mind.
A module that narrates our actions after the fact supports the claim that no unified self is in charge. Wright cites Michael Gazzaniga's split-brain work and the interpreter idea.

books.thesis: People are more decent than cynical theories assume, and some famous studies show less than claimed.
books.summary:
Rutger Bregman asks whether people are, underneath, selfish and dangerous, as many theories of civilisation assume. He argues that most people are more decent than that, and that the opposite belief, which he calls veneer theory, has shaped institutions in harmful ways.

He goes back to famous studies and stories and retells them. He claims the Stanford prison experiment was staged more than discovered, that the real story of boys stranded on a Pacific island ended differently from Lord of the Flies, and that tales of bystanders ignoring crime were exaggerated. He then describes cooperation, from soldiers in the First World War to schools and prisons run on trust. Critics say Bregman picks evidence to suit his case and is less sceptical of his own sources than of his targets. Others have also questioned several of the studies he challenges.
ideas: Veneer theory, the belief that goodness is a thin coat over human selfishness, is old, popular and mostly unsupported, Bregman says.
Six boys stranded on a Pacific island looked after one another, Bregman says. He retells the story as the reverse of Lord of the Flies.
The Stanford prison experiment was shaped by its organisers, he argues. It therefore does not show that ordinary people turn cruel when given power.
The famous story that many neighbours watched a woman's murder and did nothing was inflated by the press, in Bregman's account.
Humans evolved to cooperate, he argues. The same traits that make us friendly also make us easy to teach and to trust.
Soldiers in the First World War who held fire or shared the lines at Christmas are, for Bregman, signs that people resist killing.
Critics say Bregman is selective and applies less scrutiny to evidence that fits his view. He admits that people can also be cruel.
Humans may have domesticated themselves by selecting for friendliness, in what Bregman calls the Homo puppy hypothesis. He cites the Russian fox experiment as a parallel.
Many of Milgram's subjects went on, Bregman argues, not from blind obedience but because they were persuaded they were doing something worthwhile.
Easter Island was not ruined by its own people, Bregman says. He holds that disease and slavery brought by outsiders did most of the damage.

books.thesis: Humans dominate through accumulated culture, the collective brain, not individual intelligence.
books.summary:
Joseph Henrich asks why humans, who are not especially strong or fast, came to dominate the planet. Raw intelligence, he argues, is not the answer. Success comes from culture: groups accumulate and pass on knowledge across generations, much of it more than any individual could work out alone.

Humans, he says, are cultural learners who copy what works, especially from people who seem successful or prestigious, and this shaped our bodies and brains through genes and culture evolving together. He gives examples of know-how that works without anyone understanding why, such as food processing that removes toxins, and of European explorers who died in places where locals had long thrived. Critics say he gives too little weight to individual reasoning and that cultural evolution is hard to test.
ideas: Humans owe their success to cumulative culture, the slow build-up of skills and knowledge over generations, more than to any one person's cleverness.
European explorers starved in places where local people lived well, Henrich tells. They lacked the locals' inherited knowledge.
Methods for preparing certain foods, such as detoxifying cassava, protect people from poison. Those following them may not know why they work.
People copy most from those who seem successful or prestigious. This lets useful practices spread without anyone checking them.
Young children are not better than other apes at physical puzzles, but they are far better at learning from other people. Henrich draws this from experiments comparing the two.
Culture and genes shape each other. Cooking and group living changed our bodies and brains, which in turn made us better able to learn from others.
Critics say Henrich undervalues individual reasoning and that cultural evolution is hard to test. The book still makes a case that is hard to ignore.
Copying the majority lets useful practices spread and stabilise in a group. Henrich calls this tendency conformist transmission.
Larger and better connected populations sustain more complex technology, in Henrich's idea of the collective brain. Tasmania lost tools after it was cut off from the mainland.
Groups with better norms and institutions outcompeted others, Henrich argues. He calls this cultural group selection and says it shaped human cooperation.

books.t: The WEIRDest People in the World
books.thesis: Western psychology is an outlier, produced by a particular cultural history.
books.summary:
Joseph Henrich asks why Western societies think and act so differently from most people in history. The term WEIRD, for Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic, comes from earlier work with colleagues, who showed that psychology mostly studied these societies.

His argument is that WEIRD psychology, which is individualistic, analytic, trusting of strangers and prone to guilt over shame, is the product of a specific history. Medieval Church rules about marriage and family, he claims, broke up the tight kin groups that organised most societies. That opened the way for new institutions, trust in strangers and later widespread reading. Critics say the thesis leans on a single cause and sometimes confuses correlation with explanation. His wider point, that one odd population should not be treated as typical, is widely accepted.
ideas: Most psychology studies draw their participants from WEIRD societies, Henrich notes. The acronym stands for Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic.
WEIRD people tend to be more individualistic and analytic. They value personal choice and put the self ahead of group ties.
WEIRD people show more trust in strangers and impersonal institutions. Henrich links this to the rise of markets and law.
Church policies on marriage, such as bans on marrying relatives, weakened the extended clans that had once organised life in most societies, Henrich argues.
Learning to read changes how the brain works. Henrich links the spread of literacy, helped by the Protestant stress on reading scripture, to later psychological differences.
Guilt-based moral thinking, which concerns private conscience, is stronger in WEIRD societies. Shame, which concerns reputation, is stronger in many others.
Critics say the thesis leans on one cause for a huge historical change. They add that correlations across regions do not prove his explanation.
Even basic perception differs across populations, Henrich says. Illusion experiments such as the Muller-Lyer figure show that WEIRD samples cannot stand for all people.
Economic games such as the ultimatum game show that people in market-integrated societies offer fairer splits to strangers. People in small-scale societies offer less.
Voluntary associations such as guilds, monasteries and universities, along with charter towns, built new forms of trust beyond kin. Henrich credits them with this change.

books.thesis: Desires are mostly copied from other people, and seeing the copying loosens its hold.
books.summary:
Luke Burgis asks where our wants come from. Drawing on the thinker René Girard, he says they come mostly from other people. Wanting applies mimetic theory, the idea that desire is copied, to business, relationships, careers and social media.

Burgis argues that we rarely pick our desires alone. We watch models, people we admire or compete with, and take on what they want, often without knowing it. He separates thin desires, driven by imitation and prone to leave us unsatisfied, from thick ones, which last longer and tie to what we value. He also describes how rivalry grows when we copy those close to us, and how groups can turn on a scapegoat. The book is a popularisation, and Girard's theory has few experimental tests behind it. Burgis suggests that noticing the pattern gives us some freedom from it.
ideas: People learn what to want by watching what others want, so desire is social and not spontaneous. This is Girard's central claim, and Burgis builds on it.
We tend to deny that we imitate. Burgis argues that this denial keeps the copying hidden and makes it more powerful.
Models can stand at a distance, like celebrities, or close at hand, like colleagues. Closeness is what makes rivalry likely.
Thin desires come mostly from imitation and tend to leave us restless. Thick desires hold up over time and tie to deeper values.
Rivalry grows between people who want the same thing and who are close. It can come to matter more than the object itself.
Groups in tension may settle their conflict by blaming a scapegoat. Girard developed this idea at length, and Burgis applies it to modern settings.
Seeing where a want came from can make it easier to choose whether to follow it, Burgis argues. Girard's theory has little experimental support.
Peter Thiel studied with Girard and became an early investor in Facebook. Burgis points to him as an example of how the theory moves from the seminar into business.
In Girard's metaphysical desire, we want not only the object but the being of the model. It is as if having what they have would make us who they are.
Social media increases the number of models we see and shows their reactions in real time. Burgis suggests this speeds up mimetic rivalry.

books.t: The Hero with a Thousand Faces
books.thesis: Myths worldwide share one pattern, the monomyth of departure, trial and return.
books.summary:
Joseph Campbell asks whether the stories of different cultures share one underlying shape. He argues they do: myths from around the world follow a single pattern he calls the monomyth. He draws on Jung, Freud and the comparative study of myth and religion.

The pattern has three parts. The hero leaves the ordinary world, passes through trials and revelations, and returns with something that benefits others. Campbell fills it in with stages such as the call to adventure, the refusal, helpers and guardians, the lowest point and the return. He treats these as expressions of inner psychological change, with myths serving as maps for growing up. Critics say the pattern is so general it fits nearly anything, that he selects examples to suit it, and that his hero is mostly male. The book has still been hugely influential on storytellers.
ideas: Hero stories everywhere share one structure, Campbell claims, with three parts: departure, initiation and return. He calls this the monomyth.
The hero's story typically begins with a call to adventure, which the hero may at first refuse. Aid from a helper comes next.
Crossing the threshold means entering a strange world. Figures guard it and test whether the hero is ready to go on.
The middle of the story is a series of trials that lead to a crisis, a kind of symbolic death or descent. A gain follows it.
Campbell reads these stages as images of inner psychological change. He draws on Jung's archetypes and Freud's analysis of dreams and treats myth as a kind of shared dreaming.
The return brings something back for the community. Campbell treats this as the point, since the hero's gain is meant to be shared.
Critics say the pattern is too loose, fits almost any story and was built from selected examples. They add that the hero in his account is nearly always male.
The belly of the whale is Campbell's image for the threshold passage. The hero seems to vanish, as Jonah does, and is reborn after a symbolic death.
Atonement with the father is a central crisis. The hero faces the power that rules his world and comes through to a new understanding.
The hero who returns is the master of two worlds, Campbell says. He can move between the everyday and the sacred without being trapped in either.

books.thesis: Campbell and Moyers talk about why old stories still matter once nobody takes them.
books.summary:
The Power of Myth grew out of conversations between the mythologist Joseph Campbell and the journalist Bill Moyers, filmed in the mid 1980s and broadcast in 1988. It asks why old stories still matter in a modern world that no longer believes them and what they do for people who live by them.

Because it is a conversation, the book moves loosely. Campbell argues that myths are metaphors for the experience of being alive and for stages of life, and that trouble comes when they are read as facts. He talks about heroes, rites of passage, marriage and the loss of shared stories in modern societies, and urges people to follow what makes them feel alive. Critics say he generalises across traditions, flattens real differences and slips in his own tastes. Many readers met his ideas here first, and the book offers more charm than rigour.
ideas: Myths are metaphors for the experience of being alive, Campbell says. Reading them as literal history misses what they are for.
People are looking less for the meaning of life than for the experience of being alive, Campbell suggests. Myths help them feel it.
Rites of passage once marked the move from childhood to adulthood. Campbell worries that modern societies have lost these shared ceremonies.
Marriage asks two people to give up their separate selves. In Campbell's discussion, the shared relationship is the thing to serve.
Campbell advises people to follow their bliss, meaning the activity that makes them feel most alive. He tells them to trust that doors will open.
The old myths no longer fit the modern world, Campbell argues. A new set of stories, drawing on the whole planet, is needed.
Critics say he treats different traditions as one. His easy blending of them in conversation covers over real disagreements.
Campbell lists four functions of mythology: the mystical, the cosmological, the sociological and the pedagogical. He says modern life has lost the first.
The talks include discussion of Star Wars, whose creator George Lucas said he had drawn on Campbell's work. Campbell treats the film as a modern myth.
Campbell advises people to participate joyfully in the sorrows of the world. He says one needs a sacred place where one can find oneself.

books.thesis: Wrestling, soap powder and cars carry a second layer of meaning that makes ideology look natural.
books.summary:
Roland Barthes asks what is hidden in the things a society treats as natural and harmless. Mythologies collects short essays he wrote for a French magazine in the 1950s, on subjects such as wrestling, soap powder, a car, wine and a magazine cover, and ends with a longer theoretical essay.

Everyday objects and images, he argues, carry a second layer of meaning. A picture or phrase signifies something plain, then is used to signify an idea, often a bourgeois one, in a way that makes history look like nature. He calls this layer myth. The essays are brisk and witty, and they ask readers to notice what has been made to seem obvious. Critics say his readings can be arbitrary, confident and driven by his politics, since the same image could be read another way. The book has taught generations to read advertising and popular culture with suspicion.
ideas: Myth is a second layer of meaning added to a sign, Barthes says. An ordinary image comes to carry an idea without seeming to.
Myth turns history into nature. What is made by particular people at a particular time is presented as simply how things are.
Professional wrestling is a spectacle of moral display, Barthes reads. Its gestures show suffering and justice clearly for the crowd.
A magazine cover showing a young Black soldier saluting the French flag presents empire as natural and welcome, Barthes reads.
Wine is made into a national symbol of Frenchness. Barthes says this hides how particular and unevenly shared the habit is.
Advertising turns cleaning products into stories about depth and action. Barthes shows this in his essay on soap powders and detergents.
Barthes's readings are playful and political, which critics say makes them hard to check. The closing essay, Myth Today, gives the theory behind them.
In the closing essay, Barthes defines myth as depoliticised speech. It removes the history and the human making from things and presents them as natural.
The bourgeoisie is ex-nominated, meaning it is never named and appears as the universal norm. This is why its values pass as common sense.
French playthings prepare children to be users and not makers, in the essay on toys. The essay on the brain of Einstein shows how the scientist is turned into a myth of genius.

books.thesis: Play is older than culture, and law, war, poetry and ritual grew out of it.
books.summary:
Johan Huizinga, a Dutch historian, asks what play is and what it has to do with culture. He argues that play is not a side activity of civilisation but one of its roots, older than culture itself, since animals play before humans have anything we would call culture.

He describes play as voluntary, set apart from ordinary life, bounded in time and space, and ruled by agreed limits. He follows that spirit through law, war, poetry, ritual, philosophy and art, claiming each began as a contest or a game. He ends on a worried note: in the twentieth century, he says, the real play spirit had weakened and given way to a shallow childishness. Critics say he stretches the idea of play until it covers too much, and that he is selective with evidence. The book still shaped how games and culture are studied.
ideas: Play is older than culture, Huizinga argues. Animals play and do not need humans to teach them how.
Play is free. A person who is forced to play is no longer playing, which marks it off from work and duty.
Play takes place within a boundary of time and space, a kind of magic circle. Inside it the ordinary rules are replaced by those of the game.
Every game has rules. A spoilsport who drops them destroys the game, while a cheat still respects them.
Law, war, poetry and ritual all began as contests of skill, courage or wit, Huizinga claims. He traces the play element through each of them.
Contest, in the sense of a struggle for honour and reputation, is one of the main ways play shapes social life.
In the last chapters Huizinga laments puerilism, a mix of childishness and propaganda that he thinks replaced real play. Many critics find that section dated.
Homo ludens is offered as a rival to Homo sapiens and Homo faber. The subtitle calls the book a study of the play element in culture.
Ritual and play overlap, Huizinga says. Sacred performances take place in a marked-off ground where participants hold the play to be real and also know it as play.
Play has aesthetic qualities such as rhythm, harmony and tension. Huizinga surveys words for play in many languages to show how differently the idea is divided.

books.thesis: Modern people became other-directed, steering by the approval of peers, as if by radar.
books.summary:
David Riesman, with Nathan Glazer and Reuel Denney, asks how American character was changing by mid century. The book proposes that societies produce characteristic personality types, and that a new one, steered by peer approval, was becoming dominant among the urban middle class.

The book describes three types. Tradition-directed people follow custom, inner-directed people follow values set early in life, and other-directed people steer by the signals of those around them. Riesman ties these to stages of population and economic change, and contrasts the inner-directed person's gyroscope with the other-directed person's radar. He is wary but not hostile, noting gains in flexibility and costs in anxiety. Critics said the evidence was thin and the types too loose. It was still a surprise bestseller and gave the public a vocabulary for conformity.
ideas: Riesman proposes three social characters: tradition-directed, inner-directed and other-directed. Each is linked with a stage of economic and population change.
In tradition-directed societies, people follow inherited custom and rank. Deviation brings shame from the group.
Inner-directed people take their goals from early parental teaching and hold to them through life. Riesman describes them as guided by an inner gyroscope.
Other-directed people look to their peers and to media for cues about what to want and how to act. Riesman compares them to radar.
The shift to the other-directed type is tied to the growth of cities, offices and consumer society. There, getting on with people becomes the main skill.
Other-directed people gain in warmth and flexibility. They pay for it with anxiety about approval and a thinner sense of their own aims.
Critics said the evidence was thin and the types too loose. The book was still a bestseller, and its terms entered everyday talk.
The book began as a study of the American middle class and grew into a general theory of character. Riesman wrote it with Nathan Glazer and Reuel Denney.
Each of the three types is tied to a point on a population curve: high growth potential, transitional growth and incipient decline. Each stage produces its own typical character.
The autonomous type is Riesman's ideal, a person who can conform to norms but is free to choose not to. He contrasts this with the anomic person, who is simply cut off.

books.thesis: Consumer culture, therapy and celebrity produce anxious selves that depend on other people's approval.
books.summary:
Christopher Lasch wanted to know what had happened to American character by the late 1970s, after the boom in consumerism, therapy and celebrity. He found a new kind of person: anxious, hungry for admiration and short on any stable sense of self. He borrowed the language of clinical narcissism to describe it.

He treats this as a social pattern, not a private failing. The decline of family authority, the growth of bureaucracy and experts, mass media and a therapeutic outlook that replaced older moral and political frames all pushed people toward personal growth and approval while making lasting commitments hard to trust. The book leans on psychoanalytic writers and cultural criticism more than on data. Critics call Lasch nostalgic and moralistic, and say he stretched the clinical term and cherry-picked.
ideas: Lasch uses narcissism as a cultural diagnosis. In his account it describes a social pattern that produces anxious people who depend on others' admiration.
Consumer culture feeds this pattern by selling images of a better self. It keeps people dissatisfied with what they have.
The therapeutic outlook, with its focus on personal feeling and growth, has taken the place of religion and politics as a way of finding meaning.
Experts and bureaucracies have taken over tasks once handled by families and communities. Parents are left less sure of their own authority.
Mass media and celebrity encourage people to see life as a performance, judged by an audience. Being seen comes to matter more than doing.
A survival mentality has spread, Lasch says. People cope day by day, avoid long commitments and treat relationships as things to be used.
Critics say Lasch was nostalgic and stretched a clinical term to cover a whole society. They add that his evidence is mostly anecdote and cultural reading.
Lasch draws on the clinical work of Otto Kernberg and Heinz Kohut. He describes the narcissist as having a fragile self, a need for an audience and a fear of dependence.
In his chapter on sport, Lasch argues that games have been turned from play into spectacle. Commercialism and the cult of winning have replaced the joy of taking part.
Constant self-observation leads to detachment from feeling and not to insight. Lasch calls this habit pseudo-self-awareness.

books.thesis: Empathy is biased and narrow, and rational compassion is a better guide to doing good.
books.summary:
Paul Bloom takes on an idea almost everyone accepts, that empathy is the root of kindness and the best guide to moral choices. He argues that it is a poor guide. He first separates two things people run together: understanding what another person thinks, which he grants is useful, and feeling what they feel, which he says misleads us.

Emotional empathy works like a spotlight. It favours people who are near, similar and identifiable, it responds poorly to large numbers, and it can push us toward cruelty against whoever seems to threaten the one we feel for. He also cites research suggesting that absorbing others' pain can lead to burnout. In its place he proposes rational compassion, concern for others' wellbeing that does not require sharing their feelings. Critics say he defines empathy too narrowly and that human care needs more feeling than he allows.
ideas: Bloom separates cognitive empathy, understanding what someone feels, from emotional empathy, feeling it yourself. His target is the second kind.
Empathy acts like a spotlight. It is strongest for people who are close to us, look like us or whose suffering we can picture clearly.
Empathy is poor at numbers. People respond more to one named victim than to thousands, which skews decisions about charity and policy.
Empathy can lead to cruelty. Feeling for one victim may spur anger and harsh punishment toward whoever caused the harm.
Caregivers who take on their patients' pain can burn out, while those who respond with compassion cope better. Bloom cites research to support the contrast.
Bloom proposes rational compassion, a concern for others' wellbeing that rests on thought and values. It does not depend on sharing their feelings.
Critics say he defines empathy so narrowly that it becomes easy to attack. They add that many kinds of care do depend on feeling with another person.
The girl trapped in a well drew great public attention and money, while larger disasters receive far less. Bloom reads this as a sign of how empathy chases vivid individuals.
Empathy divides in politics, Bloom argues. It flows toward our own side and can turn into hostility toward the people who seem to have hurt them.
Bloom concedes that empathy has value in private life, bringing pleasure, closeness and enjoyment of fiction. He aims his criticism at its role in moral and policy decisions.

books.thesis: James studies religious experience from the inside and judges it by its fruits, not its origins.
books.summary:
William James, philosopher and psychologist, gave these lectures in 1901 and 1902 to ask what religious experience is like for the people who have it, and how much weight it deserves. He chose the intense cases, conversions, visions and saintly lives, because he thought the extremes show the nature of the thing most clearly.

The book gathers first-person accounts and sorts them: the healthy-minded who see mostly good, the sick soul who feels evil and despair, the divided self and its sudden conversion, the habits of saints, and the states of mystics. James judges them by their fruits, what they do for a life, and not by their roots, such as whether they trace to nerves or biology. He called explaining them away that way medical materialism. His conclusion is cautious. These experiences are real and often valuable, but they bind only those who have them.
ideas: James studies religion as private experience, not as church or creed. He looks at the feelings of individuals in their solitude and sets institutions and doctrine aside.
Temperament splits believers into two real types. The healthy-minded focus on the good, while the sick soul cannot ignore evil, and James argues that both are genuine ways of seeing.
Conversion is the healing of a divided self. James describes a person at war within who becomes unified, either suddenly or by degrees.
A religious state is not discredited by its bodily causes. James calls the habit of dismissing it on those grounds medical materialism, and notes that all states have bodily causes.
James judges religious experience by its fruits, not its roots. What counts is whether it makes a person more charitable, steady and alive, whatever its origin.
Mystical states, he suggests, share four marks. They are hard to put into words, they feel like knowledge, they pass quickly and they feel as though they happen to you.

Mystical experience binds only the person who has it. James concludes that it carries authority for that person but gives others no obligation to accept it, a view critics find both modest and evasive.
The book's evidence is first-person testimony. It began as the Gifford Lectures at Edinburgh in 1901 and 1902, and its case studies come mostly from letters and memoirs.
Saintliness is a recognisable set of traits, and James tests it by its practical results. He lists charity, purity and asceticism, and asks whether the saint is better to live with.
James suggests that religious experiences come from a subliminal region of the self that opens onto something more. People then add overbeliefs beyond what the experience itself shows.

books.thesis: How we attend shapes what we find. McGilchrist wants the right hemisphere's broad attention restored.
books.summary:
Iain McGilchrist, a psychiatrist and former literary scholar, asks how the way we pay attention shapes what we find in the world. The Matter with Things is a long, two volume work that continues his earlier book on the two brain hemispheres. It argues that modern culture has come to favour one way of attending at the cost of the other.

In his account the left hemisphere attends narrowly, to what can be grasped and used, while the right attends broadly, to context, living things and what is new. He says the left has taken over and flattened the world into a mechanism. He then moves beyond neuroscience into physics, time, consciousness and value, arguing that truth, beauty and goodness are real parts of the world. Neuroscientists dispute his picture of the hemispheres as too sharp a split, and some readers find the later philosophy loose.
ideas: Attention is not neutral. McGilchrist argues that how we attend to the world decides what we find in it and what we miss.
The two hemispheres attend in different ways. The left looks narrowly and for use, while the right looks widely, to context and to living, changing things.
The left hemisphere is an emissary that has taken over from its master. His earlier thesis holds that the right hemisphere should lead, and that the emissary now runs modern culture.
The left's way of seeing turns the world into a machine of separable parts. This suits manipulation, he claims, but loses what is whole and alive.
Consciousness is not a by-product of matter. McGilchrist argues that mind and matter are more entangled than materialism allows.
Truth, beauty and goodness are real features of the world. He treats them as things we discover, not preferences we project onto it.
The hemisphere account is the most disputed part of the book. Neuroscientists object that the split is overstated, and some readers find the philosophical chapters more assertion than demonstration.
A sound view of the world needs four ways of knowing: science, reason, intuition and imagination. McGilchrist thinks modern thought leans too far on reason and measurement.
The corpus callosum may exist partly to keep the hemispheres apart. He argues that this band joining them inhibits one side so that two different ways of attending can stay distinct.
The world is better understood as made of processes and relationships than of isolated things. What lies between things is as real as the things themselves.

books.thesis: Capitalism has become the only thinkable order, and that closed horizon shapes how people suffer.
books.summary:
Mark Fisher starts from a remark often attributed to Fredric Jameson and Slavoj Zizek: it is easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism. Capitalist Realism looks at what happens to a culture when no alternative seems thinkable, and how that shows up in everyday suffering, work and education.

Fisher argues that capitalist realism is more than a belief. It is an atmosphere that limits what feels possible. He reads the film Children of Men as a picture of this closed future, calls the spread of bureaucracy and targets in public services market Stalinism, and notes students who know things are wrong yet feel unable to act. He also challenges the habit of treating depression and stress as private chemical problems. The book is short and polemical, and readers disagree on how far its diagnosis extends.
ideas: Fisher builds the book on the line that it is easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism. He treats it as a description of our mood.
Capitalist realism works as an atmosphere, not a doctrine. In Fisher's account it limits thought and action, so that no alternative to the present system seems worth imagining.
Children of Men shows a future that has been cancelled. Fisher reads the film as a picture of a world where all that remains is management.
Markets did not replace bureaucracy. Fisher argues that targets, audits and paperwork have spread through schools and services, and he calls the result market Stalinism.
Reflexive impotence keeps the system standing. Fisher uses the term for students who know the system is broken and also feel they can do nothing about it.
Depression and anxiety, Fisher argues, have social causes that get ignored. He challenges the habit of treating them as private chemical faults and points to work and precarity.
Fisher argues from teaching and cultural criticism, not from data. The book is short and combative, and critics find its evidence thin and its alternatives vague.

Business ontology is the assumption that every institution ought to be run as a business. Fisher applies it to schools, hospitals and the arts, and says it is treated as common sense and is hard to question.
Wall-E shows how critique gets absorbed. The film criticises consumerism, yet it does so as a product sold by the system it describes.
The 2008 bank bailouts did not break the spell. Fisher notes that they exposed the market's dependence on the state, yet he argues that the sense that there is no alternative survived the crisis.

books.thesis: The self is a model the brain cannot recognise as a model, and we live inside it.
books.summary:
Thomas Metzinger, a German philosopher of mind, asks what the self is and whether anything in us matches the sense of being someone. The Ego Tunnel is a popular version of his longer academic work. Its answer is bold: there are no selves, only the brain's process of modelling itself.

The brain builds a model of the body and the world, and we cannot see it as a model because it is transparent to us. We live inside it, in what he calls the ego tunnel, and take it for reality. Out-of-body experiences, the rubber hand illusion, lucid dreaming and virtual reality show how easily the model can be shifted. He then raises ethical questions about altering consciousness and about creating artificial minds that might suffer. Critics say the claim that no self exists depends on how self is defined, and the science is still unsettled.
ideas: Metzinger claims that no such thing as a self exists. What we have is a continuous process in which the brain models itself.
The phenomenal self-model is what makes us feel like a single someone. It is the brain's internal picture of the body, and it is the central notion of the book.
The self-model is transparent, so we cannot see it as a model. We look through it, take its content for the real world and think we are directly in touch with things.
Each of us lives inside an ego tunnel. It is the narrow, constructed space of experience, a bit like a private virtual reality.
The felt boundary of the body can be shifted by simple tricks. The rubber hand illusion and out-of-body experiences show this.
