Dreams are natural examples of a self-model running without sensory input. Metzinger presents dreams, and especially lucid dreams, as the brain producing a self and a world on its own.
The no-self claim is disputed, since critics say it depends on definitions. Metzinger also raises ethical questions about enhancing minds and building artificial ones that might suffer.

Agency is part of the self-model too. He treats the feeling of being the author of one's own actions as a constructed feature, and he is doubtful about a free will that would stand apart from the brain.
Clinical cases show how fragile the sense of self is. Metzinger draws on patients who deny that a paralysed limb belongs to them, where part of the self-model has failed.
A suffering machine would be a new kind of victim. For that reason Metzinger has called for a pause on work that could produce artificial consciousness.

books.thesis: We expect more from technology and less from each other, and being connected is not being close.
books.summary:
Sherry Turkle asks what technology is doing to our relationships, and why we can feel so lonely while constantly connected. A psychologist at MIT, she spent years interviewing people about robots and about networked life, and the book is organised in two halves around those themes.

The first half covers social robots, from toy pets to machines designed as companions for the old, and notes how readily people attach to something that only seems to care. The second covers phones, texting and social media, where people curate themselves and often prefer messages to calls. Turkle argues that constant connection can crowd out solitude and real conversation. Her evidence is largely interviews and observation, and critics say she worries too much and generalises from small samples. She is not against technology and hopes for more reflective use of it.
ideas: Turkle claims that we expect more from technology and less from each other. Connection, she says, is not the same as closeness.
The robotic moment is the point at which people accept machines as companions even when they know the machines feel nothing. Turkle uses the phrase for this readiness.
Simulated care raises a problem of authenticity. A robot that seems to listen may stand in for the harder work of human company.
Attachment to robot pets points to unmet need. Turkle found that children and older people formed real bonds with them, and she took this as more than a curiosity.
Texting appeals because it gives control. Many people prefer it to calling since they can manage what they say and when, and Turkle thinks this costs the give and take of conversation.
Online selves are edited, and the pressure to be seen turns life into material for sharing. Some people feel they exist only when posted.
Turkle's case rests on interviews and leans toward alarm, as critics note. She says she is not against technology and hopes for more reflective use.
Children treat robot toys as alive enough. With Furbys and Tamagotchis, the need for care leads them to feel the toys are living things, even if not quite animals.
The tethered self is always connected and finds solitude hard. Turkle describes a person who reaches for a phone to fill any gap and struggles to be alone with their own thoughts.
People feel recognised by robots even when they know the responses are programmed. Turkle writes about MIT robots such as Kismet, built to respond to faces and voices.

books.t: On Kissing, Tickling and Being Bored
books.thesis: Small everyday things tell us more about the psyche than grand theory does.
books.summary:
Adam Phillips, a British psychoanalyst, suggests that grand theories of the mind explain less than the small things people feel and do. On Kissing, Tickling and Being Bored is a collection of essays that start from trifles and use them to reach questions about desire, childhood and the odd things psychoanalysis tries to describe.

The essays build no single argument. Phillips writes in a short, playful, aphoristic way, takes up a subject, turns it over and leaves it open. Boredom is treated not as emptiness but as a state in which a child waits for desire to appear. Tickling and kissing are ordinary pleasures mixed up with fear and control. Freud and Winnicott stand in the background, and Phillips treats their theories as stories to be used, not settled fact. Readers who want conclusions may be frustrated, because he prefers questions.
ideas: Phillips doubts that large theories capture the mind. He starts from small experiences, such as a kiss or a bad afternoon, that theories tend to skip.
Boredom is a waiting state in which a child searches for what to want. Rushing to fill it may get in the way of finding a desire.
Tickling mixes pleasure with helplessness and alarm. Phillips uses it to show how closely enjoyment and loss of control can sit together.
A kiss holds a good deal of the ambiguity of wanting and being wanted. Phillips treats it as a small, everyday act.
Phillips reads Freud's ideas as stories to think with, not as proven facts. He is playful about psychoanalysis even as he draws on it.
The form carries the argument. The essays are brief and aphoristic, and Phillips raises a subject, turns it over and often ends on an open question.
Winnicott runs under several essays. His emphasis on play and on being able to be alone shapes the book, though Phillips uses it freely.
Not every part of a life is improved by being analysed. The subtitle refers to the unexamined life, and Phillips treats it as a quiet answer to Socrates.
Being tickled depends on trust. Phillips suggests that the same helplessness that is fun with a friend would feel like a threat from a stranger.
Phillips often reverses the usual view of a fault. A symptom, a habit or a mood is read as an attempt at something, not simply as a fault to be removed.

books.thesis: We keep imagining the lives we are not living, and those fantasies shape the one we have.
books.summary:
Adam Phillips asks why we spend so much of our lives thinking about the lives we are not living. Missing Out, subtitled In Praise of the Unlived Life, argues that these imagined alternatives matter. We compare our real lives with the ones we wanted, feared or missed, and that comparison shapes the life we have.

Phillips draws on Freud, literature and clinical experience in his usual essayistic way. He suggests that frustration is unavoidable in desire, since wanting means not having, and that people often cope by imagining a better self living elsewhere. He treats envy and regret as signs of this habit. The book is more suggestive than systematic and offers no method for living better. It leaves open how far we should give up the fantasies, and he seems to hold that some are necessary. Readers who like a firm thesis may find it slippery.
ideas: Phillips says each of us lives alongside the lives we did not lead. These imagined lives affect how we feel about the real one.
To want is already to miss out. Phillips treats frustration as part of wanting, since to desire something is to lack it, and so a life of wanting is always a life of some missing out.
The happier self who chose differently can make the actual life seem thin. Phillips suggests that the fantasy of that other version of ourselves does this.
Envy is a sign of the unlived life. Phillips reads it as a response to someone who seems to have what we gave up or never had.
Regret can become a way of avoiding the present. The idea that we missed our chance can excuse us from the risks of now.
Fantasy is more than an escape. Phillips holds that we need imagined lives to know what we want and to sense what is possible.
The book is an essay in the loose sense and offers no method. It draws on Freud and on writers, which some readers find slippery.
The promise that we can have it all makes ordinary satisfactions feel like losses. Phillips contrasts that modern promise with the fact of limits.
Missing out is built into growing up. Phillips reads the Oedipus story as a tale of what a child must give up.
Parents can hand their unlived lives to their children. The child is then asked to live out what the parent missed, Phillips suggests.

books.thesis: Domination begins where mutual recognition fails, and love needs two people who can each be a subject.
books.summary:
Jessica Benjamin, a psychoanalyst and feminist thinker, asks why domination and submission recur in love and in society, and what it would take for two people to meet as equals. The Bonds of Love uses psychoanalysis to argue that domination begins where mutual recognition fails.

Each person needs recognition from another, but recognition only counts if the other is independent, so the need carries a built-in tension. When people cannot hold it, one may try to control the other, and the relationship turns into master and servant. She reads this in Freud and Hegel, in how children separate from their mothers, in gender roles and in erotic submission, including the novel The Story of O. Critics have pressed her on how far the account depends on psychoanalytic assumptions, and on its use in politics.
ideas: Recognition is a paradox. Benjamin starts from the point that we need another person to confirm us, but only a separate person can do so in a way that counts.
Domination begins when mutual recognition breaks down. Each person may then try to control the other, and the relationship hardens into domination and submission.
Hegel's master and slave story pictures this failure. As Benjamin reads it, one party's independence is bought at the cost of the other's.
Mother and child both need recognition. In her account the child must be recognised by the mother as a separate person, while the mother also needs to be seen as a person with a life of her own.
Gender roles grow out of this history. The mother is often cast as an object and the father as the model of independence, and both split what should be shared.
Erotic domination acts out the failure of recognition. Benjamin discusses The Story of O as an example.
Mutual recognition is an ideal that is never fully reached. Critics question how far her psychoanalytic picture explains politics.
Infants are active partners in exchange from early. Benjamin draws on infant research, including the work of Daniel Stern, and this replaces the picture of a passive infant.

The other becomes real by surviving aggression. Using Winnicott, Benjamin argues that the child needs to test the other with aggression and find that the other survives, which shows the other to be separate and not a projection.
The ideal of the independent, rational self hides the dependence and care it relies on. Benjamin links that Western ideal to domination.

books.thesis: Modern life speeds up just to stay in place, and the present shrinks until little can last.
books.summary:
Hartmut Rosa, a German sociologist, asks why people in modern societies feel they never have enough time, even though technology saves it. Social Acceleration says life has sped up in three ways at once, and that this is now a structural pressure.

Rosa separates technological acceleration, such as faster transport and communication; acceleration of social change, as jobs, families and knowledge go out of date more quickly; and acceleration of the pace of life, as more actions are crammed into each hour. These feed one another and are driven by competition and a cultural promise of more. People must run just to stay in place, a state he calls frenetic standstill. His worry is that the present shrinks and leaves no stable ground for lasting commitments. Critics say he generalises about a diverse world from one view of modern life.
ideas: Acceleration comes in three kinds that reinforce one another. Rosa identifies technological acceleration, acceleration of social change and acceleration of the pace of life.
Technology saves time on each task and leaves us with less time overall. The freed time is filled with more tasks and rising expectations.
Social change makes knowledge, jobs and relationships go stale faster. What was reliable for one generation no longer holds for the next.
The present shrinks. Rosa's phrase, the shrinking of the present, names how stable ground shortens, so people can make fewer assumptions about what will last.
Competition and a cultural promise that faster is better push acceleration forward. Rosa argues that individuals can hardly step out of it.
Frenetic standstill is lots of motion with no sense of direction. Rosa uses the term for the feeling that nothing changes or leads anywhere.
Acceleration produces a new alienation from time, from places and from ourselves. Critics say Rosa's theory is dense and generalises from one view.
Different spheres speed up at different rates, which Rosa calls desynchronisation. Politics and law, for example, move more slowly than the economy, so democratic decisions fall behind events.

None of the forms of slowness reverses the trend. Rosa lists natural limits, islands of deceleration, side effects such as traffic jams and burnout, and deliberate resistance, and argues that none turns the overall trend around.
Identity becomes situational. Instead of building a life around a lasting project, people adjust themselves from one moment to the next to changing demands.

books.thesis: A good life depends on resonance, the moments when the world answers back, and speed and mastery erode it.
books.summary:
Hartmut Rosa asks what makes a life good, and his answer in Resonance is that it depends on the quality of our relationship to the world. He makes resonance the central concept: a responsive relation in which something outside us touches us and we answer in turn. He sets it against alienation.

Resonance cannot be forced or bought. It happens when a piece of music, a landscape, a person, a task or a belief speaks to us and changes us a little, and it needs an openness that can be neither controlled nor guaranteed. He describes three axes along which it occurs: with other people, with things such as work and school, and with larger frames such as nature, art and religion. Modern society, driven by growth and speed, tends to turn the world into something to be mastered, and so resonance is under threat.
ideas: Resonance is a responsive relation to the world. Rosa defines it as being touched by something and answering back, so that we change in the process.
Alienation is the opposite of resonance. The world seems mute, indifferent or hostile, and we can only use it or endure it.
Resonance cannot be commanded or purchased. Rosa says it is always partly out of our control, and trying to engineer it tends to kill it.
Rosa separates horizontal from diagonal resonance. Horizontal resonance is with other people, such as family and friends, and diagonal resonance is with things such as work, school and objects.
Vertical resonance concerns the larger frames of life, such as religion, nature and art. Rosa argues that modern life has weakened many of them.
Growth and speed shut out resonance. Rosa says modern society is driven by them and so treats the world as something to be mastered.
The concept is hard to test, critics say. They find it vague and note that it is hard to tell what would count as a failure to resonate.

Resonance is different from an echo. An echo returns only my own voice, while resonance needs a counterpart with a voice of its own, so it can include friction and disagreement and is not the same as harmony.
A good life is measured by the quality of our relation to the world. Rosa argues that resources, options and money are means and not ends.
Teaching works through resonance. Rosa argues that it succeeds when teacher, pupil and subject respond to one another and fails when it is organised around performance targets alone.

books.thesis: Pain destroys language and shrinks a person's world, which is why torture can unmake people.
books.summary:
Elaine Scarry starts from a plain observation. Physical pain is nearly impossible to describe, and a person in agony loses the ability to speak in sentences. The book asks what that silence does to the sufferer, to the people around them, and to the world they live in.

The argument has two movements. The first shows how pain shrinks a person's world to the size of a body and takes language with it, and how torturers exploit this by turning the prisoner's surroundings and voice against him. The second turns to making. Tools, buildings, poems and beliefs are the human answer to pain, ways of extending the body and its feeling into a shared world. Scarry draws on Amnesty reports, the Bible and Marx. Some readers find the second half more speculative than the first, and she leaves open how far imagining can repair what pain undoes.
ideas: Pain has no object. Fear and desire are about something, but pain is about nothing outside itself, which is part of why it is so hard to put into words.
Pain resists language and, at its extreme, destroys it. The person in agony is pushed back toward the cries and groans that come before speech.
Pain is certain for the sufferer and easy to doubt for everyone else. Scarry builds her account of suffering around this gap between certainty and doubt.
Torture is built around interrogation, yet Scarry argues the questions are beside the point. The real work is staging the prisoner's own voice as something that can be broken and used.
Torture turns ordinary objects against the person. A chair, a bed or a door becomes an instrument of pain, and the shelter a room normally gives is made to attack the person inside.
War, like torture, rests on injuring bodies. Scarry argues that wounded and dead bodies are used to settle which side's contested beliefs will count as real.
Making and imagining run in the opposite direction from pain. A chair, a poem or a law carries human feeling outward into the world and gives it a shape others can share.
Severe pain shrinks the world to the size of the body. The sufferer loses the usual sense of a wider world beyond it.
Descriptions of pain borrow the language of weapons. Scarry notes that people speak of a stabbing or burning pain, and so refer to an agent that is not there.
Torture produces a show of power for a regime whose authority is in doubt. Scarry argues that the prisoner's pain is turned into a display of strength the regime does not truly have.

books.thesis: Jobs, identities and bonds no longer hold their shape, and freedom now arrives with unease.
books.summary:
Zygmunt Bauman begins with a metaphor. Solids keep their shape and liquids do not, and he thinks that fits life since the late twentieth century. Jobs, institutions, neighbourhoods and identities used to be built to last. Now they are expected to change, and the book asks what it feels like to live with nothing settled to lean on.

Bauman works through the idea in sections on emancipation, individuality, time and space, work and community. Early modernity, he argues, melted old traditions in order to cast firmer ones, while the present keeps melting with little rebuilding. People are freer to choose, but they carry the whole burden of choosing and the blame when things fail. Power belongs to those who can move, and capital moves faster than anyone. The book is a long essay, not an empirical study, so its sweeping claims are more suggestive than proven.
ideas: Liquid modernity melts without promising a replacement. Solid modernity melted inherited orders so that better, sturdier ones could replace them, but now nothing is expected to last.
Individuals are handed the task of building their own identities. When the larger system fails them, Bauman says, the failure tends to be read as a personal shortcoming.
Power has become light and mobile. Capital can move on quickly, while those tied to a place, such as workers and local communities, are left with whatever it leaves behind.
Work has stopped being a lifelong project. Short contracts and constant restructuring make it hard to plan a career or build lasting trust with colleagues.
Time, not distance, becomes the scarce resource. With distance easy to cross, speed and the ability to move on quickly turn into marks of status.
Freedom arrives with a loss of company. As class, neighbourhood and tradition loosen, people gain freedom and lose guidance and the comfort of knowing what is expected of them.
Unease drives people toward groups defined by sameness. The search for security can harden into suspicion of strangers.
The agora is emptying out. Bauman worries that the space where private troubles can be turned into public issues is vanishing, so people are left to deal with shared problems alone.

Freedom on paper is not freedom in practice. Bauman separates individuals de jure, who are formally free to choose their lives, from individuals de facto, who have the means to do so, and sees the gap as a mark of the liquid age.
Solid-era power rested on fixed routines and mutual dependence. Bauman uses the Fordist factory and Bentham's panopticon as images of it, set against the present ease of moving on.

books.thesis: We want close bonds but keep an eye on the exit, and consumer habits have seeped into love.
books.summary:
Zygmunt Bauman turns his liquid modernity argument toward intimacy. People want close bonds, yet they watch the exit, anxious about being left or being stuck. The book asks why relationships have become so frail and what that does to the people in them.

Bauman argues that consumer habits have seeped into love. A partner is weighed like a purchase, judged on satisfaction and replaced if the return disappoints. Commitment looks like a risk that closes off other options, while a life without it feels lonely and unprotected. A market of advice, columns and guides thrives on this uncertainty, and he extends the worry to how we treat strangers and neighbours. The tone is that of an essayist, not a researcher, and he offers no remedy. He suggests only that love needs a willingness to be vulnerable, which a culture of keeping options open works against.
ideas: Bonds are entered with an exit in view. People want closeness and also want to stay free to leave, and the two wishes pull against each other.
Connections are easy to make and easy to cut. Bauman contrasts them with relationships, and says phones and online networks make connections easier still.
Consumer habits seep into love. A partner gets judged like a product on satisfaction and is expected to be replaceable if the experience disappoints.
Commitment and its absence both frighten. Commitment feels like a risk that closes off other options, yet a life without it leaves people lonely and insecure, so they are stuck between two fears.
Love advice sells because people distrust their own judgement. Bauman notes that advice columns and relationship experts often treat love as a skill to be bought and practised.
Sex is increasingly treated as a self-contained episode. It carries no duty to continue afterwards, which fits a culture that prizes keeping options open.
The old call to love your neighbour is under strain. Bauman asks how it holds up when strangers are mostly seen as a risk.
Semi-detached couples hedge against a bond that is hard to leave. Bauman discusses couples who keep separate homes and lives.
Virtual proximity makes contact easy, frequent and thin. Bauman suggests it may wear away the skills needed to sustain lasting ties.
A child can become an object of emotional consumption. Bauman notes that, as other bonds feel fragile, a child is treated as a dependable source of feeling, which places a heavy load on the child.

books.thesis: A world that sees skin first and the person second deforms the inner life of those it labels.
books.summary:
Frantz Fanon was a psychiatrist from Martinique, and in this book he tries to describe what colonial racism does to the mind of a Black person. He asks why Black men and women in the Antilles and in France so often measure themselves against a white standard, and what it costs to live in a world that sees skin first and a person second.

He looks at language, at desire and relationships across racial lines, and at how a sense of inferiority is laid on people from outside. He argues with psychoanalysts such as Octave Mannoni and borrows and bends Hegel's account of recognition. The prose moves between case analysis and personal testimony. Some of his claims about women and about homosexuality have been sharply criticised. The book ends without a programme and asks for a person to be free of both history's weight and a fixed racial identity.
ideas: Mastering French brings approval and a loss of self. In the Antilles, speaking good French counts as a step toward being treated as fully human, and Fanon shows what adopting the colonizer's language costs.
Inferiority is produced from outside. Fanon argues that economic and social conditions lay a sense of inferiority onto the skin, and that it is no private trait of the individual.
The white gaze fixes the Black man as an object. On a train in France a child says, Look, a Negro, and Fanon describes feeling reduced to a thing, no longer a person with his own body and view.

Fanon reads interracial desire as an attempt to escape inferiority. He applies this to the desire of some Black women for white men and of Black men for white women, though critics have found his treatment of women unfair.
Dependence is made by the colonial situation. Fanon rejects Octave Mannoni's claim that colonised peoples are dependent by temperament from the start.
The Black man is denied real recognition. Using Hegel, Fanon argues that the slave's freedom was handed over by the master and never won, so reciprocal acknowledgement is missing.
Fanon closes by refusing to let the weight of the past or a fixed racial essence define a person. He asks for a life open to questioning.

A full diagnosis of the disorder must be social. Fanon argues for sociogeny alongside ontogeny and phylogeny, meaning the social origin of the disorder, which he finds in colonial and racial relations.
The Black person as a symbol of evil is learned, not inherited. Fanon rejects Jung's idea of a collective unconscious as an inherited feature and points to comics, stories and schooling.
Sartre's Black Orpheus left Fanon feeling that his experience had been placed inside someone else's argument. The essay treats negritude as a passing stage in a larger dialectic.

books.thesis: Colonial violence is psychological as well as political, and so is the violence of resistance.
books.summary:
Fanon wrote this book while dying of leukaemia and serving the Algerian independence movement. A psychiatrist, he treats colonial rule as a system that damages minds as well as economies. The question running through it is how a colonised people can become free without copying the order that ruled them.

Fanon argues that the colonial world is split into two zones kept apart by force, so decolonisation is a violent process. He presents violence as a way for the colonised to recover self-respect and unity. Critics including Hannah Arendt have disputed this, and how to read it remains debated. The national bourgeoisie, he says, tends to inherit the colonial machinery and use it for itself, and he warns against nationalism without a social programme. The final chapter presents clinical cases from the Algerian war.
ideas: The colonial world is cut in two. Fanon describes the settler's town and the native quarter as a world of opposites, kept apart by police and soldiers.
Decolonisation is always violent, in Fanon's account. It replaces one order of people with another, and no colonial power gives up its position out of politeness.
Fanon calls violence freeing for the colonised. It frees the native from a sense of inferiority and from passivity, a claim Arendt and others have disputed.
The national bourgeoisie inherits the colonial machinery and imitates the old rulers. In Fanon's account it lacks the means or will to build a new economy for everyone.
Fanon looks to the peasantry as the main revolutionary force. He thinks the urban workers have been partly bought off by a share in the colonial economy.
National consciousness without a social programme decays. It turns into narrow nationalism or tribalism, and Fanon warns of single-party rule and leaders who take the place of the people.
The colonial war leaves psychological wounds on both sides. In the last chapter Fanon presents clinical cases of Algerian fighters and French torturers whose disorders he links to the war.

A living culture is made in the struggle, not dug up from the past. In the chapter On National Culture, Fanon warns that intellectuals who recover pre-colonial traditions to restore pride risk freezing them.
Rural revolt needs political education. Fanon is wary of its spontaneity and argues for leaders who explain and listen to the people instead of giving orders.
Fanon urges the Third World not to imitate Europe. He ends by calling for a new humanism and a new kind of person.

books.thesis: Patriarchy harms men too, because it teaches them to fear and hide their feelings.
books.summary:
Bell hooks wrote this book to speak to men, and she begins from an uncomfortable observation. Many men say they want love yet feel little of it, and many of the women around them find them emotionally closed. She asks why men are so often cut off from their own feelings, and she answers by looking at how boys are raised.

Hooks defines patriarchy as a system of domination that shapes men as well as women. Boys learn early to hide feeling, and the lesson is often taught by shaming or violence. In short chapters on work, sex, violence and love, she argues that patriarchal masculinity ties a man's worth to power and provision and teaches him that vulnerability is weakness. She is clear that women also help sustain the system. Her proposal is that men can choose honesty and emotional openness, and that love is a real alternative to dominance.
ideas: Patriarchy is something men live inside and not simply benefit from. Hooks defines it as a system of domination that boys and men are socialised into.
Boys are taught early to bury what they feel. The lesson is often delivered through shaming, punishment or violence, sometimes by their own parents.
Many men want love and have learned that needing it is weak. Hooks argues that they settle for control, silence or distance instead.
Women help sustain patriarchy too. Hooks says mothers and partners often teach and reward the same emotional restraint in boys and men.
Male violence is tied to the demand that men prove themselves through dominance. Hooks suggests it often covers an unspoken pain.
Patriarchal ideas of work tie a man's worth to status and provision. His sense of self is then left fragile when that standing is lost.
Men can change by choosing honesty and emotional openness. Hooks presents love as a real alternative to the will to dominate.
Earlier feminist writing, hooks says, left men out. She criticises it for treating them only as enemies, which gave men no picture of how they might change.
Patriarchal men learn to treat sex as a performance or a conquest cut off from feeling. Hooks argues that this leaves sex lonely and intimacy out of reach.
Popular images of Black men tie manhood to dominance and violence. Hooks sees this as an exaggeration of ideas held across society.

books.thesis: Gender is a performance repeated until it looks natural, and it could be repeated differently.
books.summary:
Judith Butler challenges an assumption in feminist thought, that there is a stable group called women whose interests politics should serve. She asks what produces that category, who it leaves out, and what an inner gender identity rests on.

Butler argues that the split between biological sex and cultural gender breaks down, because ideas about sex are already shaped by gender. Gender is performative: produced by repeated acts, gestures and speech that make it look natural, within a heterosexual matrix that expects sex, gender and desire to line up. Drag shows how imitation can expose the lack of an original. Performativity is often misread as choosing a gender each morning, which Butler denies. The book is famously dense, and critics dispute its style and its politics.
ideas: The category women is less stable than feminism often assumes. Butler argues that it leaves people out and is itself made by the power it hopes to challenge.
Sex is no more natural than gender. Butler holds that the split between biological sex and cultural gender does not stand, because our ideas about sex are already shaped by gender.
The heterosexual matrix expects sex, gender and desire to line up, as in a male body, masculine behaviour and desire for women. Deviations get treated as failures.
Gender is performative. There is no doer behind the deed: repeated acts, gestures and speech produce the appearance of an inner identity, and repetition makes it look natural.
Performativity does not mean choosing a gender each morning. Butler says the acts are constrained by norms nobody picked, so freedom lies in how they are repeated.
Drag shows gender as imitation. It hints that the supposed original is itself an imitation, though critics dispute how subversive drag is.
Change comes through subversive repetition, which shifts the terms of gender from within. The book's difficult style has drawn complaints from readers who want the argument stated more plainly.

Gender identity is partly formed through gender melancholy. Drawing on Freud, Butler argues that a lost same-sex attachment is taken in and not mourned, because the taboo on homosexuality forbids grieving it.

Becoming a woman is shaped by norms, not simply chosen. Butler reads Beauvoir's line that one is not born but becomes a woman, asks whether that becoming is a matter of choice, and concludes that it is not.
Gender norms depend on excluded and disavowed bodies. Borrowing from Mary Douglas and Julia Kristeva, Butler argues that bodily boundaries are policed through the idea of the abject.

books.thesis: Science runs on imaginative pictures, and the image of society as separate self-interested units is one.
books.summary:
Mary Midgley argues that human thinking runs on imaginative pictures, and that science is no exception. She uses the word myth for a deep, shared image that organises how people see things. She does not mean that it must be false.

She takes aim at several: society as a pile of separate, self-interested individuals, nature as a machine, and progress as a steady climb. She is sharply critical of popular science that dresses opinions about human nature up as results, with the selfish gene as her chief example. Her method is a philosopher's habit of asking what a metaphor is doing. She also holds that no single science can describe everything, so different kinds of explanation have to live together. Some scientists found her too hostile to reductionism, and the book is more a set of provocations than a system.
ideas: A myth, for Midgley, is a deep imaginative pattern and need not be a falsehood. Progress is one example, and such patterns organise how people think.
Science runs on images such as nature as a machine. They are picked up early, shape which questions get asked, and are rarely checked.
The picture of society as built from separate, self-interested individuals is an old story. Midgley argues it ignores how dependent humans are on one another from birth.
Metaphors such as the selfish gene slip a view of human nature into what is presented as plain science. Midgley criticises this move.
Progress is itself a myth. Midgley questions throughout the book the belief that history climbs steadily and that science will solve everything.
Descartes's picture of mind as separate from the rest of nature feeds the fantasy of a detached, purely rational thinker. Midgley treats it as a myth about ourselves.
No single science covers everything. Different kinds of explanation, including those of the humanities, have to be allowed to coexist.
The picture of evolution as a ladder leading up to humans is a myth of progress dressed as biology. Midgley criticises the view of evolution as an escalator.
The claim that minds are computers is another version of the machine myth. Midgley is wary of it and of the idea that brains can be copied.
Images such as Gaia remind us that we belong to an interdependent whole. Midgley suggests this holds whatever their scientific standing, and the machine picture hides it.

books.thesis: Emotional life and market logic have merged, and intimacy has grown cooler and more calculating.
books.summary:
Eva Illouz, a sociologist, begins with a puzzle. We talk about our feelings more than any earlier generation, in therapy, in offices and in relationships, yet intimacy often feels calculated and thin. She asks how the economy and the language of emotion became so tangled together.

Her answer is a concept she calls emotional capitalism, in which economic life takes on the vocabulary of feeling and emotional life takes on the logic of the market. She traces how twentieth century managers drew on psychology to understand workers, how therapeutic language moved from the clinic into the home, and how skills such as communication became things to measure. Online dating is a late example, with partners appearing as profiles ranked against criteria. The book is an argument about culture, not an experiment, and critics say it paints the past as warmer than it was.
ideas: Emotional capitalism is Illouz's term for the mutual shaping of economy and feeling. Economic life takes on the vocabulary of feeling, and emotional life takes on the logic of calculation.

Psychology entered the workplace as a tool of management. Early twentieth century managers used it to understand workers and raise productivity, which brought talk of emotion and communication into work.
Therapeutic language moved from the clinic into the home. Words such as communication, needs and boundaries treat relationships as something to be worked on and negotiated.
Emotional skills came to be measured like job skills. Feeling is judged as competence, so a person can look emotionally better or worse equipped.
Online dating turns partners into profiles. Illouz uses it to show how people begin to evaluate each other like goods, compared against criteria.
The ideal of the emotionally healthy person becomes a norm. Unhappiness can then look like a personal failure to be fixed and not a shared problem.
Feminism and therapy together made marriage easier to question and to leave. Illouz argues that they promoted an ideal of equal, communicative marriage.
The therapeutic story of the self tells a person's past as an injury to be overcome. Illouz reads this narrative as now spread widely through self-help books and talk shows.
Advice writers such as Dale Carnegie link emotional skill to commercial success. Illouz reads them as teaching people to manage their feelings in order to get along and win cooperation.

Online, people form attachments to a textual self. In her chapter on online dating Illouz argues that the Internet favours imagination over bodily presence in early contact, so people are often let down at a first meeting.

books.thesis: Choosing partners freely ties love to self-worth, so rejection reads as a verdict on who we are.
books.summary:
Eva Illouz, a sociologist, starts from a puzzle. Love seems to hurt more now that people choose their partners freely. She says a large share of the pain comes from the social conditions of choosing.

In earlier eras, family, rank and moral character gave romantic choice firm footing. Today the choice rests on the self, so being chosen or rejected feels like a verdict on one's worth. The internet and the sexual marketplace add endless comparison, and Illouz speaks of uncertainty about what we want and feel. She also claims that men and women hold unequal power in that marketplace, a point critics dispute. The book offers a diagnosis and no cure. It does not suggest going back to constrained courtship, and it leaves open how people might love well under conditions that make love so exposed.
ideas: Much of love's pain comes from social arrangements, Illouz argues. Psychology tends to treat it as individual damage, which she thinks misses the larger picture.
Austen's novels serve as a contrast case. There, social rank and moral character gave romantic choice firmer footing than it has today.
Free choice ties romance to self-worth. Being chosen or rejected feels like a verdict on the person, so rejection hurts as recognition withheld.
Endless options and easy comparison keep people browsing. Helped by the internet, they measure each prospect against others, which makes commitment harder.
Uncertainty about desire is built into modern romantic choice. Illouz says people have become unsure what they want and what the other person wants.
Sexual freedom gives men and women unequal power in the sexual marketplace, Illouz argues, because men can often delay commitment more easily. Critics say this is overstated.
The book offers a diagnosis and no cure. It does not argue for going back to arranged or tightly controlled courtship.
Time bears unequally on the sexes. Illouz points to age and the fertility timeline weighing on women far more than on men, and says this shapes who can afford to delay commitment.
Psychology and self-help have rationalised romance, in the sense Max Weber gave the word. People learn to assess relationships by standards of fit, satisfaction and communication.
Idealising imagination sets people up for disappointment. Illouz argues that people build a picture of a partner in advance and suffer when the real person differs.

books.thesis: Treating yourself as you would a friend builds more resilience than self-criticism does.
books.summary:
Kristin Neff, a psychologist, starts from a practical puzzle. When we fail or suffer, we are far harsher on ourselves than on a friend. Most of us half believe the inner critic keeps us honest and driven, and Neff tests that belief against the research.

She breaks self-compassion into three parts. Self-kindness replaces harsh self-judgement, common humanity sees failure as a shared experience, and mindfulness means seeing painful feelings without burying them or being swept away. She separates it from self-esteem, which rises and falls with success and often depends on feeling above others. Drawing on studies, including some of her own, she reports links between self-compassion and lower anxiety and depression, and argues it does not breed complacency. The book includes short exercises. Her Buddhist roots shape the approach, and some critics think the research is still young.
ideas: Self-compassion means treating yourself as you would a struggling friend. It offers warmth in place of the usual inner scolding.
Neff splits self-compassion into three parts: self-kindness, a sense of common humanity, and mindfulness. Each answers a different habit of harsh self-treatment.
Common humanity counters the feeling of being uniquely flawed or alone. It means seeing that failure and suffering are shared parts of life.
Self-esteem and self-compassion differ. Esteem rises and falls with success and often depends on comparison, while self-compassion stays available when things go badly.
Mindfulness means seeing pain before being kind to it. Neff uses it for noticing painful feelings as they are, without pushing them away or being carried off by them.
Self-criticism motivates less well than people think. Neff cites research suggesting that people who treat themselves kindly tend to try again after failure.
The book offers short practices for building the habit. One is a brief self-compassion break combining a calming phrase and a soothing touch.
Self-compassion is not self-pity. Self-pity is absorbed in one's own troubles and forgets that others suffer too, while self-compassion keeps the shared human view in sight.
Kindness toward oneself is not self-indulgence. Neff argues that a person who cares about a friend wants them to grow, so a kind inner voice can still ask for change.
Harsh self-talk tends to backfire for a bodily reason. Drawing on emotion research, Neff describes self-criticism as triggering the body's threat response, while kindness engages a soothing system.

books.thesis: When a way of life ends, courage may mean hoping for a good that cannot yet be imagined.
books.summary:
Jonathan Lear, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, takes up the story of Plenty Coups, the last great chief of the Crow nation. When the buffalo disappeared and the Crow were confined to a reservation, the activities that gave their lives shape, such as hunting and war, became impossible. Lear asks what courage can mean when the way of life that defined it comes to an end.

He argues that a culture can collapse in a way beyond physical loss. Plenty Coups, guided by a dream of the chickadee, led the Crow to adapt and hold on to a hope Lear calls radical. It is hope for a future good that the people cannot yet picture, because the concepts to describe it do not exist. The book offers a picture of hope at the edge of what a culture can understand, and does not offer a method.
ideas: Lear's main case is Plenty Coups, the last great chief of the Crow. He led his people through the end of the buffalo-hunting life and into reservation confinement.
A culture can collapse in a way beyond physical loss. When counting coup and warfare became impossible, the Crow lost the terms that made their lives intelligible.
Plenty Coups's boyhood dream held up the chickadee as a model. The small bird survives by listening and learning, and Lear reads the dream as preparation.
After the buffalo were gone, Plenty Coups said, nothing happened. Lear reads this as a sign that the Crow could no longer tell events as stories with a point.
Radical hope is hope for a future good that exceeds our present ability to conceive it. It has no content yet, so it depends on trust that the world is basically good.
Courage is usually defined by a culture. Lear asks what it means when that culture is gone, and suggests that then courage is the hope itself.
Lear presents radical hope as a picture of hope under extreme conditions. He does not offer it as a recipe or claim that every choice of Plenty Coups was right.

The Crow decision to side with the United States against rival tribes was made without being able to picture the future. Lear reads Plenty Coups as judging that resistance would lead to the Crow's destruction.
Every way of life is vulnerable. Lear speaks of the vulnerability of a culture, which rests on concepts that can cease to make sense, and its members may not see this coming.
Lear's source is a retelling and not the chief's own text. His main source is the life of Plenty Coups recorded by Frank Linderman, and Lear is aware of that.

books.t: Happiness, Death, and the Remainder of Life
books.thesis: Read together, Aristotle and Freud show what a good life asks of us once we accept that it ends.
books.summary:
Jonathan Lear sets side by side two thinkers rarely read together, Aristotle and Freud. Both are concerned with how a human being can live well, and both worked with a view of the mind in which reason and desire pull against each other. Lear asks what a good life demands once we take seriously that it will end.

He reads Aristotle's account of happiness as an activity carried out across a whole life, and notes Aristotle's tension between a life of ethical action among others and a life of contemplation. Freud, in Lear's reading, adds that much of what moves us is unconscious, so a person may think he is living well while hiding conflict from himself. Lear is also a practising psychoanalyst and treats analysis as an ethical practice. It is better at framing the question of how to live in the time that remains than at settling it.
ideas: Lear pairs Aristotle's ethics with Freud's psychoanalysis. He assumes that both are trying to say what it takes for a human being to live well.
For Aristotle, happiness is an activity of living well across a whole life. It is no passing feeling, so it can only be judged over time.

Aristotle sketches two pictures of the best life, and they pull against each other. One is a life of virtuous action among other people and the other a life of contemplation, and Lear examines the strain between them.
Death presses on both thinkers. A good life must be one a person could stand behind while knowing that it will end.
Freud adds that much of what moves us is unconscious. A person can believe he is living well while hiding a conflict from himself.
Lear treats psychoanalysis as an ethical practice. He is a practising analyst, and sees it as aimed at living more honestly with one's own desires.
The remainder of life is the time left to a mortal creature. The book asks how that time can be lived well once death is taken seriously.
No one can be called happy until death, said Solon, and Lear draws on Aristotle's discussion of the saying. It shows that the shape of a life is only fixed at its end.
Freud's late idea of a death drive is treated as a serious question, not a settled doctrine. Lear reads it as an attempt to think about repetition and the pull toward ending.
Making the unconscious conscious has an ethical side. Lear suggests that a person's character is shaped by what he can bear to know about himself.

books.thesis: Photographs let us feel we possess the world, and that possession thins our experience of it.
books.summary:
Susan Sontag collected six essays in this book, and she starts from an everyday fact. We live among photographs and take for granted what they do to the way we see. The book asks what changes when experience becomes something a person can capture, keep and collect.

Sontag argues that photographing is a way of taking possession. It lets us feel that we own a place or a person while keeping a safe distance, and it turns the world into a stock of images. She compares our situation to Plato's cave. Photographs seem to be pieces of the real, which gives them authority, though framing and choice shape what they show. She draws on surrealism, on Diane Arbus and on the habits of tourists. Some of her claims, particularly about Arbus, have been disputed, and she later revised her view that images simply numb us.
ideas: We live among images that tell us what the world is like, and we take them as a replacement for it. Sontag returns to Plato's cave to make the point.
Photographing is a way of taking possession. The traveller with a camera has a souvenir of the place and a protection from meeting it.
The vocabulary of photography is borrowed from hunting and violence. People load, aim and shoot, and Sontag suggests that photographing people treats them as things.
A photograph's authority comes from seeming to be a piece of the real. It looks like a trace taken directly from the scene, though framing and selection shape what it shows.
Every photograph is a reminder of mortality. It holds a moment from a life that has moved on, and old pictures of people long dead carry that quality.
Sontag links photography to surrealism and its taste for the overlooked and shabby. She reads Diane Arbus's pictures of outsiders as cold, a view critics have disputed.
As images multiply, shock wears off. A culture of images changes what counts as real and what we feel we need to look at.
Families use photographs to build a portrait chronicle. Sontag notes that taking snapshots has become part of the ritual of family life, at weddings and on holidays.
The photographer's role is one of non-intervention. To record a scene of suffering is to stand outside it, Sontag argues, and the camera can become a way of not acting.
An American taste for treating all things as equally worth seeing runs from Whitman through Walker Evans to Arbus. Sontag says this democratic vision can flatten moral distinctions.

books.thesis: Metaphors about disease add shame and blame to suffering, so they are best resisted.
books.summary:
Susan Sontag wrote this short book after her own cancer treatment, though she keeps herself out of its pages. She noticed that diseases do more than make people sick. They attract meanings, and those meanings can cause suffering of their own. She asks what is added when tuberculosis and cancer are described in terms of character, passion, repression and war.

She compares the two. TB was romanticised in the nineteenth century as a disease of sensitivity and passion that refined the sufferer. Cancer, in the twentieth, was cast as a shameful condition linked to repression and growth gone wild. In both cases the patient is hinted to be responsible. She also criticises military language, such as wars on cancer and invading cells, which makes death a defeat. Her answer is to resist metaphor and look at illness plainly, though she admits that this is hard.
ideas: The healthiest way of being ill is the one most free of metaphor, Sontag argues. The wish to see illness plainly drives the whole book.
Tuberculosis was romanticised in the nineteenth century as a disease of sensitivity and passion. It lent the sufferer a refined, interesting look.
Cancer in the twentieth century was imagined as shameful. It was tied to repression and uncontrolled growth, which made it feel like a judgement on the person.
Both diseases get read as expressions of character. The patient is hinted to be partly responsible, which adds blame to the pain of being sick.
Military metaphors turn the patient into a battlefield. The war on cancer and talk of invading cells make dying look like a defeat.
Moral meaning gathers around diseases with unknown causes and no sure cure. As understanding and treatment improve, the aura begins to fade.
Sontag's remedy is to resist metaphor and speak about illness plainly. She admits that metaphor is hard to avoid and that people use it for understandable reasons.
She keeps her own case out of the essay. Sontag wrote it while being treated for cancer, but she writes as a critic of language and ideas.
Political language that borrows illness can license harsh measures. Sontag notes that a society is said to be sick or a group is called a cancer.
Doctors in some countries used to withhold a cancer diagnosis from patients. Sontag observes that the word carried so much shame and dread.

books.thesis: Images of suffering do not guarantee compassion, and they can numb as well as move us.
books.summary:
Susan Sontag opens with Virginia Woolf's Three Guineas, where Woolf thought pictures of war's victims might unite people against war. Sontag asks whether that is true, and what we do when we look at images of other people's suffering. She also revisits her own earlier view, from On Photography, that a steady diet of such images numbs us.

She now argues that compassion is unstable. A picture can move a viewer, but the feeling fades or freezes if nothing can be done with it. The same image can serve opposite sides depending on its caption and context, and early war photographers sometimes arranged their scenes. She looks back to Goya's etchings and forward to the way memory increasingly works through pictures. A recurring warning is against assuming a shared us when we look at the pain of others, since safe viewers do not stand where the sufferers do.
ideas: Sontag begins by doubting Virginia Woolf's hope. In Three Guineas, Woolf thought pictures of war's victims might unite people against war, and Sontag doubts the simple version of that hope.
Sontag revises her earlier claim that images numb us. The problem, she says, is that compassion cannot last unless it turns into some kind of action.
The same picture of suffering can serve opposite sides. A caption and a context decide what it is taken to prove.
Photographs were never raw records. Early war photographers sometimes arranged their scenes, as Roger Fenton is said to have done in the Crimea, and a famous Capa photograph is still disputed.
The shock of images belongs to more than photography. Goya's etchings of war's cruelty show that art made it hard to look away long before cameras did.
There is no shared we when looking at pictures of others' pain. Sontag warns that safe viewers do not stand where the sufferers do.
Memory increasingly works through pictures. A vivid image can stay with us while a narrative, which might help us understand, slips away.
The dignity of being shown is unevenly given. Sontag notes that news pictures show the far-off dead of other peoples in ways seldom used for a nation's own dead.
An existing antiwar movement gave Vietnam photographs their force. Sontag suggests that the movement, and not the photographs alone, did this.
People feel an appetite to look at horror. Sontag acknowledges this and treats it as a fact to be faced and not only as a vice.

books.thesis: Crowds and rulers grow from one root: the wish to survive others.
books.summary:
Elias Canetti asks what crowds are, why people join them and how they relate to those who rule. He starts from the fact that humans dislike being touched by strangers. A crowd is the place where that fear is briefly reversed, as individuals feel themselves equal.

The first half is a taxonomy of crowds, including open and closed ones, baiting and flight crowds, and the images, such as fire and sea, that societies attach to them. The second half turns to power. Canetti argues that commands leave a sting in whoever obeys, and that the root of power is the survivor, someone who stands among the dead and feels the satisfaction of having lived. He reads Daniel Paul Schreber's memoirs as a portrait of paranoia as the illness of power. The book is free association, not proof, and many readers treat it as a meditation more than a theory.
ideas: Canetti starts from the dread of being touched by strangers. A crowd is where that fear reverses, and he opens the book with this ordinary observation about how people guard their personal space.
Discharge is the moment a crowd forms. Differences of rank and status fall away and everyone feels equal.
Open and closed crowds have opposite lives. Open crowds grow without limit but can vanish quickly, while closed crowds keep their boundaries and last longer.
Crowd symbols carry the character of the crowd. Societies attach fire, sea, rain, forest and grain to crowds, and Canetti reads each as expressing a quality of the crowd it represents.
Every command leaves a sting in the person who obeys. People tend to pass that sting down to others beneath them, which creates chains of command.
The survivor sits at the root of power. Standing among the dead, he feels the satisfaction of having lived, and the ruler wants to be the one who survives everyone.
Paranoia is the characteristic illness of power. Canetti reads the memoirs of Daniel Paul Schreber as a portrait of it.

Crowds can be classified by their dominant feeling. Canetti names baiting, flight, prohibition, reversal and feast crowds, and adds the double crowd, such as two armies or two sexes facing each other.
Crowd crystals give a crowd its shape. They are small, tight groups, such as armies or religious orders, that keep it from dissolving.
Secrecy is central to power. The ruler conceals his intentions while demanding to know everything about others.

books.thesis: Intelligent people embrace a total ideology because certainty is easier than facing the truth alone.
books.summary:
Czesław Miłosz, a Polish poet who left his country's diplomatic service in 1951, wrote this book to explain how intelligent writers and thinkers came to accept Stalinist rule. Educated people who could see what was happening chose to believe, and he wants to know why.

He uses two borrowed images. The Pill of Murti-Bing, from a novel by Witkiewicz, makes its swallower serenely content with the new order. Ketman, a term Miłosz took from Gobineau's account of Persia, is the art of outward conformity while holding inward reservations. Four portraits of Polish writers, labelled with Greek letters, show how each made peace with the regime for different reasons. A complete doctrine, he argues, gives people certainty and a place in history, a relief after war. It is a personal essay, not a study, and later readers have matched some of its sketches to real people.
ideas: The Pill of Murti-Bing is Miłosz's image for intellectual conversion. It comes from a novel by Witkiewicz, and swallowing it makes a person cheerfully content with the new order.
Ketman is the art of outward conformity while holding inward reservations. Miłosz borrowed the word from Gobineau's account of Persia and describes several varieties of it.
A total doctrine offers relief from uncertainty. It gives answers and a place in history, and Miłosz suggests this was especially tempting to minds exhausted by war.
There was no single route into accommodation. Miłosz draws four portraits of Polish writers, named with Greek letters, who each reached an accommodation with the regime for different reasons.
Fear alone does not explain it. Miłosz insists that many intellectuals took up the new belief out of conviction and hunger for meaning.
Playing a role long enough can change the player. Miłosz suggests that the mask of Ketman can harden into belief.
Miłosz does not treat those who gave in as fools. He writes as someone who felt the temptation himself, and that is why the book unsettles.
The four portraits are given types as labels: Alpha the Moralist, Beta the Disappointed Lover, Gamma the Slave of History and Delta the Troubadour. Each shows a different route into accommodation.
Ketman comes in varieties with respectable excuses. Miłosz describes national, professional and aesthetic Ketman, in which a person defends a compromise as serving the nation, his craft or beauty.
Socialist realism made art a service to the doctrine. Writers had to praise the order they lived under and were judged by their usefulness to the Party.

books.thesis: Cioran's aphorisms attack hope and the fact of birth with wit, and many readers find them consoling.
books.summary:
Emil Cioran was a Romanian writer who settled in Paris and wrote in French, and this collection of aphorisms is one of his late books. It circles one idea: being born is the original trouble, the one fact no argument can undo. The fragments, each in its own mood, deal with birth, sleeplessness, God, time and the thought of ending it all.

Cioran is hostile to hope, plans and progress, which he sees as ways of postponing a plain fact. He comes back often to suicide, as a thought that makes life bearable more than as an act. He is drawn to saints and mystics while having no faith, and he praises music, Bach especially, with something close to gratitude. The surprise is the tone. The despair arrives with wit, and many readers find the book consoling and good company.
ideas: Birth is the original misfortune, and nothing can correct it. The whole book circles the idea that having been born at all is a trouble no argument or achievement can undo.
Suicide works for Cioran as a thought and not as a plan. He keeps it in reserve, and knowing the exit is there is what makes life bearable.
Sleepless nights give him his sharpest material. Awake, lucid and alone, he feels existence most plainly as a burden.
Hope, plans and progress are all postponements of one plain fact. Cioran scorns them because they let people avoid looking at it.
Music, Bach above all, gets something close to gratitude from a writer who thanks almost nothing else. It is one of the few places where his tone softens.
Saints, mystics and Buddhists draw his envy. He admires a faith he cannot share, and the admiration shows what his own position lacks.
The book is built from fragments, each a mood and not an argument, and the despair comes with wit. Many readers find that combination oddly consoling.
The French title, De l'inconvénient d'être né, speaks of an inconvenience. That word gives the complaint a dry, understated tone which the English title only partly keeps.
God appears as a flawed creator to be complained about, not as the subject of a doctrine. Cioran uses the figure to give his grievance somewhere to land.
Writing is a way of getting through bad days. It manages his despair and does not claim to overcome it.

books.thesis: Cioran's first French book makes exhaustion and doubt its subject, in formal, polished prose.
books.summary:
A Short History of Decay was Emil Cioran's first book in French, published in 1949 after years of writing in Romanian. He is said to have rewritten it several times, and the prose has a formal, polished edge. Its subject is exhaustion, doubt and the sense of coming at the end of something.

The book is a series of short essays and aphorisms with no single argument. Cioran treats lucidity as a kind of illness, doubt as a habit that cannot even spare itself, and civilisations as organisms that tire and fall. He distrusts enthusiasm and system building and prefers failure and disillusion to the comfort of belief. Readers divide over whether this is nihilism or a perverse tonic, and the book gives no help in deciding. What is clear is the force of the sentences. Cioran makes weariness a subject with a style.
ideas: Lucidity is an illness in Cioran's telling. Seeing the human situation clearly wears the observer down and does not set him free.
Doubt in this book is turned on everything, itself included. Cioran finds exhaustion behind every system of belief offered to him.
Civilisations age like organisms. Late cultures turn inward and tire, a theme that echoes Spengler.
Cioran wrote this book in French, his adopted language, after years of writing in Romanian. The formal, polished prose gives his despair a classical shape.
Weariness becomes a form of knowledge and not a problem to be cured. From fatigue, Cioran gets a vantage point on modern life.
Enthusiasm looks to Cioran like fanaticism waiting to happen. He reads the energy of movements and causes with suspicion and prefers disillusion.
The essays are bleak and ironic, and readers split on the effect. Some take it for nihilism, others for a strange comfort.
Cioran prefers the moralist, the mystic and the aphorist to the system builder. For him philosophy is closer to temperament than to proof.
Time dissolves every conviction in the end. Cioran lets that slow erosion give all human projects a sense of futility.
Critics point to Cioran's writing in 1930s Romania, which showed sympathy for the fascist Iron Guard, and ask how it bears on his later pessimism.

books.thesis: People become what they practise, so religion and philosophy are best read as training systems.
books.summary:
Peter Sloterdijk takes his title from the last line of a Rilke poem, in which a viewer before an ancient headless statue of Apollo feels the stone telling him to change. Sloterdijk's answer is that humans are creatures who practise, and that most of what we call character, belief and culture comes from repeated exercise.

He calls the study of this anthropotechnics, and he reads religions, monastic orders, athletic regimes and artistic discipline as training systems. Religion, he suggests, has been misread as a matter of belief when it is closer to a programme of exercises. He describes a vertical tension, the pull between higher and lower ways of living. Toward the end he turns to global risks and asks what shared practice might be needed. Critics find the central claim stretched across too many cases, and its secular reading of religion is contested.
ideas: The title comes from a Rilke poem in which a headless statue of Apollo seems to order the viewer to change. Sloterdijk takes that demand as his motto.
Humans are creatures who practise, and repetition makes us what we are. Sloterdijk calls the study of this anthropotechnics.
Religions are better read as training programmes than as systems of belief, Sloterdijk suggests. On this view their core is a set of exercises.
The word asceticism comes from the Greek for exercise, and that links monks, athletes, philosophers and artists. All of them shaped themselves by practice.
Vertical tension is the pull between a higher and a lower way of being. Exercise is how people try to climb.
Modern culture has lost the language of practice and treats people as producers and consumers. Sloterdijk wants practice back, in a secular form.
The book ends on shared global risks. Sloterdijk asks what common training a threatened world might need.
Pierre Hadot read ancient philosophy as spiritual exercises, and Sloterdijk builds on that reading. He stretches it into a general theory of human self-formation.
Nietzsche appears here as a thinker of training. Sloterdijk reads the overman as a figure of rising through practice and not as a biological type.
Co-immunism is Sloterdijk's closing proposal, a shared protective system built through common practice. He offers it as a response to global risks.

books.thesis: Torture destroys trust in the world, and resentment can be a moral stance against forgetting.
books.summary:
Jean Améry was an Austrian-born essayist who was tortured by the Gestapo in Belgium and then sent to Auschwitz. He wrote these essays more than twenty years later. They ask what intellect can do in a camp, what torture destroys, and what survivors owe to those who would prefer them to forgive.

The title essay argues that learning and culture gave little protection in Auschwitz. In the essay on torture, Améry describes how the first blow shatters trust in the world and reduces the victim to a body at another's mercy. Other essays deal with exile and the loss of home, with being made a Jew by one's persecutors, and with resentment. He insists that resentment can be a moral stance, since it refuses a forgiveness that would let the crime fade. The book is bleak and offers no reconciliation, and Primo Levi disagreed with him on several points.
ideas: Culture gave an intellectual little protection in Auschwitz. In the title essay Améry argues that the camp's reality outran any aesthetic or philosophical comfort.
The first blow of torture destroys trust in the world. The victim learns that he cannot count on help from others and never fully regains that confidence.
Torture reduces the person to a body in another's full power. Améry describes the torturer as becoming sovereign over him.
Time does not heal, in Améry's account. Those who have been tortured stay tortured, and the experience does not turn into a lesson.
The essay on exile asks how much home a person needs. It shows that language, scenery and belonging stay with us after they are lost.
Améry was made a Jew by his persecutors. They defined him that way although he had no religious tie, so the label came from the enemy.
Resentment is a moral stance, Améry argues. Refusing to forgive keeps the crime in view when a world eager to move on would like it to fade.
The German title, Jenseits von Schuld und Sühne, means Beyond Guilt and Atonement. It points to the book's concern with guilt and to its German readers.
The torture essay draws on his own arrest by the Gestapo in Belgium for resistance work. He was hung by his arms during questioning.
The Muselmann is the camp figure Améry describes as a prisoner worn down past hope. For such a man, intellectual and moral life had stopped.

books.thesis: A chemist records, calmly and precisely, how Auschwitz tried to strip people of their humanity.
books.summary:
Primo Levi was a young Italian chemist and partisan when he was arrested in 1943 and sent to Auschwitz. The title asks the reader to decide whether a person stripped of name, clothes, hair and any work worth doing, and forced to live at the edge of starvation, is still a man.

He describes the arrival, the tattooed number, the bowl and spoon, the hunger, the camp economy of small trades and the sickness ward. He is precise and calm, in the manner of a scientist taking notes, and the restraint makes the book hard to forget. He also records small moments that kept something human alive, such as a civilian who brought him bread and an attempt to recite Dante to a fellow prisoner. Levi insists that he is a witness, and that the worst is known best by those who did not return.
ideas: The opening poem asks whether a person who works in mud, knows no peace and dies for a yes or a no is a man. That is the title question, put to the reader.
The camp set out to erase the person before it killed him. On arrival prisoners are stripped of clothes, hair and names and given tattooed numbers.
A guard tells Levi, who has reached for an icicle, that here there is no why. Levi takes the answer as the camp's refusal to give any reasons.
Survival hung on small things such as a bowl, a spoon, shoes and bread. A camp economy of trades and theft made every one of them count.
Levi divides prisoners into the drowned, who gave up and went under, and the saved. The saved usually lived through luck, skill or compromise, and he rejects any claim that they were the best.
A civilian Italian worker named Lorenzo brought him bread and food over months. Levi credits him with keeping alive a belief that goodness still existed.
On a walk to fetch the soup, Levi tries to recite and translate Dante's canto of Ulysses to a fellow prisoner. For a moment the exchange feels like being human again.
A fellow prisoner, Steinlauf, insists on washing every day even without soap. He argues that prisoners must keep some form of dignity so as not to become beasts.
Levi says in the preface that the book is documentation and not a new accusation. He offers it for a calm study of certain aspects of the human mind.

Luck and training shaped Levi's survival. His chemistry led to a place in the camp laboratory, which spared him outdoor work in winter, and scarlet fever left him in the infirmary when the camp was evacuated.

books.thesis: Levi's last book weighs memory, survivors' shame and the grey zone, where simple judgment fails.
books.summary:
Primo Levi wrote this book near the end of his life, four decades after Auschwitz, and it reads as a stock-taking. He asks how the camps should be understood and what has happened to the memory of them. The questions are hard ones: how reliable memory is, why survivors feel shame, and where fair judgment of the people caught in the camps ends.

Levi warns that memory fades and reshapes itself, in survivors and perpetrators alike. He describes the grey zone, the space between victim and oppressor where some prisoners were forced into cooperation, and discusses the Jewish ghetto elder Rumkowski as an ambiguous figure. He also writes of the shame of surviving, of the failure of communication, and of violence that served no purpose. Levi urges caution in judging. The book closes with no verdict, only a sharper sense of what cannot easily be judged.
ideas: Memory is fallible, and Levi says so about everyone. Survivors' recollections fade and reshape themselves, and perpetrators bend their own memories to fit what they can live with.
The grey zone lies between victim and oppressor. Some prisoners were forced into collaboration, and Levi urges against hasty condemnation.
Rumkowski, the Jewish elder of the Łódź ghetto, cannot be read simply as villain or victim. Levi uses him to test how far judgment can go.
Shame is common among survivors, who feel they lived by taking another's place. Levi also suggests, with pain, that on the whole the worst survived.
Communication failed in the camps. Prisoners who could not understand orders in a babel of languages were often punished or killed for it.
Much camp violence served no purpose beyond humiliation and cruelty. Levi gives it a chapter of its own.
Levi disputes the idea that educated prisoners fared either worse or better at Auschwitz. In the chapter on the intellectual he disagrees with Améry in part.
The SS told prisoners that none would live to tell the story and that no one would believe them if they did. That threat shaped the survivors' sense of a duty to testify.

The Sonderkommando, prisoners forced to work in the crematoria, represent for Levi the most demonic crime of the National Socialist state. He still urges that no one has the right to judge them lightly.
In the chapter on letters from Germans, Levi reads responses to his book, some sincere and some evasive. They show how a nation's memory of the camps was managed.

books.thesis: We build selves from scripts that others supply, and freedom has to work inside them.
books.summary:
Kwame Anthony Appiah asks how much of who we are is up to us. We think of identity as personal, yet the labels we live under, such as nation, race, gender and religion, come from other people.

Appiah starts from a liberal idea he takes from Mill, that people should be able to shape their lives by their own lights. He argues, though, that nobody builds a self from nothing. Language and social categories supply the scripts, and individuals work within them. Collective identities help people find company and meaning, but they come with demands, and they can become a tyranny. He doubts that a state should protect cultures against change when members choose differently, and he asks how far communities may shape children. The book is philosophy that leaves many questions open, and critics ask how much room it leaves for group claims.
ideas: No one writes a self from nothing. Language, categories and roles supply the scripts we choose from, and every life is shaped by social materials.
Appiah starts from Mill's idea that people should shape their lives by their own lights. He then asks how that works when we depend on others for the tools.
Collective identities such as gender, race, religion and nation give people company and meaning. They also make demands, and Appiah warns they can turn into a tyranny.
A true self waiting to be discovered is a doubtful idea for Appiah. Making a self is a continuing conversation with others and with the labels on offer.
The state need not preserve cultures against change, Appiah argues, when the individuals inside them make other choices.
Parents and communities shape children's identities, and Appiah asks how far they may go. He asks where a liberal state may step in to protect a child's future choices.
Race is a label with social force and little biological support. Appiah uses it to show how labels shape the people who carry them.

Demanding public respect for group identities can push individuals into a script, Appiah warns in criticising Charles Taylor's politics of recognition. The script might dictate how a Black person or a gay person should behave.
Classified people change in response to the label, an idea associated with Ian Hacking and called looping effects. The category itself then changes over time.
A label that began as medical or insulting can be taken up and given positive meaning. Being gay is Appiah's example of how identities are made over time.

books.thesis: We can owe things to strangers without asking everyone to become alike.
books.summary:
Kwame Anthony Appiah wrote this book for general readers. It asks how people can live together among strangers who do not share their values, and what, if anything, we owe to people far away.

Appiah separates two strands of the cosmopolitan idea. One says our obligations reach beyond family and nation. The other says we should take the value of particular human lives seriously, including the different ways people live. He argues the two fit together, so a cosmopolitan does not want everyone to become alike. He welcomes the mixing of cultures and calls the idea of a pure culture a fiction.
