ideas: The native informant is the figure from whom colonial knowledge was drawn but who is not permitted to speak as a thinker. Spivak finds traces of this figure in philosophy and literature.
Kant, Hegel and Marx each rely on a place outside their system held by the colonized. Spivak reads them closely to show that their central concepts of the subject, history or economy depend on it.
The subaltern is a person cut off from the routes through which a voice is heard. Spivak revisits her earlier claim that the subaltern cannot speak in that sense.
Bhuvaneswari Bhaduri, a young woman who killed herself in 1926, is Spivak's example of an act that was misread. Her message, Spivak argues, was not heard as she meant it.
Spivak reads a Mahasweta Devi story about a tribal community and an outsider trying to understand it. She uses it to ask how intellectuals approach people they cannot assume speak for themselves.
Giving voice to the oppressed is not a simple favor, in Spivak's view. Speaking on behalf of others can silence them, and she asks that this be examined.
Postcolonial criticism needs to read the major texts of European thought carefully, not discard them, Spivak argues. The book's attention to the history of reason is meant to show why.
Spivak borrows foreclosure from Lacan to describe how the native informant is written out of European texts. The figure is needed for the argument and then barred from it.

In the literature section Spivak revisits Jane Eyre, Wide Sargasso Sea and Frankenstein. She argues that Bertha Mason is sacrificed so that Jane can complete her story as a heroine of feminist individualism.
Kant's account of the human subject relies on figures at the edge of humanity, such as the man in the raw state. Spivak reads these asides as signs of where the colonized are placed in philosophy.

books.thesis: Concepts that claim to be universal were made somewhere, and should be read that way.
books.summary:
Dipesh Chakrabarty takes up concepts such as citizen, modernity, science and capital, which present themselves as universal. Historians of India and other places can hardly do without them, yet they do not fit cleanly. The subtitle, Postcolonial Thought and Historical Difference, frames the task: to use these ideas while recognizing where they come from and where they strain.

He argues that historicism treats Europe as first and others as not yet, as if Indians and Africans sat in a waiting room of history. Building on Marx, he describes two kinds of history, one that stands for the logic of capital and another made up of ways of life that do not fit it. He reads Bengali middle-class life, including the adda or talking circle, and the world of mill workers who dealt with gods. Some critics ask how far the book escapes the European thinkers it relies on.
ideas: Concepts presented as universal, such as citizen, modernity and the individual, were formed in European history. To provincialize Europe is to read them as local.
European thought is both indispensable and inadequate, Chakrabarty says. Scholars outside Europe cannot do without it, but it does not capture their experience in full.
Historicism, the idea that societies go through stages, puts Europe at the front. Chakrabarty describes it as an imaginary waiting room, with others told to wait.
Drawing on Marx, Chakrabarty separates two histories. History 1 presents the story of capital as universal, and History 2 covers the local ways of life that capital meets and cannot fully absorb.
Adda, the Bengali habit of sustained and aimless conversation, resists Western categories. Chakrabarty uses it as a social form that the notions of public sphere and civil society handle poorly.
Jute mill workers in Bengal lived among gods and spirits as well as among labor contracts. Chakrabarty asks how a historian can write about that without treating belief as error.
Provincializing Europe does not mean rejecting it or putting an Indian tradition in its place. Chakrabarty asks historians to use European ideas while attending to what they leave out.

Historicism's verdict is always "not yet". Colonized peoples were told they were not yet ready for modernity, and Chakrabarty says the delay is built into the structure of the story and not into the facts.
Chakrabarty turns his criticism on the Subaltern Studies project he writes from within. He says it sometimes treated the religion of peasants as an early stage of consciousness waiting to mature.
Chakrabarty engages Heidegger as well as Marx. He uses Heidegger's idea of ways of being in the world to ask how gods and spirits can be real to those who live among them.

books.t: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World
books.thesis: Anticolonial nationalism did not simply copy the West, because it claimed a domain of its own.
books.summary:
Partha Chatterjee asks whether anticolonial nationalism was only a copy of European ideas. The subtitle, A Derivative Discourse?, poses the question, and the book answers no. Looking at Indian nationalism, he shows that nationalists accepted much of the West's science and statecraft while insisting on India's difference and its own right to rule. The puzzle is how a movement can borrow so much and still say something new.

He follows Indian nationalist thought through three stages: the moment of departure, the moment of maneuver and the moment of arrival. Bankim stands for the first, Gandhi for the second, and Nehru for the third. He uses Gramsci's idea of passive revolution to describe how the elite absorbed popular energy without giving up control. Critics have asked whether the three moments make too tidy a sequence, and whether the story describes mainly the educated elite.
ideas: Nationalism in the colonies is often judged an imitation of European models. Chatterjee argues that this overlooks what anticolonial thinkers did with those models.

Chatterjee separates the problematic, the framework of knowledge a thinker works within, from the thematic, the claims made inside it. Nationalism shared colonial frameworks while arguing against colonial themes.

The shared framework set limits. Chatterjee suggests that, shaped by ideas about the East, it constrained how far nationalism could depart from colonial thought even while it challenged colonial rule.
The moment of departure is when nationalist thought emerges from the encounter with colonial rule. Chatterjee associates it with Bankim.
In the moment of maneuver, nationalism turns to the masses and uses their symbols. Gandhi stands here, drawing in peasants without giving them power.
In the moment of arrival, nationalist thought settles into the framework of the state and planning. Chatterjee connects this with Nehru and his ideas of order and progress.
Chatterjee uses Gramsci's passive revolution to describe how the leading classes took in popular movements while preserving their own authority.
Nationalism was derivative in its framework but not in its claims. This is Chatterjee's answer to the question posed in the subtitle, A Derivative Discourse.

Chatterjee reads Gandhi's Hind Swaraj as an attack on modern civilization itself and not just on British rule. This is why Gandhi could speak to peasants and why he fit awkwardly in the later nationalist state.
Chatterjee takes Said's Orientalism as a foil. He agrees that colonial knowledge worked as power, but asks why Said leaves little room for the colonized to answer back.

books.t: The Collected Essays of A. K. Ramanujan
books.thesis: Essays on folklore and translation that describe a culture without flattening it into a few principles.
books.summary:
A. K. Ramanujan was a poet, translator and folklorist. His collected essays gather writing on folktales, classical poetry, translation and the idea of an Indian way of thinking. One concern runs under them: how to describe a culture without flattening it into a few principles, and how stories carry meaning from one setting to another.

In an essay on whether there is an Indian way of thinking, he proposes with caution that Indian thought and ethics are often context sensitive, where Western universals are context free. In an essay on the Ramayana, he follows how the story changes across many languages and traditions, with no single original. Some readers find his generalizations too tidy, and he was wary of them himself.
ideas: Ramanujan asks whether there is an Indian way of thinking, and answers with caveats. He offers the idea that Indian thought is often context sensitive while Western thought leans toward context free universals.
In Indian traditions, rules of conduct often depend on who a person is and what situation they are in, Ramanujan argues, instead of applying one law to everyone.
The Ramayana has no single original, in Ramanujan's essay. He describes many tellings in different languages and traditions, with changes in plot and attitude.
Folktales travel across languages and regions, and each teller adapts them to a setting. Ramanujan treats this variation as part of the tale's life, not a corruption.
Translating classical Tamil and Kannada poetry is hard, Ramanujan wrote, because a poem carried into another language can turn into something familiar.
Ramanujan lived among several languages, writing in English and Kannada and translating from Tamil. His essays treat that mix as an ordinary condition of Indian culture.
His Ramayana essay became the subject of controversy when it was removed from a Delhi University reading list. The episode shows how contested the retelling of stories can be.
Ramanujan translated three bodies of poetry: Kannada vachanas in Speaking of Siva, Tamil love and war poetry in The Interior Landscape, and Nammalvar's hymns in Hymns for the Drowning.
Classical Tamil poems divide into akam, interior poems about love, and puram, exterior poems about war and public life. Ramanujan uses the pair to show how a tradition maps feeling onto landscape.
Women's oral tales in Kannada form a counter-system, Ramanujan says in an essay on women's tales. They give a different view of marriage and family from the textual tradition.

books.thesis: Philosophy should start from pure experience, before the world is split into subject and object.
books.summary:
Nishida Kitaro's first book tries to start philosophy from the place before ideas harden into categories. He asks what experience is like before we split it into a self that sees and a world that is seen. His term is pure experience, a direct awareness that comes before judgment, such as the moment of hearing a melody or looking at a color without thinking about it.

The text moves in four parts: pure experience, reality, the good and religion. Nishida argues that thinking, feeling and willing are all forms of this unified activity, and that the good lies in the full realization of the self. He ends by describing God as the unifying ground of reality, not as a being apart from it. Readers disagree about whether the book fits Western philosophy or a Zen outlook, and its terms are not easy to pin down.
ideas: Pure experience is awareness that comes before the split between subject and object. Nishida describes it as experiencing facts just as they are, before any added judgment.
In the moment of hearing a melody or seeing a color there is no separate self reflecting on it, only the experience itself. These are Nishida's examples of pure experience.
Nishida reverses the usual order. Experience does not belong to an individual who stands first, and the individual arises within experience.
Knowing, feeling and willing are phases of one unifying activity of consciousness, not separate faculties. Nishida says this can be seen at work in attention and in thought.
The book is built on a single ground. Its four parts move from pure experience to reality, then to the good, and finally to religion, and each builds on that idea.
Nishida defines the good as the realization of the self. Acting well means becoming whole, which is not the same as following rules or pursuing pleasure.
In his last section God is the unifying ground of the universe, not a being outside it. Critics have asked whether this stays close to a Zen view.
The phrase pure experience comes partly from William James. Nishida also drew on his Zen practice, which shaped how he treated direct experience.
Love, Nishida says, is the union of subject and object. To know something fully is to lose the gap between oneself and it.
An Inquiry into the Good was Nishida's first book and is seen as the start of the Kyoto School. He later judged pure experience too psychological and moved toward the idea of basho, or place.

books.thesis: Ethics studies the human being as betweenness, at once an individual and a relation.
books.summary:
Watsuji Tetsuro wrote his major work on ethics in the 1930s and 1940s. Its key word, rinrigaku, names ethics as the study of rin, the relations between people. In Japanese the word for human being, ningen, joins the characters for person and for between, and Watsuji reads this as a clue. A person is individual and relational at once, and ethics studies that twofold existence.

Watsuji argues that the individual and the community each arise by negating the other. A person separates from the group and then returns to it, and this movement is the structure of moral life. He criticizes Heidegger for describing human existence in terms of time and neglecting space, and links his ethics to a companion study of climate and landscape. Later critics note that his emphasis on the whole fit uncomfortably with support for state authority in his time.
ideas: Ethics, for Watsuji, studies ningen, the human being understood as person and as the between. The word's characters themselves point to a being defined by relations.
Watsuji rejects the isolated individual that much Western ethics starts from. A person cut off from others is an abstraction, he argues, because human beings exist in relation from the first.
The individual arises by negating the community, and the community arises by negating the individual. Watsuji describes this movement back and forth as the basic structure of moral life.
Ethics deals with family, neighborhood, economy and state, Watsuji argues. Each is a form of betweenness, a nested set of human connections within which people act.
Watsuji faulted Heidegger's Being and Time for treating human existence mainly through time. He thought the work gave too little place to space and to the shared world.
Place and climate shape human existence, Watsuji holds. His book on climate asks how landscape shapes ways of living and of relating.
Critics note that his emphasis on the whole and on the state made his ethics compatible with the nationalism of his era. How far that is inherent remains debated.
The word rinri carries the argument. Rin means fellows or companions and ri means principle or order, so ethics is the order of human fellowship and not a rulebook for the lone will.
His climate book, Fudo, sorts regions into monsoon, desert and meadow types. Watsuji links each to a characteristic temperament, such as a receptive, patient one for the monsoon lands.
Reading Being and Time in Germany in 1927 and 1928 shaped his response. Watsuji concluded that human existence is spatial and social before it is temporal.

books.thesis: Iki is allure held at a distance, erotic tension kept alive by never quite closing.
books.summary:
Kuki Shuzo tried to explain a Japanese word that no European language seems to translate. Iki names a quality of style in dress, manner and flirtation, associated with the pleasure quarters of Edo. It is stylish, a little cool, a little erotic and a little sad. Kuki had studied in Europe, and the book applies philosophy from Paris and Germany to a sensibility he missed while abroad.

Kuki says iki has three parts. One is bitai, a flirtatious attraction to another person that stays alive by never being fulfilled. The second is a spirited pride, and the third is a calm resignation that refuses to cling. He then lists its forms in color, pattern and gesture, noting that vertical stripes and gray tones suit it. Some readers see an elegant piece of cultural analysis, and others a nationalist claim for Japanese uniqueness.
ideas: Iki is a style prized in the Edo pleasure quarters, a way of dressing and bearing that is refined without being showy. Kuki treats it as a distinctive form of Japanese taste.
Flirtation, bitai, is the first element of iki, and it depends on staying unfulfilled. Kuki says iki keeps the attraction of one person to another alive without reaching its fulfillment.
The second element, ikiji, is spirited pride or backbone. It keeps allure from collapsing into dependence and makes the person in iki seem self-possessed.
The third element, akirame, is resignation. This calm comes from knowing that attachments are fleeting, and it gives iki a cool and slightly melancholy tone.
Parallel lines are Kuki's image of iki, because they approach each other but never meet. He applies the idea to stripes in textiles.
Iki shows in muted blue gray tones and plain designs, Kuki says, in preference to bright ornament. Subdued surfaces suggest restrained feeling.
Critics debate whether the book is a philosophical study of an aesthetic or a case for Japanese uniqueness. Kuki himself treats the term as only partly translatable.
A Japanese taste is described here with European tools. Kuki wrote after years in Europe, where he met Heidegger and studied phenomenology.
Iki is defined in part by what it is not. Kuki maps it against neighboring tastes such as shibui, which is astringent, hade, which is flashy, and yabo, which is boorish.
Kuki treats iki as a way of being of a people, and approaches it by interpretation. He works out the meaning as it is lived and does not define it from outside.

books.thesis: Doi uses the Japanese word amae, the wish to be indulged, to explain how closeness works.
books.summary:
Takeo Doi, a Japanese psychiatrist, noticed while working in the United States that English had no good word for a feeling he knew well from home. The word is amae: the wish to be indulged, to lean on another person's goodwill and be forgiven for it. Doi asks whether this feeling explains a pattern of closeness in Japanese life, and whether it is more widely human than the language suggests.

He starts from the bond between mother and infant and follows the same wish into friendship, work and religion. Along the way he discusses the inner and outer circles of obligation and the gap between public stance and private feeling. Critics say the book makes Japanese uniqueness too neat. Others accept that amae is real but argue that it exists in many societies, a point Doi himself half admits.
ideas: Amae comes from a verb meaning to depend on another's goodwill. Doi describes it as the wish to be indulged, usually first felt by an infant toward the mother.
Doi found no English word for amae while working in the United States. He took this gap as a sign that Japanese and Western cultures notice different feelings.
Amae does not end with childhood. Doi sees it in friendships, in relations between boss and employee and in the way Japanese people expect to be understood without saying everything.
Amae is easier within the uchi, the inner circle, than with the soto, the outer one. Doi notes that stiffer manners hold with outsiders.
Amae thrives in private feeling and is hard to express openly. Doi notes the contrast between public stance and private feeling.
Western psychology tends to treat dependence as immaturity, Doi argues. He says this may be an expression of a culture that prizes independence.
Critics suggest that amae is a universal feeling and not a mark of Japanese uniqueness. Doi's own work partly allows this, and the debate over how culture specific the concept is continues.

Japanese words for sulking and resentment, such as suneru, higamu and uramu, belong to a vocabulary of thwarted amae, Doi shows. The language records what happens when the wish for indulgence is refused.
Doi sets amae beside giri and ninjo, obligation and human feeling. Amae sits at the center of ninjo, which explains why obligation can feel both binding and warm.
Doi engages Ruth Benedict's The Chrysanthemum and the Sword. He argues that Japanese guilt and shame are shaped by fear of losing others' goodwill, which a plain shame culture label does not capture.

books.thesis: Fei pictures rural China as ripples of obligation, with each person at the center of widening circles.
books.summary:
Fei Xiaotong, a Chinese sociologist trained in anthropology, wrote these short essays in the 1940s on village China as he knew it. The book asks what holds people together in a society where most live close to the land and know everyone around them. Fei looks at habits Westerners might overlook, such as how people speak of the family, settle disputes, and trust those they have long known.

His best known image is the ripple. A person is like a stone dropped in water, and relations spread outward in circles of decreasing closeness. In such a society the family can stretch or shrink with the situation, and morals depend on how near someone stands. Fei calls rural life an acquaintance society, run by custom and rites more than law. The essays sketch one place and period, so how far they fit China as a whole is open to question.
ideas: Fei describes rural China as a society of ripples. Each person stands at the center of circles of relations, with obligation weakening as the circles widen.
Western society, in Fei's contrast, follows an organizational mode in which individuals belong to groups like sticks in a bundle of firewood, with clear edges and equal standing inside.
Because each person sits at the center of their own circle, the boundaries of the family are elastic. It can shrink to a household or expand to a wide kin network.
Moral standards in a society of ripples depend on closeness. What is owed to a relative differs from what is owed to a stranger, so public principles are harder to apply evenly.
Rural China is an acquaintance society, in Fei's phrase. People live among those they know from birth, and trust rests on long familiarity and not on written agreements.
Ritual and custom learned in childhood do the work of law in such a society. Fei argues it works because everyone knows what is expected, with no law enforced from outside.
Fei's account is a sketch of a type of society as he saw it in the 1940s. Readers have asked how well it describes later or different parts of China.

Trust comes from staying put. The Chinese title uses xiangtu, the earthbound, and Fei argues that rural people stay where their ancestors lived, which is what makes trust through long familiarity possible.

Chinese families run on a feedback model, in Fei's account, where the Western model is a relay. In a relay each generation hands the baton on, and in the feedback model the young are expected to repay their parents by supporting them.
Writing matters less in a society of acquaintances, Fei suggests, because speech and shared habit carry most meaning. He uses this to explain why village life could run without written contracts.

books.thesis: Lu Xun's first stories show a China asleep in old habits, and ask whether waking it is a kindness.
books.summary:
Lu Xun's first story collection, published in 1923, gathers short fictions about Chinese people at the end of the old order. In the preface he says he gave up medicine after seeing a slide of a Chinese man executed as a spy while other Chinese looked on, and decided that curing minds mattered more than bodies. He also describes an iron house with no windows, where sleepers will soon suffocate, and asks whether waking them only adds suffering.

In "A Madman's Diary" a man comes to believe that history and the people around him are devouring one another. "Kong Yiji" shows a failed scholar mocked in a tavern, and "Medicine" follows a family that buys a folk remedy for a dying son. "The True Story of Ah Q" gives the book its best known figure, a poor man who turns every humiliation into an imagined victory.
ideas: Lu Xun left medicine after seeing a slide of an execution in which Chinese onlookers stood watching. The preface says he turned to writing to change minds.
The preface's iron house with no windows frames the whole book. Sleepers inside are about to suffocate, and Lu Xun asks whether it is kind to wake them. The stories are his answer.
In A Madman's Diary the narrator thinks the people around him are cannibals. Reading history, he sees the words eat people between the lines of benevolence.
Kong Yiji shows cruelty in ordinary onlookers. He is a failed scholar in a tavern who wears a scholar's long gown and is laughed at by the customers.
In Medicine, superstition and indifference share the stage. A family buys a roll dipped in the blood of an executed revolutionary, believing it will cure their son.
Ah Q wins every defeat in his mind, and the story treats this spiritual victory as a national habit. When beaten, he tells himself it is like a son beating his father.
Lu Xun keeps hope slight. The collection ends with no promise that waking the sleepers will help, and readers still argue over whether the book is bitter or loving.
A Madman's Diary is counted as the first modern story in vernacular Chinese. It appeared in New Youth in 1918, and its title is borrowed from Gogol.

Hope is compared to paths on the earth in Hometown. The narrator returns to a village and finds it changed, and the story ends with the thought that there were no paths at first, but when many walk the same way, a path appears.
Ah Q's end repeats the preface's image of the watching crowd. He is a village drifter without a home who is executed for a robbery he did not commit, and the crowd watches the execution as a show.

books.t: The Myth of the Lazy Native
books.thesis: Colonial writers built the image of the lazy native to justify rule, and the image outlived empire.
books.summary:
Syed Hussein Alatas, a Malaysian sociologist, took on an image European colonizers repeated for centuries: the native who prefers idleness to work. He looks at accounts of Malays, Filipinos and Javanese from early European contact through the nineteenth century. His answer is that the image was an ideology. The colonial economy wanted labor, and local people often did not want to give it on the terms offered.

Alatas reads administrators, travelers and scholars and shows that their picture of laziness rested on colonial needs and prejudice more than on observation. He argues that the image belonged to a larger set of ideas that excused rule and later shaped local elites. He also criticizes how it survived the end of empire, even in the writing of some of the colonized themselves.
ideas: Alatas treats the image of the lazy native as an ideology built for a purpose, not as a neutral observation. He studies it in colonial writing about the Malays, Filipinos and Javanese.
The lazy label turned a political and economic quarrel into a fault of character. Colonial plantations and mines needed cheap labor, and people who refused harsh terms were called idle.
The accounts rest on colonial assumptions about what counts as work, Alatas argues. They overlook the labor local people did, such as farming, fishing and trade.
The image did not stand alone. Alatas places it among other stereotypes that justified rule, in which natives were childlike, backward or in need of supervision.
The same economy judged different peoples by what they gave it. Alatas compares attitudes toward groups seen as industrious, such as the Chinese migrants, with those toward the natives.
The image survived the end of empire. Alatas shows local elites repeating it about their own people, and treats this as a sign of how thoroughly colonial ideas were absorbed.
Alatas analyzes texts as a form of ideology. Critics say the book generalizes across diverse colonies, but its central claim that stereotypes can serve power is widely accepted.
The pattern holds across Spanish, Dutch and British sources. Alatas draws on writings by colonial officials, travellers and missionaries from the sixteenth to the twentieth century.
Jose Rizal traced whatever idleness existed to colonial conditions, Alatas notes. In his essay on the supposed indolence of the Filipino, forced labor and heavy taxes are the cause, not character.
The lazy native myth is a case study of the captive mind. Alatas used that term for scholars in formerly colonized countries who take Western frameworks without question.

books.thesis: A nation is an imagined community: members never meet, yet print and shared time let them picture each other.
books.summary:
Benedict Anderson asks why people feel so strongly about a group of millions they will never meet. His answer begins with a definition. A nation is an imagined political community, imagined as limited and sovereign. It is imagined because no member will know most of the others, yet each carries an image of belonging. The book asks how that became possible, and why it spread worldwide.

He points to the decline of religious communities and dynastic kingdoms, the rise of print capitalism and vernacular languages, and a new sense of time in which people share the same calendar moment. Novels and newspapers let readers picture a society moving through that time. He traces the first nationalisms to Creole officials in the Americas. Later editions add chapters on the census, the map and the museum.
ideas: A nation is an imagined political community, imagined as both limited and sovereign. It is imagined because members will never meet most of their fellow members, yet feel a bond with them.

Nations needed older forms of belonging to fade first. Before them, people lived within religious communities and dynastic realms, and Anderson argues that the decline of both made room for a new way of imagining belonging.
Print capitalism gave readers a shared language. Publishers sold books and papers in the vernacular, and readers of the same language began to see themselves as part of a shared community.
The novel and the newspaper make a new sense of time visible. Anderson borrows from Walter Benjamin the idea of homogeneous, empty time, in which many events happen at once across a society.
Reading a morning newspaper is a ceremony done by many people at once. Each reader knows that thousands of others are doing it too, which links strangers.
The first nationalisms, Anderson argues, emerged among Creole elites in the Americas. They were born in the colonies and excluded from the highest posts by officials sent from the mother country.
Colonial states used the census, the map and the museum to give nations their shapes, in chapters added to later editions. Critics say the book neglects oral culture.

The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier works because it is empty of a name. Everyone knows what it stands for, yet no one knows whose remains lie inside, and that emptiness is what lets millions identify with it.
Official nationalism was the answer of dynasties such as the Romanovs and the Habsburgs to popular nationalism. They adopted national language and identity from above to stay in power.
Nationalism became modular, Anderson says. Once the Creole, linguistic and official models existed, later movements could copy and adapt them, so nationalism spread as a pattern.

books.thesis: Said argues that Western writing about the East worked as an instrument of power, not neutral knowledge.
books.summary:
Edward Said, a literary critic born in Jerusalem, saw that European writing about the Middle East and Asia kept returning to the same few images: the sensual, despotic, unchanging East. He begins from the thought that the East of European writing is a made thing, shaped by writers and then taken for fact.

He argues that Orientalism, the study and description of the East, grew alongside European empire and became a way of managing it. He draws on Foucault for the link between knowledge and power, and on Gramsci for how culture supports rule. He follows the pattern from Napoleon's Egypt expedition through British officials like Cromer and Balfour to American experts after the Second World War. Critics say he treats the West as a single block, ignores scholars who resisted the pattern, and offers little on how the East should be described instead.
ideas: Said argues that the Orient is a European construction. It was produced through writing, scholarship and administration, and it says more about those who imagined it than about those it describes.
Orientalism, in Said's sense, is a style of thought that sets East against West. The East is cast as irrational, sensual and unchanging, the West as rational and capable of progress.
Said uses Foucault to argue that knowledge is tied to power. Describing a people is part of ruling them, and the scholar's authority serves the interests of empire.
Napoleon's expedition to Egypt is Said's example of scholarship and conquest coming together. Scholars were attached to the army to study the country.
British officials such as Balfour and Cromer explained why Britain should rule Egypt in terms of what Egyptians were said to be like. Said quotes them to show it.
Said distinguishes latent Orientalism, a stable set of assumptions about the East, from manifest Orientalism, the particular statements made at different times by different authors.
Critics such as Bernard Lewis and Aijaz Ahmad argue that Said treats the West as one unit, overlooks scholars who did not fit, and offers no alternative way of describing the East.
Orientalism has three meanings in Said's book: an academic discipline, a style of thought based on a distinction between East and West, and a corporate institution for dealing with the Orient.

Said traces modern Orientalism to philologists such as Silvestre de Sacy and Ernest Renan. Renan's treatment of Semitic languages as limited and primitive is his example of scholarship that passes judgment.

Flaubert's encounter with the Egyptian courtesan Kuchuk Hanem shows how the Orient was imagined as sensual and available. Said's last chapter follows these habits of thought into the American scholarship of the postwar era.

books.thesis: Freire contrasts "banking" education, which fits people to the world, with dialogue that lets them name it.
books.summary:
Paulo Freire wrote this book in exile after the 1964 coup in Brazil, drawing on his work teaching adults to read in poor communities. He asks what education looks like when its aim is freedom instead of fitting people into the world as it is. Education either helps people accept their situation or helps them question it, and it settles who gets to name the world.

Freire describes a banking model, in which a teacher deposits information into passive students, and sets against it problem-posing education, in which teacher and students investigate the world together through dialogue. He says the oppressed can take in the oppressor's image of them, so that freedom is also feared. Critics say his language is abstract and his proposals hard to carry out in schools, and Freire invites that testing.
ideas: In the banking concept of education, the teacher deposits facts into students, who receive, memorize and repeat them. Freire says this trains people to adapt to the world as it is.

In problem-posing education the teacher learns too. Teacher and students learn together through dialogue, the teacher is also taught by the students, and the topic is drawn from the world they live in.

Conscientizacao is the process of becoming aware of the social conditions that shape one's life and of one's ability to change them. Freire thinks this awareness arises through reflection joined with action.
The oppressed can take in the oppressor's picture of themselves, so that they come to feel ignorant or unfit. For this reason, Freire says, freedom is also frightening to them.
Freedom is feared on both sides, Freire says. The oppressed may prefer the security of a known place, and the oppressor may fear losing a position of advantage.
Praxis is reflection and action together directed at changing the world. Action without reflection is activism, Freire says, and reflection without action is empty talk.
Freire warns revolutionary leaders not to manipulate the people they want to free or to treat them as an object. Liberation has to be undertaken with them.
Freire's method begins with generative themes drawn from the lives of the learners. Teachers and students investigate them together and codify them in pictures or situations to be discussed.
Freire lists anti-dialogical actions: conquest, divide and rule, manipulation and cultural invasion. Against them he sets dialogical ones: cooperation, unity, organization and cultural synthesis.

Dialogue, in Freire's account, needs love, humility, faith in people, hope and critical thinking. He wrote the book in exile in Chile after the 1964 coup in Brazil, drawing on his literacy work with adults.

books.thesis: Ibn Khaldun explains dynasties' rise and fall by asabiyya, the group feeling that comfort wears away.
books.summary:
Ibn Khaldun wrote the Muqaddimah in 1377 as the introduction to a larger history, and it became a book about how to read history at all. He lived in North Africa and Spain, held political posts and saw dynasties fall. He asked why groups rise to power and why states weaken after a few generations. He treated society as having its own regularities, which he calls the science of civilization.

His central idea is asabiyya, group feeling or solidarity, which gives a tribe the strength to take power. Once in power, the rulers move into city life, grow used to comfort, and lose the cohesion that made them strong. A hardier group then takes their place. He also faults historians who repeat reports without testing them against what is plausible. Modern readers argue about how far his cycle fits other places, and whether he foresaw economics and sociology.
ideas: Ibn Khaldun proposes a science of civilization, a study of the regular patterns in how human societies form, grow and decline. He sees it as a way to test historical reports.
Historians should test reports against what is plausible about how societies work, Ibn Khaldun says. He criticizes chroniclers who repeat reports without checking them.
Asabiyya is the group feeling that binds people together, usually through kinship or shared life. It is the force that lets a group defend itself and take power.
Nomads and desert peoples are tougher and more cohesive than city dwellers, he argues. They can conquer settled lands because their solidarity has not been softened by luxury.
Comfort undermines the group that wins power. Once a ruling group moves to city life and grows used to comfort, its solidarity weakens and the dynasty becomes vulnerable to a new group from outside.
A dynasty lasts about three generations, or a hundred and twenty years, in Ibn Khaldun's view. The first is hardy, and by the third the roots of its strength are forgotten.
Heavy taxation can reduce a state's revenue, Ibn Khaldun argues, by discouraging work and trade. Some modern economists cite this as an early version of an idea now well known.
The Muqaddimah is the introduction to a longer world history, the Kitab al-Ibar, and Ibn Khaldun made the introduction into a separate science of society.
Umran, his term for civilization or social organization, has two forms. He divides it into bedouin umran, the life of nomads and rural people, and sedentary umran, the life of towns.
Religion can add to group feeling, he says. A call to a religious cause helps a dynasty gain power by joining the solidarity of its members to a larger purpose.

books.thesis: Anzaldúa treats life between cultures and languages as a place to see from, as well as a wound.
books.summary:
Gloria Anzaldúa grew up on the Texas side of the US border with Mexico. Her book, part essay and part poetry, shifts between English, Spanish and Nahuatl without translation. It asks what it means to live where cultures meet and rub, and to belong to none of them completely. She writes as a Chicana, a lesbian and a writer, and treats these positions as a place to see from as well as a place of pain.

Anzaldúa introduces the mestiza consciousness, a way of thinking that tolerates ambiguity and holds contradictory parts together. She writes about the Aztec past, the Virgin of Guadalupe and the figure of Malinche, and about the policing of language, which she calls linguistic terrorism. Critics have asked how accurate her mythic history is, and some find the mixed form hard to follow.
ideas: Anzaldua calls the border an open wound, a place where one world grates against another and bleeds. She treats it as both a physical line and a condition of life.

Anzaldua refuses to translate. She moves between English, Spanish, Tex-Mex and Nahuatl, and the shifting language mirrors the life she describes, so readers who lack one language are made to feel the border.
The mestiza consciousness is a way of thinking developed by those who live between cultures. It involves tolerance for ambiguity and an ability to hold contradictions without choosing one.
Linguistic terrorism is Anzaldua's term for the shaming of people for how they speak. She says that being told your language is wrong is being told that you are wrong.
Anzaldua reaches back to the Aztec past and to the idea of Aztlan, claiming a long history for people of Mexican descent in the American Southwest. Critics debate the accuracy of this.
The Virgin of Guadalupe, Malinche and La Llorona are women whose stories have been used to define what women may be in Mexican and Chicano culture. Anzaldua examines them.
As a queer woman in a culture that often condemned her, Anzaldua writes of standing outside more than one boundary. She presents that edge as a place to see from.
The book's form follows the border it describes. The first half is prose essays and the second half is poetry, and both use the same mixed language.
The Coatlicue state is a stage of paralysis and crisis that Anzaldua draws from the Aztec earth goddess. It is a necessary period of being stuck before a new consciousness emerges.

Chicano Spanish is a border tongue and not a corrupted one, Anzaldua says. In How to Tame a Wild Tongue she opens with a dentist who tries to make her mouth behave, and then lists the several languages Chicanos speak.

books.thesis: Paz reads Mexican character through the mask, the fiesta and a solitude he ties to the Conquest.
books.summary:
Octavio Paz wrote these essays on Mexico in 1950, as a young poet and diplomat. He asks what it is to be Mexican, and he looks for the answer in behavior he thinks reveals it: the mask, the love of fiestas, the closed manner, the attitude toward death. He treats the national character as a way of being alone in the world that people of other countries may feel as well but do not live in quite the same way.

Paz begins with the pachuco, a young Mexican American in Los Angeles who lives between two cultures. He turns to the Mexican as son of the violated mother, linking national feeling to the Conquest, and to the festival as a release in which the mask comes off. Critics argue that he turns a diverse country into a single type, and that his picture of Mexican women is limited.
ideas: Paz opens with the pachuco, a young Mexican American in Los Angeles with a defiant style of dress and speech. He uses the figure to show life between two worlds.
The Mexican wears a mask, in Paz's description. Politeness, irony and silence keep others at a distance, which he treats as a defense of a lonely and wounded self.
Paz reads the Conquest as a founding wound. The Mexican is the child of the violated mother, which he connects to the word chingada and to ambivalence toward origins.
The fiesta is a break from ordinary life. People spend heavily, shout and mix, and for a time the mask comes off and solitude is eased.
Death is a familiar presence for Mexicans, Paz suggests. It is joked about and celebrated instead of hidden, which shows an attitude to life as much as dying.
Paz discusses the Mexican Revolution as a search for a national face, an effort by the country to discover and affirm what it was, after years of imported forms.
Critics say that Paz makes a diverse country into a single type and that his account of women is thin. The book is an interpretation, and he offers it as one.
Paz contrasts Mexicans and North Americans in a phrase. North Americans see the world as something to be perfected, while Mexicans see it as something to be redeemed.
The postscript Postdata reads the 1968 killings at Tlatelolco as a return of old sacrificial patterns in Mexican politics. Paz added it after the massacre.

Imported ideas widened the gap between a nation and its self-image, Paz argues. The nineteenth century brought liberal and positivist ideas that did not fit the country, and the gap between the ideas and daily life added to the mask.

books.thesis: Du Bois describes double consciousness: seeing yourself through the eyes of a society that despises you.
books.summary:
W. E. B. Du Bois published these essays in 1903, when he was a young scholar at Atlanta University. He opens with the question white acquaintances put to him, how it feels to be a problem, and with the claim that the problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color line. The book asks what it is like to see yourself through the eyes of a society that despises you.

Du Bois describes double consciousness, the sense of always looking at yourself through the eyes of others, and the veil that separates Black and white Americans. He surveys the aftermath of emancipation, the Freedmen's Bureau, life in the rural Black Belt of Georgia, and the sorrow songs, which he treats as the nation's finest music. Some readers, then and now, have questioned his elitism, and he later revised parts of his thinking.
ideas: Du Bois names the color line as the central problem of the twentieth century. He opens with the unspoken question white Americans put to him.
Double consciousness is the feeling of always looking at yourself through others' eyes. Du Bois describes a person both American and Black, with two warring ideals in one body.
The veil is Du Bois's image for the barrier between Black and white worlds. Black people can see through it, though white Americans often cannot or will not.
Du Bois criticizes Booker T. Washington for accepting economic progress without political rights. Giving up the vote and higher education, he argues, would keep Black Americans in subordination.
The Freedmen's Bureau was a brief and incomplete effort, in Du Bois's account. It was set up after emancipation to help formerly enslaved people with land, schools and justice.
In the Black Belt of Georgia, Du Bois travels through rural counties and shows the effects of debt and tenant farming on Black families after the war.
The sorrow songs are the finest American music, Du Bois writes, and a record of a people's grief and hope. He places them at the center of the book's closing pages.
Of the Passing of the First-Born is a lament for Du Bois's infant son, Burghardt. It is a plain and personal piece set among essays on politics and history.
Of the Meaning of Progress shows how little changed for the families Du Bois taught. He describes teaching in a rural school in Tennessee and returns years later to find little different.
Of the Coming of John is fiction. A Black man comes home from his education and finds that he no longer fits, and the town's racism decides his fate.

books.thesis: Freud splits the mind into id, ego and superego, and leaves the ego serving three harsh masters.
books.summary:
By 1923 Freud had found his early picture of the mind, built on conscious and unconscious, too crude for clinical facts such as unconscious guilt and the resistance of patients who wanted to get well. The book asks how the mind is organized and why part of the self works against the person.

Freud proposes a structural model. The id holds the drives, the ego develops from it as a surface that deals with reality, and the superego forms from internalized parental authority. The ego must balance the demands of id, reality and superego, and this strain is a source of anxiety. The model is hard to test, and critics note that the three agencies read more like metaphors than measurable systems.
ideas: The id is the reservoir of instinctual drives. It operates by the pleasure principle and has no sense of time, logic or negation.
The ego develops out of the id through contact with the outside world. It represents reason and caution, and works by the reality principle.
Freud compares the ego to a rider who must guide a stronger horse. The rider often ends up steering it where it already wants to go.
The superego arises from the resolution of the Oedipus complex. The child internalizes parental prohibitions as conscience and ideal.
Much of the ego is itself unconscious, so Freud drops the equation of the unconscious with the repressed alone.
A sense of guilt can be unconscious. Freud says this explains why some patients cling to their symptoms and resist cure.
The ego is threatened from three sides: the external world, the id's libido and the superego's severity. Anxiety signals each danger.
Freud writes that the ego is first and foremost a bodily ego. It is derived from bodily sensations, chiefly those from the surface of the body, and is a projection of that surface.
The word id comes from Georg Groddeck, who used das Es, the It, for the forces by which we are lived. Freud adopts it for the unknown and uncontrollable part of the mind.
Freud reduces the instincts to two classes, Eros and the death instinct. He says the harsh superego can become a pure culture of the death instinct.

books.t: Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality
books.thesis: Freud argues that sexuality begins in infancy and develops in stages, so adult desire reflects its history.
books.summary:
Freud's 1905 book takes on the question of what sexuality is and where it comes from. Common opinion held that it appears at puberty with a fixed aim of reproduction. Freud asks how perversions, childhood behavior and the wide range of adult desire can be explained within one account.

His answer is that the sexual drive is present from infancy, attaches to different bodily zones in turn, and only later organizes under genital primacy. Adult variation then reflects how development went, and no outcome is wholly natural or unnatural. The book was revised across several editions. Many of its claims about childhood and gender are now rejected, though its broad view that sexuality is shaped by development remains influential.
ideas: Freud argues that sexual life starts in infancy and not at puberty. He reads thumb sucking as pleasure sought for its own sake, apart from feeding.
The sexual drive has a source, an aim and an object, and each of the three can vary. This lets Freud describe sexual variation without setting up a single norm.
Development runs through oral, anal and genital phases, then a latency period. During latency, in the years before puberty, the drive is held back.
Freud calls the infant's disposition polymorphously perverse. Before the drive is organized, it can find satisfaction in many ways.
Adult perversions, on Freud's account, come from fixation or regression to earlier stages. He does not read them as signs of a degenerate constitution.
Freud calls neuroses the negative of perversions. The repressed wishes do not find open expression and return as disguised symptoms.
Finding a sexual object at puberty is a refinding. The first object of the infant's drive was the mother's breast.

Freud maps the body into erotogenic zones, such as the mouth and anus, that give sexual pleasure. The component instincts tied to these zones act separately at first and only later come together under the genitals.

Freud refuses to treat inversion, or same-sex object choice, as degeneration. He notes it occurs in people of otherwise sound health, and he says everyone has the capacity to choose an object of either sex.
Children carry out their own sexual researches, driven by curiosity about where babies come from. Freud says their theories are mistaken, yet he counts them as an important step in development.

books.thesis: Freud traces religion and morality to a primal crime: sons kill the father, then live with the guilt.
books.summary:
Freud asks how the earliest human communities came to hold their taboos and totem animals. He notes that tribal customs resemble the obsessions of neurotic patients, and asks whether the similarity points to a common source.

He answers with a speculative story. A tyrannical father who kept all the women was killed and eaten by his sons, who then felt remorse and created the totem and the incest prohibition. This, he says, is the origin of religion and moral law. Anthropologists criticized it at once, since there is no evidence for such an event and the story depends on the idea that guilt is inherited. Most readers now treat it as a myth that clarifies Freud's thinking more than as history.
ideas: Freud sees taboos as resembling the prohibitions of obsessional neurosis. In both, the forbidden act is one people are drawn to and also fear.
Totemism forbids killing the totem animal and marrying within the totem clan. Freud connects these two rules to the two crimes of the Oedipus complex.
The primal horde, as Freud tells it, was ruled by a violent father. The brothers banded together to kill him and then identified with him through a totem meal.
Guilt after the killing turned the sons into followers of the father's former prohibitions. Freud treats this obedience as the basis of social order.
Freud sets animism, religion and science as three stages of human thought. They run from belief in the power of thoughts to reliance on reason.
Ambivalence, the mixture of love and hate toward the same person, runs through taboo. Freud finds it also in the feelings of the living toward the dead.
The weakest step in the argument is the assumption of a collective mind. Freud needs it to carry the memory of the crime across generations.
The book moves in four essays, from incest horror to the return of totemism in childhood. In between come taboo and ambivalence, then animism and magic.
Freud's own contribution is to join three borrowed sources with the Oedipus complex. The sources are Darwin's primal horde, Robertson Smith's totem meal and Frazer's anthropology.
Little Hans serves in the last essay as a childhood version of totemism. His fear of horses, in Freud's reading, has the horse stand in for the feared father, as the totem animal does.

books.thesis: Freud calls religion an illusion born of childhood helplessness, one he hopes reason will outgrow.
books.summary:
Freud asks what religious belief is and why it holds such power over civilization, which needs restraint on the drives to survive. He wants to know whether people can hold together morally without religious faith.

His argument is that religious ideas are illusions, meaning beliefs driven by wish and not by evidence. They answer the helplessness people feel before nature and fate by recalling the protective father of childhood. Freud hopes humanity will outgrow them through education and the slow voice of reason. Critics, including Freud's own imagined opponent in the text, say he underrates how belief meets human needs. He does not claim that religion is false, only that it lacks proof.
ideas: Freud holds that civilization rests on renunciation of instinct, and that people resent it. Culture therefore needs ways to make the burden bearable.
Freud classes religious ideas as illusions, meaning beliefs in which wish fulfillment is a prominent motive. Whether they happen to be true is a separate matter.
God, in Freud's account, is a projected exalted father. The adult's feeling of helplessness revives the child's need for a father.
Religion does two jobs at once. It consoles people against nature, fate and death, and it gives moral rules a divine sanction.
Freud compares religion to a universal obsessional neurosis of humanity. He hopes people may grow out of it as they grow out of childhood neuroses.
Morality, Freud proposes, can be justified by its usefulness to civilized life and not by divine command.
Science is no illusion, Freud says, because it can correct itself. The belief that science cannot supply what we need would be the real illusion.
An illusion differs from a delusion. A delusion contradicts reality, while an illusion might turn out true but is held because of a wish.
Freud proposes an education to reality. Children would not be raised on religious doctrine and would be prepared to meet the world as it is.
Freud ends on modest hope. He writes that the voice of the intellect is a soft one, but it does not rest until it has gained a hearing.

books.t: Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego
books.thesis: Freud says groups hold together through ties to a leader, who stands in for each member's ego ideal.
books.summary:
Freud asks why individuals in a crowd think, feel and act differently than they do alone, and what binds a group together. Earlier crowd theorists such as Le Bon had described the effects but offered little explanation.

Freud proposes that the answer lies in love, in the broad sense of libido. Members are tied to the leader and thereby to each other, and in the Church and the army the leader takes the place of the ego ideal. Identification with one another explains the shared emotion. The account rests on a limited range of examples, and its picture of crowds as regressive has been questioned by later social psychologists who stress shared identity and rational behavior.
ideas: Freud accepts Le Bon's picture of the group mind as suggestible, impulsive and unreflective. His own question is what produces those traits.
Group cohesion, Freud argues, rests on libidinal bonds. These are aim-inhibited love, tying each member to the leader and to each other.
Church and army are his model groups. Each depends on the illusion that the leader loves every member equally.
Identification is the earliest form of emotional tie to another person. It can replace object choice by taking the object into the ego.
Being in love and hypnosis both put an object in the place of the ego ideal. Freud uses this to explain the credulity of the hypnotized and of the crowd.
Panic comes when the tie to the leader breaks. Each member's anxiety is then freed and the group dissolves.
The leader, for Freud, is a return of the primal father. This links the group back to the primal horde.
Social feeling arises, Freud argues, from a reversal of envy and rivalry. Members who would compete demand equal treatment instead, and this becomes group spirit.
Such groups are loving inside and intolerant of outsiders. Freud notes that churches, which preach love, have been harsh toward those who do not belong.
Freud's phrase narcissism of small differences names the hostility between close neighbours, such as the English and the Scots. Small differences, he says, can stir up more feeling than large ones.

books.thesis: Freud separates grief, which lets go of a lost object, from melancholia, which turns the loss on the self.
books.summary:
This 1917 paper asks why mourning is a normal response to loss while melancholia, a similar state, is pathological. Both involve painful dejection and loss of interest in the world, yet only melancholia includes a drop in self-regard.

Freud argues that in mourning the person slowly detaches libido from the lost object, testing reality bit by bit. In melancholia the loss is often unconscious, the object is taken into the ego, and the hostility meant for it is turned against the self. The essay is short and speculative, and later work on grief, including attachment theory, has revised its picture of mourning as a task of detachment.
ideas: Mourning is a normal reaction and not an illness. It answers the loss of a loved person or of an abstraction such as a country or an ideal.
Mourning does its work slowly because reality must be tested again and again. Each memory of the lost object has to be withdrawn from.
Melancholia adds something mourning lacks, a striking fall in self-esteem. The patient reproaches and belittles himself.
The melancholic's reproaches often fit the lost person better than the patient. Freud reads the self-accusations as displaced anger.
In melancholia the lost object is introjected. The shadow of the object falls upon the ego, and the ego is then judged as the object was.
The loss in melancholia may be unconscious. The patient knows whom he lost but not what he lost in him.
Freud ties melancholia to ambivalence and to a regression toward the oral stage. He also notes that it can swing into mania.
In mourning, Freud writes, it is the world that has become poor and empty. In melancholia it is the ego itself, and this is his main contrast between the two.
Freud notices a critical agency in the ego that judges and punishes the rest of it. It is a forerunner of the superego, which he develops in The Ego and the Id.
Suicide, Freud says, becomes possible only when the ego treats itself as an object. It then turns on itself the hostility meant for the lost person.

books.thesis: Freud says the uncanny is the familiar made strange, a return of what was repressed or once believed.
books.summary:
Freud's 1919 essay takes up an unusual topic in aesthetics, the feeling of dread that comes from something both known and alien. He asks what makes certain things uncanny and why the feeling differs from simple fear.

He begins from the German word unheimlich, whose meaning runs into its opposite, heimlich, which means both homely and hidden. He argues the feeling arises when repressed infantile complexes or surmounted primitive beliefs are revived by some event. His main example is Hoffmann's story "The Sandman." The essay is loosely organized, and readers dispute both his reading of the story and the limits of the concept in fiction, where Freud admits the rules differ.
ideas: The German word unheimlich shows why the uncanny belongs to the familiar. Heimlich means both homelike and concealed, so the two meanings meet.
Freud finds Jentsch's account of the uncanny insufficient. Jentsch had linked it to intellectual uncertainty, such as whether a doll is alive.
In The Sandman, Freud reads the fear of losing the eyes as a substitute for the fear of castration. The fear is tied to the father figure.
The double was once a protection against death and later became a sign of death. It is an image of the self that appears elsewhere.
Repetition and coincidence feel uncanny because they recall the compulsion to repeat that Freud finds in the unconscious.
Freud separates two sources of the uncanny. One is repressed complexes that return, and the other is primitive beliefs, such as animism and the power of thought, that seem confirmed again.
Fiction can create uncanny effects the real world cannot. It can also remove them if it announces that its world follows different laws.
Freud quotes Schelling's definition: the uncanny is everything that ought to have remained secret and hidden but has come to light.
Dead bodies, ghosts, severed limbs and the return of the dead are among Freud's examples. They feel uncanny, he says, because they revive an old belief in the dead returning.
Freud treats the fear of being buried alive as the reverse of a fantasy of life in the womb. The most uncanny places, in his account, are those that recall the first home.

books.thesis: Breuer and Freud trace hysterical symptoms to forgotten trauma and report that talking it out relieves them.
books.summary:
Breuer and Freud ask what causes hysterical symptoms, such as paralyses and lost speech, that have no organic basis, and whether they can be treated. The book collects case histories, including Breuer's Anna O. and Freud's patients such as Emmy von N. and Elisabeth von R.

Their argument, laid out in the Preliminary Communication, is that symptoms derive from memories of events whose emotion was never discharged. Recalling the event and voicing the feeling relieves the symptom. Freud's later chapters move from hypnosis toward free association and begin to stress resistance and repression. The cases are told selectively, and later scholars have questioned the claimed cures, notably in the case of Anna O.
ideas: Hysterics suffer mainly from reminiscences, as the authors put it. These are memories of events that continue to act on the patient.
A trauma produces symptoms when the emotional reaction to it was suppressed. Abreaction, the discharge of that affect, can relieve them.
The cathartic method uses hypnosis to bring forgotten memories into awareness. Anna O. called it her talking cure.
Freud found that not all patients can be hypnotized. He developed the concentration technique, which leads toward free association.
Resistance is the patient's reluctance to recall. Freud takes it as evidence that a force has kept the memory out of mind.
Symptoms are often symbolically tied to the trauma. A painful memory can show up as pain in a particular part of the body.
Freud's cases suggest that the traumas are mostly of a sexual or conflict-laden kind. He pursues this idea after the book.
The cases come from both authors. Freud's are Frau Emmy von N., Miss Lucy R., Katharina and Fraulein Elisabeth von R., while Anna O., the case that started it, was Breuer's.
Freud's pressure technique was a step between hypnosis and free association. He placed his hand on the patient's forehead and promised that a memory would come.
Breuer explained hysteria through hypnoid states, while Freud argued for defense, the active pushing away of intolerable ideas. The disagreement foreshadowed their break.

books.thesis: Freud presents slips, dreams and neuroses as products of one theory: repressed wishes in conflict.
books.summary:
Delivered to a general audience at the University of Vienna during the First World War, these lectures ask how an educated layperson should understand psychoanalysis. Freud presents its method and findings in a single account, starting with everyday phenomena.

The lectures run in three parts, on parapraxes, on dreams, and on the general theory of the neuroses. Freud argues that all three show meaningful mental acts produced by repressed wishes in conflict with a censor. He is open that some claims are provisional, and he answers objections as he goes. The work is still a common way into his thought, though the theory of libido and his dismissal of critics have aged less well.
ideas: Slips of the tongue and forgetting have meanings. Each can be traced to an interfering intention the speaker did not know he held.
Dreams are wish fulfillments in disguise. The manifest content is a disguised form of latent dream thoughts, made by dream work.
Dream work uses condensation, displacement and symbolic representation. It gets past the censor by distorting the wish.
Neurotic symptoms are compromise formations. Each expresses a forbidden wish and the defense against it at once.
Repression and resistance are the basic tools of the theory. The analyst meets resistance in the patient's reluctance to bring up painful material.
Transference is both the main obstacle and the main means of cure. The patient turns old feelings toward the analyst.
Freud treats anxiety as the central problem of neurosis. He ties it to libido that has not been discharged.
The Oedipus complex is a core part of childhood development in these lectures. The child's early desire for one parent and rivalry with the other leave traces in adult life.
Free association is the basic method, and Freud calls it the fundamental rule. The patient reports whatever comes to mind without editing.
Freud divides the mind into the conscious, the preconscious and the unconscious. He argues that a censor guards the border between the last two.

books.thesis: Jung reads Job as showing a God who is not wholly good and is changed by human moral growth.
books.summary:
Jung reads the Book of Job as a psychological drama. He asks why a just God would let Job suffer on a wager, and what this shows about the image of God in the Western mind and the unconscious from which it comes.

Jung argues that Yahweh is shown as unconscious of his own dark side, and that Job, by holding to his integrity, becomes morally more conscious than his maker. God then answers by becoming man in Christ, and the process continues, in Jung's view, in the 1950 dogma of the Assumption of Mary. Theologians and Jungians have both objected. Jung treats images of God as psychic facts and not metaphysical claims, which he says is the limit of his argument.
ideas: Jung reads the God of the Old Testament as a mixture of opposites. Goodness and unreflective violence sit together, and God is unaware of his own contradictions.
Job is more conscious than Yahweh, in Jung's reading. He is wronged and does not give up his moral standing, which calls for a divine response.
Jung takes the Incarnation as God's answer to Job. It lets God share human suffering and atone for what he did.
Sophia, divine wisdom, is linked by Jung to the feminine element that was long suppressed in the Christian God image.
Revelation shows the unresolved shadow of God. Jung sees its violent apocalypse as the return of the dark side.
Jung treats the 1950 dogma of the Assumption as an advance in the symbol of the Trinity. In his view it moves toward a fuller divine image.
Jung insists he writes of psychic reality. Archetypal images of God exist in the psyche, whatever their ultimate source.
Job's faith in an advocate in heaven shows, Jung says, that he knows Yahweh is divided against himself. This knowledge puts Job morally ahead of God.
Jung reads the wager with Satan as a sign of Yahweh's suspicion and moral weakness. God lets a faithful servant suffer on a whim.
Jung takes the book of Ezekiel as a sign that God is turning toward humanity. The prophet is addressed as Son of Man, a human being.

books.thesis: Jung says mother, rebirth, spirit and trickster are inherited patterns that shape dreams and myth.
books.summary:
This small volume collects four essays in which Jung asks how the archetypes of the collective unconscious show up in myth, religion and the lives of individuals. He wants to show that universal forms recur in widely different cultures.

Jung treats each archetype as an inherited tendency to form images, filled with different content in each setting. He traces the mother archetype and its positive and terrible aspects, rebirth in its several types, the spirit in fairy tales, and the trickster in Native American myth. Critics say his method of amplification by comparison is selective and hard to test, and that the idea of inherited images lacks biological support.
ideas: An archetype is a form without fixed content. It is a tendency in the unconscious to produce images that vary with culture and person.
The mother archetype has loving and devouring sides. It appears in figures from the Great Mother goddess to the witch.
Jung distinguishes the personal mother from the mother archetype. A person's feelings can attach to a larger image than the real parent.
Rebirth takes forms such as transmigration, resurrection and transformation. Jung ties it to the process of individuation.
In fairy tales the spirit appears as an old wise man who gives counsel when the hero is in need. He represents a moment of insight.
The trickster of Winnebago myth is an early, undeveloped figure, both creator and fool. Jung reads him as a shadow of the collective.
The trickster's gradual change into a more civilized figure is read by Jung as a record of growing consciousness.
The collective unconscious is a layer of the psyche shared by all people. The personal unconscious, by contrast, holds forgotten and repressed individual material.
Archetypes are known only through their images, Jung argues. We infer them from dreams, myths and fairy tales and cannot observe them directly.
Jung reads later figures such as the medieval carnival fool and the alchemical Mercurius as echoes of the same early trickster pattern.

books.thesis: Jung proposes that some meaningful coincidences reflect an acausal connecting principle.
books.summary:
Jung takes on events that coincide in time with a shared meaning but have no causal link, such as a dream matched by an outer event. He asks whether such coincidences are chance or point to a principle beyond cause and effect.

He proposes synchronicity, an acausal principle linking inner psychic states with outer events through meaning, usually when an archetype is activated. He draws on his clinical cases, the I Ching, astrology and J. B. Rhine's ESP experiments, and he discussed the ideas with the physicist Wolfgang Pauli. Most scientists reject it, since the statistical evidence is weak and selective perception can account for the cases he offers.
ideas: Jung defines synchronicity as two or more events that coincide in time and are linked by meaning, without a causal connection.
The standard example is a scarab. A patient dreamed of a golden scarab while a scarab beetle tapped at the window during her session.
Jung proposes that synchronicities happen when an archetype is constellated. This usually occurs at moments of emotional intensity or transition.
Causality, Jung argues, is a statistical truth and not an absolute law. This leaves room for acausal events.
The I Ching and astrology are treated as methods that rely on the meaningful moment. Jung ran an astrological marriage experiment of his own.
Jung cites Rhine's card-guessing results as evidence that the psyche can work independently of space and time.
Jung suggests that a fourth principle could join space, time and causality in the physicists' framework.
The scarab case worked, Jung says, because the patient was stuck in an overly rational outlook. The coincidence helped break it open.
Acausal connecting principle is Jung's term for meaning that links an inner state with an outer event. He separates it from a cause that works across a distance.
In Jung's reading, the astrological marriage experiment gave results that depended on the expectations of those running it. It compared the charts of many married couples.

books.thesis: Jung's inner visions were the raw material of his psychology, and he staged them as an illuminated book.
books.summary:
The Red Book is the record of the self-experiment Jung began in 1913, when he allowed fantasies and figures to appear in waking imagination after his break with Freud. The question it takes on is what lies behind the surface of the mind and how one can meet it without being overwhelmed.

Written in calligraphy and illustrated with paintings, the text follows Jung in dialogue with figures such as Elijah, Salome and Philemon, and describes a descent into the underworld and a search for his soul. He later said it held the source of all his work. It was published only in 2009. Readers disagree about whether it is a mystical text, a case record or a psychological experiment, and its style is deliberately strange.
ideas: Jung began deliberately entering fantasies in late 1913, a method he called active imagination. He recorded them first in the Black Books, before the Red Book.
Jung meets inner figures such as Elijah, Salome and Philemon. He treats them as autonomous beings that speak back to him.
The book begins with two conflicting claims on his soul, the spirit of the depths and the spirit of this time.
Recovering the soul requires a journey downward, away from rational control. The book treats this as a necessary loss of ordinary certainty.
Jung's lengthy commentary on the images shows how concepts like the shadow, the anima and the self began as personal experiences.
Near the end the book depicts a mandala-like painting. Jung came to see it as a map of psychic wholeness.
Jung held that he spent the rest of his life working out in scientific form what he had first seen in these visions.
The book is as much a work of art as a record. It is written in the style of a medieval illuminated manuscript, with calligraphic script and large painted images.
Jung describes a period in which he feared he was losing his mind. He chose to follow the images instead of resisting them.
Jung kept the book private during his life. It was published only in 2009 by the Philemon Foundation and his heirs, with Sonu Shamdasani as editor.

books.thesis: Horney says neurosis grows from basic anxiety, met by moving toward, against or away from others.
books.summary:
Horney asks what drives neurotic conflict and why people hold contradictory needs that tear at their lives. She wants a theory that rests less on instinct and more on the person's relations with others, and on culture.

She argues that a child who feels isolated and helpless develops basic anxiety and adopts one of three strategies: moving toward people, against them or away from them. In a healthy person the three can be balanced, but the neurotic is rigid and divided, and tries to solve the conflict through an idealized image of the self. Her view is clinical and drawn from her patients. It has been criticized for lacking empirical testing, though the three trends influenced later personality work.
ideas: Basic anxiety, in Horney's account, is the child's feeling of being isolated and helpless in a potentially hostile world.
The compliant type moves toward people. It needs affection and approval, and fears conflict and self-assertion.
The aggressive type moves against people. It needs to win, to control and to be admired, and it sees others as threats.
The detached type moves away from people. It values self-sufficiency, privacy and freedom from obligation.
In neurosis the three trends become compulsive and cannot be balanced. The person feels torn between them.
The neurotic builds an idealized self-image to escape the conflicts. The gap between it and the real self creates self-hatred.
Cure, for Horney, means giving up the idealized image and accepting the real self. She connects this with a person's capacity for wholeheartedness.
The tyranny of the should is Horney's name for a set of rigid inner demands. The neurotic person tries to meet them in order to match the idealized self.
The search for glory is a drive toward absolute perfection, mastery and recognition. Horney says it grows out of the need to escape inner conflict.
Resignation is the stance of a person who tries to settle conflict by giving up on striving. Horney sees it as a way of withdrawing from life.

books.thesis: Berne says many social exchanges are scripted games with hidden payoffs that people repeat.
books.summary:
Berne's 1964 bestseller asks what goes on when people interact, and why the same painful patterns repeat in relationships, families and work. He wanted a plain language that laypeople could use to understand it.

Drawing on transactional analysis, Berne divides the personality into Parent, Adult and Child ego states and analyzes the transactions between them. Games are repeating sequences with a hidden payoff, played out with set roles, and he sets them apart from honest intimacy. The catalogue of named games is vivid and readable. Critics regard the framework as more descriptive than rigorously tested, and its popular uptake went well beyond Berne's clinical aims.
ideas: Berne gives each person three ego states, Parent, Adult and Child. Communication works well when the states respond as expected.
