A crossed transaction produces conflict or breaks off communication. A transaction is Berne's unit of social exchange.
A game is a series of complementary transactions with an ulterior motive. It ends in a predictable payoff.
Players in games take named roles and switch among them. These are the Persecutor, the Rescuer and the Victim.
Games have names and set patterns. Examples include Why Don't You, Yes But, Now I've Got You, You Son of a Bitch, and Kick Me.
Berne separates games from rituals, pastimes and activities. Intimacy stands apart from all of them as a candid, game-free relationship.
Escape from games requires awareness, spontaneity and the capacity for intimacy. These let a person drop the script.
People crave strokes, Berne's term for units of recognition, so strongly that they will accept negative ones over none.
Berne ranks games by degree. A first degree game is socially acceptable, a second degree game is one the player would hide, and a third degree game ends in serious harm.
A script, for Berne, is an unconscious life plan formed in childhood. His later work on scripts grew out of the study of games.

books.thesis: Skinner argues that freedom and dignity are myths that block social design, since consequences shape behavior.
books.summary:
Skinner asks why humanity, facing problems like war, overpopulation and pollution, still resists applying a science of behavior. His answer is that the ideas of autonomous man, freedom and dignity stand in the way of such a science.

He argues that behavior is controlled by its environment and its reinforcement history, not by inner choice. Because control is unavoidable, he says, we should design cultures deliberately so that useful behavior is reinforced. Critics, including Chomsky, objected that this ignores the mind and invites authoritarian control. Skinner replies that the real danger is control that goes unexamined.
ideas: Autonomous man, the inner agent who originates actions, is a pre-scientific explanation. Skinner says it survives in our talk of freedom and merit.
Operant conditioning shapes behavior. Actions followed by reinforcement become more likely.
Skinner calls punishment, which most societies rely on, a poor way to control behavior. It produces avoidance and resentment.
The literature of freedom mostly fights aversive control. Skinner says that is worth doing but wrongly assumes freedom is a general goal.
Dignity and credit are given when we cannot see the causes of an act. They shrink as the causes come into view.
Control cannot be removed, only changed. The question for Skinner is who designs it and with what ends in view.
A culture survives when its practices help the group. Designing practices for survival is the aim of a technology of behavior.
The idea of autonomous man leads us to praise and blame, Skinner argues, and to ignore the environment that produces behavior.
Skinner sees positive reinforcement as less harmful than punishment. He says the best control is one the controlled hardly notice because it feels like choice.
Mentalistic terms give the appearance of an explanation, Skinner says. What is called a feeling or state of mind should be explained by the history of reinforcement.

books.thesis: Pollan finds it plausible that psychedelics can treat mental illness and also deepen ordinary consciousness.
books.summary:
Pollan takes up the revival of research on psychedelics after decades of prohibition. He asks what these substances do to the mind, whether they can help in depression, addiction and the fear of death, and what they might tell us about consciousness.

He combines history, interviews with researchers and underground guides, and his own journeys with psilocybin, LSD and 5-MeO-DMT. The central scientific idea is that psychedelics quiet the default mode network, which loosens the ego and may let people see their thinking afresh. Pollan is cautious about the evidence, which came from small trials, and acknowledges that personal experience is not proof.
ideas: Psychedelic research in the 1950s and 60s was promising before it was shut down. Pollan describes it ending amid the backlash against the counterculture and its political fallout.
Modern trials at Johns Hopkins and NYU found that guided psilocybin sessions eased anxiety in patients facing terminal illness.
Robin Carhart-Harris proposes that psychedelics reduce activity in the default mode network, which is tied to the sense of self.
A mystical experience, with a sense of unity and meaning, seems to predict lasting benefit. The setting and the set shape what happens.
Following Aldous Huxley, Pollan suggests the ego can work like a reducing valve. Psychedelics temporarily open this filter.
Pollan raises the idea that depression and addiction involve rigid patterns of thought. A psychedelic experience may break them.
Pollan reports that his own trips changed his sense of mortality and of his self. He is wary of overclaiming from them.
Albert Hofmann first synthesized LSD in 1938 and discovered its effects by accident in 1943, as Pollan tells it.
Pollan covers the Beckley Foundation and the Imperial College group. Their brain imaging showed reduced blood flow in parts of the default mode network.
Legal and cultural barriers keep these treatments outside regular medicine, Pollan points out. He visits guides who work in underground therapy settings.

books.thesis: Brewer says craving drives habits from sugar to phones, and curiosity about the feeling loosens it.
books.summary:
Brewer, a psychiatrist and addiction researcher, takes on a puzzle: why people stay caught in habits they know are harmful, and why willpower so often fails. He seeks a view of addiction that covers smoking, eating, worry and screens in one account.

He argues that habits run on a reward loop of trigger, behavior and reward, and that craving is its engine. Mindfulness works, he says, by making the actual reward of the behavior visible and by replacing the urge with curiosity. His evidence comes from his lab's trials on smoking and eating, which are promising but modest in size. The book is aimed at a general reader and draws on Buddhist ideas, which he treats as practical.
ideas: Habits form through a loop of trigger, behavior and reward. The brain learns by reward-based learning.
Craving is the sense of wanting that makes the loop run. It arises from the brain's pursuit of a reward, with dopamine involved.
Willpower is a weak tool against cravings. The prefrontal cortex that supports it goes offline under stress, exactly when cravings hit hardest.
Mindfulness lets a person notice what the behavior feels like. The real reward often disappoints.
Brewer teaches the acronym RAIN, which stands for recognize, allow, investigate and note. He offers it as a way of handling urges.
Curiosity about a craving feels better than the craving. It can be used in place of suppression.
The same loop applies to thinking habits. Brewer discusses craving for approval and for a self-image as drivers of unhappiness.
Brewer links craving to a dopamine-driven positive reinforcement loop first seen in animals. He says it also helps explain smoking and overeating.
Brewer describes a clinical trial in which mindfulness training for smoking cessation outperformed a standard program. He uses it as evidence for the method.
The self can be a habit too. Brewer says the mind forms a story about who we are, and that story is rewarded by approval and then craved.

books.thesis: Lembke says pleasure and pain share one balance, so modern abundance tips us into compulsion and pain.
books.summary:
Lembke, a psychiatrist who runs an addiction clinic, starts from a puzzle: in an age of abundance people feel more anxious and depressed, and compulsive use of drugs, phones, food and gambling has spread widely.

She argues that the brain processes pleasure and pain on the same balance, like a seesaw, so heavy pleasure is followed by a pain that pulls users back. Her remedy includes a period of abstinence to reset the balance, and a deliberate use of discomfort. She builds the account from patient stories. Some neuroscientists say the pleasure-pain seesaw simplifies dopamine's role, which is tied to wanting more than to pleasure.
ideas: The brain balances pleasure and pain like a seesaw. Each push toward pleasure is met by an opposite push toward pain.
Repeated use leads to neuroadaptation. The baseline falls, and the person needs more of the substance to feel normal.
Dopamine signals reward and motivation, and modern products deliver it in high doses with little effort.
A month of abstinence from the problem substance or behavior can level the seesaw. It restores sensitivity to small pleasures.
Lembke advises self-binding, with physical, time and category limits, to make compulsive use harder.
Deliberate hardship, such as cold showers or exercise, can set off a balancing pleasure response. It does so without the cost of a drug.
Radical honesty about one's behavior, shared with others, helps break the shame and the lies that sustain addiction.
Using a drug or habit to escape pain makes the pain worse once the effect fades, Lembke argues. She names this as a pattern among her patients.
Lembke illustrates the pleasure-pain balance with patients she treats for compulsive overuse of media, sex and gambling.
Recovery often fails through relapse, Lembke warns, so patients should plan ahead for triggers. Cues in the environment can revive craving long after use stops.

books.t: Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking
books.thesis: Dennett offers thinking tools, chiefly thought experiments, that show what plain intuition hides.
books.summary:
Dennett offers a toolkit for thinking about hard topics such as evolution, meaning, consciousness and free will. He asks what makes a thought experiment useful and how to avoid being misled by intuitions that feel compelling but may be wrong.

The book presents around seventy tools, which he calls intuition pumps, along with some general rules of thumb for criticism. He applies them to defend his own positions, including a naturalist view of evolution as a process that builds competence without comprehension, and a view of consciousness as having no inner theater. Critics argue some pumps are rigged to produce his conclusions, and he concedes that an intuition pump is only as good as its fit with the facts.
ideas: An intuition pump is a thought experiment designed to pump intuitions. Dennett says it should be tested by varying its details.
Rapoport's rules ask a critic to restate the target's position so well that the target would say thanks. Only then may the critic offer any criticism.
Sturgeon's law holds that ninety percent of everything is crud. Dennett's advice is to judge a field by its best work, not its worst.
Evolution shows competence without comprehension. Natural selection builds clever designs without understanding anything.
The intentional stance predicts behavior by treating a system as a rational agent with beliefs and desires.
Dennett criticizes the Cartesian theater, the picture of a place in the brain where consciousness comes together for an inner viewer.
Dennett calls Searle's Chinese Room a misleading pump. He questions its claim that running a program could not yield understanding.
Dennett lists a set of tools for criticizing, including how to compose a successful critical commentary and the use of reductio ad absurdum.
A deepity is a statement that seems profound because it is true on one reading and trivial on another. On the reading that sounds deep, it is false or empty.
Dennett uses the zombie as a pump. He argues that a being that acts exactly like a conscious person cannot be coherently said to lack consciousness.

books.thesis: Having too little of anything narrows the mind, and that narrowing explains many poor choices.
books.summary:
People who are short of money, time or food often make decisions that deepen their shortage. Mullainathan, an economist, and Shafir, a psychologist, argue that the usual answers about character or culture miss the point.

They propose that scarcity captures attention and leaves less mental capacity for everything else. The focus helps with the pressing problem, but it causes tunneling, neglect of the future and weaker self-control. Experiments with shoppers, sugarcane farmers and others support the claim. A caveat is that some of the lab findings on scarcity and cognition have been harder to replicate, and the book's policy suggestions are modest rather than proven.
ideas: Scarcity captures the mind. When we lack something, our attention goes to it automatically, which the authors call the scarcity mindset.
Scarcity brings a benefit in focus. People under it can be good at managing the pressing need, such as stretching a tight budget.
Tunneling is the cost of that focus. Things outside the urgent problem get neglected, including long-term plans and other tasks.
Scarcity imposes a bandwidth tax. Worry about the shortage uses up mental capacity, which lowers measured fluid intelligence and self-control.
Indian sugarcane farmers scored lower on cognitive tests before harvest, when money was tight, than after it. The comparison involved the same people.
Poverty is explained by context and not by weak character. The authors argue that anyone placed in scarcity would show the same lapses.
Slack is valuable. Buffers, such as fewer deadlines or simple automatic defaults, help people who have little spare capacity.
Juggling is the authors' term for the constant trade-offs faced by those with little. They say it makes small mistakes more costly.
At a mall, thinking about a large car repair bill reduced reasoning scores in low income shoppers but not in the better off.
Payday loans and late fees show how scarcity creates traps. A short term fix leaves a person with even less to work with later.

books.thesis: Taleb says people should bear the costs of their own decisions, or systems drift toward fragility.
books.summary:
Advisers, experts and institutions often gain when they are right and pay nothing when they are wrong. Taleb takes on that problem, and asks what keeps decision makers honest and systems robust.

His argument is that symmetry of risk is both an ethical rule and a practical filter. People with exposure to downside decide better, and those without it should be doubted. He also argues that small committed minorities can set the rules for a majority, and that survival of the whole matters more than the average outcome. The book is polemical and combative, and critics note that its sweeping claims and personal attacks are not always supported by evidence.
ideas: Skin in the game means having something to lose. Taleb treats it as a requirement for fairness and for reliable judgment.
The silver rule is a negative form of reciprocity: do not do to others what you would not want done to you. Taleb prefers it to positive moral advice.
The intellectual yet idiot is a credentialed person who shapes policy and opinion without bearing the consequences of errors.

Ergodicity matters because group averages can hide individual ruin. The outcome for a group on average can differ from the outcome for one person who can be wiped out, so avoiding ruin comes before maximizing gain.
The minority rule says that an intransigent minority can impose its preferences on a flexible majority. Taleb uses examples such as halal and kosher food labeling.
Antifragile systems depend on the failures of their parts. Entrepreneurs who fail teach the system, which only works if they pay for failure.
Soldiers, artisans and risk takers hold knowledge that pundits who bear no cost for being wrong tend to lack, Taleb argues.
Taleb uses the Lindy effect to defend old ideas and traditions. The longer a non-perishable thing has lasted, the longer it is likely to last.
The bureaucrat has no stake in outcomes, Taleb says. He contrasts this person with someone who must live with the results of their choices.
Taleb argues that the payoff from risk should be tied to responsibility. He cites the Code of Hammurabi, in which a builder was punished if a house fell and killed its owner.

books.thesis: Ariely says our judgment errors are systematic, not random, which makes them predictable and sometimes usable.
books.summary:
Classical economics assumes that people weigh options rationally. Ariely tests behavior directly and asks why people err in the same direction again and again.

Through experiments, many run with students, he shows that choices depend heavily on relative comparisons, on the word free, on arousal and on social versus market norms. His conclusion is that irrationality has patterns, and understanding them can improve design and policy. A caveat is that several well-known results, including some on honesty and priming in his work, have faced replication problems, and Ariely himself has been involved in a data-integrity controversy, so the specific findings deserve care.
ideas: Relativity shapes choice. People judge options by comparison, so a decoy option that nobody picks can shift which of the other two they choose.
Free is a powerful emotional trigger. Zero price makes people take a worse deal, because it removes the sense of loss.
Social norms and market norms follow different rules. Paying a small amount for a favor can ruin willingness to help, while a gift keeps it.
Arousal changes judgment. In experiments with young men, sexual excitement shifted their stated preferences far beyond what they predicted for themselves while calm.
Procrastination and self-control fail in predictable ways. Commitment devices, which restrict future choices, can help.
Ownership raises value, so people overvalue what they already have. Expectations also shape experience, as in the beer experiment where a hidden ingredient changed ratings once it was named.
The dishonesty section argues that most people cheat a little but not a lot. Reminders of morality reduce it.
Anchoring lets an arbitrary number sway what people will pay. Ariely's example is the last digits of a Social Security number.
The Economist subscription case shows a decoy at work. Adding a decoy offer changed how many readers chose the print and web bundle.
Coherent arbitrariness means an early arbitrary price shapes later choices. People stay consistent with the anchor without knowing it.

books.thesis: Boredom signals that we want to engage and cannot, which is neither laziness nor a lack of stimulation.
books.summary:
Boredom feels unpleasant, and Danckert and Eastwood ask what it is for. Both are psychologists who study the topic, and they set out to treat boredom as a serious psychological state and not a trivial one.

They argue that boredom is the mind's way of telling us that our current activity does not meet our desire to be engaged, and that it pushes us to seek meaning. Chronic or poorly managed boredom is linked with risky behavior, poor mental health and a pull toward distraction. The book is a readable overview of a small research field, and some of its links between boredom and later outcomes are correlational, so causes remain open.
ideas: Boredom is the state of wanting to be engaged but being unable to. The authors define it by this mismatch and not by a lack of things to do.
Boredom works as a signal, like hunger or pain. It tells us our current situation is not satisfying a need to engage.
Three ingredients combine in boredom. A person is unable to focus, wants to do something, and finds nothing to satisfy that wish.
Boredom proneness differs between people. Those who score high are more likely to report depression, anxiety, risk taking and problems with attention.
Reaching for a phone or other quick stimulation relieves boredom briefly. It does not fix the underlying lack of meaning.
Boredom is linked to agency. People who feel they have little control over what they do tend to feel bored more often, which also links to boredom in school and work.
Handled well, boredom can motivate people to find new goals and creative activity. The authors advise using it as information and not escaping it.
Simple boredom differs from existential boredom. The latter is a deeper sense of meaninglessness that cannot be fixed by adding more activity.
The authors cite a study in which people chose to give themselves mild electric shocks rather than sit alone with their thoughts for a few minutes.
Boredom can be a sign that a person has lost a sense of purpose. The authors argue that the cure lies in finding meaning and not in more entertainment.

books.thesis: Haidt says phone-based childhood replaced play-based childhood and drove the rise in teen mental illness.
books.summary:
Rates of anxiety, depression and self-harm among adolescents climbed sharply in the early 2010s in many wealthy countries. Haidt, a social psychologist, takes up the cause for a general audience.

His argument is that children lost free play and independence in the real world while gaining smartphones and social media around 2010 to 2015, producing what he calls a great rewiring of childhood. He proposes four norms, including no smartphones before high school and no social media before 16. Critics, including some researchers in the field, say the evidence for causation is weaker than the book suggests, and that the data are mixed and the effect sizes small.
ideas: Haidt calls the shift from a play-based childhood to a phone-based one the great rewiring. He dates it to roughly 2010 to 2015.
Children are overprotected in the real world and underprotected online. They are kept from risk outdoors but exposed to harmful content on screens.
Haidt names four harms: social deprivation, sleep deprivation, attention fragmentation and addiction.
Social media hits girls hardest through comparison, relational aggression and perfectionism. Boys, Haidt says, withdraw into video games and pornography.
Collective action problems explain why parents give in. A child without a phone is excluded when peers have them, so norms must change together.
Haidt proposes four norms: no smartphone before high school, no social media before 16, phone-free schools and far more unsupervised play.
Anxious and depressed teenagers are a trend visible across the English-speaking world and parts of Europe. Haidt treats the timing as evidence for the cause.
Haidt argues that the four harms reach spiritual life as well, leading to what he calls spiritual degradation.
The screen world opens a gap with the real world, which Haidt describes as a loss of embodied experience. This includes play, touch and shared presence.
Haidt contrasts a discover mode with a defend mode. He argues that children need risky play to move from fear to confidence.

books.thesis: Peterson argues that myth and religion encode how humans meet the unknown, with real psychological content.
books.summary:
Peterson begins from the question of how belief systems can drive people to atrocity, and asks how people build meaning at all. The twentieth century gives him his examples of what ideologies can do.

The book argues that myths across cultures share a structure of order, chaos and the hero who mediates between them, and that this structure reflects how the brain meets novelty. It draws on Jung, Piaget, neuroscience, Eliade and others. It is dense, sprawling and unusual in its method, and critics find its claims about universal archetypes and its use of evidence loosely argued. Readers should treat it as a speculative synthesis and not as established science.
ideas: Peterson divides the world into explored and unexplored territory, which he calls order and chaos. Myth often draws them as masculine and feminine.
The hero goes into the unknown, confronts chaos and brings back new order. Peterson finds this pattern in stories across many cultures.
Anomalies, events that violate expectations, trigger fear and exploration. Peterson links this to research on orienting responses in the brain.
Myth is a map of behavior and not a map of objects. It tells people how to act in a world full of significance.
The adversary is the force in myth that resists the hero. Peterson treats it as a figure of rigid belief or deliberate evil, depending on the story.
Totalitarian ideologies, Peterson says, are attempts to deny anomaly. He argues that believing one's own system is complete leads people to destroy those who disagree.
Peterson draws on Jung's archetypes, such as the Great Mother and the Wise King, to argue that stories share recurring characters across cultures.
In Peterson's scheme the known is explored territory and the unknown is unexplored territory. The knower is the process that moves between them.
Peterson uses the Babylonian creation myth as an example of the hero confronting the unknown. In it Marduk defeats the chaos dragon Tiamat.
The hero myth sets as its ideal the individual who takes responsibility and tells the truth, Peterson argues.

books.t: Women Who Run with the Wolves
books.thesis: Women carry an instinctive Wild Woman nature that society suppresses, and old stories can restore it.
books.summary:
Estés, a Jungian analyst and cantadora (a storyteller in the Latina tradition), asks what happens to a woman's creativity, intuition and sense of self when she is taught to be tame and compliant. She answers through myth and fairy tale, not clinical argument.

She retells tales such as Bluebeard, The Ugly Duckling and Vasalisa the Wise, and reads each as a map of psychic life. Her central figure is the Wild Woman, an archetype of instinctive knowing. The book is poetic, influential and widely loved. Scholars note that its use of sources is loose and that a universal archetype is a matter of faith more than evidence, so it works best as inspiration and not as research.
ideas: Estés argues that the Wild Woman, an archetype of the instinctive, creative, intuitive self, is natural to women and often suppressed.
Estés treats fairy tales as medicine. They are living guides that give psychological direction and are more than entertainment.
In Bluebeard, the dangerous husband stands for a predatory force inside the psyche. The heroine's intuition is her protection.
The Ugly Duckling is read as the story of a child in the wrong family. She must find her own kind and her own nature.
Vasalisa the Wise shows trust in an inner knowing, symbolized by a small doll. It guides a girl through dangerous tasks.
La Loba, an old woman who gathers bones and sings them into life, is Estés's image of creative restoration.
Reclaiming the instinctive self means setting boundaries, resting, making creative work and leaving relationships and roles that cage a woman.
Estés presents herself as a cantadora, a keeper of stories in the Latino tradition. She draws on that heritage in retelling the tales.
The Handless Maiden describes a woman whose creative power is given away through a bad bargain. She must regain it through a long journey.
The Red Shoes is read as a tale about a woman who loses touch with her instinctive life. Her compulsive dancing needs to be stopped.

books.t: Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds
books.thesis: Crowds go mad in a group, and they recover their senses one person at a time.
books.summary:
Mackay, a Scottish journalist, set out in 1841 to catalog episodes of collective folly. His subject is how whole societies pour money and belief into schemes that look foolish in hindsight.

His chapters cover financial manias such as tulip mania, the Mississippi Scheme and the South Sea Bubble, along with alchemy, witch hunts, prophecies, fashions in thinking and the Crusades. His claim is that groups can be swept up in shared delusion, and that sanity returns slowly, person by person. The book is anecdotal and moralizing, and historians have shown that parts of it, notably the tulip story, were exaggerated. It is better as a source of patterns than as reliable history.
ideas: Crowds fall into shared delusions, Mackay holds, while individuals recover their judgment slowly. He repeats the saying that men think in herds.
Tulip mania in the Dutch Republic is Mackay's example of speculation driven by a belief that prices could only rise. Later historians dispute how severe it was.
The Mississippi Scheme in France, run by John Law, turned a paper-money system and a promised colonial fortune into a bubble and collapse.
The South Sea Bubble shows speculation spreading through the English public, including the educated. Many companies with no real business were launched.
Alchemy and fortune-telling show that false authority attracts followers who want hidden knowledge.
Witch hunts show moral and religious fervor turning into mass violence. Mackay pairs them with the Crusades.
Folly appears even in light matters, Mackay shows, in fashions such as haunted houses and odd tastes in hair and beards.
In the bubble chapters, early gains draw in new buyers, so that more people join just before the collapse.
The chapters on slow poisoners and on the duel show how a fashion or a fear can spread through a society.
Mackay treats the Crusades as a long lasting popular frenzy that drew in whole nations.

books.thesis: Creating means facing the unknown, and that takes courage as much as talent.
books.summary:
May, an existential psychotherapist, asks what creativity demands of a person and why it so often feels frightening. His interest is the moment someone brings something new into the world, and what that moment costs them.

He argues that creativity is an encounter between a person and the world, marked by intensity, commitment and risk, and that courage is the virtue it requires. He draws on art, myth and clinical work, with discussions of the daimonic, form and limits, and the role of the unconscious. The book is short and reflective, closer to philosophy than to experimental psychology, so its claims rest on interpretation and example.
ideas: Creativity requires courage, which May defines as moving ahead despite despair and not as the absence of fear.
Creative acts come from an encounter. A person absorbed in a task meets the world, and that gives the work its intensity.
Form and limits are essential to creativity. May says constraints such as the rules of a sonnet give shape to freedom.
The daimonic is a drive, such as love or anger, that can take over the whole person. It can create or destroy, and creative people must engage with it.
Creativity works partly through the unconscious. Breakthroughs often come in moments of insight after effort and rest.
May distinguishes creative work from mere talent or hobby. Real creation means entering a risk of losing one's former self.
Conformity threatens courage. Those who follow the crowd avoid the commitments that creative work requires.
May separates courage into physical, moral, social and creative kinds. Creative courage, he says, is the discovery of new forms and symbols.
The creative person must give up some personal certainty and enter a sense of being alone. May calls this a kind of solitude necessary for work.
In May's account the artist meets the world and gives it a form. That act of giving form is what completes the encounter.

books.thesis: Self-actualization is not the top of a pyramid. Security and growth are both needed for a full life.
books.summary:
Kaufman, a psychologist, revisits what Maslow meant by self-actualization. His starting point is that the hierarchy of needs has often been misread as a rigid pyramid, with higher needs reachable only after lower ones are met.

He proposes a revised model pictured as a sailboat, with security needs as the hull and growth needs as the sail, and adds ten characteristics of a self-actualizing person. He draws on current research in personality and well-being. Some critics note that the original studies of Maslow's exemplars were small and subjective, and that Kaufman's update leans on his own selection of research.
ideas: Maslow did not draw the pyramid that carries his name. Kaufman argues that people pursue several needs at once instead of climbing them in a fixed order.
Kaufman replaces the pyramid with a sailboat. The hull holds the security needs of safety, connection and self-esteem, and the sail holds the growth needs of exploration, love and purpose.
Security and growth depend on each other. A person needs a sound hull to sail, and the sail is what takes them somewhere.
Self-actualization appears as a set of traits and not as a single achievement. Kaufman's list includes a love of truth, openness to experience, a sense of purpose and creative engagement with life.
Maslow's later thinking points beyond the self. Kaufman describes transcendence as connecting to something larger than oneself.
Hardship does not rule out growth. Kaufman rejects the idea that only comfortable conditions allow self-actualization, and he says trauma can sit alongside it.
Adversity can lead to posttraumatic growth, but Kaufman says this is not guaranteed. It depends on support.
The ten characteristics overlap and continue through life. Kaufman says people move among them across a life instead of finishing them in order.
Wholeness means integrating the different parts of oneself. The book contrasts this with growing by only one measure.
Maslow revised his own model late in life. Kaufman notes that he added a stage of transcendence beyond self-actualization.

books.thesis: Conflict eases when we state needs and feelings instead of judgments, and listen with empathy.
books.summary:
Rosenberg, a clinical psychologist and mediator who worked in many conflict zones, asks how people can speak honestly without attacking. Ordinary conversations slide into blame and defensiveness, and he wants a way to stop that.

He teaches a four-part process of observations, feelings, needs and requests, paired with empathic listening to the other person. The idea is that behind every judgment lies an unmet need, and naming that need opens connection. The method is practical and widely taught. Critics find it can sound formulaic or stilted in daily conversation, and it does not guarantee that the other person will cooperate.
ideas: Honest speech has four parts in Rosenberg's method. You observe without evaluating, state a feeling, name the need behind it and make a clear request.
Observation and evaluation are separate acts. Saying what happened is different from calling someone lazy or rude, and the second invites defense.
Many sentences that begin with a feeling word state a thought instead. Rosenberg asks people to name an emotion and not a judgment in disguise, such as feeling ignored.
Needs such as respect, safety and autonomy are shared by everyone. Rosenberg says understanding them keeps attention off the particular strategies for meeting them.
A request is only a request if the other person can say no. Rosenberg wants requests to be specific and doable, and he says that if a person cannot say no, it is a demand.
Empathy means listening for the feelings and needs of others without advice or reassurance. Rosenberg says this can calm anger.
Rosenberg calls evaluative, moralizing language life-alienating communication. His preferred style is giraffe language, named for the animal's large heart.
Demands often arrive dressed as requests. Rosenberg suggests that the listener hear a request as an offer from the heart.
Appreciation has three parts. Rosenberg says to state what the person did, the need it met and the feeling it brought.
Rosenberg allows force when its aim is protection. Protective use of force prevents harm, while punitive force aims to make the other person suffer.

books.thesis: Codependents lose themselves controlling and rescuing others. Recovery means returning attention to oneself.
books.summary:
Beattie, writing from her own recovery in the 1980s, gives a name to a pattern. A person organizes life around someone else's problems, such as an addicted partner or a troubled family, until their own needs fade from view.

She describes codependency as a set of habits, including caretaking, controlling, denial and low self-worth, and offers steps for detachment, setting boundaries and self-care, drawing on twelve-step ideas. The book was a bestseller and shaped popular language about relationships. Critics note that codependency is not a formal diagnosis, that the definition is broad enough to fit almost anyone, and that the book rests on personal experience more than research.
ideas: Beattie defines codependency by two things together. It is letting another person's behavior affect you and being obsessed with controlling that behavior.
Rescuing tends to keep problems alive. Codependents take on responsibility for others' feelings and problems, and that can keep those problems going.
Denial and low self-worth sit under the habits. Codependents often do not see how much another person's problem shapes their own life.
Detachment is separation without hostility. Beattie describes stepping away from the other person's problems with love while still caring.
Boundaries say what you will and will not accept. Beattie ties them to ending the pattern of rescuing.
Self-care starts with a plain inventory. Beattie lists naming your own feelings, needs and wants as a practical step.
Recovery borrows from twelve-step programs. These include accepting what you cannot control and finding support in groups such as Al-Anon.
Letting others face the results of their choices is part of letting go. Beattie argues that a person is not responsible for the choices of others.
Beattie describes codependency through a list of common traits. They include caretaking, low self-worth, repression of feelings and an urge to control.
Saying no without guilt is a skill the book teaches. Beattie also encourages readers to ask directly for what they need.

books.thesis: Depression comes from distorted thinking. Changing thoughts changes mood.
books.summary:
Burns, a psychiatrist who trained with Aaron Beck, asks whether depression can be treated without relying only on drugs or long analysis. He presents cognitive therapy to a general audience as a self-help method.

He lists ten cognitive distortions, such as all-or-nothing thinking and mind reading, and teaches readers to write down negative thoughts and replace them with more realistic ones, alongside activity scheduling. Controlled studies of the book as bibliotherapy have shown benefits for mild to moderate depression. It can seem to oversimplify, it is less suited to severe depression without professional care, and later cognitive therapy has added more than the book covers.
ideas: Mood follows thinking. In Burns's cognitive therapy, a person who thinks in negative patterns feels depressed, and changing the pattern changes the mood.

Burns catalogues ten distortions that make thinking gloomy. They include all-or-nothing thinking, overgeneralization, mental filter, mind reading, fortune telling, emotional reasoning and should statements.
The triple-column technique answers a thought in writing. The reader records the automatic thought, names the distortion and writes a rational response.
Mood logs and activity schedules make patterns visible. They also help people notice pleasure and mastery in small tasks.
Perfectionism is treated as a source of misery. It sets standards that cannot be met.
The book reaches beyond depression. Burns addresses guilt, anger and low self-esteem, with techniques for each.
Burns does not offer the book as a replacement for professional care. A chapter covers antidepressant medication, and he advises discussing severe symptoms with a professional.
Procrastination gets a 'no-lose' approach. The person plans small steps and records the results.
A self-test lets readers measure their own mood. Burns includes one for depression so they can track it from week to week.
Burns has readers argue back to negative thoughts. In the technique he calls 'externalization of voices', the person answers the thought as if it were another speaker.

books.t: Complex PTSD: From Surviving to Thriving
books.thesis: Chronic childhood abuse and neglect leave lasting wounds, but recovery is possible with specific tools.
books.summary:
Walker, a psychotherapist who has worked with survivors and has his own history, asks how the trauma of chronic childhood abuse or neglect differs from that of a single frightening event. He writes a guide for people living with the effects.

He describes complex PTSD through four responses to threat: fight, flight, freeze and fawn, and shows how each can shape an adult personality. He also covers emotional flashbacks and the inner critic, then offers steps such as grieving, self-compassion and building safe relationships. The book is practical and widely read. It rests on clinical experience, not controlled research, and C-PTSD was added to the ICD-11 but not to the DSM-5.
ideas: Complex PTSD comes from prolonged relational trauma in childhood. Walker distinguishes it from PTSD after a single event.
Survival responses carry into adulthood as styles. The four Fs of fight, flight, freeze and fawn each persist in adult life and relationships.
An emotional flashback has feeling without a picture. It is a sudden regression into childhood fear, shame or despair, with no visual memory.
The inner critic is the internalized voice of an abusive parent. Walker describes steps for shrinking it.
Toxic shame is the core wound. It is a deep sense of being defective that came from abandonment, and Walker says it drives many symptoms.
Grieving is part of recovery because old pain was never allowed expression. Crying and anger release it.
Healing happens between people. Walker stresses that safe people and a good therapist are central to recovery.
Walker holds that Complex PTSD is often hidden behind other diagnoses. He proposes it as a more accurate name, since symptoms can look like depression, anxiety or personality disorders.
Each of the four Fs has a matching adult type. The fight type tends toward narcissism and the flight type toward obsessive work.
Walker teaches a thirteen-step routine for managing flashbacks. It begins with saying 'I am having a flashback' and reminding oneself that the danger is past.

books.thesis: Every part of us means well, and healing comes from leading with a calm Self, not fighting parts.
books.summary:
Schwartz, the founder of Internal Family Systems (IFS), asks why we feel pulled in different directions, and why inner critics, addictions and anxieties seem so hard to dislodge. This book offers the model to a general reader.

He holds that the mind is naturally multiple, made of parts that take on roles, some protective and some carrying pain. At the center is the Self, which has qualities such as curiosity and compassion. Therapy means helping the Self relate to the parts instead of fighting them. IFS has growing clinical use but a limited research base, and the claim that the Self is an inborn core goes beyond what can be tested.
ideas: Schwartz treats having parts as normal. He describes the mind as made of subpersonalities and not as a sign of disorder.
Destructive behavior comes from a part trying to protect. Schwartz says there are no bad parts, only parts that use extreme methods.
Parts fall into three roles. Managers try to prevent pain, firefighters react when pain breaks through, and exiles carry the hurt of earlier events.
Beneath the parts sits the Self. Schwartz marks it with the eight Cs, which include curiosity, calm, compassion and clarity.
Unburdening lets a part put down what it carried. The part releases the beliefs and emotions it took on from past hurt.
Burdens are acquired, not original. They are extreme beliefs and feelings picked up in childhood or from the culture, and they are not a part's true nature.
Schwartz extends the model beyond the individual. He argues that systems of parts exist in families and society as well as in people.
Schwartz holds that the Self cannot be damaged, only blocked by parts. He calls this the basis for healing without the therapist having to supply it.
Legacy burdens pass down through families and culture. Schwartz gives beliefs about race, gender and worth as examples.
A protective part can be asked to step back. With its trust, Self energy can then reach the exile.

books.thesis: Short case stories from a psychoanalyst show how people avoid, defend and slowly face themselves.
books.summary:
Grosz, a psychoanalyst with decades of practice, asks what people bring into a therapist's room and what happens as they change. He answers with short case stories in place of a theory.

Each chapter follows a patient, with identifying details changed, and draws a lesson about loss, lying, change, love or the stories we tell about ourselves. The recurring idea is that behavior is often an attempt to avoid a pain we do not know we feel. The book is humane and well written. As a collection of anecdotes from one clinician, it offers insight but not evidence, and the narrator naturally shapes each story to fit its lesson.
ideas: Behavior often serves to avoid a feeling. Patients repeat patterns that protect them from loss or fear, even when the patterns cause harm.
Lying is a way of managing unbearable truths. Grosz treats lies to others and to ourselves this way, and he shows how honesty can slowly emerge in therapy.
Change is hard because even unwanted situations are familiar. Giving them up feels like another loss.
Praise can backfire with children. Empty compliments can make them avoid challenges for fear of not living up to them.
Grief takes forms that are not obvious. An unexpressed loss can shape behavior for years.
The stories we tell about our past are edited. Therapy examines which parts we leave out.
Careful listening is a form of help in itself. The point is to attend to another person without hurrying to fix.
A patient who could not hold on to money was acting on a belief about what she deserved. Grosz shows the habit expressing something she never said.
Silence can protect. Grosz gives the example of a child who refuses to speak of a lost parent.
What we want and what we think we should want are easily confused. Grosz suggests that therapy can help separate the two.

books.thesis: Attention is eroded by many forces at once, so fixing it takes social change as well as personal discipline.
books.summary:
Hari, a journalist, asks why it feels harder to concentrate than it used to. He interviews researchers across many fields to trace the loss of focus through modern life.

He names twelve causes, including technology designed to hold attention, constant switching, poor sleep, junk food, pollution, stress, and the decline of mind-wandering and play. His claim is that the problem is partly structural, so individual willpower is not enough. The book is lively and wide ranging. Critics say it presents some contested findings, such as links to specific additives and the scale of tech's effect, with more confidence than the evidence allows.
ideas: Hari names twelve causes of lost focus. They include the speed-up of life, multitasking, sleep loss, poor diet, air pollution and children's lost freedom to play.
Technology companies design products to capture attention. Hari points to techniques such as variable rewards and endless feeds.
Multitasking is mostly rapid switching, and switching has a cost. Hari argues that it leaves people worse at both tasks.
Mind-wandering is a needed state. Constant stimulation robs people of time for it and for deep thought.
Sleep loss harms attention. Hari points to long-term studies showing that most people need more rest than they get.
Rising ADHD diagnoses raise a question about environment. Hari asks how much of the rise comes from surroundings and not only from the individual.
Solutions have to be collective as well as personal. Hari points to rules on the attention economy and a shorter working week, alongside personal habits.
Interruptions cost more than the interruption itself. Hari describes Gloria Mark's finding that workers took on average about twenty three minutes to return to a task.
Self-help can place the burden on the wrong party. Hari discusses cruel optimism, which tells people to fix their own focus while the systems around them stay the same.
Phone and app design works as persuasion at scale. Hari tells of a visit to Tristan Harris and builds on that idea.

books.thesis: Maté argues ADD stems from early stress, not a fixed defect, and that understanding it can heal.
books.summary:
Maté, a physician who was diagnosed with ADD as an adult, examines the condition through his own history and his years of practice. He asks what attention deficit disorder is and where it comes from.

He argues that ADD is not purely genetic. Early childhood environment, especially stress in the parent-child relationship, affects how the brain develops, he says. He then describes ways to live with the traits and recover. The view is contested: most researchers regard ADHD as strongly heritable, and the book's claim of environmental origin is stronger than the evidence supports. Its emphasis on compassion has still been welcome to many readers.
ideas: Maté argues that ADD is developmental. Early environment shapes it as well as temperament.
Early family stress can teach a child to tune out. Maté says this stress often passes from parent to child across generations.
ADD is a way of coping with emotional pain. Maté includes a loss of connection with self in that pain.
Maté rejects blame. Parents of children with ADD are usually stressed themselves, not bad people.
Maté uses his own history as evidence. He describes losing himself in work and music and neglecting his family.
The brain can change because its development depends on experience. New relationships and practices can reshape it.
Treatment goes beyond medication. Maté recommends structure, support, awareness and a compassionate relation to oneself.
Inattention can work as a form of dissociation. Maté says the child learns to tune out distress.
ADD carries gifts as well as costs. Maté names creativity and sensitivity, though they are often hidden.
Attunement shapes attention. Maté says a parent's emotional presence in the first years helps set the pattern of the child's attention.

books.thesis: Modern culture produces illness, and many health problems are the cost of adapting to unhealthy conditions.
books.summary:
Maté, writing with his son Daniel, asks why chronic illness and mental distress are so common in rich societies. He argues that the usual medical focus on individual biology misses the wider context.

The book claims that trauma, defined as a wound that disconnects us from ourselves, together with social pressures such as inequality, isolation and consumer culture, lies behind much disease. It proposes compassionate inquiry and healing through authenticity. The idea of mind-body unity is widely discussed, but some critics say the book overstates the role of trauma in conditions like cancer and autoimmune disease and relies on selected research.
ideas: Maté locates trauma in the wound and not in the event. It is what happens inside a person as a result of hardship.
Mind and body are one system for Maté. He argues that suppressed emotions can contribute to illness such as autoimmune disease.
Normal is not the same as healthy. A culture that rewards overwork and disconnection can make illness a common result.
A child faces a trade between attachment and authenticity. When forced to choose, Maté says, the child gives up authenticity to keep the bond.
Compassionate inquiry is a way of asking questions. It helps a person see how past experience shapes present behavior.
Social conditions belong in medicine. Maté argues that poverty, racism and isolation affect health and that medicine should consider them.
Healing means returning to authenticity. Maté names awareness, grief and connection as the route, and not simply symptom control.
Modern medicine rests on a split between mind and body. Maté calls the separation a cultural myth.
Maté lists four A's of healing: authenticity, agency, anger and acceptance. He links them to the way the body responds to stress.
The word normal hides a sick society. Maté treats it as a statistical idea that disguises how common conditions reflect cultural illness.

books.thesis: The mind is a set of computational organs that natural selection shaped for ancestral problems.
books.summary:
Pinker, a cognitive scientist, tries to explain perception, reasoning, emotion and social life within one framework. The question he starts from is what the mind is and how it does what it does.

His thesis joins the computational theory of mind with evolutionary psychology. The brain is a set of modules built by natural selection to solve problems faced by hunter-gatherers. He applies this to vision, intelligence, emotions, family, art and humor. The scope is wide and the prose lively. Critics dispute how modular the mind is, and say evolutionary explanations for traits like music and humor are speculative and hard to test.
ideas: Pinker defines the mind as what the brain does. He describes thinking as information processing, or computation.
Natural selection explains the design of the mind. It shaped the mind to solve problems like finding food, avoiding danger and dealing with kin.
The mind is modular and not one general learning device. Pinker points to specialized systems for tasks such as vision, language and social reasoning.
Vision is a showcase of inference. We see in three dimensions through inference, and optical illusions reveal the assumptions the system makes.
Emotions are adaptations that serve goals. Fear helps avoid danger, and emotions act as commitments that make threats and promises credible.
A mind built for ancestral conditions meets a modern world. Pinker says the mismatch explains some of the problems of modern life.
Art, music and humor may be by-products. Pinker treats them as possible spin-offs of other adaptations, and he calls music auditory cheesecake.
Thought may run on a language beneath speech. Pinker discusses mentalese, a proposed language of thought, to explain how we think without words.
Reverse engineering is the method. Pinker says the question to ask of any trait is what it was designed to do.
Family feeling and cooperation have an evolutionary logic. Pinker uses kin selection and reciprocal altruism and treats them as part of the design of human nature.

books.thesis: Reason, science and humanism have improved human life, and the long-run data show it.
books.summary:
Pinker takes on the widespread belief that the modern world is sliding into decline. He asks whether the record of health, wealth, safety and knowledge supports that mood, and why intelligent people keep reading the news as a story of collapse.

He argues that life has improved on most measurable fronts over two centuries, and credits the Enlightenment ideals of reason, science and humanism. Progress is not automatic, he says, but the result of problem solving. Critics say he picks favorable indicators, plays down inequality, climate and catastrophic risks, and treats a past trend as a promise about the future.
ideas: Pinker defends four ideals as the source of modern gains. Reason, science, humanism and progress are presented as a living source and not an outdated creed.

The long-run numbers show large gains. Life expectancy has roughly doubled in developed countries since the 1800s, child mortality has collapsed, and the share of humanity in extreme poverty has fallen sharply.
Progress is not a law of nature. Entropy and the indifference of the universe mean things go wrong by default, so improvement requires knowledge and effort.
News coverage skews perception. Through the availability heuristic, bad events are reported and gradual improvements are not, which feeds what Pinker calls progressophobia.
Violence has declined over the long run. This covers war deaths, homicide and cruelty, and it extends the argument of his earlier book The Better Angels of Our Nature.
Pinker treats existential threats as problems to solve. Nuclear war and climate change call for institutions and technology, and he does not take them as proof that doom is certain.
Pinker defends science against the charge of scientism. He argues that scientific ways of thinking should inform the humanities and that moral progress depends on evidence.
The second law of thermodynamics explains why order is rare. Pinker invokes it to say that order must be created against a constant trend toward disorder.
Happiness, literacy and leisure also show improvement. Pinker displays the data as graphs.
Tribal politics and motivated reasoning threaten reason. Pinker argues that institutions such as science and open debate help correct them.

books.t: Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents
books.thesis: Emotionally immature parents leave children lonely, and recovery starts with seeing it clearly.
books.summary:
Gibson, a clinical psychologist, writes about adults who feel unseen or drained by a parent who looked fine from outside. She asks how parents who fed and housed their children, yet stayed emotionally unavailable, still shape a child's sense of self and relationships.

She describes four types of emotionally immature parent: emotional, driven, passive and rejecting. Children adapt as internalizers or externalizers. Her remedy is to stop hoping the parent will change, set limits and build a truer self. The book rests on clinical experience rather than controlled research, and the labels can be applied too widely to ordinary imperfect parents.
ideas: Gibson describes these parents as self-focused, low in stress tolerance and poor at empathy. The child learns to manage the parent's feelings.
Gibson names four types. Emotional parents are driven by moods, driven parents push and control, passive parents avoid, and rejecting parents withdraw.
Children adapt in two ways. Internalizers take on blame and try to help, externalizers act out and take risks, and Gibson treats both as survival strategies.
Emotional loneliness is the central wound. It is the sense of being unseen even in a family that looks intact.
A role-self can replace the true self. Many adult children build one to keep the relationship going, and the true self has to be rebuilt.
Hoping the parent will finally change keeps people stuck. Giving up that fantasy is part of healing.
The practical steps are modest. Gibson suggests observing the parent without taking the bait, limiting contact, setting boundaries and choosing relationships with emotionally mature people.
Role reversal marks these families. The child cares for the parent's needs in place of the other way around.
Gibson sets the immature parent against a mature one. A mature parent can reflect on their behavior, take responsibility and respond with empathy.
Gibson advises keeping contact light and brief. She says not to expect emotional closeness from such parents.

books.thesis: Chasing happiness and fighting bad feelings backfires. Valued action and acceptance work better.
books.summary:
Harris challenges the idea that a good life means feeling good, and that painful thoughts and feelings must be removed first. He asks why this approach leaves so many people anxious and stuck, and presents Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) as an alternative for general readers.

His argument is that struggling against inner experience makes it worse, so people should accept thoughts and feelings, step back from them, and act on chosen values. The skills include defusion, mindfulness and committed action. ACT has good research support, but it is not clearly better than other therapies for every problem, and a self-help book does not replace treatment for severe conditions.
ideas: Harris says the trap rests on four myths. They are that happiness is the natural state, that unhappy people are defective, that you must get rid of negative feelings to live well, and that you should be able to control your thoughts.
Avoiding unpleasant inner states backfires. Experiential avoidance tends to increase suffering and shrink a person's life.
Defusion loosens a thought's hold. Harris teaches people to see thoughts as passing words and images, for example by noticing 'I am having the thought that' instead of treating a thought as fact.
Acceptance means making room for pain. Harris calls this expansion and sets it against fighting feelings.
The observing self gives a stable place to watch from. Mindfulness lets thoughts and feelings be watched without being obeyed.
Values are a chosen direction, distinct from goals. Committed action means doing what matters even when discomfort is present.
Dropping anchor is a short exercise for strong emotion. The person acknowledges their feelings, connects with their body and engages with what is around them.
The struggle switch makes anxiety about anxiety worse. When it is on, the fight adds a second layer of distress, and Harris suggests turning it off.
The mind is a storyteller. Harris suggests treating thoughts such as 'I am worthless' as that habit, using the labels 'the storyteller' and 'the thinking self'.
The choice point is a daily decision. At any moment a person can move toward their values or away from them.

books.t: What Life Could Mean to You
books.thesis: A life is judged by how a person meets work, community and love. Social interest is the test of health.
books.summary:
Adler, the founder of Individual Psychology, writes for the general reader about what gives a human life meaning and why people end up with such different outlooks. He looks to each person's early circumstances to explain how they face the demands of living.

He argues that children feel inferior and strive for significance, and that healthy striving is joined to concern for others, which he calls social interest. Each person forms a style of life early, and it shows in how they handle three tasks: work, community and love. Many of his claims, such as those on birth order, are hard to test, and later research on them is mixed.
ideas: Everyone starts with feelings of inferiority. Adler says the drive to overcome them is the engine of development, and it can be healthy or turn into a superiority complex.
Adler measures psychological health by social interest. Gemeinschaftsgefuhl is the capacity to feel connected to others and contribute.
Life sets three main tasks: occupation, community or friendship, and love and marriage. Adler says failure to meet them shows in a person's behavior.
Style of life is set in early childhood and works as a private logic. It guides later choices and can be read from early memories.
Birth position shapes outlook without fixing it. Whether eldest, second, youngest or only child, Adler said it does not determine character.
Pampering and neglect both distort a child's view of life. The pampered child expects others to serve them, and the neglected child distrusts everyone.
Dreams and early recollections reveal a person's goals. Adler uses them to read the style of life, and he says the cure for maladjustment is to widen social interest.
Meaning is made and not given. Adler holds that the meaning of life is shaped by what each person makes of it, and that no one lives in a world of pure fact.
The inferiority complex is weakness used as an excuse. Adler describes people using feelings of weakness to avoid the tasks of life.
Heredity and environment do not fix fate. Adler says the person's interpretation of them matters more.

books.thesis: The good life is activity of the soul in line with virtue, and character is built by habit and judgment.
books.summary:
Aristotle asks what the highest human good is and how people can achieve it. He treats ethics as a practical inquiry into how to live, not a set of abstract rules, and wants to know what makes a life go well for a creature with our nature.

He argues that the good is eudaimonia, flourishing, which comes from exercising reason and the virtues over a whole life. Virtues are habits formed by practice and guided by practical wisdom. Interpreters dispute whether he ranks contemplation above civic life, the doctrine of the mean is vague in practice, and his views on slaves and women are plainly dated.
ideas: Every action aims at some good, and the highest is eudaimonia. Aristotle takes it to be an activity over a complete life and not a feeling or a state.
The function argument ties the human good to what is distinctive of humans. Aristotle locates it in doing well the activity of the rational soul.
Moral virtues are acquired by habituation. Courage and temperance are a mean between excess and deficiency, relative to the person and the situation.
No virtue is complete without practical wisdom. Phronesis is the capacity to see what to do in particular cases.
Praise and blame depend on voluntary action. Aristotle requires that the agent knows what they do and that the source of action is in them.
Aristotle sorts friendship into three kinds: utility, pleasure and character. Friendship of character is the most lasting, and friendship as a whole is central to a good life.
Contemplation is the highest and most self-sufficient activity. Pleasure is a completion of activity and not the goal of life.
Ethics is not an exact science. Aristotle warns that one should look for only as much precision as the subject allows.
Akrasia names knowing what is best and acting against it. Aristotle discusses this weakness of will.
Justice has a distributive and a corrective form. Aristotle compares it to a kind of proportion.

books.thesis: A just city and a just soul are ordered by reason, and only philosophers should rule.
books.summary:
Plato asks what justice is and whether being just is better for a person than seeming just. Starting from a challenge by Glaucon and Thrasymachus, he builds an imagined city to see justice at large scale before looking for it in the individual.

He argues that justice is each part of city and soul doing its own work under the guidance of reason, and that rulers must be trained philosophers who know the Form of the Good. Readers dispute whether he means the ideal city as a program or as a model, and critics such as Popper read it as authoritarian, given the censorship, guardian class and noble lie.
ideas: The ring of Gyges poses the challenge. Glaucon claims people are just only from fear of punishment, and the rest of the book answers it.
The ideal city is just when each class does its own work. It has three classes: producers, auxiliaries and guardians.
The soul mirrors the city with three parts. Reason, spirit and appetite make up the soul, and a just person is one in whom reason rules with the help of spirit.
Only philosophers should rule, because only they know the Good. Plato proposes a long education and shared property for the guardians.
Knowledge is an ascent. The sun, the divided line and the cave describe a climb from images and opinion to understanding of the Forms.
Plato regulates poetry and music because they shape character. He also admits a founding falsehood, the noble lie, to bind the city together.
Regimes decline in a set order: aristocracy, timocracy, oligarchy, democracy and tyranny. The tyrant is shown as the most wretched person.
Justice in the soul is each part doing its own work. This, Socrates says, is why the just person is happier than the unjust.
The myth of Er closes the book with a story of the afterlife. Souls choose their next lives and are responsible for their choice.
The guardians would have no private families. Plato argues that women could take part in guarding the city if they have the ability.

books.thesis: Love begins as desire for one body and can rise to the contemplation of beauty itself.
books.summary:
Plato's subject is Eros, or erotic love, and what it is for. Set at a drinking party in Athens, the dialogue has a series of guests give speeches in praise of love, and it asks what love wants and why it matters for a human life.

The speeches build to Socrates, who reports a lesson from the priestess Diotima. Love is a desire for the good to be one's own forever, and it can ascend from bodies to souls, laws and knowledge, ending with the Form of Beauty. She describes Eros as the child of Poverty and Resource, always lacking and always seeking. Critics, notably Vlastos, argue that this ladder treats individuals as steps and not as people worth loving for themselves.
ideas: Four speakers treat love in different ways. Phaedrus, Pausanias, Eryximachus and Agathon present it as a source of courage, a matter of two kinds of Aphrodite, a cosmic principle and a god.
Aristophanes explains love as the search for a lost half. In his myth, humans were once double beings split by Zeus.
Diotima, through Socrates, says Eros is not a god. He is a spirit between mortal and divine, born of Poverty and Resource, always needy and always seeking.
Love is the desire to possess the good forever. That explains why people seek immortality through children, fame and works of the mind.
The ladder of love moves upward. It runs from one beautiful body to all bodies, then to souls, laws and knowledge, and finally to Beauty itself.
The Form of Beauty differs from beautiful things. It is unchanging and pure, while beautiful things come and go, and seeing it is the goal of correct love.
Alcibiades breaks in drunk and complicates the neat theory. He describes Socrates as a man who resists his advances, which shows philosophy in practice.
Eryximachus, a doctor, treats love as a force in body and cosmos. He links it to harmony and health.
Agathon praises Love as the youngest, most beautiful and best of the gods. Socrates then questions each of these claims.
The setting is a banquet for Agathon's victory in a tragedy contest. The guests decide to give speeches in praise of love instead of drinking heavily.

books.thesis: Socrates faces death on the belief that an examined life and obedience to justice matter more than survival.
books.summary:
These four Platonic dialogues center on the trial and death of Socrates in 399 BC. They ask what a philosopher owes to his city, to the gods and to his own principles when he is charged with impiety and corrupting the young.

Euthyphro tests definitions of piety, Apology gives his defense, Crito has him refuse to escape prison, and Phaedo gives his final conversation about the soul. Together they present him as a model of integrity. Plato is not a neutral reporter, the historical Socrates is hard to separate from Plato's portrait, and many readers find the Phaedo's arguments for immortality weak.
ideas: In Euthyphro, every definition of piety fails. This shows Socrates' method of questioning and his claim that he knows he does not know.
Socrates says the Delphic oracle started his mission. In Apology, it led him to test those thought wise and to urge Athenians to care for the soul.
He would not stop philosophizing even to save himself. He says the unexamined life is not worth living.
Crito argues against returning wrong for wrong. Socrates holds that escaping would break an agreement with the laws that raised him.
The personified Laws of Athens give an early social-contract argument. It rests on benefits received and continued residence.
In Phaedo, Socrates offers arguments for the soul's survival, from opposites, recollection and affinity with the Forms. He also says a philosopher practices dying.
The death scene presents his calm as the fruit of his philosophy. It includes the hemlock and his last words about owing a cock to Asclepius.
Socrates is charged with corrupting the young and not believing in the gods of the city. In reply he describes his daimonion, a divine sign that holds him back.
In Phaedo, friends such as Simmias and Cebes press objections. One asks whether the soul might fade like the harmony of a lyre.
Socrates declines to beg the jury for mercy. After conviction he proposes that his fitting penalty would be free meals at public expense.

books.thesis: Freedom comes from caring only about what is up to you, namely your own judgments and choices.
books.summary:
Epictetus, a former slave who taught Stoicism in Nicopolis, asks how to live well when so much of life lies outside our power. The Discourses, written down by his student Arrian, are lectures and exchanges aimed at practice rather than theory.

His answer is that some things are up to us, namely our judgments, desires and choices, and others are not, such as body, reputation and property, which he treats as indifferent to our happiness. Peace comes from focusing on the first and accepting the second. The text is mediated by Arrian, and critics argue the stance can drift into passivity, though Epictetus insists on duties to family and city.
ideas: Epictetus divides everything into what is up to us and what is not. Opinion, impulse, desire and aversion are ours, while body, wealth and reputation are not.
Prohairesis, the faculty of choice, is the true self. No one can compel it, not even a tyrant.
People are disturbed by their judgments about events and not by the events. Training therefore means examining impressions before assenting to them.
Epictetus teaches three disciplines. Desire covers what to want, action covers how to act towards others, and assent covers how to think.
Roles carry duties. Son, citizen and brother each call for acting well regardless of how others behave.
Providence governs the world. One should accept what happens as a good actor accepts the part given by the playwright.
Philosophy is a daily practice and not doctrine to recite. Epictetus compares the philosopher's school to a hospital.
Epictetus was born a slave and later became a teacher. His Discourses survive because his student Arrian wrote them down.
The use of impressions is the key task. Epictetus suggests telling oneself 'you are an impression and not at all the thing you appear to be'.
An insult injures only through judgment. Epictetus holds that the choice to be angry or calm belongs to us, and he asks students to see that the injury lies in the judgment.

books.thesis: Reason can cure anger, fear and wasted time, and a good life is one in which we use our days well.
books.summary:
Seneca, Stoic philosopher and adviser to Nero, writes about the practical troubles of a Roman life: anger, grief, busyness, insecurity and the fear of death. These dialogues and essays offer advice on how to meet them with reason.

His argument is that virtue is the only good, that most distress comes from false judgments, and that time is the thing we waste most. He is especially hard on busyness, noting that people guard their money carefully yet give their time away freely. The essays blend Stoic doctrine with Roman moral rhetoric. Seneca's own wealth and political compromises have long been used against him, and his sharpest advice sits uneasily beside his life.
ideas: Anger should be prevented and not merely restrained. On Anger calls it a brief madness and advises checking the first impulse and delaying a response.
Life is long enough if used well. On the Shortness of Life says people waste it on busyness, pleasure and the pursuit of other people's approval.

Wealth can be preferred without being good. On the Happy Life holds that happiness lies in virtue and that wealth is a preferred but indifferent thing, which Seneca defends against charges of hypocrisy.
Restlessness eases with measure. On Tranquility of Mind advises a measured level of public involvement, simple living and acceptance of change.
Hardship is training from a rational universe. On Providence uses this to answer why good people suffer.
Grief is met with the view that loss belongs to nature. The consolations to Marcia, Helvia and Polybius also recommend remembering the dead with gratitude.
Imagining misfortune in advance softens it. Premeditation of evils reduces the shock of loss, and the wise person holds all external goods lightly.
Seneca ends the day with an audit of his own faults. He reviews them each night and cites the habit as one he took from the philosopher Sextius.
The sage cannot be injured. On the Constancy of the Wise Man argues that insults and losses touch only what is external.
Withdrawal from public life can still serve the public. On Leisure explains that a person may serve through study and thought when active public life is closed to them.

books.thesis: Fortune cannot give or take true happiness, which lies in the highest good that no one can remove.
books.summary:
Boethius, a Roman statesman imprisoned and awaiting execution around 524, asks how a just person can fall so low and what, if anything, can console him. The work is a conversation between the prisoner and Lady Philosophy, written in alternating prose and verse.

She argues that fortune is changeable by nature, that worldly goods cannot satisfy, and that true happiness is the supreme good, which she identifies with God. Evil is powerless and providence orders all. Scholars note that the book is explicitly philosophical and hardly mentions Christianity, and many find its reconciliation of divine foreknowledge with free will unconvincing.
ideas: Lady Philosophy diagnoses the prisoner as having forgotten his own nature. Her treatment is gentle at first and then more rigorous.
Fortune's wheel shows that rising and falling are her nature. Complaining about reversals therefore mistakes what she gave.
Wealth, honors, power and fame cannot make a person happy. Each is partial, unstable or dependent on others.
True happiness is the highest good, which is one with God. People seek it in mistaken forms.
Evil people are in a sense powerless. They fail to reach the good that every will aims at, and wrongdoing is its own punishment.
Providence and fate are one order seen two ways. Providence is the divine plan seen as a whole and fate is its unfolding in time, so apparent injustice has a place within a larger order.
Eternity is not endless time. It is the complete and simultaneous possession of unending life, and God's knowledge of future events does not remove human freedom.
The prison setting shapes the form of the book. Boethius wrote it in prose and verse while held and awaiting execution on charges of treason.
The supreme good is also the source of all being. Philosophy presents it as what people seek whenever they seek anything.
God knows the future differently from the way we foresee it. Philosophy answers the problem of free will against foreknowledge by saying that God sees all at once.

books.thesis: Fixed views and fixed names narrow us, and freedom comes from following the Way and letting things change.
books.summary:
The Zhuangzi, a Daoist text attributed to Zhuang Zhou, asks how to live when human values, judgments and categories look partial and shifting. It works through stories, jokes and paradoxes instead of systematic argument.

Its central claim is that every perspective is limited, that right and wrong depend on where one stands, and that a person who responds spontaneously to the Way finds ease and freedom. Death is treated as one more transformation. The book is a composite, only the inner chapters are usually credited to Zhuang Zhou, and readers disagree on whether it teaches skepticism, mysticism or a practical skill.
ideas: Free and easy wandering is the ideal. It means moving through life without being tied to fame, usefulness or fixed goals.
'This' and 'that' depend on each other. The Qiwulun chapter argues that disputes cannot be settled from within any single standpoint.
The butterfly dream unsettles our categories. Zhuang Zhou cannot tell whether he is a man who dreamed a butterfly or a butterfly dreaming a man.
