Cook Ding shows skill as following natural patterns without strain. His carving of an ox is a model for acting in line with the Way.
Uselessness can protect. The tree survives because carpenters ignore it, and that frees it.
Zhuangzi drums and sings when his wife dies, after first grieving. He accepts death as part of the cycle of change and not as something to resist.
Fasting of the mind empties oneself of fixed ideas. The aim is to respond to things as they arise.
The Inner Chapters are traditionally credited to Zhuangzi himself. The outer and miscellaneous chapters are thought to have been added by later followers.
Small creatures laugh at the giant bird Peng. The text opens with the fish Kun that becomes Peng, and the laughers mistake their own range for the whole.
Each voice speaks for itself. In the image of the pipes of heaven, wind blows through hollows and makes different sounds.

books.thesis: A ruler who wants to keep power must act by what works, not by what is conventionally good.
books.summary:
Machiavelli asks how new rulers gain and hold power, and why they so often lose it. Writing in 1513 for the Medici after the fall of the Florentine republic, he sets aside imagined ideal states and looks at what happens in politics.

He argues that a prince needs virtu, meaning skill and force of character, to cope with fortuna, the unpredictable element of events, and that he must be ready to act against conventional morality when the state requires. His most famous advice is that if a prince cannot be both loved and feared, it is safer to be feared. Readers dispute his purpose: some see a manual for tyrants, others a satire or a republican in disguise, given his Discourses on Livy.
ideas: Machiavelli judges politics by outcomes. He promises to follow the effectual truth of things and not how rulers ought to behave in theory.
Virtu meets fortuna. Virtu is a mix of boldness, skill and adaptability, and fortuna is chance, which he compares to a river that can be channeled by preparation but not stopped.
New principalities are harder to hold than hereditary ones. The new ruler must secure the support of the people and eliminate rivals decisively.
Cruelty is judged by how it is used. It can be well used if committed at once and for security, and badly used if repeated, and a prince should keep his promises only when it serves him.
Being feared beats being loved if one cannot be both. A prince must still avoid being hated, especially by taking property or women.
Citizen armies are safer than hired ones. Mercenary and auxiliary armies are unreliable, so a state needs its own soldiers to be secure.
Cesare Borgia is offered as a model of skill. The final chapter urges the liberation of Italy from foreign rule.
A prince needs both the lion and the fox. He must have the strength to scare wolves and the cunning to avoid traps.
The choice of advisers tests a prince. He should choose wise ministers and let them speak freely only when asked.
Chapter 18 says the public judges by appearances and results. A prince must therefore seem to have the good qualities.

books.thesis: Without a sovereign power to keep the peace, life reverts to war, so people rationally submit to authority.
books.summary:
Hobbes, writing during the English Civil War, asks why people should obey political authority and what makes a commonwealth stable. He builds his answer from a materialist account of human nature and a thought experiment about life without government.

He argues that in the state of nature, people are roughly equal and driven by fear and desire, producing a war of all against all, so they covenant to give up their rights to an absolute sovereign. Critics doubt his bleak view of human nature, object that absolute power invites abuse, and note that his account of religion was controversial in his day.
ideas: Without a common power, life in the state of nature is, in Hobbes's famous phrase, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish and short.
Equality breeds quarrel. Equality of ability produces equality of hope, and competition, diffidence and glory-seeking become three causes of quarrel.
The laws of nature are rational rules. Seeking peace and keeping covenants follow from the desire for self-preservation.
Covenants without a sword are only words. A sovereign with the power to enforce them is needed to make them binding.
Sovereignty is created by a covenant among subjects. They authorize one man or assembly, and the sovereign's authority is not subject to their judgment.
One right cannot be given up. Subjects keep the right to resist force against their own life, though this is not a right to rebel in general.
Hobbes puts the church under the sovereign. The later parts attack clerical claims that he saw as weakening civil peace.
The commonwealth is an artificial man. Hobbes calls it a 'mortal god', whose soul is sovereignty and whose body is made of its subjects.
Hobbes denies that there is any fixed highest good. He describes human life as a 'perpetual and restless desire of power after power, that ceaseth only in death'.
Liberty is the absence of external impediments. Subjects remain free wherever the law is silent, and acting from fear is still free action.

books.thesis: Government is legitimate only with consent, and it must protect natural rights to life, liberty and property.
books.summary:
Locke challenges the claim that kings rule by divine, inherited right. Written in the context of the Exclusion Crisis and published in 1689, the work asks what gives anyone the right to rule over others.

The First Treatise attacks Filmer's patriarchalism. The Second argues that people in a state of nature have rights under natural law, form government by consent to protect them, and may resist when it breaks that trust. Property begins when people mix their labor with what nature provides. Critics point to his property theory's ties to colonial dispossession, his own involvement in slavery, and the vague role of tacit consent.
ideas: The First Treatise refutes Robert Filmer. Locke argues that scripture and reason do not support the view that kings inherit Adam's authority, or absolute monarchy.
The state of nature has a law of its own. It holds that no one may harm another in life, health, liberty or possessions.
Property arises from labor. A person mixes labor with something held in common, subject to leaving enough and as good for others and wasting nothing.
Money allows unequal holdings. It lets people keep more than they can use without spoilage, and Locke accepts the result.
The lack of an impartial judge pushes people into government. They form a commonwealth by consent to gain settled law and enforcement.
Power is a trust. The legislative must be supreme but is limited by the ends of government, and it is kept distinct from the executive.
The people may remove rulers who act against the public good. Locke defends this as a safeguard against tyranny and not an invitation to disorder.
Political power differs from paternal and despotic power. Locke argues that a father's authority over children is temporary and ends when they reach reason.
Living under a government implies tacit consent. Simply enjoying its protection counts, though only express consent makes one a full member.
Prerogative lets the executive act for the public good where the law is silent or even against its letter. Locke says the people are the final judge of its abuse.

books.thesis: Human understanding rests on habit and feeling, not on reason alone, and we know less than we think.
books.summary:
Hume sets out to build a science of man on the model of Newton's natural philosophy. He asks what the mind can know, how passions move us, and where moral distinctions come from, using experience and observation instead of speculation.

He argues that all ideas derive from impressions, that causation is a habit of expectation and not a perceived necessity, and that the self is a bundle of perceptions. In morals, reason serves the passions and virtue is based on sentiment. Hume was dissatisfied with parts of the book, especially on personal identity, and it attracted little notice on release.
ideas: Every simple idea comes from a prior impression. Perceptions divide into vivid impressions and fainter ideas, so ideas without such a source are empty.
We never observe a necessary connection between cause and effect. Causation is constant conjunction plus a habit of mind.
Induction cannot be justified by reason. Expecting the future to resemble the past is itself an assumption drawn from past experience.
There is no impression of a self. A person is a bundle of perceptions in perpetual flux, and the sense of identity is a fiction produced by memory and imagination.
Reason alone cannot move us to act. Hume says it is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions.
Moral distinctions come from feeling and not from reason. They arise from approval and disapproval, and Hume remarks on the gap between 'is' and 'ought'.
Justice is an artificial virtue. It is invented through convention to meet the needs of society, while others such as benevolence are natural.
Ideas link through three principles of association: resemblance, contiguity and cause and effect. Hume calls this a kind of gentle force that works like attraction among ideas.
Sympathy carries passions from person to person. Hume uses it to explain how moral approval can be shared.

Skeptical doubt gives way to ordinary life. At the end of Book One Hume is anxious and isolated, and he finds relief only in dinner, backgammon and company, which shows that nature overrides philosophical argument.

books.thesis: Our knowledge of the world rests on custom, not proof, and we should hold beliefs in proportion to evidence.
books.summary:
Hume's later, shorter statement of his theory of knowledge asks how far human reason can reach. Written for a broader readership than the Treatise, it considers what we can know about causes, the future, freedom and the claims of religion.

He divides knowledge into relations of ideas and matters of fact, argues that reasoning about the latter depends on custom, and recommends a mitigated skepticism. He argues that we have no rational proof that the future will resemble the past. The essays on miracles and design press against religious claims. Critics say the argument on miracles is weaker than it looks, and Kant and later Quine questioned the sharpness of his divide.
ideas: Hume's fork splits knowledge in two. Relations of ideas are known by reasoning alone, while matters of fact depend on experience and can always be otherwise.
Nothing in past experience can prove that the future will resemble it. This is the problem of induction, and our expectations rest on custom.
Necessary connection is felt and not seen. The idea comes from a habit of expecting the effect after the cause, not from anything in objects.
Hume reconciles liberty and necessity by defining liberty as acting according to the will. This compatibilist view holds that human actions are as regular as natural events.
A wise person proportions belief to evidence. On miracles, testimony for a violation of natural law will almost always be less likely than that the witness is mistaken or lying.
The design argument rests on a comparison we cannot make. We have no experience of other universes to set ours against, so Hume finds the inference to a designer weak.
Mitigated skepticism favors modest, limited inquiry into everyday matters. Hume holds that extreme doubt cannot be sustained in practice.
Animals show that inference from custom needs no reasoning. They learn from experience and act on expectation, which Hume takes as evidence.
The missing shade of blue is a possible counterexample. It tests the claim that every idea is copied from an impression, though Hume treats it as too small to overturn the rule.
Belief in an external world rests on instinct and not argument. We only ever have perceptions before the mind and cannot step outside them to check.

books.thesis: Everything follows from the nature of God or Nature, and freedom is understanding our place within it.
books.summary:
Spinoza asks what reality is, what the human mind is, and how a person can live well without superstition. Presented in geometrical form with definitions, axioms and proofs, the Ethics tries to deduce the whole of human life from first principles.

He argues that there is only one substance, God or Nature, whose attributes include thought and extension, and that everything follows with necessity. Freedom is not free will, which he rejects, but understanding why things must be as they are. Humans are in bondage to passions until adequate ideas free them. Many readers find the geometrical form opaque, the monism is contested, and in his time the work was condemned as atheism.
ideas: God and Nature are one thing, and nothing exists outside it. Everything else is a mode of this single infinite substance, so Spinoza leaves no creator standing apart from the world.
Mind and body are one thing seen under two attributes. Thought and extension belong to the same substance, and the order of ideas matches the order of things, so neither is the cause of the other.
Spinoza denies free will in the usual sense. Everything happens by necessity, and he says the belief in free choice comes from ignorance of the causes that move us.
Every thing strives to persevere in its being, and Spinoza calls this striving conatus. He takes it to be the essence of each individual.
Emotions are changes in the body that raise or lower our power to act. Spinoza treats desire, joy and sadness as the basic ones.
Bondage means being governed by passive emotions, and the way out is understanding. Freedom grows as we form adequate ideas and learn the causes of our feelings.
The highest knowledge is intuitive: seeing things as following from God. Spinoza says it brings the intellectual love of God and a lasting kind of blessedness.
Ethics can be argued like geometry, in Spinoza's view. The book proceeds by definitions, axioms, propositions and proofs, treating human emotions as if they were lines and planes.
Knowledge comes in three kinds, and only two give adequate ideas. Opinion or imagination does not, while reason and intuitive knowledge do.
Good and evil are relative to our power of acting. What raises that power is good and what lowers it is bad, and the free person, guided by reason, thinks of death least of all things.

books.thesis: Moral judgment grows out of sympathy and the imagined view of an impartial spectator.
books.summary:
Smith, writing before The Wealth of Nations, asks where moral approval and disapproval come from. He wants to know how self-interested creatures come to judge conduct, feel for others and hold themselves to standards, and he answers from observation of ordinary social life.

He argues that we judge by imagining how an impartial spectator would feel, and that conscience is that spectator internalized. Sympathy lets us share another's feelings, and we want to be praiseworthy, not merely praised. Scholars have long debated how this fits with the later book, and critics worry that the spectator mirrors social convention.
ideas: Approval is a match of feelings. Sympathy is the imaginative sharing of another person's situation, and we approve when our feelings agree with those of the person concerned.
Conscience works as an imagined observer. Smith calls this figure the impartial spectator, or the man within the breast, and we judge our own conduct through its eyes.
People want to deserve praise, not only to receive it. Smith calls this praiseworthiness, and it matters even if no praise ever comes.
Smith splits moral judgment into two questions. Propriety asks whether an action fits its cause, while merit and demerit ask what reward or punishment its effects deserve.
Justice can be enforced, but kindness cannot. Justice forbids harm to others and is the pillar of society, while beneficence is a grace that no one can be required to give.
Admiring the rich and powerful corrupts our moral sentiments. People mistake wealth for happiness and pursue it beyond what satisfies them.
Self-command is the virtue the others depend on. It restrains our passions in line with the spectator's view, and Smith holds it essential to all the other virtues.
We judge actions by their results even though intentions should count. Smith treats this as a flaw, and he says nature built it in for practical reasons.
The 'invisible hand' also appears here, in a passage on the rich. Pursuing their own ends, they divide the necessaries of life with the poor almost as if the earth had been shared equally.
General rules of morality grow out of repeated experience of what we approve and disapprove. A sense of duty is respect for these rules when feeling alone would fall short.

books.thesis: Easy optimism fails against real suffering, and the only workable answer is modest, practical effort.
books.summary:
Voltaire's satirical tale attacks the philosophy of optimism, the idea that this is the best of all possible worlds. Written after the Lisbon earthquake of 1755 and the Seven Years' War, it asks how such a view survives war, disease, slavery and natural disaster.

Candide is taught optimism by Pangloss and is then thrown through a series of disasters across Europe and the Americas that refute it while Pangloss keeps defending his creed, ending with the advice to cultivate our garden. Voltaire caricatures Leibniz's actual position, and the ending is ambiguous, since it can be read as wisdom or as a retreat from larger questions.
ideas: Pangloss repeats that all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds, and Voltaire makes him a target. His doctrine is a distorted version of Leibniz's optimism.

Voltaire tests optimism by piling disasters on Candide. After his expulsion from Westphalia come war, shipwreck, the Lisbon earthquake and the Inquisition, and each one sets the doctrine against experience.
The church, the military and the aristocracy are all shown as cruel and hypocritical. Voltaire's targets include clergy who preach morality while acting without it.
The slave in Surinam shows what European prosperity is built on. He has lost a leg and a hand, and Candide's reaction to him marks a turn away from optimism.
Eldorado is a utopia of reason and tolerance, and Candide leaves it anyway. This suggests that an ideal society is no remedy for human restlessness.
Martin the Manichean scholar is as pessimistic as Pangloss is optimistic. Set side by side, they show that neither extreme fits the facts.
The closing line, to cultivate our garden, recommends useful work and modest aims. It replaces speculation about the world's ultimate design.
The Old Woman shows that suffering reaches every rank. She tells of losing half a buttock and of years of misery, and she observes that many wish to die yet still cling to life.
The romantic quest ends in a deflation. Cunegonde has grown ugly and sharp tempered, and Candide marries her out of duty because he keeps his promise.
The Turkish farmer gives the practical answer. He tells Candide that work keeps away three great evils, boredom, vice and need, which prepares the closing call to cultivate the garden.

books.thesis: Legitimate authority rests on the general will of free citizens, not on force or birth.
books.summary:
Rousseau opens with the problem that people are born free yet everywhere live in chains. He asks what could make political rule legitimate, given that no one has a natural authority over others and force creates no right.

His answer is a contract in which each person gives themselves wholly to the community and so obeys only a law they share in making. The general will, aimed at the common good, is sovereign and cannot be represented. He separates it from the will of all, which is only the sum of private interests. Critics, from Constant to Berlin, argue that the idea of being forced to be free can license tyranny over dissenters.
ideas: Rousseau begins with man born free, and he says political chains need a justification. Neither force nor paternal power creates a right to rule.
In obeying the law, citizens obey themselves. Each individual alienates all rights to the community and receives them back as a citizen.
The general will is not the will of all. It concerns the common interest, while the will of all is only the sum of private wishes.
Sovereignty belongs to the people and cannot be alienated or represented. For this reason Rousseau is suspicious of representative government and favors direct assembly in small states.
Someone who refuses the general will may be compelled to obey it. Rousseau describes this as forcing them to be free.
Rousseau separates the sovereign from the government. The sovereign makes law, and the government is a magistracy that executes it and can be changed by the people.
Laws need a shared moral sentiment, so Rousseau proposes a civil religion and a lawgiver figure. Later readers have found these ideas uncomfortably illiberal.
The general will is always right, but the judgment that guides it is not always enlightened. This is why Rousseau says a people needs good guidance.
Rousseau counts three kinds of liberty. Natural liberty is limited only by force, civil liberty by the general will, and moral liberty means obeying a law one prescribes to oneself.
No one form of government suits every state. Democracy, aristocracy and monarchy fit states of different size and climate, and Rousseau thinks pure democracy fits only a small state.

books.thesis: Rousseau claims that a life told with unsparing candor shows one man's inner nature and his wrongs.
books.summary:
Rousseau's Confessions is often called the first major modern autobiography. He asks what it would mean to show a human being exactly as he is, and sets out to give a complete account of his character, shameful acts included, so that readers can judge him with the full truth in hand.

The book follows him from a Geneva childhood through years of wandering, patronage, love affairs and literary fame, stressing feeling over reason as the source of his character. He presents himself as basically good yet damaged by society. Readers have long noted that his memory is selective and self-justifying, and that his claim to total honesty is hard to sustain.
ideas: Rousseau claims to be doing something no one has done before. He opens by declaring that he is undertaking a work without precedent, showing a man in all the truth of nature, himself.
He puts his worst acts on record. He confesses stealing a ribbon and blaming a servant girl, and he admits abandoning his five children to a foundling hospital.
Childhood shapes the adult in his account. He treats experiences such as a punishment by Mlle Lambercier as formative of his later tastes and temperament.
Feeling comes before reasoning in Rousseau's picture of himself. He presents his sensibility as the key to his character and his writing.
Mme de Warens is the warmest and most formative relationship of his life. He portrays her as a mix of mother figure, patron and lover.
The later books darken into quarrels and suspicion. He describes disputes with Diderot, Voltaire and Hume and a growing belief that he is the target of a conspiracy.
The book invites judgment but steers it. Its self-justifying tone and gaps in fact make it as much a work of self-fashioning as of record.
Rousseau addresses the book to the last judgment. When the trumpet sounds, he says, he will present it to the Sovereign Judge and say he was what he was.
A road to Vincennes launched his fame. Reading a prize question there brought a sudden illumination that produced his First Discourse.
He values independence over security. He earns his living copying music and has success with his opera The Village Soothsayer, yet he refuses a royal pension.

books.thesis: Cut off from society, Rousseau finds a quiet happiness in the pure sense of existing.
books.summary:
Written near the end of his life, the Reveries asks what remains of a person once he is rejected by everyone and can no longer defend himself. Rousseau, convinced he has been cast out by his contemporaries, turns to examine himself without an audience.

Across ten walks he reflects on memory, botany, lying, charity and moral duty, and arrives at the experience of existing in the moment as a self-sufficient happiness, like floating on the Lake of Bienne. The work is unfinished, and its serenity sits beside real bitterness and fears of persecution, which readers have to weigh when judging its calm.
ideas: The first walk frames the book as a record of his own state of mind. Rousseau presents himself as alone in the world, outcast by his contemporaries, and makes no case for others.
Pure existence is his picture of happiness. The mind rests in the present with no desire or fear and feels only the sentiment of being.
The fifth walk, at the island in Lake Bienne, shows this happiness in practice. He drifts in a boat, watches the water and gives himself to idle reverie.
The fourth walk separates harmful deceit from harmless fiction. Rousseau holds that truthfulness is owed where someone is wronged.
Botany takes him out of self-torment. It becomes a gentle pastime, a way of attending to nature without expecting anything.
He uses episodes from his life to study his own experience. His accident with a Great Dane in the second walk asks what such events show about how he feels pain and recovery.
The peace is only partial. The tone moves between serenity and resentment, and the book is unfinished, so his sense of persecution sometimes undercuts it.
Good deeds can turn into burdens. In the sixth walk he says habit and obligation attach to them, and he values freedom from constraint above benevolence on demand.
Persecution had one benefit, he suggests in the eighth walk. It drove him inward and taught him to find contentment within himself.
The tenth walk breaks off unfinished. Written shortly before his death, it recalls his first meeting with Mme de Warens on Palm Sunday.

books.thesis: Space, time and the categories come from the mind, so knowledge cannot reach past possible experience.
books.summary:
Kant asks whether metaphysics can ever be a science. Mathematics and physics seem to give knowledge that is both necessary and informative, so how is that possible? And what happens when reason tries to go beyond experience to God, the soul and the world as a whole?

His answer is transcendental idealism. Space, time and the categories, the mind's basic concepts such as cause, are contributed by the knower, so we know appearances, not things in themselves. When reason presses past experience, it falls into illusion and contradiction. The thing in itself remains a lasting dispute, since critics doubt that Kant can say it exists and also say it cannot be known.
ideas: Kant's central question is how synthetic a priori judgments are possible. These are claims that add to our knowledge yet hold independently of experience, as in mathematics and the principles of physics.
Space and time are forms of intuition that the mind brings to experience. This is why geometry applies to everything we can perceive.
The categories make experience of objects possible. Concepts of the understanding such as causality and substance apply to all appearances, which the Transcendental Deduction argues.
We know things only as they appear to us. Kant distinguishes phenomena from noumena, things as they are in themselves, and holds that only the former can be known.
Reason falls into illusion when it overreaches. The Transcendental Dialectic shows this in attempts to prove the soul's nature, the world's beginning or God's existence from concepts alone.
On the world as a whole, reason contradicts itself. The Antinomies set out four pairs of opposed arguments, such as whether the world has a beginning, to show what happens when reason oversteps.
Kant calls his reversal a Copernican revolution. Objects must conform to the structure of our cognition and not the other way around, and by limiting knowledge he leaves room for faith.
A single subject holds experience together. The unity of apperception says the 'I think' must be able to accompany all my representations, which grounds the unity of experience.
Existence is not a real predicate, which is why Kant rejects the ontological argument for God. Adding existence to a concept does not enlarge the concept.
Knowledge needs both sensibility and understanding. Kant's slogan says thoughts without content are empty and intuitions without concepts are blind.

books.t: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
books.thesis: Morality rests on a law that reason gives itself, the categorical imperative, not on outcomes or desires.
books.summary:
Kant asks what the supreme principle of morality is, and whether duty can have a basis that does not depend on what people happen to want. He looks for a standard that binds every rational being, whatever their inclinations or circumstances.

He argues that only a good will is good without qualification, and that an action has moral worth when it is done from duty. The categorical imperative, stated in several formulations, tests maxims for universality and for respect for persons, and the will's autonomy is what grounds it. Critics ask whether the formulations amount to one test, and whether the view is too rigid when duties conflict.
ideas: Only a good will is good without qualification. Talents and happiness can be misused, Kant says, so they cannot be good in that way.
Moral worth comes from acting out of duty, not merely in line with duty or from inclination. His example is the shopkeeper who deals honestly out of self-interest.
Imperatives come in two kinds. A hypothetical imperative commands means to an end we want, while a categorical imperative commands unconditionally and is the form of moral requirement.
The Formula of Universal Law is a test for maxims. You ask whether you can will your maxim to become a universal law, and Kant applies the test to false promises and neglect of talents.
The Formula of Humanity forbids treating people merely as tools. Humanity, in yourself and in others, must always be treated as an end and never merely as a means.
Autonomy of the will means rational beings are bound by laws they give themselves. This makes dignity, not price, the mark of a person.
The kingdom of ends pictures what moral life would look like. It is a community of rational beings legislating shared laws.
Duties differ in how strict they are. Perfect duties, such as not making false promises, admit no exceptions, while imperfect duties, such as helping others, leave room for choice about when and how.
Moral philosophy must be pure and rest on reason, not on empirical anthropology. A law that binds all rational beings cannot come from observing human nature.

Freedom has to be assumed in acting. The third section argues that we must act under the idea of freedom, and Kant uses two standpoints, the sensible world and the intelligible world, to make room for morality.

books.thesis: Consciousness develops through contradiction toward absolute knowing, and self-awareness needs recognition.
books.summary:
Hegel sets out to trace how consciousness moves from the simplest claim to know something to a full understanding of itself and the world. He wants to show that knowledge, freedom and social life all grow out of one historical process.

The book follows shapes of consciousness. Each one falls into contradiction and gives way to a richer one, from sense certainty through self-consciousness, reason, spirit and religion to absolute knowing. Self-awareness, on his account, is achieved only through recognition by another self. The book is famously dense and its final stage is contested. Readers dispute whether it describes history, an individual's education or a logical structure.
ideas: Even the simplest claim to know a thing fails. Hegel starts with sense certainty and shows that it depends on universals, so it cannot hold up as immediate knowledge.
Each shape of consciousness is undone by its own standard. It tests itself, finds a contradiction and gives way to a new shape, a process Hegel calls determinate negation.
Self-consciousness needs another to recognize it. In the master and slave passage, the bondsman gains independence through labor while the master depends on him.
Stoicism, skepticism and the unhappy consciousness show self-awareness retreating inward. It seeks a perfect otherness that it cannot reach.
Freedom is realized in shared institutions. The chapter on Reason and Spirit places individuals in ethical life, culture and history, not only in the private will.
Pure inwardness and absolute freedom destroy themselves. The Beautiful Soul and the Terror of the French Revolution are Hegel's examples.
Absolute knowing is the point where spirit recognizes itself in its own history. Interpreters dispute whether this closes the system or is a philosophical standpoint.
The Preface says the true is the whole. Hegel mocks the Absolute of Schelling as a night in which all cows are black.

The search for laws behind appearances turns back on itself. In the chapters on Perception and on Force and Understanding, consciousness looks behind appearances, and this prepares the way for self-consciousness.
Recognition begins with a struggle. Before the master and slave relation, each self-consciousness risks its life to be recognized, and the one who yields becomes the bondsman.

books.t: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
books.thesis: Women seem inferior because they are denied education, and reason should guide both sexes.
books.summary:
Wollstonecraft takes on the claim that women are naturally weaker in mind and fit mainly to please men. She asks whether the faults attributed to women come from nature or from the way girls are raised.

She argues that a poor education trains women to value beauty and manners over understanding, which makes them dependent and turns them into frivolous companions. She calls for national, coeducational schooling and for women to be treated as rational beings, who would then be better mothers and citizens. Later readers note that she still accepts some traditional roles for women and is sharp in her criticism of the women of her day.
ideas: Reason is common to both sexes, so Wollstonecraft sees no basis for claiming that women are made for submission.
Women's apparent weakness is an effect of upbringing. It teaches them to cultivate charm and cunning at the expense of understanding.
Rousseau's Emile is a main target. He gives Sophie an education aimed at pleasing Emile, and Wollstonecraft rejects that picture.
Valuing women for beauty and sensibility is a kind of slavery. She says it corrupts both men and women.
Boys and girls should be educated together. She proposes a system of national, coeducational day schools where they learn together and form habits of reason and companionship.
Marriage should be a friendship between equals. Women's rational virtue, she says, would make them better mothers and more useful citizens.
Tyranny in the home and tyranny in the state are linked. Reform of women's status is bound up with the wider cause of liberty and the critique of hereditary power.
The book is a direct appeal to revolutionary France. It is dedicated to Talleyrand and urges the government to include women in its plans for national education.
Conduct books teach women the wrong lessons. Wollstonecraft attacks writers such as Fordyce and Gregory for telling women to value docility and appearances over understanding.
Women and soldiers are trained alike. Both are taught obedience and surface polish, she says, and so lose the habit of thinking for themselves.

books.thesis: Simplifying life and living deliberately free a person from labor and conformity that crowd out what matters.
books.summary:
Thoreau asks how a person should live, and what it costs to spend life earning the means of living. In 1845 he moves to a cabin by Walden Pond to test how little a person needs and what he can learn from nature.

Drawing on his two years at the pond, he describes the economy of necessities, the seasons, the pond itself and the habit of close attention. He says he went to the woods to live deliberately. He argues that most people are driven by needless possessions and borrowed opinions. Critics note that he lived near town and leaned on friends and family, and that his stance can seem privileged or self-satisfied.
ideas: Most people live lives of quiet desperation, Thoreau holds. They work to maintain possessions and a standard of living they do not need.
The cost of a thing is the amount of life exchanged for it. In the chapter on Economy he counts costs this way and shows how little shelter, clothing and food are required.
He went to the woods to live deliberately. His aim was to face only the essential facts of life and see whether he could learn what it had to teach.
Solitude is not loneliness for Thoreau. He finds companionship in nature, in reading and in his own thoughts.
Close attention makes the ordinary world worth seeing. The chapters on Sounds and The Ponds follow the pond and the seasons in detail.
Inventions such as the railroad are often improved means to unimproved ends. Thoreau distrusts progress measured by speed or commerce.
The book ends with spring and renewal. Thoreau says the sun is but a morning star, a call to wake up and keep living in new ways.
Thoreau keeps exact accounts to show how cheaply real needs can be met. In Economy he says his cabin cost a little over twenty-eight dollars.
Serious reading is a deliberate effort to stay awake. The chapter on Reading urges the study of the ancient classics in the original.
Work in The Bean-Field becomes a lesson in self-cultivation. He hoes rows of beans and calculates his profit, and the labor teaches him about cultivating himself as well as the soil.

books.thesis: Society may restrict individual liberty only to prevent harm to others.
books.summary:
Mill asks what limits society may legitimately place on the individual. He worries less about government tyranny than about the pressure of majority opinion and custom, which can crush dissent and individuality without any law at all.

He sets out what is called the harm principle. He then argues for freedom of thought and discussion, since even false opinions help test the truth, and for individuality as a condition of human progress. Opinion left unchallenged, he warns, hardens into dead dogma. His utilitarian grounding is questioned, as is the line between self-regarding and other-regarding acts, which proves hard to draw in practice.
ideas: Power over a person against his will is justified only to prevent harm to others. This is Mill's harm principle, stated for members of a civilized community.
Silencing an opinion is wrong for three reasons. It may be true, a false opinion still helps clarify the truth, and unchallenged truth becomes dead dogma.
The majority can tyrannize without law. Mill warns that its power works through social stigma and custom as well as legal penalty.
Individuality is a part of well-being. Mill thinks people should be free to try experiments in living.
Mill draws the line at conduct that affects others. Self-regarding conduct is the individual's own business, while conduct that affects others society may regulate.
The principle covers only some people. It applies to adults of developed faculties, and Mill excludes children and what he called backward societies governed by despotism for their improvement.
Liberty needs limits even on Mill's own terms. A rule against selling oneself into slavery shows a tension with his own principle.
Liberty has three spheres. They are the inward domain of conscience and opinion, the liberty of tastes and pursuits, and the freedom to unite with others for any purpose that does not harm them.
The state may require education but should not provide it. In the last chapter Mill applies his principle to cases, and holds that this avoids a single mold for all minds.
Custom can become a despotism. Mill cites China as a society that was once advanced and then frozen by conformity.

books.thesis: Johannes treats a young woman as material for aesthetic play, and the book exposes how empty that life is.
books.summary:
Presented as found papers, this work asks what an existence devoted to aesthetic pleasure looks like from the inside. Kierkegaard gives voice to the aesthetic life, where interest and enjoyment outrank commitment and ethics.

Johannes plans and carries out the seduction of Cordelia, a young woman. He works patiently on her feelings and her engagement, then loses interest once he has her. The diary form lets the reader watch his method from inside. Kierkegaard published the text within Either/Or as one side of a choice, and many read it as a critique of the aesthetic stance, not an endorsement. Its elegance keeps that reading debated.
ideas: Kierkegaard keeps Johannes at a distance. The diary is framed as papers found by an editor, and Johannes is a pseudonymous voice, not Kierkegaard's own view.
Johannes treats seduction as an art. He values the interesting over the beautiful, and the process of winning over the result.
He engineers Cordelia's sense of free choice. Studying her, he arranges meetings, letters and an engagement so that she comes to feel she freely chooses what he has planned.
The engagement is a tool, not a goal. Johannes uses it to make Cordelia break from convention, then ends it once he has what he wanted.
The aesthetic life treats feeling as an end and people as objects of interest. The account shows a life in which feeling is cultivated for its own sake.
Either/Or sets the diary against the ethical life. Judge William's letters defend ethical commitment such as marriage, so the reader is asked to weigh the two ways of life.
Readers disagree about whether the text exposes the emptiness of aestheticism or invites admiration for Johannes's skill. It also reflects Kierkegaard's broken engagement to Regine Olsen.
Edward serves as a foil. Johannes places this young suitor near Cordelia so that her attention turns toward himself by contrast.
The pursuit begins in the street. Johannes sees Cordelia, follows her, and then arranges to enter her aunt's household as a harmless visitor.
The aesthetic life is only the first of three stages. Kierkegaard later adds the ethical and the religious, so the diary shows what the aesthetic way of life lacks.

books.thesis: Happiness depends chiefly on what a person is, not on what he has or how others see him.
books.summary:
Schopenhauer takes up the old question of how to live well and asks what contributes most to a happy life. He weighs personality, possessions and reputation, and writes in the spirit of a practical guide even though his wider philosophy is pessimistic.

He divides goods into what one is, what one has and what one represents in the eyes of others, and ranks them in that order. Health, cheerfulness and a rich inner life matter most, while honor, rank and fame matter least. His advice leans toward solitude and moderation. It reflects his own temperament, so it may not suit those who find meaning in society.
ideas: Happiness has three sources, and the first is the largest. Schopenhauer sorts life's goods into what a man is, what he has and what he represents, and holds that what he is matters most.
Personality shapes happiness more than circumstance does. Health, temperament and intellect matter most because each person experiences the world through his own mind.
Wealth is useful only as protection from want and boredom. Schopenhauer advises against hoarding it or chasing more than is needed.
People give too much weight to the opinions of others. Schopenhauer argues that honor, rank and fame are poor sources of contentment.
Boredom and suffering are the two enemies of human life. A person with rich inner resources suffers less from both.
Solitude suits those with inner wealth. Sociable people, he says, tend to depend on company to fill an emptiness.
Schopenhauer treats freedom from pain, not pleasure, as the aim of life. He recommends a mild, steady approach, avoiding great hopes and fears.
Health and cheerfulness are worth more than wealth. Schopenhauer remarks that a healthy beggar is happier than a sick king.
Desires should be limited to the natural and necessary. Drawing on Epicurus, he sorts desires into natural and necessary, natural but unnecessary, and neither.
Experience changes how we read our own earlier years. The first forty years of life, he says, give the text and the next thirty the commentary.

books.t: On the Suffering of the World
books.thesis: Life is dominated by suffering and striving, so compassion, not optimism, is the fitting response.
books.summary:
Schopenhauer asks what the world is worth, and whether the common belief that life is good survives an honest look. This short collection draws on his larger work to argue that pain is the normal condition and pleasure only its temporary relief.

He holds that the world is driven by blind will, which produces endless wanting and conflict, so existence is better understood as something to be endured. He proposes compassion, ascetic denial of the will and aesthetic contemplation as partial relief. Critics find the pessimism one-sided and note that it rests on his metaphysics of will, which many reject.
ideas: Suffering is positive and pleasure is only its absence. Schopenhauer concludes that happiness is a brief pause in want.
Desire is never fully satisfied because the will is blind. He describes the will as a striving at the root of all things, and in human beings it appears as ceaseless desire.
Life swings like a pendulum between pain and boredom. As soon as want is met, boredom arrives.
Schopenhauer rejects optimism as a cruel mockery of human suffering. He calls this the worst of all possible worlds in the sense that it could not last were it worse.
Compassion follows from seeing that all beings are fellow sufferers. In his view it is the foundation of morality.
Music and other aesthetic experience offer temporary release. The will is quiet while one contemplates something without desire.
Lasting relief comes only through denial of the will to live. He links this path of asceticism to Indian and Christian thought, though he says it is rare.
The principle of individuation is the way the world divides into separate things in space and time. Schopenhauer says that seeing through it reveals that individuals are appearances of a single will.
Fear of death rests largely on a confusion about what we are. Death destroys the individual but not the will itself, which he calls the thing in itself.
Dante took the material for hell from this world. Schopenhauer observes that he then had nothing left to build heaven from.

books.thesis: Greek tragedy came from Apollonian order joined to Dionysian ecstasy, and Socratic rationalism killed it.
books.summary:
Nietzsche asks how Greek tragedy came to be and why it matters to modern culture. He wants to understand how a people so aware of suffering could produce such affirming art, and what has been lost since. Tragedy, he says, lets people face suffering and still affirm life.

He argues that tragedy blends two drives: the Apollonian love of form and illusion, and the Dionysian dissolution of the self in music and intoxication. Euripides and Socrates broke the balance with optimistic reason, and Nietzsche hopes Wagner might revive it. He later criticized the book himself, and it is often faulted for weak classical scholarship and its attachment to Wagner.
ideas: Nietzsche names two artistic forces. The Apollonian is tied to dream, form and individuation, and the Dionysian to intoxication, music and the loss of self.
Tragedy arises from the union of these forces. The chorus and music carry the Dionysian, and the stage action gives it visible shape.
The Greeks answered the terror of existence with beauty. The Olympian gods are an example, and they made life worth living.
Tragedy lets the audience feel the unity of life. It gives the joy of creation and destruction, which affirms existence in spite of suffering.
Rationalism killed tragedy, in Nietzsche's account. Euripides brought rational argument and ordinary characters onto the stage, and Socrates stands for the faith that knowledge can correct existence.
Existence is justified only as an aesthetic phenomenon. This famous line ties his view of life to art.
He hoped Wagner would revive tragic culture. In the closing sections he looks to Wagner's music drama for its rebirth, a hope he later dropped as he turned against Wagner.
The story of Silenus gives the darkest Greek view. Silenus tells King Midas that the best thing is never to be born and the second best is to die soon.
Tragedy began in ritual. Nietzsche traces it to the chorus of satyrs in Dionysian ritual, which he thinks gave the audience a sense of being part of a larger life.
Nietzsche later judged the book harshly. In 'Attempt at a Self-Criticism' he calls it badly written and heavy with Schopenhauer and Wagner, though he still defends its central questions.

books.thesis: Many ideals thought to be pure, from morals to art, have humble and psychological origins.
books.summary:
Nietzsche asks what we find when we examine high ideals with the tools of history and psychology. Written after his break from Wagner and Schopenhauer, the book tests the claim that morality, religion and art come from something beyond the human.

In aphorisms, he traces such ideals back to ordinary drives, habits and fear. He recommends a cooler, more scientific approach, and free spirits who think for themselves. The book marks a turn from romantic metaphysics to a more skeptical style. The aphoristic method scatters the argument, and some of its claims, such as those on women or race, have not aged well.
ideas: Values have a history, so philosophy should study how they arose. Nietzsche holds that there are no eternal facts or absolute truths.
Moral feelings have lowly sources. Pity and conscience can be traced to custom, utility and fear instead of to a higher source.
Metaphysical beliefs came from errors about dreams, language and cause. Now that we understand the history, we can see their origins.
Great works come from steady labor, not inspiration. Art and religion offer consolation, but Nietzsche suspects that the genius is a figure of myth.
The free spirit breaks from inherited convictions. This person sees the world with detachment, and the book is dedicated to such readers.
Nietzsche values method over discovery. He encourages a scientific, humble attitude toward knowledge.
The aphorism form is a choice with a cost. Numbered aphorisms let him try ideas from different angles but leave the argument open and sometimes inconsistent.
The book marks a break. It appeared in 1878, is dedicated to Voltaire, and separates Nietzsche from Wagner and from Schopenhauer's metaphysics.
The will is not free, so guilt and punishment need rethinking. Nietzsche argues that actions have causes.
The book kept growing. Later volumes, including Assorted Opinions and Maxims and The Wanderer and His Shadow, extend it, and the whole was gathered into a second edition in 1886.

books.thesis: Long-standing idols of philosophy and morality sound hollow when struck, and should be tested and overturned.
books.summary:
Nietzsche's late short work aims to summarize his philosophy and to ask which cherished beliefs can stand up to hard questioning. He uses the image of tapping idols with a hammer to hear whether they ring true or hollow.

He attacks the Socratic equation of reason and virtue, the idea of a true world behind appearances, the notions of free will and guilt, and Christian morality as anti-life. The subtitle is How to Philosophize with a Hammer. A short passage tells how the true world finally became a fable. The tone is polemical and compressed, and his pronouncements on race, nationality and others have drawn criticism.
ideas: Nietzsche sounds out idols with a hammer. He treats inherited beliefs as things to test and not to revere.
Socrates is a symptom of decline. By equating reason with virtue and happiness, Nietzsche says, he reflects a need to master unruly instincts.
The idea of a true world ends as a fable. In How the True World Finally Became a Fable, Nietzsche traces the idea from Plato through Christianity and Kant to its collapse.
Blame rests on four great errors. They include confusing cause and effect and imagining free will, and Nietzsche holds that these serve to assign blame and guilt.
Moralities that condemn the passions are hostile to life. In Morality as Anti-Nature he argues that the passions should be spiritualized, not condemned.
Skirmishes of an Untimely Man collects his comments on artists, writers and thinkers. It also treats the aesthetic state of intoxication as a source of creativity.
What does not kill me makes me stronger, a motto that reflects Nietzsche's emphasis on health and strength. The book is also tied to the Dionysian affirmation of life.
The book opens in a spirit of mischief and attack. Its first section is Maxims and Arrows, a set of short barbed sayings.
Moral systems that claim to improve people often work by weakening them. In The Improvers of Mankind he argues this, citing the priestly law of Manu as a case of taming.
German education neglects thinking. What the Germans Lack criticizes German culture, and he says teaching to think, speak and write has been neglected.

books.thesis: Teaism turns the plain act of drinking tea into a way of seeing beauty in imperfection and simplicity.
books.summary:
Writing in English for a Western audience around 1906, Okakura asks what tea means in Asian life and why the West misreads it. He presents tea as a philosophy and a form of aesthetic discipline that shaped Japanese art, architecture and manners.

He traces tea from medicine to drink to ideal, which he calls Teaism, and shows how Taoism and Zen shaped the tea ceremony, the tea room and flower arrangement. The central theme is an appreciation of the imperfect and the incomplete. The book is also a polite argument against Western contempt for Asia, and some readers find its picture of Japanese culture idealized.
ideas: Teaism is the worship of beauty amid ordinary life. Okakura calls it a cult founded on the adoration of the beautiful among the sordid facts of everyday existence, a way to find harmony in small acts.
Tea changed its role over time. It moved from medicine to beverage to a way of life, from China through Song and Ming practice to Japan.
Taoism and Zen shaped the tea ideal. They bring an emphasis on the relative, the empty and the spontaneous, as in the Taoist idea that usefulness lies in emptiness.
The tea room is plain and small on purpose. It holds a few people in calm, and its beauty lies in simplicity and the absence of ornament.
Imperfection is valued because the viewer completes the idea in the mind. Okakura prizes the unfinished.
The tea master uses flowers with restraint. The chapter on flowers criticizes wasteful display of cut blooms.
Okakura pleads for understanding between East and West. He also reflects on how the tea masters met death, with the story of Rikyu.
Okakura points to a Western double standard. Westerners called Japan barbarous while she practiced the quiet arts of peace but civilized once she fought on Manchurian battlefields.
Tea was prepared in three ways across three dynasties. The Tang boiled cake tea, the Song whipped powdered tea and the Ming steeped leaf tea.
Understanding art needs sympathy between viewer and work. Okakura retells the Taoist tale of the harp that only the right player could tame.

books.thesis: Philosophy offers no final answers, but its questions enlarge the mind and free it from prejudice.
books.summary:
Russell asks whether any knowledge is so certain that no reasonable person could doubt it, and what we can know about matter, truth and the world. He writes a short introduction for general readers, not a technical treatise.

He begins with appearance and reality and defends the existence of matter as the best hypothesis. He separates knowledge by acquaintance from knowledge by description, argues for universals and a priori knowledge, and closes on the value of philosophy. Later philosophers, including Russell himself, revised specific positions such as sense data and his theory of truth.
ideas: Even a table raises a problem of knowledge. Russell starts from the way a table looks different from different angles and asks what, if anything, we know about the real table behind appearances.
Matter is the simplest and best explanation of our sense data. Russell argues it cannot be proved with certainty.

Knowledge by acquaintance differs from knowledge by description. Acquaintance is direct awareness of things, such as sense data, while description gives knowledge of things through definite descriptions.
Logic and mathematics are known a priori. Russell defends this against empiricism, and against Kant's view of such knowledge as shaped by the mind.
Universals exist apart from particular things. Whiteness and resemblance are examples, and Russell says they are needed to account for general terms.
Truth is correspondence between belief and fact. Russell rejects the coherence theory as insufficient.
Philosophy is valued for its questions more than its answers. The last chapter says they free the mind from narrow ideas and bring a kind of greatness of thought.
Berkeley's idealism rests on a confusion, Russell argues. A thing being known by us does not imply that it exists only in a mind.
Induction cannot be proved by experience. Experience supports it only if it is already assumed, and Russell uses the chicken that expects food until the day its neck is wrung.
Knowledge is more than true belief. One may believe something true by luck or from a false premise, a point Russell raises in the chapter on knowledge, error and probable opinion.

books.thesis: Happiness comes from outward interest and sensible habits, not from self-absorption.
books.summary:
Russell asks why so many people in comfortable circumstances are unhappy, and what an individual can do about it. He writes a practical guide that first lays out the common causes of unhappiness and then the conditions of a satisfying life.

The first half examines causes such as competition, boredom, fatigue, envy, a sense of sin and fear of public opinion, many of which he traces to self-focus. The second half recommends zest, affection, work and impersonal interests, and a balance of effort and resignation. The advice is commonsensical and sometimes dated, and it reflects a comfortable social position.
ideas: Much unhappiness comes from habits of thought. Russell says self-absorption is among them, and a person can recognize and change such habits.
Competition as the central aim of life breeds anxiety. Russell argues for more attention to enjoyment than to winning.
A life of constant stimulation cannot bear quiet. Russell links boredom and excitement in this way.
Envy is a major cause of unhappiness. He suggests comparing oneself less with others and finding pleasure in what one has.
Fear of public opinion and a sense of sin hold people back from their own lives. He advises a more rational approach to morality.
Zest is the best mark of happiness. It is a broad interest in things and people, and affection and work provide steady satisfaction.
Effort and resignation need balancing. Russell recommends working to improve what can be changed, accepting what cannot, and widening interests so that no single loss is devastating.
Byronic unhappiness is a pose. The proud who think the world is against them are among the first causes Russell names, and he treats it as fashionable rather than a deep truth.
Worry fades when the worst is faced. Russell advises thinking through the worst that could happen until it loses its terror, which he says brings calm and clears the mind.
The happy person lives objectively. With free affections and wide interests, such a person finds happiness through contact with the world and not through self-regard.

books.t: Why I Am Not a Christian
books.thesis: The arguments for God and for Christianity's moral standing do not withstand rational scrutiny.
books.summary:
Russell asks what it means to be a Christian and whether the faith's beliefs and moral claims are justified. The title essay, a lecture from 1927, is joined here by other writings on religion, morals and freedom of thought.

He reviews the classic arguments for God, such as the first cause, natural law and design, and finds each unconvincing. He then challenges the character of Christ, the doctrine of hell and the church's effect on moral progress, and argues that fear lies behind religion. His case is rational and polemical, and critics say it overlooks more sophisticated theology and the role of religion in lived experience.
ideas: Russell tests each part of the definition of a Christian. He defines one as someone who believes in God and immortality and in Christ as the best and wisest of men, and he questions each element.
The first cause argument defeats itself. If everything needs a cause then God needs one, and the world may simply have no cause.

Natural law and design do not prove God either. The argument from natural law confuses descriptions of regularities with commands, and the argument from design does not explain the imperfect nature of the world.
Morality cannot rest on God as its source. If right and wrong are God's commands then they are arbitrary, and if not, God is not the source of morals.
Christ was not above criticism. Russell points to the teaching on hell and the cursing of the fig tree as marks of moral limits, and says other historical figures were wiser or kinder.
The church has hindered moral progress. Russell gives its views on divorce, sex and birth control as examples.
Religion rests on fear and the wish for a protector. A good world needs knowledge, kindness and courage instead.
The world's injustice does not prove a God who will set things right. Russell replies that the universe as we see it gives no ground for that inference.
Mind seems bound to the body, so personal immortality is doubtful. Memory and character change with changes in the brain.
A good life is one inspired by love and guided by knowledge. This is Russell's famous line.

books.thesis: A sudden awareness of the bare, contingent fact of existence strips away the meaning we assume things have.
books.summary:
Sartre's novel, written as the diary of Antoine Roquentin, asks what happens when a person stops taking the world for granted. Roquentin, a historian living in a provincial town, begins to feel a strange disgust at objects and at his own existence.

The nausea reveals that things exist without reason or necessity, and that human life has no given purpose. He tests escapes such as his research, other people and love, and finds them insufficient. He then glimpses a modest way forward through creating something, perhaps a book. The novel dramatizes ideas later set out in Being and Nothingness, and some readers find its conclusion thin.
ideas: The nausea starts with small things going strange. Roquentin records a growing sense that something has changed in him, and a pebble by the sea and a door handle feel uncanny to touch.
Existence has no necessity behind it. The nausea reveals contingency: things simply are there without reason, and Roquentin is superfluous like everything else.
The chestnut tree root scene is the key moment. He sees that the root has no explanation and that words and categories do not reach its bare existence.
Roles and rank hide freedom. The Self-Taught Man and the townspeople in the portrait gallery represent bad faith, hiding behind roles, humanism or social rank.
The past cannot be recovered. His historical research on the Marquis de Rollebon fails as he realizes it cannot be given the stable meaning he sought.
Perfect moments and adventure are only stories. His relationship with Anny shows that the old idea of perfect moments cannot be revived, and that adventure is imposed on life.

Creation offers a way out. A jazz song, Some of These Days, suggests escape by creation, and he decides to write something that might justify his life to others, a hint of the existential idea that meaning is made.
The novel is framed as a found diary. It is presented as a diary among Roquentin's papers, opening with a publisher's note and undated pages.
The Self-Taught Man's humanism fails in a humiliating scene. He is caught in an incident with a boy in the library and thrown out, which exposes its limits.
Roquentin names the respectable citizens salauds. In the portrait gallery they hide their contingency behind rights and duties, and at the end he leaves Bouville for Paris.

books.thesis: Science advances by bold conjectures tested against refutation. Verification never settles a theory.
books.summary:
Popper takes on the problem of demarcation: what separates genuine science from metaphysics and pseudo-science. He also faces Hume's problem of induction, since no number of observations logically proves a universal law.

His answer is falsifiability. A theory is scientific if it forbids certain outcomes and so can be shown wrong by observation. Scientists should propose risky conjectures, try hard to refute them, and keep the survivors only tentatively. The book is dense and technical. Critics such as Kuhn and Lakatos argue that real science does not follow strict falsification, since researchers often protect core theories from awkward data.
ideas: Induction cannot justify scientific laws. Finite observations never logically entail a universal statement, and Popper holds that science does not actually rely on induction.
Falsifiability marks the line between science and non-science. A theory that no possible observation could contradict is not scientific, however well it seems to fit the facts.
Science works by deductive testing. Consequences are derived from a hypothesis and checked against observation, and a failed prediction counts against the theory.
Good theories take risks. The more a theory prohibits, the more informative it is and the higher its empirical content.
Surviving tests is not proof. A theory that has survived severe tests is provisionally accepted, but corroboration is not confirmation, and the theory is never shown to be true or even probable.

Even observations are accepted by convention. Basic statements, the observations used in tests, remain open to revision, and Popper rejects the idea that science rests on a firm bedrock of experience.
Rescuing a threatened theory by ad hoc moves lowers its scientific standing. Popper sets methodological rules against evasive moves that reduce testability.
Popper keeps the psychology of invention out of logic. He separates the context of discovery from the context of justification and says the logic of knowledge concerns only the second.

Informative theories are improbable ones. Popper argues that the more content a theory has, the lower its logical probability, so aiming at highly probable theories works against aiming at informative ones.
Demarcation is not about meaning. Popper opposes the positivist view that meaningful statements must be verifiable, and says demarcation concerns scientific status.

books.thesis: Knowledge grows through bold guesses and criticism. Error is the engine of progress.
books.summary:
This collection of essays and lectures asks how human knowledge grows and why some theories deserve more trust than others. It carries Popper's philosophy of science into history, politics and the question of how reason relates to tradition.

Popper argues that we learn by proposing conjectures and trying to refute them, never by piling up confirmations. He applies the idea to Marxism, Freudian and Adlerian psychology and the history of philosophy, and he links the critical attitude to the open society. Some readers find the essays loosely connected. Others think he was unfair to Marx and Freud.
ideas: A theory that explains every case tells us nothing. Popper counts it a weakness that certain Marxist and psychoanalytic theories can explain any event.
Knowledge begins with problems, not observations. We approach the world with expectations and revise them when they clash with experience.
All learning proceeds by trial and error, from animals to scientists. The difference is that scientists consciously criticize their guesses.
The critical tradition started with the Presocratics. Popper presents them as founders of a tradition in which ideas are open to challenge by pupils and rivals.
Science aims at verisimilitude, or closeness to truth. No theory is ever known to be true.

Historicism, the belief in laws of historical destiny, is both logically flawed and politically dangerous. Popper says the course of history cannot be predicted because it depends on a growth of knowledge we cannot foresee.
Rationalism is the willingness to learn from criticism. Popper ties this attitude to tolerance and to the open society.
Risk separates Einstein from Freud and Adler. The 1919 eclipse test was a risky prediction that could have failed, while Freud's and Adler's theories were ready to absorb any case.
Theories are conjectures, not tools or definitions of essences. Popper compares instrumentalism, essentialism and his own view, and holds that theories can be tested.
The right question is how to detect error, not where claims come from. In the essay on the sources of knowledge, Popper says we should ask how errors can be eliminated.

books.thesis: Modern life has damaged private life. One can no longer live rightly within a wrongly organized society.
books.summary:
Written in exile after the Second World War, this book asks what remains of ethics and personal life when society is organized around exchange, administration and the culture industry. Its subtitle, Reflections from Damaged Life, names the condition.

Adorno writes 153 short aphorisms on marriage, gifts, intellectuals, houses, manners and art. Each shows how domination and commodity logic reach into private habits. He declines to offer a program, and the style is deliberately difficult and pessimistic. Critics find it elitist and cheerless, and some say it leaves little room for action, though admirers value its refusal to console falsely.
ideas: Wrong life cannot be lived rightly. Adorno denies that individuals can be fully good inside a society built on exploitation and conformity.
The whole is the false. Truth lies not in system or totality but in fragments and in the details that resist being absorbed.
Private life has withered into a sphere of consumption. The home, the family and friendship are shaped by market and administrative pressures.
The culture industry flattens experience. It trains people to want what they are given, which weakens independent judgment.
Gift giving has decayed into obligation and calculation. Real giving requires a spontaneity that exchange society undermines.
Intellectuals are compromised by the world they criticize. Adorno applies the same suspicion to his own position as a critical thinker.
The fragmentary form is deliberate. A smooth system would falsely suggest a reconciled world, so Adorno writes in aphorism and fragment.
The subtitle names the subject. Written in exile during the 1940s and dedicated to Max Horkheimer, the book is subtitled Reflections from Damaged Life.
Adorno attacks psychoanalysis through its exaggerations. He remarks that nothing in it is true except the exaggerations, and uses the line to criticize adjustment to a sick society.
Not being at home in one's home is part of morality. Adorno says dwelling has become impossible in the old sense.

books.thesis: A healthy society meets the soul's needs for obligation, order and belonging. Modern uprooting has starved them.
books.summary:
Written in London in 1943 for the Free French, this work asks what France and Europe would need in order to be rebuilt after the war. Weil wants to know what human beings need beyond rights, and how a society can fail those needs.

Weil starts from obligations, not rights, since rights depend on duties owed to every person. She lists needs of the soul such as order, liberty, obedience, equality, honor, security, risk, truth and, above all, roots. Uprooting through conquest, money and industrial work is the main disease, and she calls for rooted work and spiritual life. Her proposals are idiosyncratic, some critics find them authoritarian or nostalgic, and the text was left unfinished.
ideas: Obligations come before rights. A right has force only because others have a duty to respect it, and every human being is owed unconditional respect.
Weil names the needs of the soul. They include order, liberty, responsibility, equality, hierarchy, honor, punishment, freedom of opinion, security, risk, private and collective property, and truth.
Rootedness is the most important and least recognized need. It means taking an active part in a community that preserves treasures of the past and hopes for the future.
Conquest and money both uproot people. Weil sees money as destroying other motives for action.
Industrial labor uproots workers. Factory work severs them from understanding and meaning in what they do, and she urges a spiritual rethinking of manual work.
Patriotism should rest on compassion, not pride. Weil wants love of a country's fragility, and she criticizes the idolatry of the nation and the cult of power.
Truth deserves reverent attention. Weil would protect it from propaganda, and she proposes limits on the press to keep it so.
The book was a plan for rebuilding France. It was written in London in 1943 for the Free French, as a study of what a renewed France would need after the war.
The structure moves from diagnosis to remedy. It has three parts, The Needs of the Soul, Uprootedness and Rootedness.
Weil reads Hitlerism as European methods of conquest coming home. She treats it as the return to Europe of methods Europeans had used abroad, a product of the same cult of force.

books.thesis: Spiritual life comes through attention and affliction. We wait for God and cannot force a meeting.
books.summary:
This collection of letters and essays, including the Spiritual Autobiography, asks how a person oriented toward truth and the good can come to God while standing outside the church. It also asks what suffering means.

Weil argues that prayer is attention in its purest form, that school study trains this capacity, and that affliction, which combines physical pain, social degradation and a sense of abandonment, can bring a person into contact with Christ. She writes of love of neighbor as the question 'what are you going through?' and stays outside baptism by choice. Theologians still dispute her severe asceticism and unorthodox views.
ideas: Attention is the substance of prayer. It means emptying the mind and waiting, open to the truth, without grasping.
School studies train attention, even geometry. They serve spiritual growth whether or not the pupil believes.
Affliction is more than suffering. It marks the soul and body with social degradation and a feeling of being abandoned, and Weil calls it a path toward God.
Love of neighbor means giving attention to the afflicted. This treats them as real persons, which is rare and difficult.
Love of God can be implicit. It appears in love of neighbor, love of the order of the world, love of religious practices and friendship.
In the Spiritual Autobiography Weil describes being seized by Christ. She also describes her decision to stay at the threshold of the Church.
Christianity should be catholic in the original sense. Weil wants it open to the truth found in other traditions, and she worries about the church's exclusions.
She recited the Our Father in Greek each day. She describes being seized by Christ while saying George Herbert's poem Love.
Two moments shaped her religious life. She recalls a small chapel at Assisi where she was moved to kneel, and Holy Week at Solesmes.
Accepting necessity is a form of love. She sees the beauty of the world as the trace of God and necessity as matter's obedience to God.

books.thesis: Objective thought has limits. The subjective point of view cannot be fully absorbed into an impersonal one.
books.summary:
Nagel asks how a person can combine a particular, inner perspective with an objective picture of the world that includes that person. The tension runs through mind, knowledge, ethics and the meaning of life.

He argues that pushing for objectivity is valuable but leaves out something real, namely what experience is like from the inside, so reductive theories of mind fail to account for consciousness. He defends a form of realism about value and rejects pure subjectivism. He leaves several conflicts unresolved and says so. Critics find his positions on consciousness and on values mysterious and insufficiently argued.
ideas: Objectivity works by stepping back from your own point of view to a more detached one. Each step back reveals features of reality that were hidden before.

A purely physical description of the mind leaves out what experience is like from the inside. Some facts about consciousness can be grasped only from a subjective standpoint, so Nagel holds that such a description misses an essential feature of mind.
Nagel's version of the mind-body problem is that no current reduction explains how experience could arise from brain processes. He treats this as an open gap in present theories.
Reality may exceed what humans can understand, so Nagel rejects idealism. Idealism limits reality to what we can conceive, and he will not accept that limit.
Some reasons apply to everyone equally, and Nagel defends these agent-neutral reasons in ethics. He also describes a real conflict between them and the pull of personal projects and relationships.
Free will is hard to reconcile with the objective view. From outside, our actions look like events with prior causes, and Nagel leaves the difficulty open.
Detachment and personal life both make legitimate demands. Nagel concludes that a mature outlook must live with the tension between them.
The objective self is the part of us that can view ourselves as one person among others. Nagel asks how this standpoint relates to the unique 'I' that is each person's own point of view.
In the last chapters on birth, death and the meaning of life, Nagel treats absurdity as the result of the clash between the two standpoints.
Mind and body may be aspects of something more basic that we do not yet grasp. Nagel offers this as a suggestion, and he treats current reductions as inadequate.

books.thesis: Natural selection is a universal algorithm. It explains design in life, mind and culture without any designer.
books.summary:
Dennett asks what follows if Darwin's theory is true. He wants to show that evolution by natural selection is more than a biological claim, and that it reshapes how we think about meaning, mind, morality and culture.

He calls natural selection a 'universal acid' that eats through traditional concepts, and argues that design arises through mindless algorithmic steps. He champions adaptationism, defends memes as cultural replicators and attacks 'skyhooks', which claim to explain design from above.
