books.thesis: People can rationally become someone with new values. Aspiration is how we pursue what we do not yet grasp.
books.summary:
Callard takes on a puzzle. Learning to love classical music, becoming a parent or growing morally good all mean wanting something whose value you cannot yet fully see. Standard accounts of action assume we pursue what we already value, so they struggle to say how such change can be rational.

Her answer is that aspiration is a distinct kind of agency. The aspirant acts for the sake of a value she only partly grasps, guided by proxies such as teachers, and her understanding grows through the effort. A limit is that the account may be too permissive about what counts as rational. Critics also ask how it differs from ordinary learning, and her reply to L.A. Paul on transformative experience is still contested.
ideas: Aspiration is a rational process, not a leap in the dark. Callard argues that people can work toward a value they do not yet have in a way that is guided by reasons, and so the change is something an agent does.

The aspirant cannot fully see the value in advance. A person who wants to appreciate music hears little at first, and that gap between the wish and the ability is what makes the project hard to explain.
Aspiration differs from ordinary ambition. The ambitious person wants to get something she already values, while the aspirant wants to change what she values, so the goal is the growth itself.

Aspirants rely on value proxies. Because she cannot see the good directly, the aspirant borrows judgment from someone who can, a teacher or a trusted friend, and treats their guidance as a stand-in for her future understanding.
Proleptic reasons explain how action can precede understanding. Callard says the aspirant acts for reasons that are only partly hers yet, and as she practices, the reasons become fully her own.
Aspirants often act before they feel the right thing. She goes to concerts, reads and practices while still bored, which can look like pretense but is part of how the real taste is formed.

Change is gradual, so the choice can be rational. In reply to L.A. Paul's claim that transformative choices cannot be rationally made, she says the aspirant moves in small steps and is not choosing blind.

Aspiration is rarely solitary. Because the aspirant depends on others who already have the value, institutions such as schools and teachers, and relationships of apprenticeship, are central to how it works.

Moral growth is a case of aspiration. Becoming a better person involves acting justly before one fully understands justice, much as Aristotle describes habituation, and Callard treats the moral learner as an aspirant.
The self is both author and project. The subtitle names an agency of becoming, meaning that a person can take responsibility for who she is turning into, not only for what she does from fixed values.

books.thesis: Honest self-examination yields more truth than doctrine, and doubt makes for a wiser, kinder life.
books.summary:
Montaigne wrote in France during the Wars of Religion, when certainty about God, truth and virtue was getting people killed. He retired to his tower library and began testing his own judgment on whatever came to mind, from thumbs to cannibals to death.

His answer is a method, not a system. A person can only report how he thinks and lives, and that report shows human beings to be changeable, inconsistent and badly suited to dogmatism. Doubt, summed up in his motto "What do I know?", leads to tolerance and a modest life well lived. The limit is that his skepticism often defers to custom and the established order. The essays make no case for reform, so some readers find him evasive.
ideas: A person is a shifting series of moods, not a fixed character. Montaigne says he paints the passing, not the being, and finds himself different from one hour to the next, which makes him distrust any neat theory of the self.

Writing honestly about yourself counts as a study of humanity. He holds that each person carries the whole human condition, so a candid self-portrait with its faults left in teaches more than a general treatise.

Doubt is a better guide than certainty. In the long "Apology for Raymond Sebond" he piles up examples of how reason, the senses and learned authorities mislead us, and concludes that confident doctrine is mostly vanity.

Custom shapes belief far more than reason does. In "Of Cannibals" he notes that people call barbarous whatever differs from their own habits, then argues that the tortures practised in Europe's religious wars were worse than the rites he was told of.

Education should build judgment, not stock the memory. In "Of the Education of Children" he prefers a well-formed head to a well-filled one, and mocks the scholar who can quote everything and decide nothing.

Preparing for death by philosophy turns out to be less useful than living plainly. Early essays follow the Stoic line that to philosophize is to learn to die, but "Of Experience" notes that ordinary people die well without any training.

True friendship is rare and cannot be explained by qualities. His account of La Boétie in "Of Friendship" rests on a bond with no stated reason, and he sets it above family ties and ordinary affection.
Cruelty is the worst vice. In "Of Cruelty" he says he hates it more than any other fault, including in the treatment of animals, and he judges it more serious than ordinary weakness or lust.
The body and its pleasures belong to wisdom. In "Of Experience" he treats eating, sleep and health as parts of a good life, and rejects the idea that the soul gains by despising them.
Public duty should never swallow the private self. As mayor of Bordeaux he lends himself to office but keeps what he calls a back room that is entirely his own, where he stays free.

books.thesis: Modern Europe's danger is the mass man, who claims rights and comfort but refuses discipline and excellence.
books.summary:
Ortega y Gasset wrote in 1930, as Europe moved toward fascism and communism. He asks why a civilization with unprecedented wealth, science and comfort feels in crisis. His answer is that the crowds, once in the background of history, have moved to the center of public life.

"Mass man" is a type, not a class. He is found among workers and aristocrats alike, and the narrow specialist is a prime example. This person takes civilization's benefits as natural, owes nothing to the past, feels no duty, and wants his tastes to rule. The limit is that Ortega's talk of noble minorities is elitist and vague. He never says how such an elite would be chosen, so critics read him as hostile to democracy.
ideas: The mass man is a psychological type, not an economic class. Ortega finds him among the educated and the wealthy as often as among the poor, because the mark is satisfaction with oneself exactly as one is.

The crisis is the arrival of the crowd in the center of social life. Places once reserved for a few, such as theaters, hotels and public office, are now full, and Ortega treats this crowding as the opening fact of the age.
Abundance has bred ingratitude. Mass man meets the comforts of civilization as if they were natural features of the world, like air, and so never sees that they must be maintained by effort.
The scientific specialist is a new kind of learned ignorant. He knows his corner well, feels competent about everything else, and speaks with authority outside his field.
A noble life is one that sets itself demands. For Ortega, nobility means obligation and self-imposed effort, while the mass way of living means drifting with what one already is.

Mass man favors direct action over discussion. Ortega sees violence, syndicalism and fascism as ways of skipping argument, and he calls liberal democracy a rare act of generosity that grants rights even to opponents.
The modern heir is a spoiled child. Ortega's "satisfied young gentleman" inherits a world he did not build, assumes it belongs to him, and treats every limit as an insult.
Life needs a project, and the mass man has none. Ortega sees people at their best when they aim at something beyond themselves, and the crisis is a loss of direction as much as a loss of order.
The age feels high and empty at once. Ortega says people now believe they live at a greater height than any earlier period, yet no one knows where to go, so the age feels both powerful and lost.
The state is the largest risk. When bureaucracy absorbs social life, Ortega warns, the state becomes the mass man's tool, and he argues for a united Europe that rests on a common future project.

books.thesis: Treating life as possession dulls our sense of being, which we meet in presence, fidelity and participation.
books.summary:
Marcel, a French Christian existentialist, wrote against a modern world that treats people as functions and bundles of useful traits. The book joins a philosophical journal with essays on the contrast between being and having. He asks what is lost when we relate to everything, ourselves included, as something to own.

Having creates dependence, he argues. The more I possess, the more anxious I am about losing it, and the more I am defined by it. Being appears where I am present to someone or something without trying to hold it. Marcel works through concrete examples and returns to them, not through a system. The journal form is loose, and terms such as "mystery" are never sharply defined, so many readers find the book suggestive more than rigorous.
ideas: Having makes the owner a hostage. What I possess can be lost or stolen, so my peace comes to depend on it, and Marcel treats this dependence as the hidden cost of ownership.
A problem stands outside me, but a mystery includes me. Marcel separates questions I can examine from a distance from those, such as evil or love, that I cannot study without being part of them.
My body is not a tool I own. Marcel notes that I seem to have a body, yet I cannot put it down or step outside it, so the language of having starts to fail where it matters most.
Having can spread to opinions, talents and virtues. A person who holds a belief as a possession defends it like property, and this closes the mind and kills what made it living.
Hope differs from optimism. Hope does not calculate odds or demand a particular result, but trusts that reality holds more than what I can see and control.
Fidelity is more than consistency. To stay faithful to someone, even when feelings change, creates a reality that did not exist before, and it is a way of being instead of a rule followed.

Availability is the opposite of being encumbered by oneself. A person who is available can give attention and take on another's need, while a self-absorbed person has all attention tied up in his own concerns.
A person present to me differs from a person who is merely informed about me. Presence is felt as a kind of openness, and it cannot be produced by gathering facts about someone.
Love treats the other as a "thou" and not as a "he". Marcel holds that once I turn someone into an object with a list of features, I stop knowing them.
Philosophy should start from concrete experience. The journal form is a deliberate choice, because Marcel thinks the real questions come up in particular situations and cannot be settled from above.

books.thesis: America's refusal to see its own racial history harms everyone, and only clear-eyed love can change it.
books.summary:
Baldwin published these two essays in 1963, a century after emancipation and at the height of the civil rights struggle. The first is a letter to his nephew. The second recounts his boyhood in Harlem, his teenage years as a preacher, and a meeting with the Nation of Islam's leader. He asks what it costs Black and white Americans to live inside a lie about race.

He argues that white innocence is the national crime. Whites who refuse to know the past are trapped by it, and Black Americans must reject the idea of their own inferiority without answering hatred with hatred. Love, for Baldwin, is a hard demand that makes others face the truth. The limit is that his prophetic tone offers little concrete program, and critics find the appeal to love weak against economic and political structures.
ideas: Innocence is the central offence. In the letter to his nephew, Baldwin says the crime of white countrymen is that they have done harm without knowing it and without wanting to know.

Black Americans must refuse the verdict of worthlessness. He tells his nephew that the country has tried to make him believe he is inferior, and that survival means rejecting that judgment while remembering where it came from.
White Americans are also trapped. Baldwin writes that people who do not understand their history are imprisoned inside it, so racism limits the people who profit from it.
Love is a demand, not a mood. He calls on Black Americans to love whites in a way that forces them to see themselves as they are, which is a harder task than sentiment.
Harlem left few exits. In the second essay, he describes the streets as offering religion, crime or ruin to a boy with little money, and says his conversion at fourteen was partly an escape.
The church gave Baldwin power and then disappointed him. He preached for several years as a teenager, and he came to see that a Christianity serving whiteness had no moral force left to claim.

The Nation of Islam inverts white supremacy without ending it. Baldwin meets Elijah Muhammad and understands the pull of his message, yet he rejects the answer of replacing one racial hierarchy with another.
Racism is partly a refuge from white fear. Baldwin suggests that whites project onto Black people the parts of their own lives that they cannot face, which keeps both sides from freedom.

Integration into a corrupt house is not the goal. He doubts that Black Americans should want to join a nation that has not changed, and says they have a duty to help change the country's idea of itself.
The title is a warning. It draws on a spiritual that promises no more flood, but fire next time, and Baldwin presents the choice as change now or a more destructive reckoning later.

books.thesis: A justice system shows its character in how it treats the condemned, and no one is only their worst act.
books.summary:
Stevenson is a lawyer who founded the Equal Justice Initiative. The book follows his early work defending poor prisoners in Alabama, many on death row. It takes on mass incarceration: the death penalty, children sentenced to die in prison, the mentally ill locked away, and the role of race and poverty in who gets punished.

The main thread is the case of Walter McMillian, a Black man convicted of a murder in Monroeville, Alabama, on weak and pressured testimony. Stevenson argues that outcomes depend more on money, race and the quality of a lawyer than on guilt, and that mercy is a moral duty, not a favor. The book follows unusually dramatic cases and one hero's story. Critics say it underplays victims' views and the structural change needed beyond rescuing individuals.
ideas: Poverty decides outcomes more than guilt does. Stevenson argues that the opposite of poverty is justice, and shows that people without money get overworked lawyers and little investigation.
Change requires getting close to the people affected. Proximity is a core belief for Stevenson: he says moral understanding comes from standing near suffering and not from analysis at a distance.

A conviction can survive on thin, coerced testimony. In McMillian's case, the evidence came largely from a man under pressure from officials, and the book shows how that kind of testimony was accepted without scrutiny.

Monroeville's literary pride sits next to its injustice. The town was the home of the author of To Kill a Mockingbird, and Stevenson contrasts that image of fairness with how it treated a Black defendant.
Judicial override made death sentences easier. Alabama allowed judges to impose death even when the jury had recommended life, and McMillian's sentence came about this way.

Children are not small adults. Stevenson's work on juveniles sentenced to die in prison rests on the claim that young people are less culpable and more able to change, a view that influenced later court rulings.
Mental illness and trauma are often ignored at sentencing. Stevenson presents clients, including veterans and people with long histories of abuse, whose conditions were not given proper weight.
Everyone is broken, and that is the basis of mercy. Stevenson ties compassion to recognizing one's own failings, so condemning others stops looking like a clean moral act.
Wins are slow and partial, and some clients are lost. The book does not hide executions that followed failed appeals, and presents hope as something to keep up despite defeat.
The death penalty cannot fix its errors. The risk of killing an innocent person, which McMillian's years on death row show, is a main reason Stevenson opposes it.

books.thesis: Teaching that values are only feelings leaves us with no ground to resist those who engineer us.
books.summary:
Lewis began with a school English textbook that told pupils a waterfall is not really sublime, since the word only describes the speaker's feelings. He saw a quiet philosophy behind it: facts are real, values are projections. The book asks what happens to a society whose teachers believe this and raise children on it.

Schooling must train feelings to fit what is admirable, or it produces people with intellect and appetite but no moral core. The basic values he calls the Tao cannot be proved from outside, and every rival ethic borrows from it. Once they are explained away, whoever shapes the next generation acts on impulse, and humanity becomes raw material. Critics doubt the Tao is as uniform across cultures as Lewis claims, and his handling of the is-ought problem is brief.
ideas: A school textbook can do more damage than a philosophical treatise. Lewis opens with an English primer, which he calls The Green Book, because its authors teach children that value words describe only the speaker's feelings, and children absorb that without ever hearing an argument for it.

Calling a waterfall sublime is a claim about the waterfall. Lewis recalls the story of two tourists, one who calls it sublime and one who calls it pretty, and holds that one reaction fits the object and the other does not.

Good education trains the emotions to match reality. Lewis says older thinkers such as Plato and Aristotle wanted pupils to like and dislike the right things, while the modern aim is to inoculate them against feeling anything unearned.

Modern schooling produces what Lewis calls men without chests. The chest is the trained sentiment that lets reason command appetite, and societies that remove it still demand courage and enterprise from people they have taught to mock honour.

No value can be derived from facts about instinct or survival alone. Every such attempt already assumes that survival or instinct is worth obeying, so Lewis concludes that a value always enters through some prior judgment that cannot itself be proved.

The Tao is Lewis's name for a body of basic values found across many cultures. It includes duties to parents and children, honesty, mercy and justice, and an appendix gathers sayings from ancient traditions to show how widely they recur.
Debunking cannot go on for ever. Lewis argues that to see through everything is the same as seeing nothing, because a window is useful only when there is something solid beyond it.

Rival ideologies are fragments of the Tao that have broken away and begun to claim the whole. A reformer who sets out to overthrow all received values usually keeps one, such as the welfare of the species, and exempts it from the doubt applied to the rest.

Man's power over Nature turns out to be the power of some men over other men. Lewis points to inventions like the aeroplane, the wireless and contraception, where the later generation is always the one being acted upon by the earlier one.

The final conditioners are the least free people of all. Having explained away every standard, they have no reason to shape others in any one way rather than another, so their choices rest on impulse, and that is the sense in which man is abolished.

books.thesis: Mindfulness is the habit of noticing new things. It needs no meditation, and mindlessness is the default.
books.summary:
Langer starts from a simple observation: much of ordinary life runs on autopilot. We take in information once, file it under a category, and then act on the category rather than the situation in front of us. She asks what this costs in learning, health and work, and whether it can be reversed.

Her mindfulness is not meditation but active attention: drawing new distinctions, staying open to context and holding more than one view. She backs it with field experiments, including ones on choice among nursing home residents. She claims that stress and many limits we accept come from fixed mental sets. Several classic studies were small, her broader health claims are suggestive rather than settled, and her sense of the word differs from the meditative one.
ideas: Langer's mindfulness has little to do with meditation. She defines it as the active drawing of novel distinctions, which keeps a person sensitive to context and aware that the same thing can look different from another angle.

Mindlessness is often learned from a single exposure. She calls this a premature cognitive commitment: we accept information without thinking of alternatives, and later the idea feels fixed and obvious.
Categories help us cope and then blind us. Once we label a person or a problem, we respond to the label and stop looking, and the same label can hide the detail that would change our response.

Practice can make a skill automatic and so make it blind. When a task is overlearned, people stop attending to it, and Langer suggests that deliberately varying the way you do things keeps attention alive.

People often accept a reason without checking whether it is one. In a well-known study of line-jumping at a copy machine, requests that included any "because" tended to be granted, even when the reason said nothing.

Teaching facts as absolute truths breeds mindlessness in pupils. Langer reports that learning material in conditional terms, as how something could be, leaves people better able to use it later in new ways.

A focus on outcomes can crowd out the doing. Langer argues that people who worry about whether they will succeed attend less to the task itself, while those who concentrate on how they are doing it perform and feel better.
Stress comes from the meaning we assign to an event more than from the event. She argues that a mindless judgment of threat can be loosened by looking for other readings of the same situation.
Choice and responsibility have real effects on health. In her nursing home study, residents who were given control over small decisions and a plant to care for fared better than those who were not.
Certainty is a comfort that costs us flexibility. Langer encourages a stance in which answers are held as true for now and in some context, so that surprises become information instead of threats.

books.thesis: Statecraft is a discipline: a ruler who masters economy, spies and strength secures his people's welfare.
books.summary:
The Arthashastra is a manual of statecraft in fifteen books, attributed to Kautilya, the minister traditionally linked with Chandragupta Maurya. It asks how a ruler can win territory, hold it and make it prosper while rivals, corrupt officials and rebellion threaten. It treats this as a craft with rules, not a branch of moral instruction.

Its answer is a thorough system. The state has seven parts, officials are watched, taxes are collected by design, and superintendents run much of the economy. Foreign policy follows options chosen by relative strength, spies are everywhere, and the king must discipline himself first. Scholars dispute authorship and date, since the text looks compiled over time. The label Indian Machiavelli also misleads, because the text ties power to the people's welfare and to dharma.
ideas: The state is treated as a body of seven parts. The king, ministers, countryside, fort, treasury, army and ally each have a role, and a weakness in any one of them endangers the rest.

The king's welfare is bound up with his subjects' welfare. The text says his happiness lies in theirs, and it prescribes relief in times of famine, so the ruler's own interest argues for caring for the people.

Without a strong ruler the strong eat the weak. The idea called matsya nyaya, the law of the fishes, is the book's argument for enforced justice and for punishment (danda) as the thing that holds society together.
A neighbouring state is a natural rival, and the state beyond it a natural friend. This circle of states, the mandala, gives the king a map for choosing alliances and finding the next target.

Foreign policy is a choice among six measures and depends on relative strength. Peace, war, waiting, marching, seeking shelter and a double policy each suit a particular balance of power, and the weaker king is told to avoid unwinnable fights.
Wealth is the foundation of everything else. A full treasury pays the army and the army secures the land, so the book spends a great deal of its length on revenue, mines, forests and trade.
Espionage is built into the state. The text describes agents posing as ascetics, merchants and students, and it advises testing ministers with covert temptations before trusting them with power.

Officials are assumed to be corruptible, and the system is designed around that. Kautilya lists many forms of embezzlement and sets up audits, rotation and informers because he expects the treasury to leak.

The state takes an active role in the economy. Superintendents oversee agriculture, markets, mines, weights and measures, and even ships and animals, which makes the ruler more of a manager than a distant lord.
Self-mastery is the king's first task. His daily schedule is laid out in detail, he must control his senses and temper, and he must guard against plots from within his own family.

books.thesis: The Soviet camp system was not one tyrant's aberration. It was a machine run by ordinary people.
books.summary:
Solzhenitsyn set out to document the Soviet network of prisons and labour camps, which the state denied and many citizens preferred not to see. He had served eight years in it himself. The book asks how a vast system of arrest and forced labour could grow, who kept it running, and why so little was said.

He calls it an experiment in literary investigation, built from his own experience and the testimony of many prisoners. He argues that the system began under Lenin, not Stalin, that ideology gave persecutors a clear conscience, and that the camps tested the souls inside. His figures for the dead are much higher than most historians accept, some accounts rest on secondhand memory, and his portrait of Lenin is disputed. The central picture is widely corroborated.
ideas: The camps were a system with its own geography. Solzhenitsyn calls it the Archipelago because it lay across the country in scattered islands, linked by transports, and its prisoners formed an unseen nation.
He traces the terror to Lenin's time and refuses to blame only Stalin. Camps, hostages and show trials appear in the early years after the revolution, which he presents as an unbroken line.
Arrests followed the system's needs more than guilt. The catch-all Article 58 let almost any act or word be called counter-revolutionary, and people were swept up to fill planned numbers.

Interrogation is described as a method for producing confessions and not for finding truth. Sleeplessness, threats and exhaustion break people, and Solzhenitsyn insists on understanding those who signed instead of condemning them.

Shock and passivity helped the arrests proceed. Victims often assumed their own case was a mistake while the system was correct, and he suggests that this habit of compliance made mass arrest far easier than resistance would have.
Ideology gave the persecutors a clear conscience. He contrasts Shakespeare's villains, who feared their own deeds, with men who could call cruelty progress and thus kill without feeling guilt.

The line between good and evil runs through every human heart. He says this after reflecting on his own conduct as an officer, and it is why he does not treat guards and interrogators as a separate species.

Prison could be a place where conscience grew. In the section on the soul he describes how deprivation stripped away his old certainties, and he writes of camp as a moral education for some who endured it.
Camp hierarchies rewarded the wrong people. Common criminals were favoured over political prisoners, and prisoners who took soft jobs close to the administration were the ones most likely to survive.

A system that is never judged is able to return. Solzhenitsyn laments that nothing like the Nuremberg trials took place in the USSR, and he treats the book itself as the substitute: a record assembled from many voices.

books.thesis: Education is the choice of what to pay attention to, and that choice shapes how you live.
books.summary:
This Is Water began as a commencement speech given at Kenyon College in 2005 and was printed in 2009. Wallace asks what a liberal arts education is for once the diploma is in hand and a long ordinary adult life begins, with its commutes, queues, work and fatigue.

His answer is that real learning is control over how and what you think. We are built to see the world as centred on ourselves, and the daily grind worsens that. With effort, we can choose other readings of the people around us. He adds that everyone worships something, and the usual objects, such as money or looks, wear us down. He presents himself as no wise elder and admits the discipline is hard. The speech is anecdotal and says little about cases where frustration is justified. Some find its advice thin next to its fame.
ideas: Real education is the freedom to choose what you attend to. Wallace says learning how to think means exercising some control over how and what you think, which is more practical than the usual talk of critical thinking.
The most important realities are the ones nobody says aloud. He opens with a story of two young fish who are asked by an older fish how the water is, and one asks what water is.
Each of us is hard-wired to feel like the centre of the universe. Everything you perceive and feel is right in front of you, so your own needs seem urgent and everyone else's seem to be in your way.
Adult frustration is concentrated in dull places. He describes a tired shopper in a packed supermarket after work, because that is where the choice about attention gets made.
You can deliberately try other explanations for what annoys you. The person ahead of you may be having a worse day than you, and Wallace says that trying such stories is a practice, not proof.
Everyone worships something, and the only choice is what. He names money, beauty, intellect and power, and says each one eats you alive in its own way if it becomes the main thing you serve.
The freedom he cares about is plain and daily. It means attention, awareness and discipline, and being able to care for other people and sacrifice for them over and over in small unglamorous ways.

Intellect alone can trap a person in their own head. He warns that a mind lost in abstraction can become the enemy, and says a lot of clever people live on a constant, low sense of having lost something large.
Awareness has to be renewed every day, because the default returns. He says this takes effort and the work is never finished, and the stakes show up in the way you live day in and day out.

The speaker disclaims authority. Wallace says he is not the wise old fish and that the message is about life before death, which he suggests is the real subject that a liberal arts degree is supposed to prepare you for.

questions: Why do people stay in relationships they know are bad?
Why do people stay in toxic relationships?
Why do I want something less once I get it?

tensions.q: Is narcissism a wound or a fortress?
a: A developmental arrest. Respond with empathy.
tensions.pa: If empathy is the treatment, why do so many narcissistic patients turn the therapist's attunement into more admiration to feed on? Kernberg's clinical point is that unchallenged grandiosity tends to grow, not heal.
tensions.pb: Confrontation assumes the person can survive the shame it triggers. Kohut's answer is that for a fragile self, confrontation repeats the original injury, and people simply leave.

tensions.q: After the silence, faith or revolt?
tensions.pa: Camus asks what entitles you to the leap. If the reason is that the silence is unbearable, the leap answers your need, not the world.
tensions.pb: Kierkegaard would ask whether revolt rests on any more evidence than faith does. Lucid defiance is also a stance chosen without proof, just a darker one.

tensions.q: Should you fear the time after you die?
a: No more than the time before you were born.
b: Yes, because it takes what you would have had.
tensions.pa: Nagel: you couldn't have been born much earlier and still be you, but you could have lived longer. From where you stand, the two eternities aren't symmetrical.
tensions.pb: On the deprivation view, every death is a loss, even at 110. If no amount of life would ever be enough, the badness of death may say more about wanting than about death.

tensions.pa: If meaning is found, where is it before you find it? Sartre would say that calling your choice a discovery is a way of not owning it.
tensions.pb: If meaning is simply made, a torturer's chosen project is as meaningful as a caregiver's. Most people don't experience meaning as arbitrary, and Frankl takes that experience seriously.

tensions.q: Must a self be a story?
b: No. Some lives are episodic, and fine.
tensions.pa: Strawson's challenge: many people live well without a life story, and the pressure to have one turns every event into a plot point. Does your story fit you, or do you fit your story?
tensions.pb: Even 'episodic' people answer 'who are you?' with something story-shaped. And the link between redemption narratives and well-being is hard to explain if narrative doesn't matter.

tensions.q: Did Milgram show obedience or belief?
b: People followed a cause they identified with.
tensions.pa: When the experimenter gave a direct order ('You have no other choice'), almost everyone refused. Pure obedience predicts the opposite.
tensions.pb: Belief in a cause doesn't explain the visible distress: the sweating, the nervous laughter, the protests. Many participants seemed to go on against their own judgment, not because of it.

quotes.q: That it will never come again is what makes life so sweet.
quotes.n: Scarcity as the source of sweetness. Time-horizon research reaches the same point by experiment.

quotes.q: I think where I am not, therefore I am where I do not think. I am not whenever I am the plaything of my thought; I think of what I am where I do not think to think.
quotes.n: A knot: the “I” that thinks and the “I” that is occupy different places. We act from rooms we never consult.

quotes.q: To dare is to lose one's footing momentarily. Not to dare is to lose oneself.
quotes.n: The cost of risk is momentary and visible; the cost of avoiding it is slow and invisible. That asymmetry is why we misjudge both.

quotes.q: People know what they want because they know what other people want.
quotes.n: Desire doesn't arrive pre-formed; it is calibrated by watching others. “I know what I want” can simply mean “I haven't noticed whom I'm copying.”

quotes.q: We are what we pretend to be, so we must be careful about what we pretend to be.
quotes.n: A warning about role-play: pretence trains. The costume becomes a habit, and the habit becomes the person.

quotes.q: There are two ways to be fooled. One is to believe what isn't true; the other is to refuse to believe what is true.
quotes.n: Credulity and cynicism are the same failure of attention. The cynic mistakes refusal for insight.

quotes.q: Everybody is identical in their secret unspoken belief that way deep down they are different from everyone else.
quotes.n: Uniqueness is the most widely shared belief. It makes everyone a little private and a little lonely, each assuming the others are more connected.

quotes.q: If anyone tells you that a certain person speaks ill of you, do not make excuses about what is said of you but answer, "He was ignorant of my other faults, else he would not have mentioned these alone.
quotes.n: A reply that defuses an insult by raising the number of true criticisms. It works because a secure self has nothing in particular to protect.

quotes.q: Artists are people driven by the tension between the desire to communicate and the desire to hide.
quotes.n: Expression and concealment are one gesture. A work, like a self, is a way of being found while staying safe, which is why the best of it carries a trace of hiding.

quotes.q: On an incredibly simplistic level, you can think of depression as occurring when your cortex thinks an abstract thought and manages to convince the rest of the brain that this is as real as a physical stressor.
quotes.n: Depression as a story-induced stress response: a brain built for lions answers an abstract thought as if it were a physical threat.

quotes.q: Pleasure is never as pleasant as we expected it to be and pain is always more painful. The pain in the world always outweighs the pleasure. If you don't believe it, compare the respective feelings of two animals, one of which is eating the other.
quotes.n: His eater-and-eaten test is deliberately brutal: compare satisfaction in the one with pain in the other. Pleasure is faint, pain is sharp, and pessimism is an argument from asymmetry.

quotes.q: Man only likes to count his troubles; he doesn't calculate his happiness.
quotes.n: We keep an itemised ledger of grievances and none of gifts. The twist isn't a miscount; it's a preference.

quotes.q: We never love anyone. What we love is the idea we have of someone. It's our own concept—our own selves—that we love.
quotes.n: A person you love is partly a character you wrote. That explains the intensity, and the grief when they step out of the script: you are mourning a collaborator who never agreed to the part.

quotes.q: Originality is being different from oneself, not others.
quotes.n: Novelty is measured against the self, not against the neighbours. That is why it can't be faked by contrast.

quotes.q: We all desire to be understood, but no one enjoys being obvious.
quotes.n: Wanting to be understood and wanting to stay unpredictable pull against each other. We want to be known without being solved.

quotes.q: We learn from history that we do not learn from history.
quotes.n: History's lessons become visible only afterward and from outside, exactly when they stop being useful to the people inside the events.

quotes.q: Good men and bad men alike are capable of weakness. The difference is simply that a bad man will be proud all his life of one good deed - while an honest man is hardly aware of his good acts, but remembers a single sin for years on end.
quotes.n: Moral self-assessment is asymmetric: the bad remember one good act, the good remember one sin. The calibration of your conscience says more than your record.

quotes.q: What loneliness is more lonely than distrust?
quotes.n: Distrust isolates by design, because it keeps every connection permanently under audit.

quotes.q: what has happened to us has happened to everyone or only us; if to everyone, then it's no novelty, and if only to us, then it won't be understood.
quotes.n: A trap in the logic of sharing pain: if it is common it feels trivial, and if it is rare it feels unshareable. Either way it goes unsaid.

quotes.q: He soon felt that the fulfillment of his desires gave him only one grain of the mountain of happiness he had expected. This fulfillment showed him the eternal error men make in imagining that their happiness depends on the realization of their desires.
quotes.n: The mistake isn't wanting too much; it's forecasting. We picture a goal as a place we will live in, when it is an event we will pass through.

quotes.q: To increase desires to an unbearable level whilst making the fulfillment of them more and more inaccessible: this was the single principle upon which Western society was based.
quotes.n: A diagnosis of consumer economies: keep wanting high and satisfaction out of reach, and you have a stable market and an unstable person.

quotes.q: Man is not what he thinks he is, he is what he hides.
quotes.n: What we conceal is steadier than what we show, because it is the part that never has to be performed. Character as the shape of our avoidances.

quotes.q: If only we could see in advance all the harm that can come from the good we think we are doing.
quotes.n: We take credit for good intentions as though they came with foresight of their side-effects. Moral certainty is partly a forecasting failure.
quotes.s: Six Characters in Search of an Author

quotes.q: Idealism increases in direct proportion to one’s distance from the problem.
quotes.n: Principles are cheapest at a distance. Nobody who has to do the work gets to keep a position clean, so distance is what makes a position feel pure.

quotes.q: When we ask for advice, we are usually looking for an accomplice
quotes.n: Asking for advice is often a request for ratification. We have decided; we want someone to share the cost if it goes wrong.

quotes.q: I was not a hypocrite, with one real face and several false ones. I had several faces because I was young and didn't know who I was or wanted to be.
quotes.n: Multiplicity can be immaturity rather than hypocrisy. A hypocrite has a real face to hide; a young person doesn't yet.

quotes.q: Losing hope is not so bad. There's something worse: losing hope and hiding it from yourself.
quotes.n: Despair has two layers: the hopelessness, and the effort to look as though you don't have it. The second layer keeps the first from ever being treated.

quotes.q: The only lies for which we are truly punished are those we tell ourselves.
quotes.n: Other people's lies get found out; ours don't, because the auditor is the author. The bill arrives later, as a life built on a false premise.

quotes.q: There is no other way of guarding against adulation, than to make people understand that they will not offend you by speaking the truth. On the other hand, when everyone feels at liberty to tell you the truth, they will be apt to be lacking in respect to you.
quotes.n: Power degrades information: people tell the powerful what pleases them, so honesty has to be made safe at some cost to deference.

quotes.q: Human beings are so made that the ones who do the crushing feel nothing; it is the person crushed who feels what is happening. Unless one has placed oneself on the side of the oppressed, to feel with them, one cannot understand.
quotes.n: The strong don't need to track the weak, so they don't. Understanding here is a matter of position, not intelligence: you learn it only by standing somewhere you would rather not.

quotes.q: A value is like a fax machine: it’s not much use if you’re the only one who has one.
quotes.n: Many quarrels that look like disagreements about values are disagreements about which game is being played. The question about the game comes before any move.

quotes.q: Nothing is so difficult as not deceiving oneself.
quotes.n: The easiest person to deceive is the one doing the checking. Honesty with yourself fails by design, which is why it needs outside friction.

quotes.q: To be without some of the things you want is an indispensable part of happiness.
quotes.n: Happiness needs something unmet, not as a flaw but as a function. A satisfied want disappears; a pending one gives life a direction.

quotes.q: A great many people think they are thinking when they are merely rearranging their prejudices.
quotes.n: Thinking feels the same whether you are reasoning or rearranging. The feeling of thought says nothing about its quality.

quotes.q: I don't feel that it is necessary to know exactly what I am. The main interest in life and work is to become someone else that you were not in the beginning.
quotes.n: It turns identity from something to discover into something to work on. The question moves from “who am I?” to “who could I stop being?”

quotes.q: ...if you are not like everybody else, then you are abnormal, if you are abnormal , then you are sick. These three categories, not being like everybody else, not being normal and being sick are in fact very different but have been reduced to the same thing
quotes.n: Three words that sound independent, different, normal, sick, get slid onto a single scale. A category is most powerful when it feels like a description.

quotes.q: It is in the character of very few men to honor without envy a friend who has prospered.
quotes.n: Generosity toward a friend's success is a harder test of friendship than loyalty in their failure.

quotes.q: There is strong shadow where there is much light.
quotes.n: A cousin of the shadow idea: the brighter the self-image, the more it has to leave in the dark.

quotes.q: Those who do not move, do not notice their chains.
quotes.n: Constraint is felt only when tested. A comfortable system can be indistinguishable from freedom until someone tries to leave it.

quotes.q: Before mass leaders seize the power to fit reality to their lies, their propaganda is marked by its extreme contempt for facts as such, for in their opinion fact depends entirely on the power of man who can fabricate it.
quotes.n: Propaganda of this kind isn't aimed at making people believe falsehoods. It makes truth feel optional, until the public can no longer tell whether the question matters.

quotes.q: It is not so much the kind of person a man is as the kind of situation in which he finds himself that determines how he will act.
quotes.n: We explain our own behaviour by circumstance and other people's by character. That is why this finding is easy to accept about humanity and hard to accept about yourself.

quotes.q: In his younger days a man dreams of possessing the heart of the woman whom he loves; later, the feeling that he possesses the heart of a woman may be enough to make him fall in love with her.
quotes.n: The pleasure migrates from the person to the sense of having them. That is the point where love can carry on without noticing the person at all.

quotes.q: It's very hard, for most of us to tolerate being loved.
quotes.n: To be loved is to be known beyond what you believe in about yourself. Tolerating it means tolerating a self you doubt exists.

quotes.q: No man chooses evil because it is evil; he just mistakes it for happiness, the good he seeks.
quotes.n: Evil rarely announces itself. People pursue what looks good from where they stand, so moral education is mostly training of perception.

quotes.q: your handwriting. the way you walk. which china pattern you choose. it's all giving you away. everything you do shows your hand. everything is a self portrait. everything is a diary.
quotes.n: What you do without noticing is the most honest autobiography. Self-presentation is edited; handwriting isn't.

quotes.q: The struggle itself towards the heights is enough to fill a man's heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.
quotes.n: The sentence is a conclusion, not a mood. After refusing both hope and suicide, only the effort itself remains, and he argues that is enough.

quotes.q: Man is least himself when he talks in his own person. Give him a mask, and he will tell you the truth.
quotes.n: A mask lowers the cost of saying things. The persona isn't always the opposite of honesty; sometimes it is the precondition.

quotes.q: You know you have loved someone when you have glimpsed in them that which is too beautiful to die.
quotes.n: Love may be the one place where mortality counts as an objection. Seeing something unfit to end is a quiet argument against decay.

quotes.q: The oppressed will always believe the worst about themselves.
quotes.n: Being described by the dominant becomes a voice inside the described. Oppression is finished when the verdict is delivered from within.

quotes.q: Emotion, which is suffering, ceases to be suffering as soon as we form a clear and precise picture of it.
quotes.n: Clarity as a kind of loosening: to name a feeling exactly is to stop being merely moved by it. Modern emotion research gives this a mechanism.

quotes.q: Knowing how to be solitary is central to the art of loving. When we can be alone, we can be with others without using them as a means of escape.
quotes.n: Dependence as use: someone who can't be alone treats the other person as a way out of themselves.

quotes.q: The fact that life has no meaning is a reason to live --moreover, the only one.
quotes.n: It turns despair from a verdict into a premise. If life came with a fixed purpose, living would be compliance; without one, it can only be a choice.

quotes.q: I wonder how many people I've looked at all my life and never seen.
quotes.n: To be seen you have to be looked at, and we mostly look at people as functions. A confession about how much of other people goes unseen.

quotes.q: Depression is the inability to construct a future.
quotes.n: A reading of depression as a loss of tense, not just of mood. When the future can no longer be built, the present has nothing to lead to.

quotes.q: Nothing is more desirable than to be released from an affliction, but nothing is more frightening than to be divested of a crutch.
quotes.n: A symptom can be what we hold on to when a cure would remove our excuse. Relief and fear arrive together because the problem was also a shelter.

quotes.q: It is not hard to admit that you were wrong, but very hard to admit that you are wrong.
quotes.n: Admitting an old error is cheap, because the self that made it is gone. Admitting a current one means the instrument you are thinking with is faulty.

quotes.q: Nothing thwarts happiness so much as the memory of happiness.
quotes.n: Memory competes with the present. Remembered happiness becomes a standard the present can never meet.

quotes.q: The opposite of courage in our society is not cowardice, it's conformity.
quotes.n: The enemy isn't fear but the comfort of agreement. Cowardice at least knows it is cowardice; conformity has no such alarm.

quotes.q:
All that is gold does not glitter,
Not all those who wander are lost;
The old that is strong does not wither,
Deep roots are not reached by the frost.
From the ashes a fire shall be woken,
A light from the shadows shall spring;
Renewed shall be blade that was broken,
The crownless again shall be king.

Tis true my form is something odd
But blaming me is blaming God
Could I create myself anew
I would not fail in pleasing you.
If I could reach from pole to pole
Or grasp the ocean with a span
I would be measured by the soul
The mind's the standard of the man.

Civilized people must, I believe, satisfy the following criteria:
1) They respect human beings as individuals and are therefore always tolerant, gentle, courteous and amenable ... They do not create scenes over a hammer or a mislaid eraser; they do not make you feel they are conferring a great benefit on you when they live with you, and they don't make a scandal when they leave. (...)
2) They have compassion for other people besides beggars and cats. Their hearts suffer the pain of what is hidden to the naked eye. (...)
3) They respect other people's property, and therefore pay their debts.
4) They are not devious, and they fear lies as they fear fire. They don't tell lies even in the most trivial matters. To lie to someone is to insult them, and the liar is diminished in the eyes of the person he lies to. Civilized people don't put on airs; they behave in the street as they would at home, they don't show off to impress their juniors. (...)
5) They don't run themselves down in order to provoke the sympathy of others. They don't play on other people's heartstrings to be sighed over and cosseted ... that sort of thing is just cheap striving for effects, it's vulgar, old hat and false. (...)
6) They are not vain. They don't waste time with the fake jewellery of hobnobbing with celebrities, being permitted to shake the hand of a drunken [judicial orator], the exaggerated bonhomie of the first person they meet at the Salon, being the life and soul of the bar ... They regard prases like 'I am a representative of the Press!!' -- the sort of thing one only hears from [very minor journalists] -- as absurd. If they have done a brass farthing's work they don't pass it off as if it were 100 roubles' by swanking about with their portfolios, and they don't boast of being able to gain admission to places other people aren't allowed in (...) True talent always sits in the shade, mingles with the crowd, avoids the limelight ... As Krylov said, the empty barrel makes more noise than the full one. (...)
7) If they do possess talent, they value it ... They take pride in it ... they know they have a responsibility to exert a civilizing influence on [others] rather than aimlessly hanging out with them. And they are fastidious in their habits. (...)
8) They work at developing their aesthetic sensibility ... Civilized people don't simply obey their baser instincts ... they require mens sana in corpore sano.
And so on. That's what civilized people are like ... Reading Pickwick and learning a speech from Faust by heart is not enough if your aim is to become a truly civilized person and not to sink below the level of your surroundings.
[From a letter to Nikolay Chekhov, March 1886]
Education is the ability to listen to almost anything without losing your temper or your self-confidence.
Never forget that everything Hitler did in Germany was legal.
The reasonable man adapts himself to the world: the unreasonable one persists in trying to adapt the world to himself. Therefore all progress depends on the unreasonable man.

Do not stand at my grave and weep,
I am not there, I do not sleep.
I am in a thousand winds that blow,
I am the softly falling snow.
I am the gentle showers of rain,
I am the fields of ripening grain.
I am in the morning hush,
I am in the graceful rush
Of beautiful birds in circling flight,
I am the starshine of the night.
I am in the flowers that bloom,
I am in a quiet room.
I am in the birds that sing,
I am in each lovely thing.
Do not stand at my grave bereft
I am not there. I have not left.
All generalizations are dangerous, even this one.

The worst illiterate is the political illiterate, he doesn’t hear, doesn’t speak, nor participates in the political events. He doesn’t know the cost of life, the price of the bean, of the fish, of the flour, of the rent, of the shoes and of the medicine, all depends on political decisions. The political illiterate is so stupid that he is proud and swells his chest saying that he hates politics. The imbecile doesn’t know that, from his political ignorance is born the prostitute, the abandoned child, and the worst thieves of all, the bad politician, corrupted and flunky of the national and multinational companies.

First of all, they came to take the gypsies
and I was happy because they pilfered.
Then they came to take the Jews and I said nothing,
because they were unpleasant to me.
Then they came to take homosexuals,
and I was relieved, because they were annoying me.
Then they came to take the Communists,
and I said nothing because I was not a Communist.
One day they came to take me,
and there was nobody left to protest.
Bertold Brecht, inspired by Emil Gustav Friedrich Martin Niemöller
When I was young I thought money was the most important thing in life, now that I'm old - I know it is!
Morality is simply the attitude we adopt towards people we personally dislike.
The holy grail is to spend less time making the picture than it takes people to look at it.
People seem to think if they dress like a revolutionary they don`t actually have to behave like one.
Anyone who believes in capital punishment should be shot
Nobody ever listened to me until they didn't know who I was.
Remember – it’s always easier to get forgiveness than permission
Knowledge, like air, is vital to life. Like air, no one should be denied it.
I don't think that you have any insight whatsoever into your capacity for good until you have some well-developed insight into your capacity for evil.

Women select men. That makes them nature, because nature is what selects. And you can say "Well it's only symbolic that women are nature", it's like no, it's not just symbolic. The woman is the gatekeeper to reproductive success. And you can't get more like nature than that, in fact it's the very definition of nature.
You don't get to choose not to pay a price, you only get to choose which price you pay

The television is 'real'. It is immediate, it has dimension. It tells you what to think and blasts it in. It must be right. It seems so right. It rushes you on so quickly to its own conclusions your mind hasn't time to protest, 'What nonsense!'.
Once you label me you negate me.

A fire broke out backstage in a theatre. The clown came out to warn the public; they thought it was a joke and applauded. He repeated it; the acclaim was even greater. I think that's just how the world will come to an end: to general applause from wits who believe it's a joke.
Many of us pursue pleasure with such breathless haste that we hurry past it.

No matter how old you are now. You are never too young or too old for success or going after what you want. Here’s a short list of people who accomplished great things at different ages
1) Helen Keller, at the age of 19 months, became deaf and blind. But that didn’t stop her. She was the first deaf and blind person to earn a Bachelor of Arts degree.
2) Mozart was already competent on keyboard and violin; he composed from the age of 5.
3) Shirley Temple was 6 when she became a movie star on “Bright Eyes.”
4) Anne Frank was 12 when she wrote the diary of Anne Frank.
5) Magnus Carlsen became a chess Grandmaster at the age of 13.
6) Nadia Comăneci was a gymnast from Romania that scored seven perfect 10.0 and won three gold medals at the Olympics at age 14.
7) Tenzin Gyatso was formally recognized as the 14th Dalai Lama in November 1950, at the age of 15.
8) Pele, a soccer superstar, was 17 years old when he won the world cup in 1958 with Brazil.
9) Elvis was a superstar by age 19.
10) John Lennon was 20 years and Paul Mcartney was 18 when the Beatles had their first concert in 1961.
11) Jesse Owens was 22 when he won 4 gold medals in Berlin 1936.
12) Beethoven was a piano virtuoso by age 23
13) Issac Newton wrote Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica at age 24
14) Roger Bannister was 25 when he broke the 4 minute mile record
15) Albert Einstein was 26 when he wrote the theory of relativity
16) Lance E. Armstrong was 27 when he won the tour de France
17) Michelangelo created two of the greatest sculptures “David” and “Pieta” by age 28
18) Alexander the Great, by age 29, had created one of the largest empires of the ancient world
19) J.K. Rowling was 30 years old when she finished the first manuscript of Harry Potter
20) Amelia Earhart was 31 years old when she became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean
21) Oprah was 32 when she started her talk show, which has become the highest-rated program of its kind
22) Edmund Hillary was 33 when he became the first man to reach Mount Everest

quotes.q: Freud was fascinated with depression and focused on the issue that we began with—why is it that most of us can have occasional terrible experiences, feel depressed, and then recover, while a few of us collapse into major depression (melancholia)? In his classic essay “Mourning and Melancholia” (1917), Freud began with what the two have in common. In both cases, he felt, there is the loss of a love object. (In Freudian terms, such an “object” is usually a person, but can also be a goal or an ideal.) In Freud’s formulation, in every loving relationship there is ambivalence, mixed feelings—elements of hatred as well as love. In the case of a small, reactive depression—mourning—you are able to deal with those mixed feelings in a healthy manner: you lose, you grieve, and then you recover. In the case of a major melancholic depression, you have become obsessed with the ambivalence—the simultaneity, the irreconcilable nature of the intense love alongside the intense hatred. Melancholia—a major depression—Freud theorized, is the internal conflict generated by this ambivalence. This can begin to explain the intensity of grief experienced in a major depression. If you are obsessed with the intensely mixed feelings, you grieve doubly after a loss—for your loss of the loved individual and for the loss of any chance now to ever resolve the difficulties. “If only I had said the things I needed to, if only we could have worked things out”—for all of time, you have lost the chance to purge yourself of the ambivalence. For the rest of your life, you will be reaching for the door to let you into a place of pure, unsullied love, and you can never reach that door. It also explains the intensity of the guilt often experienced in major depression. If you truly harbored intense anger toward the person along with love, in the aftermath of your loss there must be some facet of you that is celebrating, alongside the grieving. “He’s gone; that’s terrible but…thank god, I can finally live, I can finally grow up, no more of this or that.” Inevitably, a metaphorical instant later, there must come a paralyzing belief that you have become a horrible monster to feel any sense of relief or pleasure at a time like this. Incapacitating guilt. This theory also explains the tendency of major depressives in such circumstances to, oddly, begin to take on some of the traits of the lost loved/hated one—and not just any traits, but invariably the ones that the survivor found most irritating. Psychodynamically, this is wonderfully logical. By taking on a trait, you are being loyal to your lost, beloved opponent. By picking an irritating trait, you are still trying to convince the world you were right to be irritated—you see how you hate it when I do it; can you imagine what it was like to have to put up with that for years? And by picking a trait that, most of all, you find irritating, you are not only still trying to score points in your argument with the departed, but you are punishing yourself for arguing as well. Out of the Freudian school of thought has come one of the more apt descriptions of depression—“aggression turned inward.” Suddenly the loss of pleasure, the psychomotor retardation, the impulse to suicide all make sense. As do the elevated glucocorticoid levels. This does not describe someone too lethargic to function; it is more like the actual state of a patient in depression, exhausted from the most draining emotional conflict of his or her life—one going on entirely within. If that doesn’t count as psychologically stressful, I don’t know what does.

First there's immigration. Currently, 12 percent of Americans are immigrants, another 12 percent are children of immigrants, and everyone else except for the 0.9 percent pure Native Americans descend from people who emigrated within the last five hundred years. And who were the immigrants? Those in the settled world who were cranks, malcontents, restless, heretical, black sheep, hyperactive, hypomanic, misanthropic, itchy, unconventional, yearning to be rich, yearning to be out of their damn boring repressive little hamlet, yearning. Couple that with the second reason - for the majority of its colonial and independent history, America has had a moving frontier luring those whose extreme prickly optimism made merely booking passage to the New World insufficiently novel - and you've got America the individualistic.
Why has East Asia provided textbook examples of collectivism? The key is how culture is shaped by the way people traditionally made a living, which in turn is shaped by ecology. And in East Asia it's all about rice. Rice, which was domesticated there roughly ten thousand years ago, requires massive amounts of communal work. Not just backbreaking planting and harvesting, which are done in rotation because the entire village is needed to harvest each family's rice. The United States was not without labor-intensive agriculture historically. But rather than solving that with collectivism, it solved it withe slavery.

Isn't language loss a good thing, because fewer languages mean easier communication among the world's people? Perhaps, but it's a bad thing in other respects. Languages differ in structure and vocabulary, in how they express causation and feelings and personal responsibility, hence in how they shape our thoughts. There's no single purpose "best" language; instead, different languages are better suited for different purposes. For instance, it may not have been an accident that Plato and Aristotle wrote in Greek, while Kant wrote in German. The grammatical particles of those two languages, plus their ease in forming compound words, may have helped make them the preeminent languages of western philosophy. Another example, familiar to all of us who studied Latin, is that highly inflected languages (ones in which word endings suffice to indicate sentence structure) can use variations of word order to convey nuances impossible with English. Our English word order is severely constrained by having to serve as the main clue to sentence structure. If English becomes a world language, that won't be because English was necessarily the best language for diplomacy.

They could play, dance, love, and multiply their pleasures. They were the salt of the earth, and everything was given to them, everything was permitted for them, everything was possible. Later on, having started a family, having entered the adult world, they would be introduced to worry, work, responsibility, and the difficulties of existence; they would have to pay taxes, submit themselves to administrative formalities while ceaselessly bearing witness--powerless and shame-filled--to the irreversible degradation of their own bodies, which would be slow at first, then increasingly rapid; above all, they would have to look after children, mortal enemies, in their own homes, they would have to pamper them, feed them, worry about their illnesses, provide the means for their education and their pleasure, and unlike in the world of animals, this would last not just for a season, they would remain slaves of their offspring always, the time of joy was well and truly over for them, they would have to continue to suffer until the end, in pain and with increasing health problems, until they were no longer good for anything and were definitively thrown into the rubbish heap, cumbersome and useless. In return, their children would not be at all grateful, on the contrary their efforts, however strenuous, would never be considered enough, they would, until the bitter end, be considered guilty because of the simple fact of being parents. From this sad life, marked by shame, all joy would be pitilessly banished. What if the point all along has been to get along, to relate, to experience things on their own terms? Think of cocaine. In its natural form, as coca leaves, it's appealing, but not to an extent that it usually becomes a problem. But refine it, purify it, and you get a compound that hits your pleasure receptors with an unnatural intensity. That's when it becomes addictive.
Beauty has undergone a similar process, thanks to advertisers. Evolution gave us a circuit that responds to good looks - call it the pleasure receptor for our visual cortex - and in our natural environment, it was useful to have. But take a person with one-in-a-million skin and bone structure, add professional makeup and retouching, and you're no longer looking at beauty in its natural form. You've got pharmaceutical-grade beauty, the cocaine of good looks.
Biologists call this "supernormal stimulus" [...] Our beauty receptors receive more stimulation than they were evolved to handle; we're seeing more beauty in one day than our ancestors did in a lifetime. And the result is that beauty is slowly ruining our lives.

The mathematician and physicist Freeman Dyson makes a related observation about human society: The destiny of our species is shaped by the imperatives of survival on six distinct time scales. To survive means to compete successfully on all six time scales. But the unit of survival is different at each of the six time scales. On a time scale of years, the unit is the individual. On a time scale of decades, the unit is the family. On a time scale of centuries, the unit is the tribe or nation. On a time scale of millennia, the unit is the culture. On a time scale of tens of millennia, the unit is the species. On a time scale of eons, the unit is the whole web of life on our planet. Every human being is the product of adaptation to the demands of all six time scales. That is why conflicting loyalties are deep in our nature. In order to survive, we have needed to be loyal to ourselves, to our families, to our tribes, to our cultures, to our species, to our planet. If our psychological impulses are complicated, it is because they were shaped by complicated and conflicting demands.
quotes.s: The Clock Of The Long Now: Time and Responsibility

quotes.q: The technologies which have had the most profound effects on human life are usually simple. A good example of a simple technology with profound historical consequences is hay. Nobody knows who invented hay, the idea of cutting grass in the autumn and storing it in large enough quantities to keep horses and cows alive through the winter. All we know is that the technology of hay was unknown to the Roman Empire but was known to every village of medieval Europe. Like many other crucially important technologies, hay emerged anonymously during the so-called Dark Ages. According to the Hay Theory of History, the invention of hay was the decisive event which moved the center of gravity of urban civilization from the Mediterranean basin to Northern and Western Europe. The Roman Empire did not need hay because in a Mediterranean climate the grass grows well enough in winter for animals to graze. North of the Alps, great cities dependent on horses and oxen for motive power could not exist without hay. So it was hay that allowed populations to grow and civilizations to flourish among the forests of Northern Europe. Hay moved the greatness of Rome to Paris and London, and later to Berlin and Moscow and New York.

One student asks: Why should I live?
Steven Pinker answers: In the very act of asking that question, you are seeking reasons for your convictions, and so you are committed to reason as the means to discover and justify what is important to you. And there are so many reasons to live! As a sentient being, you have the potential to flourish. You can refine your faculty of reason itself by learning and debating. You can seek explanations of the natural world through science, and insight into the human condition through the arts and humanities. You can make the most of your capacity for pleasure and satisfaction, which allowed your ancestors to thrive and thereby allowed you to exist. You can appreciate the beauty and richness of the natural and cultural world. As the heir to billions of years of life perpetuating itself, you can perpetuate life in turn. You have been endowed with a sense of sympathy—the ability to like, love, respect, help, and show kindness—and you can enjoy the gift of mutual benevolence with friends, family, and colleagues. And because reason tells you that none of this is particular to you, you have the responsibility to provide to others what you expect for yourself. You can foster the welfare of other sentient beings by enhancing life, health, knowledge, freedom, abundance, safety, beauty, and peace. History shows that when we sympathize with others and apply our ingenuity to improving the human condition, we can make progress in doing so, and you can help to continue that progress.

quotes.q:
Do not despise your inner world. That is the first and most general piece of advice I would offer… Our society is very outward-looking, very taken up with the latest new object, the latest piece of gossip, the latest opportunity for self-assertion and status. But we all begin our lives as helpless babies, dependent on others for comfort, food, and survival itself. And even though we develop a degree of mastery and independence, we always remain alarmingly weak and incomplete, dependent on others and on an uncertain world for whatever we are able to achieve. As we grow, we all develop a wide range of emotions responding to this predicament: fear that bad things will happen and that we will be powerless to ward them off; love for those who help and support us; grief when a loved one is lost; hope for good things in the future; anger when someone else damages something we care about. Our emotional life maps our incompleteness: A creature without any needs would never have reasons for fear, or grief, or hope, or anger. But for that very reason we are often ashamed of our emotions, and of the relations of need and dependency bound up with them. Perhaps males, in our society, are especially likely to be ashamed of being incomplete and dependent, because a dominant image of masculinity tells them that they should be self-sufficient and dominant. So people flee from their inner world of feeling, and from articulate mastery of their own emotional experiences. The current psychological literature on the life of boys in America indicates that a large proportion of boys are quite unable to talk about how they feel and how others feel — because they have learned to be ashamed of feelings and needs, and to push them underground. But that means that they don’t know how to deal with their own emotions, or to communicate them to others. When they are frightened, they don’t know how to say it, or even to become fully aware of it. Often they turn their own fear into aggression. Often, too, this lack of a rich inner life catapults them into depression in later life. We are all going to encounter illness, loss, and aging, and we’re not well prepared for these inevitable events by a culture that directs us to think of externals only, and to measure ourselves in terms of our possessions of externals.
What is the remedy of these ills? A kind of self-love that does not shrink from the needy and incomplete parts of the self, but accepts those with interest and curiosity, and tries to develop a language with which to talk about needs and feelings. Storytelling plays a big role in the process of development. As we tell stories about the lives of others, we learn how to imagine what another creature might feel in response to various events. At the same time, we identify with the other creature and learn something about ourselves. As we grow older, we encounter more and more complex stories — in literature, film, visual art, music — that give us a richer and more subtle grasp of human emotions and of our own inner world. So my second piece of advice, closely related to the first, is: Read a lot of stories, listen to a lot of music, and think about what the stories you encounter mean for your own life and lives of those you love. In that way, you will not be alone with an empty self; you will have a newly rich life with yourself, and enhanced possibilities of real communication with others.

quotes.q: Finally, the inner accessibility and reflectiveness of theoretical knowledge which cannot basically be withheld from anybody, as can certain emotions and volitions, has a consequence that directly offsets its practical results. In the first place, it is precisely because of their general accessibility that factors quite independent of personal capacities decide on the factual utilization of knowledge. This leads to the enormous preponderance of the most unintelligent 'educated' person over the cleverest proletarian. The apparent equality with which educational materials are available to everyone interested in them is, in reality, a sheer mockery. The same is true of the other freedoms accorded by the liberal doctrines which, though they certainly do not hamper the individual from gaining goods of any kind, do however disregard the fact that only those already privileged in some way or another have the possibility of acquiring them. For just as the substance of education - in spite of, or because of it general availability - can ultimately be acquired only through individual activity, so it gives rise to the most intangible and thus the most unassailable aristocracy, to a distinction between high and low which can be abolished neither (as can socioeconomic differences) by a decree or a revolution. Thus it was appropriate for Jesus to say to the rich youth: 'Give away your goods to the poor', but not for him to say: 'Give your education to the underprivileged'. There is no advantage that appears to those in inferior positions to be so despised, and before which they feel so deprived and helpless, as the advantage of education. For this reason, attempts to achieve practical equality very often and in so many variations scorn intellectual education. This is true of Buddha, the Cynics, certain currents in Christianity, down to Robespierre's 'nous n'avons pas besoin de savants'. In speech and writing - which, viewed abstractly, are a manifestation of its communal nature - makes possible its accumulation, and, especially, its concentration so that, in this respect, the gulf between high and low is persistently widened. The intellectually gifted or the materially independent person will have all the more chances for standing out from the masses the larger and more concentrated are the available educational materials. Just as the proletarian today has many comforts and cultural enjoyments that were formerly denied to him, while at the same time - particularly if we look back over several centuries and millennia - the gulf between his way of life and that of the higher strata has certainly become much deeper, so, similarly, the rise in the general level of knowledge as a whole does not by any means bring about a general levelling, but rather its opposite.
